units: the inner circulation of the tree starts up again at the end of the cold season
the feeding liquid climbs from the root system towards the top of the tree
the pressure gap between waterlogged ground and dry air drives that rise
a very thin living tissue under the protective layer of the trunk carries this liquid
the growth organs open and let out a folded blade
through the warm season the foliage makes reserves of sugar
the tree stores those reserves in the trunk and in the roots
in the leaf-fall season the foliage loses its green colouring
through the cold season the tree keeps a faint breathing
the cycle repeats only if the base of the trunk stays sound and water keeps coming
text: As soon as the cold loosens its grip, a tree sets about a piece of work that nobody can watch. Sap climbs from the roots to the highest branches, driven by the gap in pressure between sodden ground and air that is still dry. A thin sleeve of living cells, tucked under the bark, carries that sweet flow upward. Buds swell, split, and let out a leaf folded like a fan. Through the warm months those leaves build sugars, and the tree banks them away in its trunk and in its roots. When the turn comes, the green pigment drains out of the foliage and the leaves let go. Winter looks like sleep, yet the tree breathes faintly and lives off what it has put by. The whole round begins again, year upon year, so long as the base of the trunk stays sound and the roots reach water deep down.

units: someone the narrator knows told of an incident in his hedge
he had seen a round opening dug under a shrub
he shut that opening with a slab of stone to see off a small mammal
the leaves of the shrub yellowed a fortnight after the blocking
the underground tunnel was in fact carrying away the rain
the blocking turned the foot of the bed into a hollow where water stood
the roots left without air died back
he lifted the slab away and cut a drainage channel
the shrub recovered its strength the following season
text: A fellow I know told me what happened in his hedge, and it is worth hearing. He had spotted a neat round hole under one of the shrubs, a burrow by the look of it, and he dropped a flat stone over the mouth to see off whatever small creature had moved in. A fortnight later the leaves on that shrub went a dull yellow and curled at the edges. When he dug the ground open, he saw at once what he had done to it. The tunnel had been doing the work of a drain, carrying off the rain that gathered under the hedge. Block it, and the foot of the bed becomes a basin. Water stood there, the roots had no air left to them, and they died back. He lifted the stone away, cut a channel out towards the ditch, and by the next season the shrub had come back strong. He looks at holes rather differently now.

units: a sharp cold snap at the end of the cold season can destroy an orchard crop in one night
ice crystals damage the open blossom and the recent shoots
watching the sky in the evening is advised to judge the danger
no cloud and no wind mean a high risk
watering the ground moderately before the temperature falls helps hold the warmth
wrapping the weakest trunks in a breathable cloth without tightening it is recommended
no cutting at all should be done on the branches at this time
every cut leaves a wound that the cold makes worse
at sunrise the frosted branches should be sprayed with lukewarm water little by little
writing the episode down is advised to keep a memory of the seasons
text: A late frost can wipe out an orchard crop in a single night: ice burns the open blossom and the tender young shoots. Here is how to keep the losses down. Look up at the sky late in the evening, for a clear sky with no wind is the warning. Then water the ground lightly before the temperature falls, since damp earth takes up warmth and hands it back through the night. Wrap the frailest trunks in a breathable cloth, loosely, so that air still moves around them. Cut nothing at all at this stage, however untidy the growth looks, because every cut leaves a wound and the cold makes short work of a wound. At sunrise, spray the frosted branches with lukewarm water, slowly, a little at a time. Then write the night down in a notebook. Seasons remembered will guide you better than any gadget.

units: one side of the valley is covered with dense woodland growth
there is a bed of rotting plant matter and a smell of living soil
the opposite side still carries the marks of felling done long ago
on that bare side the rock shows and water cuts grooves in it
the thin grass cover there does not hold the feeding layer of soil
a worker in charge of the area walks visitors from one side to the other
she explains that under the trees water sinks in instead of running off the surface
the water point at the foot of the valley is still flowing late in the warm season
gradual planting has begun on the stripped slope with species that root wide and shallow
the outcome will not be visible for several decades
text: On the slope that faces the sunrise the wood has taken hold again: crowded trunks, a deep bed of rotting leaves, a smell of damp earth that clings to the fingers. The far slope still carries the memory of old felling. Bare rock breaks the surface, rain scores it with runnels, and cropped grass can barely hold the fertile skin of soil in place. The warden walks visitors from one flank to the other, so that the contrast stops being an argument and becomes a thing you stand in. Under the canopy, she says, rain soaks in rather than races off, and the spring at the foot of the valley is still running when the heat has worn on. Opposite, the same shower tears downhill and hands the stream a load of red silt. Replanting has begun, shrub by shrub, with species rooted wide and shallow. The change will show in a generation, not before.

units: the outermost layer is thin and waxy and limits the loss of water
the middle layer holds salts of lime and provides the strength
the inner layer is suppler and gives the muscles their anchorage
plates set across the back keep the organs out of harm
the jointed rings of the rear part allow the body to fold
the joints of the limbs bend in one direction only
sensing bristles lodged in fine pores pick up movement in the water
this casing has the drawback of being unable to grow larger
the animal must leave its casing at intervals and wait for the fresh one to harden
through that soft spell it hides under a stone
text: The shell of a crustacean reads like armour built up plate by plate. Its outer skin is thin and waxy; it sheds water and slows the drying of the body. Beneath that lies a stiff layer, loaded with salts of lime, and this is what gives the whole thing its hardness. A third layer, suppler than the rest, lines the inside and gives the muscles something to pull against. Plates across the back keep the organs out of harm. The ringed segments of the tail let the body curl. The legs meet at hinges that bend one way and no other. Fine bristles, lodged in tiny pores, pass on every tremor in the water. All that armour carries one flaw: it will not stretch. Every so often the animal must split it, back out of it, and wait while the fresh casing hardens. Through those soft days it lies low under a pebble.

units: the author finds the lack of response to the retreat of pollinating insects unacceptable
the first warnings lay in field observations ignored some thirty years ago
successive counts then established a steady fall in numbers
fruit growers noticed that the fertilising grains were spreading badly
orchards had to fall back on artificial fertilising that is costly and unreliable
the author holds that the burden of proof should change sides
he claims that damaging practice should prove it does no harm
strips of flowers along the field edge are named as a cheap remedy
keeping the hedges and mowing less often are among the answers put forward
text: Nothing excuses the calm with which we watch the pollinating insects go. The first signals were set down a generation ago, in field notes that nobody thought worth reading twice. Then came the repeated counts, and they showed numbers falling season after season, steadily and without argument. Growers of fruit found next that pollen was moving badly, and that orchards now wanted pollination by hand, an expensive business and a fragile one. We have reached the point where the burden of proof ought to change hands: it is no longer for naturalists to demonstrate the peril, but for damaging practice to demonstrate its innocence. A strip of flowers along a field, a hedge left standing, a mower run less often, and the harm begins to mend for very little. Doing nothing is what will be paid for, and paid for long.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman heading an establishment that raises young trees had not intended this trade
she was studying the chemical make-up of soils
a disease striking the young plants of her district changed her course
the seedlings were dying with no visible cause
her study of the roots revealed a parasite organism tied to too much watering
she urged watering less often even at the cost of the weakest plants
the growers doubted at first before taking her advice
the death rate among the seedlings dropped by half
she gained the running of an establishment and set up close tracking of every batch
she now passes her experience on to beginners
text: The woman who runs a forest nursery had never meant to do this work. She was studying the chemistry of soils when a disease struck the young trees across her district, and that emergency shaped everything that came after. Seedlings were dying with nothing to show for it, so she took the roots apart and found a fungus that thrived wherever the watering had been too generous. Her advice was hard to swallow: water less often, and accept the loss of the weaker plants. The growers hesitated, then did as she said, and deaths among the seedlings dropped by half. That result won her the running of a nursery, where she brought in a record for every batch, from the seed to the planting out. She trains apprentices now, sure that a tough plant, however small it looks leaving the glasshouse, beats a forward one.

units: the narrator was let down by her first visit to an observation trail
the boards gave nothing but learned names and never said what to look at
a fine stretch of water was hidden behind tall growth and was not signposted
she came back after the trail had been rebuilt
half the boards have been replaced by questions
a gap has been cleared through towards the water
a low seat has been put in to watch the young water insects
the trail now teaches how to spot the marks that animals leave
a shortened route fit for families pushing a pram is still missing
text: Honestly, that nature trail let me down the first time round. The boards lined up learned names and never once told you where to put your eyes, so you walked it the way you walk a corridor. There was a fine pond three steps off the path, hidden behind a screen of reeds, and not a word about it anywhere. I went back after the rebuild, and the difference is plain. Half the boards have gone, replaced by open questions. A gap has been cut through to the water. There is a low bench there now, and from it you watch the larvae flicker under the surface. Fur caught on a bramble, grass pressed flat where something crossed, bark rubbed raw on a trunk: at last you are taught to read the clues yourself. What it still wants is a short loop, no steps and no loose gravel, for families pushing a pram.

units: the writer of the letter writes from her garden to a friend
she compares two cultivated beds she had already spoken of
the bed set high up takes the sun from first light to dusk
the soil of that bed dries out fast and the stems there are short and thick
the flowers of the high bed open early and go over within seven days
the lower bed is sheltered by a wall and sees the sun only from midday
the plants of the lower bed grow taller and flower twice as long
the gap comes mainly from the water in the ground since watering and feeding are identical
a rose moved from the dry bed to the damp one doubled in size in one season
she asks her friend to come before the cold arrives
text: Dear friend, I am writing from the far end of the garden with a notebook on my knees, to tell you about those two beds. The upper one takes sun from first light until it goes: the soil dries out fast, the stems come up short and thick, and the flowers open early only to go over within the week. The lower bed sits against the wall and sees nothing until midday. Everything there grows taller and softer, and the flowering lasts near enough twice as long. The difference is mostly water in the ground, since I water both squares the same and feed them from the same heap. I shifted a rose from the dry bed to the other, and in one season it doubled, throwing out supple shoots I had given up on. Come and see for yourself before the frosts, while the last blooms hold; I shall make tea and bring out two chairs.

units: the renewal of the body covering is put forward as a rebuilding and not a simple discarding
in the snake the old covering comes away in a single piece
the eyes of the snake turn cloudy before that change
the snake rubs against a rough surface to start the tear
in birds the replacement goes piece by piece so that flight is kept
the light fresh plumage grows under the worn one and pushes it off
in insects the young stage breaks down almost wholly to form a winged adult
a damaged covering no longer gives protection
an old covering does not follow an increase in size
a worn plumage keeps out the cold badly
text: What happens when an animal walks out of its own skin? Moulting is no discarded costume, it is a rebuilding. In a snake the old skin peels away whole, in one sleeve: the eyes cloud over first, and then the creature works itself against something rough to start the tear. A bird goes about it feather by feather, so that flight is never lost, and the fresh down comes up beneath the worn plumage and shoulders it off. In an insect the change goes further still, for the grub all but melts away and puts itself together again as a winged adult. And why go to such expense? Because a worn covering stops turning bites, because it cannot follow the growth of the body inside it, and because a shabby coat of feathers holds no warmth. Coming apart, in this trade, is how a creature keeps going.

units: the person leading the group states that the moisture does not fall from the sky
during the hours of darkness the ground surface gives its warmth away by radiation
that surface becomes colder than the air resting against it
moisture in the air turns into fine beads on the chilled plants
one walker reports having seen no such deposit the day before
the stirring of the air by the wind had prevented the cooling
a layer of cloud throws the warmth back downwards
the whitish haze at the bottom of the valley comes from the same process
text: The guide comes to a halt at the edge of the path and asks the walkers to look closely at the flattened grass at their feet. Dew, she tells them, never drops out of the sky, whatever most people on the hills imagine. Through the dark hours the ground gives its warmth away to an open sky, until its surface sits colder than the air resting against it. Moisture in that air then gathers as tiny beads along the chilled blades. One of the walkers objects: yesterday morning she saw nothing of the sort. The wind had been stirring the air all night, the guide answers, so the cooling never took hold. Cloud works the same trick from above, she adds, throwing the warmth back down. And that pale haze lying in the hollow below them? The same business, she says, only spread through a whole layer of air.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: growers of the older generations could do nothing against the rising water
the rising water destroyed the young plants and the pens
storage buildings were sometimes carried off
harvests were seen to be better once the water had drawn back
the muddy deposit fed the tilled ground better than animal dung
the aim became to keep the fertility without suffering the destruction
feeder channels led the flow towards shallow basins
banks were raised along the edges of the water
adjustable gates let the water in at the chosen moment
growing food stopped being left to chance
text: You are probably wondering what growers of the older generations could possibly do when the river came up and swelled. They put up with it. The flood tore out the seedlings, drowned the pens, and now and then carried off a whole store hut. Then somebody noticed something odd. Where the water had drawn back, the next harvest came in heavier, and the mud left behind fed the tilled ground better than any dung from the beasts. So the trick was to keep the enrichment and lose the wreckage. The answer arrived by degrees. Channels were dug to lead the flow into shallow basins. Ridges of clay went up along the edges. Gates were cut that a pair of hands could swing open at the chosen moment. In came the water, down went its load, and off it drained. Growing food had stopped being a gamble.

units: two agents shape the stones of a valley in different ways
running water knocks the blocks together and wears them down by rubbing
the stones carried by water end up rounded and smooth
running water sorts its deposits by size along its course
ice carries its load without rolling it
the fragments left behind by ice keep their sharp edges
glacial deposits mix huge blocks with very fine matter
a specialist knows the origin of a deposit by the look of it
this distinction makes it possible to rebuild the past of a slope with no clue left
text: Two agents shape the stones of a valley, and they do not go about the work in anything like the same way. A fast stream rolls its boulders along, knocks them one against another and wears them down by steady rubbing; out come pebbles that are round, polished and sorted by size as the course runs on. Ice, for its part, rolls nothing at all. It carries its load like a slow belt and drops it exactly as it was, so the fragments keep their sharp edges and lie jumbled together, a huge block beside a dust of clay. A specialist tells the two deposits apart at a glance. Where water has worked, the grains match one another and settle in clean layers. Where ice has passed, the sediment stays disordered. That difference lets you rebuild the story of a slope on which nothing visible now remains.

units: a child regularly brought back finds picked up in a wood
she laid out her feathers by shade, from the darkest to the palest
the shells she brought home were thin enough to break in her hand
she smelled the pieces of bark after rubbing them
a violent squall had brought down a tree in the cold season
since that tree fell she also gathered splinters of pale wood
her stone collection held three distinct kinds of rock
her elderly forebear kept none of these objects herself
that woman gave her a box and listened to her descriptions
text: The child would come back from the wood with her pockets weighed down, and nobody could ever guess what she would pull out of them. The feathers came first, laid out by shade, from the darkest to the palest. Then the empty shells, delicate enough to break in her hand. Then strips of bark, which she rubbed and held under her nose for the smell of resin and rain. A squall had brought down a beech in the cold season, and ever since she had been carrying home splinters of pale wood torn from the split trunk. Last of all lay the stones: a streaked pebble, a lump of milky-white quartz, a shard of slate that flaked apart between her fingers. Her elderly grandmother kept none of it herself. She lent a box, listened to the account of every piece, and waited for the following haul.

units: the trial plot must be marked out on an even, uncovered slope
a rigid edging driven into three sides stands slightly above the ground
the downhill side is fitted with a sloping gutter
the water collected ends up in a buried vessel bearing graduations
the amount gathered is read off as soon as a shower ends
a sample is drawn once the contents have been stirred
the suspended matter is left to settle before being dried and weighed
the slope and the state of the surface are recorded
repeating the measurement gives the solid matter carried off by surface run-off
putting in a plant cover brings that value down
text: Begin by choosing an even slope, clear of any thick cover, and mark out a square plot with wooden pegs. Drive a rigid metal edging into three of the sides, leaving it standing a hand's height above the ground. On the downhill side, fit a sloping gutter that feeds the water into a graduated drum sunk in a pit. Now you wait for a shower to fall. The moment it ends, read off the volume collected, stir the contents well, then draw a sample into a clean bottle. Leave the mud to settle overnight, pour off the clear water, dry the remaining deposit and weigh it. Finally, note down the slope of the plot and the condition of the surface. Repeat after every shower and you will have the solid load carried off by run-off, and you will watch that figure drop as soon as a plant cover takes hold.

units: a crack several paces long has opened at the edge of a farmed plateau
the authorities have closed the track that crosses this plateau
specialists put the opening down to a run of exceptional showers
water working downwards has soaked a clay layer lying beneath the crops
that soaked layer has lost its grip on what it carries
the mass above it has begun to move down towards the slope
the failure of a poorly drained retaining wall sped up the slide
the farmers fear the loss of the water point that serves their animals
the crack is diverting part of the underground flow of water
measuring instruments will be set in place before the wet season
text: A crack several paces in length opened up this week along the edge of a farmed plateau, and the authorities have closed the track that crosses it. Survey work carried out by a team of geologists puts the opening down to a run of exceptional showers. Water working downwards through the soil has soaked a clay layer buried beneath the crops; softened in this way, the layer no longer grips what it carries, and the ground above has begun to move towards the slope. Imperceptible at first, the movement quickened once a poorly drained retaining wall gave way. The farmers now fear for the spring that serves their animals, since the crack is diverting part of the underground flow. Measuring instruments will be set in place before the wet season, so that the break can be followed as it widens.

units: past a low bridge the river meets a spur of rock and changes direction
a standing eddy hollows itself out at that point
the inner side of the bend builds up fine sand
the outer side gives up about a hand's width every wet season
the roots of the bankside trees end up hanging in mid-air
a rise in the water is enough to bring down an undermined tree
the people living along the bank ruled out the use of concrete
living stakes were driven in at an angle, then linked by woven branches
the wood takes and roots, slowing the water and holding the bank
text: Just beyond a low bridge, the river runs up against a spur of rock and swings sharply away to one side. A standing eddy has hollowed itself out at that point, dark at the centre and ringed with brown foam. The inner side of the bend gathers a bank of fine sand, while the outer side gives up about a hand's width every wet season. The alder roots end up hanging in mid-air, and a tree topples over as soon as a rise in the water leaves them bare. The people living along that bank ruled out the pouring of concrete along the edge. What they did instead was drive living willow stakes at an angle into the bank under attack, then weave supple branches between them. The wood takes root, the roots stitch the soil together, and the current loses its force against the drowned foliage.

units: the writer invites us to set two ways of managing a river side by side
the first approach shuts the river in with a straightened bed and hardened banks
this approach means raising the defences at every warning
when that arrangement gives way, the water goes off faster and higher than it would naturally
the second approach gives the river back land that can flood
it means pulling buildings away and accepting the flooding of fields with nobody living on them
the spreading slows the water and lays the fertile matter down where it is useful
the writer admits that the second option means letting go of land one owns
he holds that the first option means spending for ever and costs at the worst moment
text: Honestly, we would do well to set two ways of handling a river side by side before choosing ours. The first shuts it in: the bed is straightened, the banks are hardened, the defences go up another notch at every warning. It works, right up until it does not, and then the water goes off all at once, faster and higher than it ever would have without us. The second way makes less of a show. You give the river back its flood meadows, you pull the buildings away, you accept that fields with nobody living on them will go under. The water spreads, slows, and lays its silt where it feeds instead of ruining. I know the second choice means surrendering land one owns, and surrendering has never pleased anybody. But the first commits us to spending for ever, and its bill lands at the worst possible moment.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: this water specialist comes from a family of river boatmen
the people in charge of dams turn to her for advice
her working life falls into three parts
she long drew loaded water from a cradle slung above the current
those samples served to measure the matter carried off by the river
she worked out a cheap technique for sorting grains
poorly equipped teams have taken that technique up
she trains beginners by sending them into the field before any theory
those close to her describe her as blunt but always there in an emergency
text: Nothing whatever marked out a boatman's daughter to become the water scientist whom the keepers of dams now turn to for advice. Her working life falls into three parts. There is the fieldwork first of all: whole seasons spent drawing muddy water from the middle of the current, slung in a cradle above it, to weigh what the river carries away. There is the laboratory next, where she worked out a way of sorting grains so inexpensive that distant teams with no money for equipment took it up. And there is the passing on: every season she takes in beginners and sends them wading in the silt long before she opens a textbook for them. Those close to her describe an abrupt woman, sparing with her praise, yet never able to turn down a call in the middle of the night when a bank threatens to go.

units: the visit begins in a room with almost no light
the noise of a violent wind surrounds the visitor while shadows of cloud slide across the floor
the next room shows upright samples of deposits in cases
the pale and dark bands of those samples record the turn of the seasons
the writer judges the explanatory gallery to be the weakest part
he blames the panels for repeating what the objects already show
the last room displays a damp clay surface that dries out during the visit
the cracking of that surface makes a noise you can hear in the quiet
the writer holds that a still image could not have conveyed this ageing of matter
text: The exhibition opens in a room with almost no light, and the reasoning behind it is plain from the doorway, since you listen before you see. A gale turns about the visitor while shadows of cloud slide across the floor. The second room brings out the cases at last: cores of sediment stood up like columns, leaved with pale and dark bands that tell of dry seasons and wet ones. Then comes a more instructive gallery, the weakest stretch by some way, where too many panels repeat what the objects had already said better. The final room makes up for all of it. A wall of damp clay, lit from the side, dries before your eyes and splits open during the visit; the cracking carries through the quiet. You come away having watched matter grow old, something no still image could have conveyed.

units: the writer is sending a letter to a friend from a shared allotment
the young plants were no longer coming up out of the seed
the surface of the soil had hardened into a tight crust
water slid off towards a drainage channel instead of soaking down to the roots
a grower on the neighbouring plot suggested a tried and tested remedy
the soil material was sieved to take out the stones
an organic amendment was worked in to hold water where it could be used
the surface is broken up after every watering
the plants came through after roughly three weeks
text: Dear friend, I am writing from the shared allotment I described at the start of the season. Nothing was germinating. The seeds simply sat there, and none of us could work out what was holding them back. The topsoil had baked into a tight crust, so the water ran straight across it, escaped down the drainage channel and never reached the roots. The grower on the neighbouring plot put us right; he has relied on the same remedy for years. We sieved the soil to remove the stones, then worked in well rotted compost, which retains moisture without smothering the young shoots. After every watering, somebody goes along the row and breaks the surface up with a hand fork. Three weeks or so later the first leaves pushed through, thick and sturdy. I shall send a picture once the row fills out. Do write and tell me whether your balcony is fruiting.

units: a specialist in insects compares two kinds of pollinator
hived colonies hold a very large body of workers
hived foragers travel long distances
wild species settle on their own in hollow stems or slopes of loose sand
wild species range over a small radius
wild species work flowers that the others pass over
the specialist refuses to name one kind as better
an orchard left to hives alone yields an uneven crop
ground with few flowers defeats both kinds
text: Are wild bees a match for kept bees when it comes to pollination? People ask it constantly, and an entomologist I put the question to answered with a comparison. Hived colonies work in huge numbers, she said, and their foragers will travel a long way before bringing the load home; their strength is sheer weight of workers. Wild species nest on their own, in a hollow stem or a slope of loose sand, they range only a short way, and they work flowers the others pass over; their strength is precision. So which would she pick? Neither, she laughed. An orchard left to hived colonies alone crops unevenly, because part of the blossom opens on cold days, when the hive stays shut. Ground edged with hedges and bare banks gets both services at once. Then she added a caveat: where wild flowers are scarce, neither kind will hold on.

units: the head of a laboratory presents her monitoring beside a body of water
she sets out the markers used to judge a watercourse
the insect larvae living under the stones make up the first marker
the loss of those larvae points to contamination
a spread of algae over the bed betrays fertiliser coming off the farmland
a coloured floating object serves to gauge the speed of the current
the state of the banks is among the markers that get overlooked
a bank stripped of plants gives way as soon as the water rises
bankside shrubs bind the soil and house birds
a proper assessment calls for repeated observation
text: The head of the laboratory meets us beside a shallow pool, a hand lens ready in her palm. She runs through the markers her team records to judge the health of a river. The first, she says, sits under the stones: the insect larvae clinging there cannot cope with loaded water, so if they have gone, something is getting in. The second is the algae carpeting the bed. Where it thickens, fertiliser has seeped down from the fields alongside. The third is the speed of the current, which a coloured float will gauge well enough. She ends on a marker most people overlook, the bank itself. A bare bank collapses the moment the water rises, while a bank thick with shrubs binds the soil and shelters the birds that nest close to the surface. None of this, she says, can be read off in a single visit.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: a worker in glass notices the magnifying effect of a curved piece of glass
clear stones were cut and rubbed smooth so that fine writing could be read
wooden mounts were made to hold the gap between the eye and the lens
those mounts left the hands free
a lens maker set two glasses one above the other inside a cylinder
that stacking pushed the enlargement further still
minute creatures were spotted in stagnant water
the presence of living things in a single droplet astounded the learned
the flaws of colour around the rim were cured as the craft improved
the instrument ended by making the basic unit of life visible
text: Long before science had instruments to its name, a glassworker noticed that a rounded splinter of glass swelled the threads of the cloth beneath it. Curiosity did the rest. Clear stones were cut, then rubbed smooth with sand, so that cramped writing could be read. Wooden mounts followed, holding the lens a fixed distance from the eye and leaving both hands free. A lens grinder thought of setting two glasses one above the other inside a tube, and the image swelled again. A patient watcher found tiny creatures wriggling in a drop of stale water, and the notion that a whole living thing could sit inside a droplet shook the learned world. Later hands polished better and cured the coloured fringes that blurred the rim, until the instrument laid bare the cell. What the naked eye withheld, glass gave up.

units: a dried out seed puts its biological workings on hold
that state lets it withstand extreme conditions
taking up water swells the tissues and splits the protective coat
the arrival of water wakes enzymes
those enzymes turn the stored starch into usable sugars
the root heads downwards under the pull of gravity
the shoot grows the opposite way
mild warmth speeds up the enzyme reaction
excessive heat wrecks the enzymes and halts the emergence
waterlogged soil drives out the oxygen and rots the young plant
text: While a seed stays dry, nothing stirs inside it. Its workings are on hold, and it will come through conditions that would kill a full grown plant. The moment moisture crosses the coat, the tissues swell and the pressure splits the shell open. That inrush of water wakes enzymes, and they cut the stored starch into sugars the plant can draw on. The sugars feed the embryo, which starts into growth: a root drives downwards, pulled by gravity, while a shoot climbs the other way. Warmth hurries the whole business along, since enzymes work faster in a mild medium; past a certain point, though, they break down and the seedling stalls. Too much water does something much like it. It drives the air out of the soil, leaves the tissues without oxygen, and rots the young plant before the first leaf ever shows.

units: a seed keeping station changed its procedure after a technical fault
the smallest seeds were clinging to the metal surfaces of the sorting machine
that clinging built the seeds into clumps
the weight readings were thrown out by it
the worker took an electric shock near the feed hopper
seeds rubbing against dry metal were throwing off static
replacing the equipment was beyond what the site could afford
a technician advised running the metal parts to earth through a conductor
she also called for damping the air in the room
the fault stopped during the following harvest period
text: At a seed store, a trivial mishap ended up rewriting a whole procedure. The technician on the sorting bench noticed that the smallest seeds were clinging to the metal walls of the machine and building into clumps, which threw out every weighing they made. Reaching towards the feed hopper, he took a shock, and a bluish spark jumped across to the panel. Static, thrown off by the husks rubbing against dry steel, accounted for the fault. Management first looked at replacing the plant, an outlay well beyond anything the site could find. An engineer put forward two far plainer measures: run a copper wire from every metal part down to earth, and keep the air of the room moderately damp with a fine spray. The clumps had gone by the following harvest, and the weighings could be trusted again.

units: the kit takes in a clear jar, a mesh sieve, a pouring cone, a pair of tweezers and a magnifying lens
two separate ways serve to draw the living things out of a soil sample
the two ways answer different aims
the way without water is to shake the crumbled earth on the sieve above a pale surface
the mineral grains drop through the mesh
the crawling animals are held back on top
the tweezers serve to move the animals under the lens without harming them
the way with water is to thin the sample down and then let the particles settle
roots and eggs come up to the top while the sand sinks
the first way suits looking at whole insects and the second gauging how much sand there is
text: You will need a clear jar, a fine sieve, a funnel, a soft pair of tweezers and a magnifying lens. There are two ways of separating living things from a sample of soil, and the two of them answer quite different questions. The dry way is to crumble the clod onto the sieve and shake it gently above a sheet of pale paper. Mineral grains drop through the mesh, the crawling animals stay on top, and the tweezers will lift them across under the lens without damaging them. The wet way asks you to fill the jar with water, stir the clod into it, then let everything settle before pouring the cloudy liquid through the funnel. Roots and eggs come to the top, while the sand sinks. Take the first when you want whole insects to look at, the second when you want to gauge how much sand there is.

units: a party of about twenty volunteers goes out after the sun has gone down
their aim is to count the amphibians round a body of water
two volunteers help the toads across a road
another post is netting the animals so that they can be named
the animals caught are put straight back in the water
every sighting is written down with the time and the water temperature
the woman in charge says that readings piled up over several seasons bring out shifts
one set of readings on its own is not enough to bring out those shifts
the woman in charge admits the conditions are rough and sometimes come to nothing
text: There are about twenty of them, boots on and lamps strapped to their foreheads, and they head down to the pond once the light has gone. They are volunteers, and the job comes down to a head count of amphibians. First post, the road: two of them tally the toads crossing and carry them over the bank. Second post, the water's edge: a net goes in, the species is named, the animal goes straight back. Third post, the notebook: every sighting is written down with the time and the water temperature. The coordinator explains that these figures, added up from one season to the next, bring out shifts that no single night could ever show. She owns up to the thankless side of it as well: the cold, the mud, the evenings that turn up nothing. Then a call rises from the ditch, and the whole group stops to listen.

units: the calm look of the surface hides the activity below the water
at the end of the cold season the deposit on the bed gives off bubbles
a greenish layer spreads along the edges
sticky clusters fasten themselves to the drowned plants
the embryos end by coming out of their eggs
the dark larvae gather in crowds near the warmed edge
the larvae feed on the algae coating the stones
the hind limbs form while the tail piece shrinks away
the falling level packs the last larvae into a small stretch of water
the ones that have changed leave the water for the plant cover
text: Nothing on the surface gives away what is being got ready underneath it. As the cold season loosens its hold, the mud lets go of its bubbles and a green film creeps along the edges of the pond. Jelly-like clusters show up between the stems, fastened to the reeds under the water. They pale, they fill with dark commas, and the eggs hatch at last. Black tadpoles swarm in dark clouds near the warm shallows, grazing the algae that coat the stones. Their shape alters without a sound: back legs push out, the tail shrinks away, the skin darkens. When the heat turns heavy, the level falls away, the mud cracks, and the last tadpoles crowd into one narrow puddle. The ones that have changed take to the long grass. The clear water of the season to come will keep no trace at all of any of it.

units: hedgerows are coming out faster than new ones go in
taking those hedgerows out makes it easier for farm machinery to get about
the wind sweeps the opened ground with nothing in its way
the layer of soil that feeds the crop is carried off into the ditches
rainwater tears down the slopes and cuts gullies into them
the watercourses take in more silt
the birds that used to settle in those branches have grown scarce
the drop in those predators drives up the use of sprays against crop pests
replanting is money laid out with nothing to show for it straight away
text: Hedgerows are coming out faster than they go back in, and the bill is already showing in the fields. Every screen of branches taken away makes the ground easier to work with machinery, granted. But the wind, which used to meet something living in its path, now sweeps a bare surface and carries the fertile layer off into the ditches. Storm water does the same: it tears down the slope unhindered, cuts gullies into it, and goes off to load the rivers with silt. The birds that nested in the thickness of the branches have grown scarce, and with them the predators that kept the crop pests down, so more spraying is needed. A saving in labour is paid for in lost soil, in sprays, in ditches to be dredged. Replanting costs money and returns nothing for several seasons. That is exactly why it should start now.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: one of the two scientists studies the water that lies beneath the ground
the other scientist follows the watercourses in the open air
both women study the same resource
groundwater cleans itself as it passes through permeable material
surface water carries silt and plant debris along with it
surface water has to be left to settle before it can be tested
the underground store feeds the watercourse when levels are low
spells of strong flow refill the underground store
text: One of them spends half her working life underground, lamp strapped to her forehead, notebook soaking in her pocket. The other keeps to the open air, boots planted in the current, watching the rivers run. Both women measure the same water, yet they never meet it in the same condition. Beneath the rock it threads through porous ground and clears itself as it works down through beds of sand. Out in the daylight it drags along silt, fallen leaves and drowned insects, so a sample has to stand and settle before anyone can test it. The first judges a hidden reserve by how slowly it moves, the second judges a stream by its force. Set their readings side by side and a pattern shows. The buried store feeds the visible channel when levels drop, and the visible channel refills the store once the floods have passed.

units: the visitor did not expect to enjoy the visit
a first section shows what sand does when air drives it
a face of rock crumbles in front of the public behind a glass screen
a second section shows what cold does to water that has seeped in
the rock splits when water freezes inside a crack
a third section deals with chemical attack by plants
two neighbouring pebbles compare an untouched surface with a hollowed one
the fourth section is judged disappointing because of too much written matter
a model of a coastal face closes the visit
text: Honestly, I walked into the exhibition on wearing stone expecting nothing at all, and it floored me. The first room belongs to the wind. Sand is fired at a soft face of rock and the face crumbles while you watch, safe behind glass. The second room is the cold one. Water seeps into a crack, sets hard, swells, and the rock splits open like a shell. The third was my favourite, all chemistry: quiet mosses eat into limestone, and two pebbles sit side by side to prove it, one smooth, the other bitten full of hollows. The fourth room is the weak link. Too much reading, too few objects, and you switch off fast. The ending saves it, with a model cliff the water gnaws at in front of you, over and over. I came away thinking that nothing hard stays hard, and went back the same evening.

units: the writer is writing from a shelter set up beside a pool
the spring stopped flowing with no warning sign
the team first thought the measuring device had failed
a probe revealed a blockage made of gravel
workmen cleared the blockage by hand
the water came back with force before settling down
the rock in this area breaks apart easily under pressure
the blockage happens again with every turn of the seasons
a metal guard will be fitted upstream
text: I am writing to you from the hut down by the pool, with the ink half frozen in the pen. Yesterday at first light the spring stopped flowing, no warning at all, and the team put it down to a faulty gauge. By midday the engineer had lowered a probe into the shaft and found nothing down there but a plug of gravel. Early in the afternoon two workmen cleared the passage by hand, carefully, stone after stone. The flow came back all at once. Water shot up over the rim of the basin, then eased into a steady trickle. In the evening we took our readings and set them against the week's curves. It comes down to one line. The rock up here breaks apart under pressure, and it will block the shaft again every season. A metal grille is going in upstream. I shall be home again as soon as the report has been signed.

units: water works into hollows too fine to be seen
freezing increases the space the water takes up
that increase in volume widens the crack
the crack stays open once mild weather returns
mineral deposits and roots settle into the opening
the pressure of the plants completes the break
the broken rock travels down the slope and is ground into particles
those particles help to build a soil
the bare slope and the grassland below share the same origin
moving air carries the finest fragments down to the low country
text: What becomes of a stone once the water has settled itself in its veins? It learns patience for a long while, and then it gives way. The water works into pores so fine that no eye can pick them out. Cold comes, the water stiffens and pushes outward, and the crack widens by a hair. The thaw returns, the water drains away, and the opening stays. What follows? A dust of minerals gathers there, roots take hold, and the pressure of growing things finishes the work. Should we say that the rock dies? No, it scatters. Every fragment travels down the slope, grinds against its own kind, and ends up as grains of matter that feed a soil in the making. Moving air carries the lightest of them off towards the low country. The bare slope above and the grassland below are one and the same matter, parted by a long fall.

units: the filtering system was clogging far faster than expected
the readings showed mostly clay particles
these particles turn sticky as soon as they meet damp
the clogging happens in the lower part of the system
the supervisor put forward a coarse screen at the inlet
she also put forward a settling tank ahead of the system
the technician feared a loss of flow at peak demand
two tanks used in turn solved the flow problem
the time between two clogging events has been greatly lengthened
text: The technician down at the site told the supervisor that the inlet filter was now clogging up in a fortnight rather than in six weeks. She asked him whether the load of particles had gone up. He said the analyses pointed mainly to fine clay, which turns sticky the moment it meets damp and seals the mesh from below. The supervisor put forward a coarse screen on the raw water, wide bars, ahead of everything else, and a settling tank to hold the water before it reaches the filter. The technician objected that a tank would drag the flow down at peak demand. She suggested two tanks running side by side, with a switch from one to the other. The trial was left to run for a whole season. The filter now holds for eight weeks, and the crew clean the tanks out, which costs less than replacing mesh.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the study of rock once rested on the senses of the researcher
the observer weighed the stone, tested its hardness and listened to the sound of the blow
descriptions depended on the memory of the person observing
two researchers far apart gave different names to the same material
cutting the rock into a transparent slice changed the discipline
this technique makes the crystals and their arrangement visible
the old approach was quick but confused materials that looked alike
the new approach calls for equipment and patience
the two ways of working are still used together in the field
text: Before optical instruments grew fine enough to be trusted, the study of rock rested on the hand and the eye. An observer weighed a block in the palm, scratched it with a fingernail, listened to the sound it made when struck. A description was worth no more than the memory behind it, and two scholars working far apart would file the same stone under different names. The thin section overturned all of that. Cut the rock down until light passes through it and the crystals themselves come into view, their edges and their arrangement, so that matter can be named without being handled. The older method judged the surface, the newer one questions the structure. One was quick and confused stones that felt alike. The other calls for a workshop, patience and a steady flow of cutting water. They still work together, since on the slope the hand picks what the blade will confirm.

units: three kinds of soil share the same slope
the soil in which sand dominates lets water away very quickly
its grains do not stick together between the fingers
clay soil holds water and turns sticky in the rain
as it dries clay hardens and cracks
the middle soil keeps the useful moisture and lets the surplus away
a dark surface layer holds the remains of plants
that layer feeds the vegetation
a shaping test done by hand shows which kind dominates
text: Three kinds of soil share one and the same slope, and the hand alone can tell them apart. Sandy soil lets the water slip straight through it. It is open and light, and the grains roll between the fingers without ever sticking together. Clay does the opposite. It holds on to water, turns greasy in the rain, then hardens as it dries until it cracks into plates. Loam sits somewhere between the two. It keeps back enough moisture for the roots and sends the surplus on downhill. Above these three lies a dark surface layer, thick with the remains of plants, which feeds everything that grows. A gardener checks what he is working with by rolling a damp pellet of it round in his palm. It falls apart into dust where sand rules, and rolls out into a smooth thread where clay has the upper hand.

units: the group set off before daybreak to watch a spring that flows in fits
the narrator complained about the cold on the way there
a retired stock keeper acted as guide to the group
the walk in took close to an hour along a muddy track
on arrival the site looked of no interest at all
the guide asked the group to wait in silence
a deep noise came before the puddle emptied
the water rose higher than the tops of the trees
the event was brief and left the visitors wet
the guide was recording the gap between two occurrences
text: We set off before daybreak to see the spring that empties itself in fits, and I moaned all the way there, because the cold had already got into my fingers. Our guide, a retired stockman, walked us the best part of an hour along a greasy track. When we arrived there was nothing to look at. A steaming hole, a lukewarm puddle, two birds that could not have cared less. He told us to stand still and say nothing. After a while a deep rumble came up through the ground, the puddle drained in a moment, and the water shot higher than the trees, in a warm cloud that soaked us to the socks. It was over quickly, and the quiet came back as though nothing had happened. Our guide was busy noting the gap between one waking and the next. We walked off laughing, wet, delighted, and I stopped moaning.

units: the sample is taken at the depth where the roots grow
the surface layer is set aside because it holds debris
the sample dries away from heat so that its structure is kept
the coarse material is taken out by passing it over a sieve
its weight would distort the result if it were kept
the material is then stirred into a vessel of water
the particles settle in order of decreasing weight
the depth of the bands is read from the bottom upwards
the colour is noted both wet and dry
text: Take your handful of soil at the depth where the roots are, never from the top, because the upper layer is full of debris and would throw the reading out. Spread the sample on paper and let it dry in the shade, since strong heat bursts the crumbs apart and alters the texture. Sieve the dry material to take out the gravel, or its weight will crush the fine fraction in your calculation. Tip whatever is left into a jar of clear water, shake it well, then leave it alone to settle. The heavy grains drop first, the fine ones after, and the bands can be read through the glass. Measure the depth of each band from the bottom upwards, because the order of deposit tells you what the soil is made of. Note the colour down last of all, wet and then dry, since it changes altogether as the moisture goes.

units: the current has eaten the raised bank back to the roots of the plants
the path that follows the watercourse is dropping away in sections
the people living there see the bank retreat steadily at every rise in the water
the loose nature of the ground makes it easy to tear away
the current speeding up in the bend makes the process worse
the material carried off travels downstream
a built wall was ruled out for its cost and its effect on the far bank
the chosen answer combines planting and bundles of branches
a hollow dug upstream slows the water coming in
the path will be moved further from the watercourse
text: Along the low bank the water has eaten the slope back to the roots of the shrubs, and the path that once followed the river is dropping away in whole sections. The people who live there put it plainly: every time the river rises, the bank retreats a pace. The ground is loose here, sand mixed with silt, and the current lifts it without effort as it gathers speed round the bend, carrying the loosened material away downstream. The team responsible for the catchment ruled out a concrete wall, costly and brutal, which would only have thrown the force of the water at the far bank. They chose instead to replant the slope with shrubs that root sideways, to lay bundles of branches at the foot of it, and to dig a hollow upstream to slow the water. One season was enough to hold the toe. The path will be moved uphill, out of reach.

units: a damp upland place gathers several natural habitats into a small area
a waterlogged plant carpet borders the pool
organisms fixed to the stone withstand a lack of water
hollow stems serve as shelter for young insects
the water looks clear but carries scraps of plant matter
tiny near-transparent animals move in short bursts
seeds buried in the bottom wait for a favourable period
every level depends on the others and losing one leaves the whole poorer
text: A high mountain bog brings together several quite unlike habitats within a very small stretch of ground. Along the pool spreads a carpet of sodden moss; it gives way underfoot, then springs back at once. Higher up, bare rock wears a coat of grey lichen, rough to the touch, which survives one drought after another. Between the two grow tall grasses whose hollow stems shelter minute larvae. The water counts as a habitat of its own. It looks clear from above, yet it carries scraps of plant matter that cloud it the moment you stir it. See-through insects dart about in short bursts, all but invisible. Deeper down, under the silt, seeds lie dormant and wait for a kinder season before they sprout. Every one of these layers leans on the rest, and losing a single one leaves the whole poorer.

units: artificial lighting was aimed first at the safety of public roads
it then spread to buildings and to parking areas
commercial signs shine at night above empty walkways
only the brightest stars stay visible
an orange glow hides the depth of the sky
migrating birds circle the lit buildings
insects active after sunset die beside the lamps
some local authorities have already switched the lighting off in the middle of the night without complaint
text: We have mislaid the night sky, and hardly anyone noticed. It began sensibly enough: street lamps went up so that people could walk home without fear. Then the glare crept onto building fronts, onto car parks, onto shop windows, and we took it for granted. Now signs blaze away till dawn above empty pavements. Look up and you get a handful of the fiercest stars, nothing else, since an orange wash has swallowed whatever lies behind them. Birds on migration steer by those stars, so they circle the lit towers until they drop. Moths and beetles that come out after sunset batter themselves against the lamps and die at the foot of them. Switching off after midnight would cost us little. Several local authorities have done exactly that, and no resident grumbled. It seems a pity to wait until darkness is only a memory.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman leading the team explores a network of passages not yet mapped
a fall into a crack in childhood set off her calling
she found then a chamber crossed by falling water
her parents worked a dry sloping plot of land
she understood that the water missing at the surface travelled lower down
she trained in a field devoted to the study of waters
her measurements show the deep reserves refilling faster than expected
the neighbouring authorities changed where they draw water after these results
text: The scientist who leads the team spends her working weeks underground, in a run of passages that no survey had ever put on paper. Her calling began with a fall. As a child she slipped into a narrow crack in the family pasture and landed in front of a chamber with a sheet of water pouring through it. Her parents worked a dry patch of hillside, so she grasped early on that the water missing from the surface was travelling somewhere beneath it. She trained as a hydrologist, then came back to measure what she had glimpsed. Her readings show that the deep reserves refill far quicker than anyone assumed, and the authorities round about have since reworked where they draw their supply. The map she keeps updating now serves farmers and officials alike, and her quiet manner no longer stops people listening.

units: the exhibition deals with the marine depths
the first room shows animals kept in a liquid
this display conveys neither the pressure nor the darkness of the depths
the end of the route puts this fault right
a lightless passage forces the visitor to move forward blind
projected images show jelly-like animals above people's heads
a shudder of the floor goes with that scene
the writer regrets that this choice was not applied from the start
text: You leave this exhibition on the deep sea feeling you have brushed against something vast that has been poorly served. The weakness shows in the opening room, where cabinet after cabinet holds pale specimens suspended in spirit, with nothing to suggest the crushing weight or the blackness they came from. Under a hard light, a fish that once glowed is merely another jar. The closing stretch of the route puts matters right. The designers have cut a lightless corridor there, and you edge along it by touch while projections send drifting jellyfish across the ceiling, high above your head. The floor shudders faintly. At last the intended effect arrives: a crushing body of water, thinly peopled by rare creatures. Had that instinct governed the whole thing from the door onward, the most distracted visitor would have been won over.

units: the sender reports on two methods for tracking freshwater animals
the first method uses capture devices sunk into the water
the second consists of laying plates on the ground
the underside of the plates holds moisture
the sunken devices take more mature individuals
they call for regular visits and sometimes injure the animals' limbs
the plates give fewer captures but more reliable readings
a grainy material spread under the plates suits the young ones
the sender proposes splitting the two methods across two separate sectors
text: Dear colleague, here is the account I owe you of the two protocols we settled on for tracking the amphibians in the pond. One relies on smooth-walled traps sunk into the water. The other uses plates laid flat on the ground, the rough underside of which holds the damp. The traps take more adults, but somebody has to walk the line every second evening, and they often damage the animals' legs. Plates are put down once and draw only what is looking for shelter: the yield drops, though the data comes out cleaner. One more thing worth passing on. The gritty material we spread beneath the plates appears to suit the young ones while it hampers the adults. If you agree, let us keep the plates on the upper sector and the traps on the lower one, then set the catches side by side once the season closes.

units: a handful of forest soil holds a great many living things
the combined action of these things makes the ground fertile
threads that come from fungi extend the reach of the roots
these threads take up water and dissolved minerals
they receive in exchange sugary compounds made by the leaves
the tearing of this network lets the rain strip off the surface layer
restoring damaged ground takes several decades
the measures mentioned include covering with plant waste and keeping machinery off
dark springy crumbs show that the soil is recovering
text: What does a handful of forest soil hold? Fungal threads, bacteria, mites and worms, whose combined labour is the very thing that makes the ground fertile. And what do those threads do? They reach out well beyond the tree roots, take up water and dissolved salts, and trade them for sugars sent down from the leaves. What follows when that mesh is torn? The soil loses its grip, rain strips off the upper layer, and whatever grows back grows back poorer. Can ruined ground be repaired? It can, provided one accepts a timescale of several decades: the surface is covered with plant waste, machinery is kept off it, and deep-rooted species are put back to reopen the old channels. And what tells us it is working? Dark, springy crumbs that come apart between the fingers without turning to dust.

units: the forest warden advises coming before the female returns
the group sets off in the dark without a light
the assistant notes that the nest hole sits higher than the year before
the warden climbs with the help of a ladder
he draws a young bird covered in soft down out of the hole
the bird cannot stand yet
three other chicks occupy the cavity
the visitors measure the feathers and look at the colour of the bill
the female is back at the nest shortly after the group leaves
text: “Come up before the mother starts her rounds again, or you will see nothing,” the warden had told us the evening before. So we set off ahead of daylight with no torch, following the path by nothing more than the sound of our own feet. At the foot of the beech his assistant whispered that the hole sat higher than it had the year before. He hauled the ladder into position, slipped a hand inside the opening and drew out a chick still in soft down, not yet able to stand on its legs. “Three more behind it,” he said, and settled the bird back at the bottom of the nest. We took down the length of the feathers and the colour of the bill, and disturbed nothing else. “You watch, you count, you leave,” he added on the way down, summing up his trade. The mother was back at the nest soon after we had gone.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: quarry workers found the remains of shellfish in stone lying high up
these shapes were put down at first to a whim of the rock
stonecutters noticed that the remains were stacked in a steady order
this stacking recalled the floor of still water
the same order turned up in different valleys
the explanation by chance became hard to believe
observers put forward that the stone had formed under water
this idea implied that the ground had been pushed up
the notion was accepted because what it predicted held up in the field
text: Picture the faces of the quarrymen who split a slab high above the sea and found shells lying right across the stone. For generations the answer was that the rock had simply amused itself, that it could mimic living things when it chose. Then sharper-eyed stonecutters noticed the shells were stacked in beds, in an order that never varied, exactly as they settle on the floor of a quiet bay. Since that same order turned up in one valley after another, chance became an awkward thing to believe in. Some observers put forward an unwelcome answer: the rock had formed beneath the water, and the ground had later been pushed up. The idea took decades to gain a hearing, because it forced people to accept that hills move. It won in the end by predicting correctly. Where it promised marine beds, marine beds were found.

units: a watercourse penned between straight walls sheds its water too quickly
the water reaches the lower ground abruptly in heavy rain
the low parts of built-up areas go under
the bed dries out with the first spell of real heat
the straight channel had been dug to win farming ground
that channel did away with the bends which slowed the water and let it soak in
the repair consists of handing the watercourse back a share of its former room
the works include breaking open the built banks and replanting trees
the floods grow less violent and a flow survives in dry weather
text: A river running dead straight between two concrete walls sheds its water far faster than it ought to. Hydrologists say the same thing after every flood: the whole volume lands downstream in one go, the low-lying streets go under, the water leaves, and the bed is dry by the first spell of real heat. That straight channel was dug to win ground for crops, and it did away with the bends where the flow used to slow and soak in. The remedy tried lately is to hand the river back a share of the room it once had. Built-up banks are broken open, old side channels are dug out again, trees go in whose roots knit the edges together. The water winds once more, spreads into meadows made for flooding and feeds the water table. Floods lose their punch, and a trickle survives the hot months.

units: the walkers climb a steep face and come down by the other
the face they climb is dry and stony
only short grasses grow in the cracks of the rock
the walkers' water runs out quickly on the way up
the change of face happens within a few strides at the top
the other face is deep in thick vegetation
very cold water seeps from the wall
a group of farm animals rests in the shade on that side
the narrator concludes that a hill is made of faces exposed in different ways
text: We had settled on climbing the steep face and coming down the other, with no notion at all of how sharply the two would turn out to contradict each other. The way up was dry and stony: baking slabs, tufts of cropped grass wedged into cracks, and the rasp of insects for company. Nothing there held any water, and our bottles emptied before our eyes. The switch came within three strides. Over the ridge lay a shaggy slope, deep in ferns, where the air smelt of wet moss. Threads of water seeped from the wall, cold enough to numb the fingers. We passed a flock grazing in the shade while the slope behind us went on roasting. One hill, cut in two by a ridge, was keeping two climates and two sets of living things. Since that walk, a mountain has never looked to me like one solid mass.

units: a charger in use grows warm
the current runs through a copper winding inside the device
every conducting material resists the passage of the current
this resistance turns part of the energy into heat
a greater demand for power increases the share that is lost
makers provide vents, metal contact parts and sometimes a cooling fan
a device that gets too hot slows its own pace
a soft object placed under a computer blocks the air openings
text: Put your hand on a charger you have left plugged in. It feels warm, and there is nothing odd in that. Inside the casing, current runs along thin wires and round a copper winding. No conductor lets electricity through for free; it pushes back, and that pushing back turns a slice of the energy into heat. The more power the device draws, the bigger the slice grows. Designers know as much, so they cut vents into the shell, press metal plates against the busiest components, or tuck in a tiny fan. When the heat has nowhere to go, the circuits throttle themselves to stay safe, and the machine turns sluggish. That is why a cushion slipped under a laptop smothers it: the slots close up, the air sits still, the temperature climbs. Pull the plug, give the thing room to breathe, and it will settle down again.

units: dead tablets were piling up in a repair workshop
the devices showed no sign of life at all
the explanation put forward blamed the battery
the head of the workshop doubted that diagnosis
taking one apart revealed a cracked metal joint beneath the charging socket
a light knock was enough to break it
the team built a cradle that holds the board still while the joint is redone
the repair became cheap to carry out
the workshop displays its repair notes publicly
text: At the far end of a shopping arcade, a repair workshop had been stacking up silent tablets for weeks. The verdict never varied: black screen, no response at all, a battery said to be finished. The senior repairer would not swallow so tidy and convenient a story. He opened one machine, then a second, and found beneath the charging socket a cracked metal joint, far too fine to spot without a lens. A modest knock was all it took to split it. Rather than swap out whole boards, the team shaped a cradle that grips the board firmly while a hot iron rebuilds the failed point. Putting a tablet right now costs next to nothing, and owners walk out with a machine that has woken up. Repair notes hang on a board beside the counter, so that people stop throwing away what a bead of solder would bring back.

units: two distinct ways exist to take apart an old playback device
the first means removing the screws one at a time
the first calls for noting where the parts sit on a drawing
the second means forcing the shell open with a flat tool
the second usually damages a catch
the careful method needs an adjustable lamp and a clear bench
the bundles of wire make the difference between the two approaches plain
the text recommends the careful method
putting it back together follows the reverse order
text: Before you loosen a single nut, choose your road, for an old player can be opened in two ways. The first belongs to patience: the screws come out one at a time, each dropped into a shallow saucer, each place marked on a sketch. The second belongs to nerve: a flat blade prises the lid up, a moment is saved, and a catch is lost. Patience asks for a lamp on a bendable arm and a bench swept bare; nerve asks for nothing but a firm wrist. Yet once the wiring shows itself, a thin garland pressed against the floor of the frame, the gap between them opens wide: the careful hand knows where every ribbon returns, while the hasty one pulls blind and tears. Take the first road, then. Build the thing back up in reverse order, and let the drawer spring settle back before the lid goes down.

units: the sorting line described has three complementary pieces of equipment
light sensors read the reflection to identify what the packaging is made of
jets of compressed air push aside the unwanted items
this ejection happens without anything touching the objects
belts running at unequal speeds spread the flow and stop items piling up
the manager reckons upkeep matters more than the software
a dirty nozzle sends the ejected pieces off course
a slack belt upsets the rhythm of the line
a dusty sensor takes glass for clear plastic
a worker inspects the installation regularly to clean it
text: The shed hums with a steady drone, and the guided tour opens in front of the first sorting line. Three pieces of kit work in concert here. The first is a curtain of optical sensors that measures how each pack throws light back and works out what it is made of. The second is a rail of compressed air nozzles, firing to the thousandth of a second to fling out unwanted pieces without ever touching them. The third is a run of belts whose gears turn at differing speeds, spreading the flow so that nothing rides on anything else. The operator presses a point visitors tend to miss: reliability rests less on the software than on upkeep. A clogged nozzle skews the throw; a slack belt shifts the timing; a dusty sensor takes glass for clear plastic. So a worker walks the line at set intervals, cloth in hand.

units: the assembly described follows a fixed sequence of operations
a cut sheet of metal is given its final shape under a press
a sheathed metal wire is wound around a central core
the ends of that winding are stripped of their sheath
a magnetic part sits in the outer ring and is locked by a collar
the shaft is oiled before it is fitted
the turning of the shaft is checked with no load
the wires of the winding are fixed with solder onto conducting pads
the shell closes on a seal that keeps out the dust
the finished object undergoes a load test in a booth
text: Watch an assembly line for a while and a strict order emerges, followed from the first movement to the last. A cut steel plate reaches a turning table, where a press stamps the shape of the housing into it. Winding comes next: lacquered copper wire runs round a core and builds an even coil, whose ends will later be stripped bare. A permanent magnet then drops into the outer ring and is held there by a collar. The shaft is offered up, oiled, driven home, and its turn is checked with no load on it. Once that has passed, the ends of the coil meet two conducting pads, where a machine lays down a bead of solder. The casing is closed last of all, on a soft seal that keeps the dust outside. The whole thing then goes off to the test booth, where a measured load proves how well it holds.

units: putting a household appliance back into working order has become difficult
shells are now glued together rather than screwed
the screw heads used are not sold in ordinary shops
spare parts stop being sold soon after a model goes out
the buyer gives up on repair and buys a replacement product
objects that half an hour would mend are thrown away
independent shops disappear for want of custom
technical skills are lost when those shops close
some makers show that a lid you can lift adds nothing to the bulk
the text calls for standard screws, wiring diagrams to hand and parts in stock
text: Mending a household appliance was once routine work; today it counts as a feat. The reasons are plain enough. Makers have glued the shells together instead of screwing them, settled on screw heads no ordinary shop stocks, and stopped selling spare parts a short while after a model goes out. Each of those decisions has a measurable effect. The owner gives up, buys a replacement, and something half an hour of work would have saved ends up in a skip. Independent shops close for want of custom, and the skill they carried fades with them. Slimness and sealing no longer excuse it: some makers prove that a lid you can lift adds nothing to the bulk. Asking for standard screws, a wiring diagram you can obtain and a lasting stock of parts is no fond wish for the past; it is what long use depends on.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman knew nothing of mechanical words when she started
she taught herself by taking broken toys apart
she runs a small shop set between two other businesses
her first difficulty came from the awkwardness her customers felt
the customers were afraid of getting it wrong as they described their trouble
she changed the way she receives the public
she opens the device in front of its owner and names each part as she points
customers come back having worked out the fault themselves
the shop is no longer short of custom
text: She says that at the start she muddled up a cog and a pulley, and that she taught herself by pulling old broken toys to bits. The mender of the neighbourhood now keeps a narrow shop, wedged between a launderette and a florist. Her trouble in the early days was not mechanical at all: it was how shy her customers were. Nobody dared describe a fault out loud, for fear of saying something daft. So she changed the way she takes people in. She sets the machine down on the counter, opens it up in front of its owner, and names each part aloud: here is the catch that sticks, here is the power socket, here is the gear that slips. Customers now leave having understood. A good many of them come back later with a fault they have pinned down themselves, and the shop is never empty now.

units: the two machines compared follow opposite designs
the first favours suction power and sturdiness
the first does well on thick textile floor coverings
the first makes a noise that drives the household away
the first leaves dirt in the corners
the second stands out for how well it finds its way about
the second pulls with less force and takes longer to finish the surface
the second avoids obstacles and slips under low furniture
the choice depends on the sort of floor and how cluttered the home is
both machines open and empty without a tool
text: Set side by side on the same shelf, two robot cleaners tell two opposite stories. The first backs sheer force: an eager motor, a wide brush, a generous bin, and a body that shrugs off knocks. It shines on deep rugs, but its racket drives the whole household out of the room, and its corner arm leaves crescents of dust in the angles. The second plays a finer game: careful navigation, a map you can trust, a return to base with no dithering. It pulls less hard and takes longer to cover the floor, yet it bumps into nothing and slips under low furniture. The verdict turns on the home: hard floors and tight furniture, and the second wins; deep pile and open rooms, and the first takes the lead.
