On one score they are equal: the bin tips out in a moment, and the lid lifts with no tool.

units: the writer reports on the restoration of a radio set found in the loft
the work falls into three separate tasks
the cabinet was sanded, glued at one corner and waxed
the inside was covered in a thick deposit
two wires had lost their covering
the connections were remade wire by wire
the needle of the dial no longer follows the turning knob
the writer supposes that a springy part is worn
the writer promises to write again once the set is working
text: You asked me how the radio from the loft was getting on, and I owe you an account of it at last. Three separate tasks have kept me busy. The cabinet came first: I sanded down the lifted veneer, glued a corner that had sprung open, replaced a missing beading, then rubbed in a wax that woke the grain of the wood again. The inside came second, and there my patience wavered: dust lay like a grey felt over every valve, and two wires had shed their covering. I remade the connections strand by strand, with fresh wire and a clean, bright joint. The third task holds me still: the needle on the dial refuses to follow the knob any longer, and I suspect a tired spring. When it is all ready at last, I shall set the thing by the window and write to tell you what the first voice says.

units: a specialist describes the updating of the internal software of a device
the device first checks that the file it has received is genuine
the procedure stops if that check fails
the new data is written into an area of memory apart from the one in use
this separation protects the device if the power is cut
the earlier version remains until the restart
a counter of attempts turns the start back to the old area if the writing fails
the user then notices only a slower start
the fingerprints of the two areas are compared after the switch
the space of the stale version is freed only after a session without fault
text: What actually happens when the internal software of a machine is brought up to date? The engineer we asked sets out the stages in order. First the device checks the signature of the file it has received; if that does not match, the whole procedure halts at once. The image is then written into a second area of memory, never over the one at work, so that a power cut can damage nothing. And the earlier version? It stays whole until the restart. And if the writing fails? A counter of attempts turns the start back to the old area, and the user notices no more than a slightly heavier start than usual. After the switch, a final check compares the fingerprints of the two areas. The machine frees the space of the stale version last of all, and only after a full session with nothing amiss.

units: a neighbour reports that his printing machine was damaging the paper
the user had tried rough handling without getting any result
a local repairer blames the fault on a worn drive belt
the belt had lost its grip through turning with no load
the repairer advises getting at the back of the machine
a round part must be turned one notch to retighten the belt
the machine feeds the paper properly after the intervention
the owner had thought of throwing out a repairable machine
he decides to keep the handbook within reach
text: The chap across the road got talking about his printer, which kept chewing the paper and creasing every sheet it swallowed. He had shaken it, tapped it, tugged at the tray, and got nothing out of it but another jam. Then someone who mends machines round here told him the trouble was almost certainly the drive belt: rubber goes smooth once it has spun for years with nothing to grip. Get round the back, the man said, lift the rear cover, find the grey wheel on the side and turn it one notch to take up the slack. My neighbour grumbled his way through the job. He rang the next morning sounding rather pleased with himself, since the sheets were coming through dead straight at last. He had nearly binned a sound machine over a slack loop of rubber, he said, and the handbook is going in the drawer where he can reach it.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: two ways of sending messages over distance existed side by side for a long period
the first method used tall towers carrying movable arms
one man set the arms and another read the shape through a glass
the second method sent a current along an insulated metal wire
this wire was buried beside the tracks or hung from supports
mist and darkness stopped the arm system working
the wire worked without depending on the weather
the chain of towers took up a large staff
the electric line kept only one man at each of its ends
the price of the cable held back the spread of the second method
text: Two ways of sending word across country ran alongside each other for a very long stretch of time. One of them raised towers on high ground, each crowned with jointed wooden arms that a man on duty swung into shape, while his opposite number in the next tower read the shape through a glass and repeated it at once. The other pushed a current down a copper wire sheathed in insulation, buried beside the tracks or strung between poles on open ground. Set side by side, the two are not hard to separate. Mist or nightfall stopped the wooden arms dead, whereas the current took no notice of the sky at all. A chain of towers swallowed staff by the dozen, while the wire kept one man busy at either end and nobody in between. What held the wire back was the price of the cable, and that price delayed its spread for a good while.

units: the machine described builds an object by laying matter down in layers
its bulk is comparable to that of a piece of luggage
a reel carries a plastic thread that unwinds towards the machine
a heated tip softens this thread and lays it down in fine ribbons
a moving support drops a little at every pass of the tip
the object is therefore built from the bottom upwards
a fan cools the matter laid down to stop it sagging
an electronic board orders the movements of the whole
the machine is light enough to stand on a household table
text: A machine that lays matter down layer upon layer is housed in a case hardly wider than a suitcase. Look first at the reel, where a translucent plastic filament lies coiled like a patient rope and unwinds without hurry towards the works inside. Then comes the nozzle, a heated tip that softens the thread as it arrives and sets it down in ribbons so fine they feel barely warm to the touch. Under the nozzle the bed slides along, dropping a fraction at every pass the tip makes, so that the object grows as it rises. A fan breathes over the soft trail and sets it firm before it can sag out of shape. Beneath the frame, quiet and out of the way, the board keeps count and orders every movement of the whole. None of it weighs much. The machine stands on an ordinary kitchen table and purrs away like a diligent insect at work.

units: a crew put up a mast on the roof of a technical building
the item installed is a hollow tube made of a light metal
it replaced a device cracked by vibration
the fitters bolted the base onto a thick metal plate
they checked that it stood upright before the final tightening
a rise in the wind set the mast vibrating steadily
the supervisor stopped the work and measured the frequency
the structure was resonating with the gusts
fitting two diagonal stays shifted the natural frequency
the closing measurements confirmed the performance expected
text: Work started before first light, with the crew hauling the mast sections onto the flat roof of the plant room. The aerial itself was a hollow tube of light alloy, brought in to replace one that vibration had cracked through. The fitters bolted the base plate onto a thick steel sheet, then checked that it stood true before pulling the fixings up tight. By midday the wind had freshened and the mast began to hum on one low, steady note. The supervisor called a halt, timed the oscillation and saw what was happening, for the structure was resonating with the gusts. Two diagonal stays went on, which shifted the natural frequency clear of the dangerous band. The cable was terminated as the light went, and the closing measurements confirmed the performance the design had promised.

units: the supply must be cut and the machine left to cool before any work
a hot liquid expands and may be thrown out when the union is opened
a container must be placed beneath the lower union
the draining happens through the weight of the liquid
the valve must be opened a quarter turn only
opening it too quickly draws in air and stops the flow
the bleed control at the high point lets air in at the top
filling is done through the upper opening once the valve is closed
filling slowly keeps bubbles from forming
a circuit without bubbles carries heat evenly
text: Before any work on the cooling circuit, disconnect the supply and leave the machine to cool. Hot water expands, and the pressure it builds inside the flexible hose will throw the liquid out the moment the union is opened. Set a tray beneath the lower union, since the contents drain under their own weight and nothing else. Open the valve a quarter turn and no more. Opened quickly, it draws in air, the flow stalls at once and the whole operation comes to nothing at all. Now lower the bleed lever at the high point, so that air enters at the top and drives the liquid downwards. When the tray stops filling, close the valve, wipe the union and top the circuit up through the upper opening. Filling slowly keeps bubbles from forming, and a circuit free of bubbles carries heat evenly.

units: a voluntary body takes in appliances that no longer work every week
the place used is a covered hall lent by the neighbourhood
most of the objects have a fault of small extent
the faults named are a soldered cell a corroded contact or a glued shell
makers justify these assemblies by waterproofing and slimness
the menders read them as a deliberate shortening of the working life
the workshop records every opening in a register and in pictures
the sheets produced are published for anyone to use
an associated supplier delivers batches of standard contacts
most of the appliances handed in leave in working order
text: In a covered hall lent by the neighbourhood, volunteers take in broken appliances and disheartened owners alike, week after week. Their finding is blunt. Most of what comes through the door has only a small fault: a soldered cell, a corroded contact, a shell glued shut that no ordinary tool will open without breaking it. Makers put these sealed assemblies down to waterproofing and slimness, while the menders read them as a deliberate way of shortening the working life of a product. So the workshop has answered in kind. It keeps a register of every model opened, photographs each stage and publishes the sheets for anyone to use. A parts supplier has joined in and now delivers batches of standard contacts. Since this season, two appliances in three leave the hall working again.

units: two speakers are looked at side by side
the first is a very light plastic cube
its grille imitates the look of metal
the second has a shell of folded metal and weighs more
a stretched cloth covers the front of the second one
the cube lacks power in the low sounds
the heavier one holds the bass notes without shaking
the cube is easy to carry and stands knocks
the second calls for a wall socket and a steady surface
the choice depends on the use intended
text: Stand the two speakers next to each other and the difference shows before you plug anything in. The first is a moulded plastic cube, light as an empty box, with a printed grille that pretends to be metal. The second has weight in the hand: folded sheet metal, edges turned over, and a stretched cloth across the front that hints at a proper cone behind it. Play something and the cube snaps along nicely up top, then gives way as soon as the bass drops. Its heavier neighbour holds the note, fills the room and barely shivers on the shelf. There is the other side of it, mind. The cube slips into a bag, charges overnight and takes knocks without complaint, while the other wants a wall socket and a steady corner. Each has its ground, and the ear decides by what you mean to do with it.

units: the writer disputes the praise given to the thinness of devices
the first charge concerns the battery held on with adhesive
a glued battery condemns the object as soon as its charge fades
the second charge is aimed at screws with an exclusive head
these screws keep independent workshops away from repair
the third charge concerns software that refuses an unpaired part
the three obstacles reinforce one another
the writer grants that shrinking the size forces compromises
he asks that the buyer be told before the purchase
text: We ought to stop praising a device for being thin, as though slimness were a moral achievement. The charge comes under three heads. First the adhesive, since gluing a battery to the frame does the owner no good at all and condemns the thing the moment its charge starts to fade. Then the exclusive screw, cut to a head that no common driver will fit, whose one purpose is to keep the independent workshop out. Last the software, which turns down a spare part identical in every respect because it was not paired at the factory. The three locks work together: the first makes opening risky, the second makes it awkward, the third makes it pointless. Shrinking a device does force compromises, and that much is true. The buyer might at least be told as much at the till, rather than the day after the failure.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: as a child she took the clocks of her house apart
she rarely put them back together whole
her training took place in a mechanical workshop
that workshop repaired lifting gear
her first job was greasing the grooved wheels
she saw how metal tires and how the grooves wear
once a technician she went down into the pit alone
she carried a hand crank for emergencies at her belt
she was later given the diagnoses her colleagues gave up on
she now passes her trade on to apprentices
text: As a child she took the clocks of the house apart to see what was beating inside them, and rarely got them back together whole. Her training came later, in a mechanical workshop where lifting gear was brought in for repair. Her first job was a dull one, greasing the grooved wheels, one after another, until the cable ran through without a sound. That is where she learned how metal tires and how a groove wears away under the load it carries. Once qualified, she earned the right to go down into the pit alone, a hand crank for emergencies hooked to her belt. In time the awkward diagnoses came to her, the ones her colleagues gave up on. She listens first, palm flat against the upright, and names the guilty part before the housing is even open. She teaches apprentices now, and tells them the ear comes before the tool.

units: the laptop under review weakens as soon as the load runs on
the fault comes from the shape of the machine
a powerful processor sits under a very thin lid
the heat pipe has a reduced cross-section
the heat banks up against the electronic board
the controller drops the clock to protect the chip
the fan grows noisy and the computing speed falls
the keyboard turns warm and long spells of typing suffer
a perforated stand improves the airflow without removing the cause
a thicker chassis would deliver more for the same money
text: This very slim laptop falters as soon as the load runs on for more than a moment, and the reason lies wholly in its shape. A generous processor has been fitted under a lid too thin to leave it room, which gives the heat pipe a laughably small cross-section. With nowhere to go, the heat banks up against the board, and the controller drops the clock at once to keep the silicon safe. You hear the result as much as you measure it: the fan climbs into a whine, computing speed falls by a third, then wanders instead of settling. The keyboard grows warm under the fingers, which tells against any long spell of typing. A perforated stand will improve the airflow and put off the drop, though it treats the effect and leaves the cause alone. For the same money a thicker chassis simply delivers more.

units: the writer addresses an acquaintance who had left a device with him
he takes the old device out of a cupboard and looks it over
he has just bought a recent model of the same kind
the old device weighs twice as much as the recent one
its metal shell warms up while it is being used
the screen of the recent model renders colours better
the old device opens up so that its battery can be replaced
the recent model is glued together and does not open
the writer asks his correspondent for a reply
text: Do you still think about that tablet you left with me before you went away? I dug it out of the cupboard last night and stood it beside the one I have only just bought, and the gap between the two made me laugh out loud. The old one weighs twice as much, and its thick metal shell warms up under your fingers the moment you open a second window. The recent one slips into a coat pocket, and its screen shows colours the older machine never managed. Still, I will say one thing for the old tablet: it can be mended. I have unscrewed the back myself to fit a fresh battery, whereas the later model is glued shut and will not come apart without cracking. One wins on lightness, the other on good behaviour. Guess which one stays on my desk. Write back and tell me what you make of it before you come home.

units: excess heat is what wears portable computers most
the dust that gathers blocks the air vents
that blockage stops the fan from cooling the machine
the device slows itself down to protect itself
a steady or crackling sound announces the fault
the keyboard turns hot to the touch
the computer slows down for no visible reason
the power must be cut before the casing is opened
replacing the fan costs little and is done in a single job
text: What wears out a portable computer fastest? Heat, says the repair workshop that takes us in. And where does the heat come from? From dust, which mats the vents, stops the fan turning and forces the machine to throttle itself. What warns you before the failure? Three signs, and they recur. Sound first: a steady rush of air, then a crackle as the blades catch their housing. Then the keyboard, which turns warm under your hands. Last, the slowness, which settles in with no visible cause. What should you do? Cut the power, unscrew the base plate, blow the dust outwards and screw it back. And if the noise stays? The fan needs replacing, a cheap job the workshop finishes in a single visit. Should you open it yourself? The engineer hesitates, then says a careful hand beats a smothered machine.

units: a repairer announces that she has found the fault
the person in charge of the place questions her about her diagnosis
a blinking coloured light put her on the trail
she cleaned away a corroded deposit on the board
she soldered back a conductor that had come loose
she warns that the machine must be kept away from the wall
otherwise the hot air gathers behind the device
the person in charge undertakes to move it the next day
the device lights up again once reassembled and plugged in
text: The engineer set her bag on the bench and said she had found the fault. The manager asked her what she had seen. She told him that an amber light had been blinking as soon as she lifted the casing, and that this had put her on the trail. Then she explained how she had taken out the board, scraped away a greenish crust along one track, and soldered back a wire that had been hanging loose. The manager wanted a promise. She answered that the joint would hold if the workshop stopped pressing the machine against the wall, since the hot air had nowhere to go behind it. He said he would shift it the following morning. She closed the lid, put the four screws back in the order she had laid them out, and plugged the machine back in while he stood there watching. The screen came on, a pale blue.

units: the old calculating machines worked with toothed wheels
every added wheel raised the mechanical resistance
that resistance bent the shafts that carried the movement
the number of columns therefore stayed limited
the makers wanted to do away with the moving parts
the electromechanical switch avoided gearing but wore out
it also made a sharp noise at every calculation
the vacuum tube was fast but gave off a great deal of heat
that thermal constraint led on to the solid component
text: Before electricity, adding by machine meant toothed wheels linked by pawls. Every wheel added friction, the friction called for a firmer push on the crank, and that push ended by bending the shafts. Hence the limit of such machines: past a dozen columns, the gearing jammed. Makers therefore set out to get rid of the moving part. The electromechanical relay gave them a first way out, since it switched without gears; but its contacts wore away, and its clack gave away every sum. The vacuum tube came next: quicker, and silent, yet it ran so hot that each cabinet needed its own fan and a steady supply of replacements for the burnt-out bulbs. It was that heat, as much as the cost, that pushed the workshops towards the solid component, cold, tiny, and free of anything that moves.

units: a battery that runs down early is not necessarily worn out
three habits account for the quick draining
a display kept at full brightness draws the most
some programs reach the network without being used
heat lowers the capacity of the cell for good
it is advised to lower the brightness and let it be set automatically
the updating of unused programs must be switched off
leaving the device on charge all night harms the battery
these moves put off the battery change without restoring it
text: A battery that runs flat before evening worries its owner, though wear seldom explains it. Three habits account for most cases. The first is a screen kept at full brightness, since the panel draws more than the processor does. The second is the long list of programs that reach for the network in the background, unopened. The third is heat, because a warm cell loses capacity for good. The answer falls into three moves. Lower the brightness first, and let the device set it by itself. Then switch off background refreshing for the programs you hardly ever open. Finally, keep the machine out of direct sun, and stop leaving it on the charger all night, since a cell held at the top of its range grows tired. None of this hands back a fresh cell, but it does put off the day of replacement.

units: two staff from one department are each given a pilotless flying machine
these craft are used to inspect the roofs of buildings
one of the models is heavy and can be mended on the spot
the other model is compact and easy to carry
any breakage of the compact model means sending it back to the maker
a gust comes up during the first outing
the compact craft drifts off and strikes a water channel
one of its blades snaps
its user waits two weeks for the spare part
the two machines are now used according to how exposed the site is
text: Two colleagues on the same maintenance team were handed a flying machine each in the same week, both meant for inspecting roofs. One picked a sturdy model with a thick moulded frame, whose blades can be swapped by hand in a moment. The other preferred a light craft that folds into a pocket, quicker to get airborne, though the smallest broken part means sending the whole thing back to the maker. During the first inspection the wind got up. The heavy machine held its place above the timbers while the light one drifted and struck a gutter. A blade snapped clean off. Its owner waited a fortnight for a part his colleague kept in the boot of his van. Since then, the heavy model goes up on exposed sites and the light one in sheltered yards, and they no longer argue about which is better.

units: the power must be cut before anything is handled
this precaution is presented as one that cannot be undone
a working surface has to be laid out beforehand
the tools include a fine screwdriver and a pair of flat pliers
a small container serves to keep the screws
the corner screws come out before those along the edges
the screws differ in length and their positions must be noted
a flexible ribbon joins the cover to the electronic board
a charging light that stays dark accuses the socket more often than the battery
text: Kill the power and pull the charger out before you touch anything: that is the one step you cannot undo. Then get your corner of the table ready. You want a fine screwdriver, a pair of flat pliers, a dry cloth and a small dish for the screws, or they roll off and you end up on your knees. Start at the back of the machine. Take the corner screws out first, then the ones along the edges, and note where each came from, because they are not all the same length. Lift the cover gently, never with a jerk, since a soft ribbon usually joins it to the board. Now look at the charging light: if it stays dark, the fault sits in the socket far more often than in the battery. Clean, put it back together, do the screws up without forcing, plug in, and watch the screen before you tidy up.

units: a fault in the sound at a station is reported before sunrise
the departure board then went out altogether
maintenance staff reach the plant room shortly afterwards
a backup power unit had shut itself down for protection
its red lamp stayed lit without blinking
a stalled fan had let the cabinet heat past the limit
the staff changed the fan and cleaned the filters
the board was brought back platform by platform
management now requires the cabinets to be checked every quarter
some travellers missed a change of train for want of information
text: The call came in shortly before dawn: a crackle in the loudspeakers of a station, and then the departure board going dark from end to end. A maintenance team reached the plant room half an hour later. They found first that a backup supply had shut itself down, its red lamp steady rather than blinking. By midday the cause was plain: a stalled fan had let the cabinet climb past the temperature at which everything cuts out. The team fitted a replacement fan, cleared the filters and brought the power back in the early afternoon. The board returned platform by platform, in the reverse order of its going out. Management announced that same evening that the cabinets would be inspected every quarter instead of once a year. No train ran late, but travellers missed connections for want of an announcement.

units: an adjustable light is aimed at the working surface
printed boards are stacked up waiting to be mended
a pencil mark shows the burnt patch on each board
the soldering tool rests in its cradle and still gives off smoke
the smell of resin has soaked into the walls of the room
the craftsman has done this work since the shop opened
runs of melted metal have marked the floor
the seat has left four pale round marks
the lack of a window calls for constant air extraction
the noise stopping signals a break in the power supply
text: On the mender's bench, a jointed lamp leans down over an orderly sort of mess. Green boards are waiting in a stack, each one carrying a pencil stroke where the circuit has darkened and blistered. To the right, the iron rests in its cradle, and its thin tip is still smoking with the smell of warm resin. That smell has soaked deep into the walls, for the man has been soldering here since the day the shop first opened. The floor carries the trade as well: drops of solder have melted into the covering, and the stool has worn four pale rings. Since the room has no window at all, an extractor turns above the door without pause, and its drone ends up passing for silence. When it stops, the man lifts his head, because that hole in the sound means the power has gone and the joint will be spoilt.

units: putting something right often costs more than buying it new
the writer blames this imbalance on the way products are designed
a battery held on with adhesive makes the taking apart harder
screws with an unusual head call for tools kept for them alone
a soldered link instead of a plug lengthens the job
the makers justify these choices by water resistance
a compressed seal and ordinary screws would hold just as well
the writer proposes that the board drawings be published
he asks that parts be sold at what the component costs
the obstacle is commercial and not technical
text: Mending ought to cost less than replacing, and it hardly ever does. The fault lies not with the labour but with the way the things are drawn up. A battery stuck to the frame with adhesive, screws cut to a head nobody else uses, a ribbon soldered where a plug would do: each choice adds half an hour to the job and turns a cell swap into a full strip-down. The reason offered is water resistance; yet a compressed seal and ordinary screws hold water out just as well, at a cost close to nothing. Three measures would be enough: settle on common screws, publish the board drawings, and sell spare parts at what the parts themselves cost. None of them demands a technical leap; all of them run into a trade that lives on replacement. While a sealed device costs less to build than one that opens, the bench will go on unscrewing sealed cases.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the central figure works as a repairer of technical objects
she begins by examining the energy stores
she can tell in advance which energy stores will run too hot
she is also drawn to very small drive motors
she opens waterproof casings while sparing the sealing ring
her workroom is cramped and poorly lit
she keeps her screws sorted by size
she welcomes and informs curious passers-by
she refuses to get rid of an object she has not inspected
she machines the parts that cannot be found anywhere
text: You could pass her in the street and never guess what she mends behind that door. Mending broken gadgets is her trade, and the batteries are what she reaches for first: she prises them open, coaxes them patiently back to life, and can tell from the swell of a cell which ones will run hot once they are wired in. Tiny drive motors come next, the kind you have to unpick with fine tweezers to free a bent spindle. Then the casings, above all the sealed ones, which she eases apart without nicking the rubber ring. The workshop is a single cramped room, dim beyond the reach of her lamp, with a bench and drawers of screws graded by size. She is glad to talk shop with anyone who wanders in, and she will not bin a device she has not yet opened. When a part cannot be found, she cuts it herself, filing metal half the evening.

units: the maker claimed a week of use away from the mains
unpacking gives a flattering first impression
the device is described as very light
the display stays readable under harsh light
no noise comes out of the machine during demanding tasks
after long use the shell warms near the hinge
endurance collapses once the wireless link is switched on
a software fix has not removed the lag in typing
the reviewer finds the price excessive for what is delivered
text: The makers promised a portable reader that would hold out a whole week away from the mains. Out of its box the thing does charm you: a matt shell, a hinge that holds firm under the thumb, a weight that barely registers in the hand. Early sessions bear that out. The screen stays readable in glaring light, and the machine keeps quiet even while it grinds through a heavy file. A week on, the shine wears off. The shell warms near the hinge after a long stretch of work, it takes fingerprints, and the endurance we were promised melts away the moment the wireless link goes on. An update has since tidied up part of this, though the keyboard still trails behind the fingers. The verdict, then: a pleasant enough device, roughly finished, asking a great deal more than it hands back. Better to wait and see what the next generation brings.

units: the writer is writing from his workroom
an old sound receiving set stands beside him
the addressee had predicted that the device was beyond saving
a damaged electrical lead cut the sound at the slightest knock
the writer mended the joint by soldering it again
damp had made the wooden case swell
the top would no longer sit in its housing
sanding restored the sliding of the lid
the device now keeps the writer company in the evenings
the writer invites his correspondent to come and see the result
text: I am writing to you from the workshop, the window open on the yard, with the old wireless set sitting at my elbow. You told me it was past saving, and you were nearly right: the lead inside had frayed, so the sound dropped out whenever anyone knocked the bench. I stripped the wire back, soldered the two strands together again, and the crackling stopped there and then. Damp had got into the cabinet as well; the wood had swollen, and the lid would no longer sit down in its grooves. I sanded it down, patiently, until it slid home again the way it always used to. Now the voices fill the room once darkness comes, and I drift off to them without ever reaching for the volume. You see, it took almost nothing in the end. Do come over when you can and hear for yourself how it sings, now that it breathes freely again.

units: the readings of a heat probe become inaccurate
the sensing element is generally not to blame
a deposit of particles on the wall disturbs the conduction of heat
replacing the whole unit is not necessary
cleaning followed by setting against two fixed marks is enough
checking means comparing the values with those of a control instrument
a steady offset can be made up for by the software
an erratic swing reveals a loss of sealing in the casing
the sealing ring must be renewed before readings resume
text: What is going on when a temperature probe stops giving trustworthy readings? The drift seldom starts in the sensing element itself. It comes from dust settling on the membrane, which spoils the flow of heat across it. Does that mean the whole module has to be thrown out? In most cases, no: clean the membrane, then set the instrument against two steady reference points, and the numbers fall into line again. How do you know the work has taken? Stand the probe beside a checking instrument and watch the pair of them over a long stretch. A gap that holds steady is a leftover offset, and software will take care of that. And when the gap wanders about with no pattern to it? The casing has almost certainly lost its seal, letting moisture in among the contacts. Fit a fresh ring before you begin another round of readings.

units: a technical manager questions a skilled worker about the choice of a machine
two devices are weighed against each other
the older device runs without any electrical supply
it is set going by a foot control
the newer device is markedly faster
the newer device stops by itself when something jams
the newer device calls for regular servicing
the older one is mended with rudimentary tools
the two speakers decide to keep both machines
a fresh look at the choice is planned after a season of use
text: The engineer asked the fitter which of the two machines he would sooner see kept on the shop floor. He came down on the older one: mechanical through and through, driven by a foot treadle, and needing no electrical supply at all. She countered that the newer machine works far faster and that it halts of its own accord the instant a piece jams. He granted her the point readily enough, then reminded her that the newer machine has to be serviced to a schedule, whereas the old one comes right again with a spanner and a little patience. Her suggestion was to hold on to the pair of them and bring the powered model in only for the long runs. He agreed, so long as the team learn to handle the older one first. They settled on looking at the whole question afresh once a full season of work in the shop had gone by.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: keeping sounds meant finding a way to inscribe them
the first method cut a groove by means of a vibrating point
that method made it possible to bring a voice back later
the second method rested on magnetising a ribbon coated with grains
magnetising allowed the content to be wiped and written again
the third method turned the signal into a run of separate values
each method changed practices as much as it changed devices
recordings became in turn portable, copyable without loss, then free of any carrier
this change is presented as a series of trade-offs between quality, sturdiness and ease of copying
text: Before sound could travel anywhere, somebody had to work out how to hold it still. The first answer was mechanical: a needle hung from a membrane cut a groove into soft material, and a voice could be carved there and played back afterwards. The second answer was magnetic. A ribbon coated in fine grains held the direction of a field, so what had been laid down could be wiped and written over. The third answer was numerical: the flowing signal was chopped into separate values, stored, then put together again on playback. Every one of these steps altered habits quite as much as it altered the hardware. Recordings could be carried about, then copied with nothing lost, then passed on with no carrier at all. The whole story reads as a long run of bargains struck between fidelity, toughness and ease of copying.

units: sending a message sets off its cutting into very short pieces
each piece carries a marking of the arrival address
the pieces travel first through the air to the nearest relay
obstacles of building are not enough to stop reception by that relay
the pieces carry on through wired links buried or laid under water
their route changes at every node according to crowding
the device at the far end puts the pieces back in the right order
the whole journey takes an extremely short time
a lost piece is asked for again automatically without the user noticing
text: Think for a moment about what happens as soon as you tap send. Your handset chops the message into tiny pieces first, and tags every one of them with a label saying where it has to end up. Off they go through the air to the nearest mast, which manages to pick your handset up even through the walls around you. From there they run along cables, most of them buried under the ground or laid across the seabed, and at every junction they take whichever route is least crowded. They land at last on the handset at the far end, which sorts them back into order and rebuilds your sentence. All of that takes less time than the blink of an eye, however far it has to go. And if a piece goes astray on the way, nothing is lost: your handset asks for it again straight away, and you never notice a thing.

units: the night team took no notice of the stopping of a cabinet fan
the coolness of the room put them off acting at once
the heat probe had been moved the day before because of cabling work
it was reading the temperature of a nearby passage instead of the trapped hot air
no alarm went off despite the building heat
two storage units gave out at the end of the night
the incident cut the electronic mail service for a very wide public
the inquiry puts the failure down to the unrecorded moving of the probe
a written procedure now governs any change of place of a probe
text: It began with a detail the night shift had shrugged off at first: the fan in one of the computer cabinets had gone quiet. The room itself felt cool enough, so nobody saw any reason to act before morning came. The trouble was that the heat probe had been shifted the day before to make room for cabling work, and it was now sampling the air of the corridor next door rather than the still air trapped behind the machines. Warmth built up behind them steadily, and not one alarm sounded. Towards dawn two drives gave out, and with them went the mail service for many thousands of users. The internal report puts the blame not on the hardware but on a probe that had been moved without anyone writing it down. Since then, shifting a sensor calls for a written note and a check carried out the following day.

units: a hand-cranked torch stops working when its generator seizes
it is advised to lay the object on a pale cloth
this precaution keeps the screws from going astray
the four fasteners in the base come out before the two half-shells are parted
the parting must be done gently to spare the catches
the coil turns out to be fouled by a greasy deposit
cleaning is done dry before the shaft bearing is oiled
a lasting squeak comes from the return spring, which has to be tightened again
putting it back together means not driving the screws fully home at once
the light comes back little by little after long turning of the handle
text: The torch you wind by hand tends to end up at the back of a drawer, silent, because the little generator inside it has seized. Here is how to bring it back to life. Lay it down on a pale cloth, so that no screw can slip away unseen. Take out the four screws in the base, then ease the two halves apart slowly, without straining the catches. Inside you will come upon a grey coil, matted with greasy dust that clogs the windings. Brush it clean while everything is still dry, work the shaft free, and put one drop of thin oil on the bearing. If the handle still squeaks, the fault lies in the return spring: unhook it and tighten it up. Close the shells up, start the screws without driving them home, and wind the handle for a good long while. The beam will come back to you, feeble at first, and then steady.

units: those in charge of a water supply have assessed two monitoring systems
both systems are fitted to comparable pipes
the first uses pressure sensors drawn off the main electrical supply
these sensors report through a shielded wired link
the first gives very frequent readings and flags a loss of water quickly
the second rests on standalone sensors closed inside a watertight case
the second sends its data by radio with very low power draw
the second is less precise but spares any digging work
the study recommends the cabled one on sensitive stretches and the standalone one on distant branches
both systems depend on a hydraulic model updated by staff
text: The people who run a water network have just finished weighing up two monitoring rigs fitted to a matching pair of mains. The first works from pressure sensors drawn off the electrical supply and wired back to a central controller through shielded cable; it reports at very short intervals and flags a leak well before the next round of readings. The second uses standalone probes sealed into a watertight case, sending what they gather by radio on very little power. Its resolution is coarser, but putting it in calls for no digging at all. The study comes down in favour of the cabled rig on the stretches that matter most, where a leak runs up a heavy bill. Standalone probes suit the outlying branches rather better. Both share one weakness: they lean on a hydraulic model that staff must update by hand.

units: the object described is a listening accessory set down on a piece of furniture
a coloured signal moves across the surface before the charge ends
a short sound announces that the cell is full
the shell carries marks of use along its edges
the hinged joint bends without breaking
the lead stows away in a side compartment
an opening lets the heat out towards the back
the stand can be tilted a step at a time
the whole thing folds down enough to lie at the bottom of a bag
text: Set the earpiece down on the sideboard and watch what follows. The shell warms a little, then a thin blue band creeps across the top, and at last a short chime says the rechargeable cell has taken all it can hold. Pick the case up: it sits in the palm, scuffed along the edges, its soft hinge folding over and over without ever splitting. The lead coils into a pocket in the side, out of the way. Later, once the shell has grown warm, a slotted vent pushes the hot air out at the back. The adjustable stand lifts a notch, then another, until the angle suits you at last. When the session ends, everything closes up again: the folding base slips into its sleeve, the cord follows, and the whole thing goes flat enough to lie at the bottom of a bag. Nothing bulky, nothing brittle, nothing to unscrew.

units: the text asks why electronic equipment wears out so early
a glued assembly stops any single part being replaced on its own
repair workshops see this happening
whole objects are thrown away when one joint alone has failed
makers cut short the period of software support
sound equipment becomes unusable for want of a patch
the buyer carries a double cost
local repairers lose their trade
the writer calls for an assembly that comes apart and drawings anyone can obtain
the writer asks that the cell can be changed on its own
text: Why do our machines wear out so early? Begin with the glue. Once a casing is bonded instead of screwed, no single failed part can be lifted out and replaced on its own. Anyone standing at a repair bench sees it week after week: whole objects carried off to the tip when one joint alone had let go. A second cause makes the first worse. Makers cut short the years of software support, so a sound piece of kit turns useless for want of a patch. The cost falls twice on the buyer, who pays for two machines where one would have served, and the workshop round the corner loses the trade that kept it alive. None of this is settled. Screws rather than adhesive, drawings anyone can obtain, and a rechargeable cell that comes out on its own would hand the repairer back what the glue took away.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the main figure is named by her trade as a repairer
the smell of molten metal stays on her hands after closing time
she started out with old dusty sound receivers
those sets came from a woman living nearby
at first she could not tell which part had failed
she swapped parts at random and spent her money on them
she took up the habit of writing every fault down
her notebook records the symptom and the part to blame
she now recognises recurring families of faults
she repairs almost without ever taking money
text: Her hands hold the smell of molten metal long after the shutters come down. The repairer began on dusty old wireless sets, passed on by a woman who lived along the road, which she opened without a drawing and closed without much faith. Her trouble sat in one sentence: she could not tell which part had given up, so she swapped one for another on a guess and watched her savings go with them. The way out came from a notebook. In it she writes every fault down, the sign it gave, the part to blame, the reading she took. The book has grown thick, stained, soft at the corners from handling. She reads whole families of faults in it now, and guesses before the shell is even open. Neighbours bring her dead lamps and wired keyboards. She gives them back alive, one by one, and mostly refuses to be paid.

units: two soldering devices are compared
one reaches the wanted heat far sooner than the other
that gap weighs on the pace of the workshop
the slower device offers a fine setting of the heat
the quick device gives only a few fixed positions
the heavy base of one holds better
the other shifts as soon as its lead is pulled
the softened lead on one of them soaks up knocks
the other lead stiffens in the cold
one of the two demands costly branded tips
text: Two soldering stations share one bench, and the verdict rests on gaps you can measure. The first brings its tip up to the set temperature almost at once; the second dawdles, and that delay drags on everything the workshop gets through in a day. The slow one, mind you, lets the heat be dialled to the degree, where the quick one offers three fixed positions and nothing in between. One sits on a heavy base, awkward but steady; the other slides the moment its lead is tugged. That lead tells too: supple sheathing on the first soaks up every knock, while the second stiffens in a cold room and passes each jolt straight to the point. One takes ordinary spare tips, the other insists on a costly make of its own. For a repair bench the slow and heavy machine wins in the end, waiting and all.

units: the writer is addressing the manager of a workshop
the message concerns equipment lent to a group
the embroidery machine now takes the designs the club sends over
its arm sags against thick cloth
the jointed support of the lamp no longer holds its height
the tablet works only once it is plugged into the mains
its cell no longer lasts a whole session
the trolley unit blocks the way through the room
two typing peripherals are missing from the store cupboard
the writer asks that these remarks be passed on to the technical service
text: Dear workshop manager, I am writing about the equipment lent to the assisted sewing group. First, the embroidery machine now takes the designs the club sends over, though its arm sags as soon as the cloth is at all thick. Second, the jointed lamp gives good light, but its adjustable neck will no longer stay in the high position. Third, the tablet lent to the learners remains usable provided it is left plugged in: its rechargeable cell no longer lasts half a session. Fourth, the trolley unit is too bulky for the room and blocks the way through. Lastly, two wired keyboards have gone from the dusty cupboard at the back. I should be grateful if you would pass these remarks on to the technical service, and I remain available for any checking you may wish to have carried out.

units: a visitor asks a workshop how an electronic board is made
the layout is drawn on screen first
the pattern is carried onto a metal-coated board by exposure to light
the unwanted metal is taken off in a chemical bath
a guided rotary tool drills the ways meant for the connections
a solder paste is laid down before the parts are set in place
the whole thing is taken up to a high heat to fix the joints
a camera looks over every board for a flaw
this check comes before the final assembly
text: A visitor to the workshop asks first how a printed board comes into being. The answer follows the order of the work. At the outset a layout is drawn on screen, then carried onto a metal-coated plate by exposure to light. The visitor asks next what becomes of the metal nobody wants. It is eaten away in a chemical bath, and the plate comes out with its tracks clean and fine. Then comes the drilling: a guided cutter opens the ways where the pins will sit. Is the plate ready to use, the visitor wonders. Not yet, because solder paste must be laid down, the parts set down in place, and the whole thing taken up to a heat that fixes every joint. A last question turns on the way the work is checked. Each board passes under a camera that catches the faulty track before the final assembly.

units: a man from the floor above complains about how long his drilling tool lasts
his neighbour puts the fault down to the way the tool is charged
the power pack was left sitting on its charger all the time
the casing of the pack had swollen out of shape
a measuring device was used to test the cells one by one
two cells no longer gave any current
that explains the loss of force while drilling
he is advised to store the pack half charged and somewhere cool
he must take it off the charger as soon as the green light shows
text: The man from the flat upstairs came down with his drill under his arm, saying the battery would hold nothing at all any more. My sister told him the tool was not to blame, and that it came of his habit of leaving the rechargeable pack sitting on its hot base day and night. He argued for a while, then owned up that the casing had swollen out of shape. So she fetched a wired meter out of the dusty drawer and tested each cell on its own, one after the other. Two of them gave nothing back at all, which explained why the drill lost its bite the moment the bit met the wood. Keep the pack half charged, she told him, somewhere cool, and take it off the charger as soon as the green light shows. He went back upstairs pleased, with a drill that ran again and a fresh bit into the bargain.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the first mechanical looms ran into the same blockage over and over
changing the pattern meant taking the mechanism apart
the threads had to be set back one by one
work stopped for several weeks
customers turned to the weavers who worked by hand
the answer was to hold the pattern outside the machine
a craftsman thought of a run of pierced boards laced together
whether a hole was there or not decided if the thread rose
altering the design came down to changing the band
calculating devices took the same principle up later
text: In the earliest mechanised weaving sheds one obstacle came round again and again. Changing the design meant taking the mechanism apart and setting every thread back in its place one at a time, and the work stood still for whole weeks together. Orders drifted off to the weavers who still worked by hand, slower but far more biddable. The answer came from outside the trade altogether: hold the pattern in something that sits apart from the machine. A craftsman thought of small pierced boards, laced into a supple band that the loom read as it went by. Where a needle met a hole, the thread rose; elsewhere it stayed where it lay. Altering the design now came down to changing the band. The idea soon outgrew cloth, and the calculating machines that followed still work on that same split.

units: the aerial is likened to a string that trembles as a wave goes past
the aerial makes no energy of its own
the loudspeaker runs the other way round
a current sets the cone of the loudspeaker moving
that movement shakes the air around it
in one case the energy arrives from outside and turns electrical
in the other it leaves the wire and turns into sound
neither device bears a harsh setting well
a magnetised mass of metal bends the signal
text: An aerial is less like an ear than like a taut string stretched over an invisible river. The string makes nothing of its own: it trembles while a wave goes past, and it falls quiet once the wave has moved off. A loudspeaker runs the other way round. Send a current into it, its soft cone stirs, and the air about it begins to shake. One listens, the other speaks, and both live off the same family of movements. The difference lies in which way the exchange runs. In the aerial the energy arrives from outside and turns into a faint current; in the loudspeaker it leaves the wire and turns into something you can hear. One more thing draws them together: neither bears a harsh setting. A rigid mount kills the movement, a magnetised mass bends the signal, and ear and mouth alike go deaf.

units: a failure comes up at night on a backup server
the team goes through three areas in turn
the power supply shows an odd swing in voltage
a worn capacitor lies behind that fault
a fan no longer turns evenly
its clogged bearing lets the temperature pass the allowed limit
two storage units carry areas that cannot be read
no warning had been raised about those areas
the parts at fault are replaced and the data rebuilt
the lesson drawn is that a silent fault costs more
text: The fault broke out in the middle of a maintenance night, on a backup server the team had taken for indestructible. Three lines of enquiry were worked through in order. On the power side, the reading showed an odd ripple on the main rail, the mark of a worn and swollen capacitor. On cooling, a failing fan turned in fits and starts, and its clogged bearing let the board run well beyond the temperature allowed. On storage, two drives carried sectors that could no longer be read, and no warning about them had ever come through. The repair followed the same list: capacitor renewed, fan swapped for one with a smoother bearing, drives rebuilt onto the array. The team came away from that night with a lesson that has stuck. A fault that says nothing costs far more than one that makes a noise.

units: prolonged stillness in a seated position loads the spine
the deep back muscles stiffen for want of movement
the pain is intermittent at first and later lasting
carers see this trouble appearing in ever younger adults
the trouble also affects people who have never lifted heavy loads
the cause lies in a slumped back rather than an injury
straightening up and moving often releases muscular tension
adjusting the seat height keeps the thighs parallel with the floor
the discomfort fades within a season in those who follow these measures
text: Sitting still for hours loads the spine far more heavily than most people suspect. Starved of movement, the deep muscles along the back gradually harden and tug at the lower vertebrae. A dull ache sets in, coming and going at first, then settling for good. Carers report the complaint in adults who are younger and younger, including plenty who have never lifted anything heavy in their lives. The cause is rarely an injury. It lies in a slumped back, shoulders rolled forward, pelvis tipped backwards. Putting that right costs almost nothing. Straightening up, walking about, stretching the muscles down the back of the legs already loosens what has built up. Raising or lowering the seat so the thighs stay parallel with the floor finishes the job. Those who keep to this see the discomfort fade within a season.

units: the main character breaks her ankle a second time as an adult
in childhood she had worn a splint without suffering morally
as a child she went on running and laughed at her uneven walk
the adult fall happens on a slippery step
as an adult she finds her walking aid heavy and trips about the house exhausting
she understands that inaction wears her out more than activity
what made her laugh as a child mortifies her as an adult
a fine mark stays on her skin once the bone has knitted
she takes up walking again by controlling every step
text: The second break was nothing like the first, and that was what caught her off guard. As a girl she had worn a light splint for a whole season without losing an ounce of her spirit; she half-ran, she hopped along corridors, she laughed at her lopsided walk. As a grown woman the same joint gave way on a wet step, and the whole business took on another colour altogether. The crutch felt heavy, the stairs hostile, the walk through to the kitchen endless. Idleness, she found, wears a body out faster than effort ever did. What had once amused her now shamed her, not out of vanity, but because she could measure what she had stopped taking for granted. When the bone knitted, a thin scar marked the skin, a quiet keepsake of an ordinary fall. She learned to walk again, watching where every step landed.

units: the first aid kit divides into three compartments
the first compartment brings together the material that covers a wound
the dressings must be sterile and wrapped separately
the second compartment gathers the products spread onto the skin
a soothing ointment is provided for light burns
a gel treats the bites that bring on an itch
the third compartment holds what immobilises or supports a limb
the expiry dates must be checked at every change of season
the container must be rigid and kept away from heat
text: A first aid kit worth its name falls into three clearly separate compartments. The first holds whatever is needed to cover a wound: sterile dressings sealed in individual wrappers, sticking plasters in a range of widths, a roll of fixing tape and a pair of round-tipped scissors. The second gathers everything that goes onto the skin itself: an alcohol-free antiseptic solution, a soothing ointment for the lighter burns, a gel for the bites that bring on an itch. The third carries the supporting kit: an elastic bandage, a sling for the arm, a soft splint to hold a finger or a wrist still. Check the expiry dates at every change of season and replace whatever has already been opened, without hesitating. Keep the lot in a rigid box, away from any heat and out of reach of children, then write on the lid whatever has run short.

units: a rehabilitation centre was to open in a district that had none
the works reused a disused warehouse and kept its metal frame
the first patients taken in were coming out of major surgery
these patients often moved about with a support or an immobilising device
a heated pool was opened in the cold season that followed
the heated water serves joints that cannot bear weight on the ground
a workshop on holding the back and preventing falls came next
this workshop is aimed at the older people of the area
local representatives judge the capacity insufficient and ask for an extension
text: The news broke as the mild season opened: a rehabilitation centre was to be set up in a working-class district that had never had anything of the kind. Work began without delay inside a disused warehouse whose metal frame was kept exactly as it stood. By autumn the first rooms were taking in patients discharged after major surgery, many of them leaning on a crutch or held together by a splint. The winter that followed brought a heated pool into service, which made it possible to treat joints too painful to bear any weight on the ground. Management then announced a workshop given over to posture and to the prevention of falls, open to the older people of the area. Local representatives now hold that demand outstrips the capacity planned, and are pressing for the building to be extended.

units: the heel reddens and grows slightly warm at first
rubbing against the shoe separates the surface layers of the skin
clear fluid fills the space thus opened and forms a blister
the tension of the pouch changes the way of walking
shifting the weight onto the other foot brings on an ache in the hip
the skin laid bare after bursting risks an infection
the area is covered with a clean dressing and not pierced on purpose
a greasy ointment spread on before walking reduces the rubbing
a final thickening of the skin makes the discomfort disappear
text: The heel turns faintly red to begin with, barely warmer than the skin lying around it. Rubbing against the shoe lifts the topmost layers apart, and a clear fluid seeps into the space that has opened up: the blister has formed. Its stretched roof makes standing on the foot painful and alters the gait, which throws the load onto the other leg and brings on, a little later, a dull ache in the hip. Should the pouch burst, the raw patch underneath turns tender and lies wide open to infection. That is why the place is covered over with a clean dressing rather than opened on purpose. A greasy ointment rubbed well in before a long walk cuts down the friction at the outset. Once the skin finally thickens over that spot, it holds up better and the soreness clears of its own accord.

units: the writer states that lack of sleep is treated as ordinary
drowsiness and short temper are put down to the load of work
sleep deprivation is never held responsible
evening screens push back the hour of going to bed
the stimulating drink the next day delays the following drop into sleep
the writer advises cutting the screens before going into the bedroom
the bedroom must be kept cool and dark
he recommends a steady bedtime, weekend included
the effects are felt after a handful of nights
sleep is presented as a repair that is owed and not as a privilege
text: Let us be honest: we sleep badly, and we have grown far too comfortable with it. The yawn that cuts across a meeting, the eyelids sagging halfway through the afternoon, the temper that sours over nothing, all of it gets blamed on the load of work, never on the nights we keep cutting short. Come evening, the screen wins: one clip, then another, and bed comes long after the hour we set ourselves. The morning after, we make up for it with coffee, which pushes the next drop into sleep later still. Getting out of that spiral is no mystery. Switch the screens off before going through to the bedroom, keep the room cool and dark, turn in at the same hour even at the weekend. It sounds bleak, yet the difference shows after a handful of nights. Sleep is no treat we grant ourselves; it is a repair we owe.

units: the physiotherapist receives her patients on her feet, with no desk between them
she started out on a hospital ward with injured sportspeople
there she treated sprains, tears and painful muscle contractions
the sessions there were short and the results measurable
she now practises with elderly patients in a residential district
her aim is no longer to bring a joint back to top-level sport
she teaches people to get up unaided and to climb stairs without fear
she works on standing stability in order to avoid falls
she says she likes this slower rhythm
her patients are looking for a confidence built up session after session
text: She greets her patients on her feet, at the door of her practice, with no desk standing between them. The physiotherapist began her career on a hospital ward given over mostly to injured sportspeople: sprains, torn muscles, the stubborn cramp that follows a badly prepared effort. The pace was quick there, the sessions short, the outcome easy to measure. She now works in a quiet residential district with elderly patients, and the job has changed in kind. Her aim is no longer to bring a knee back to top-level sport, but to teach someone to get up unaided, to climb stairs without dread, to hold a standing posture steady enough to keep them from falling. She says she prefers this slower rhythm. Where the athlete wanted a deadline, her patients want confidence, and confidence is built session after session.

units: the reviewer praises three aspects of the work and disputes only one
the first quality is the clarity with which the actions are described
each handling is broken into elementary movements with no obscure vocabulary
the second quality is the restraint of the writing
the author points out the limits of care given at home
the author says when a doctor's opinion becomes indispensable
the third success lies in the hand-drawn illustrations
the reviewer finds these drawings warmer than medical photographs
the passage on aching muscles is dealt with too briefly
the reader closes the book pleased but a little disappointed
text: This handbook of home care earns praise on three counts and a reservation on one. Its first strength is the clarity of the actions it sets out: laying on a dressing, changing a pad, spotting a wound that has turned septic. Each operation is taken apart into its simplest movements, with no needless jargon. Its second virtue is restraint. The author never tires of marking the limits of care given at home, and the moment when a doctor's opinion becomes compulsory. Its third success is a matter of looks: the hand-drawn plates lend the volume a warmth that clinical photography never reaches. Then comes the reservation. The chapter on aching muscles disposes of stiffness and cramp in a single page, as though complaints that common deserved no proper study. One closes the book pleased, and a little let down.

units: the sender relates what followed his operation at the request of the addressee
the operation took place under a local anaesthetic at the end of last week
the surgeon removed a piece of bone that was blocking the joint
the dressing was renewed the next day by a nurse
a rigid device has to be kept on until the check-up appointment
the pain went away in the course of the following week
an itch around the stitches signals healing according to the care team
a neutral ointment has to be spread on without rubbing
the sender now puts his foot to the ground with a single support
rehabilitation will begin once the stitches are out
text: I am writing to tell you how the operation turned out, since it was you who asked for the details. It was done at the end of last week under a local anaesthetic; the surgeon took out the fragment of bone that had been jamming up the joint. The following day a nurse changed the dressing and fitted a rigid splint, which I have to keep on right up until my check-up. Over the week that came after, the pain gave way, though an itch came up around the stitches, the usual sign of healing, so the care team tell me. They have put me on a neutral ointment, to be spread on without rubbing. Since the day before yesterday I have been putting the foot to the ground with a single crutch, and I take the stairs leading with the sound leg. Rehabilitation starts as soon as the stitches come out.

units: the night contraction hits a muscle already worked during the evening
a shortage of water and mineral salts locks the muscle fibres
the episode is harmless in most cases
the attack fades in very little time
stretching the muscle by drawing the toes back stops the signal
a warm compress laid on afterwards relaxes the fibre
this heat limits the muscle soreness of the next day
drinking enough in the evening and avoiding late effort prevent a return
certain medicines that make the body shed water must be watched
frequent attacks that break up sleep justify seeking advice
text: What sets off a cramp in the night? The muscle seizes when, already worked hard through the evening, it runs short of water and mineral salts; the fibres lock and refuse to let go. Is it a sign of illness? In most cases, no: the cause stays humdrum and the episode fades within moments. What should be done during the attack? Stretching the affected muscle gently, drawing the toes back towards you, breaks the signal that keeps the contraction going. A warm compress laid on afterwards eases the fibre and takes the edge off the soreness felt the next day. Can it be kept from coming back? Drink enough in the evening, avoid hard effort late on, and keep an eye on medicines that make the body shed water. When is advice needed? If attacks cut through sleep night after night, an examination is called for.

units: a rehabilitation specialist describes two opposite attitudes among the people she treats
the first attitude consists in locking the injured joint and never using it again
the second attitude consists in wanting to pull on the muscle from the very first appointment
the specialist judges that neither of these ways of behaving is right
the absence of movement ends up weakening the joint and hardening the muscle attachments
an effort that is too violent prolongs the irritation of the tissues
a colleague points out that the same uncertainty shows up with injuries to the hand
the two practitioners recommend moderate and frequent movements, stopped in case of strong pain
they recall that recovery is judged over several weeks and not over a single appointment
text: A physiotherapist says her patients turn up believing one of two contrary things about healing. Some want a sore ankle strapped into a rigid splint and left well alone until it settles of its own accord. Others ask to be stretched at the very first session, convinced that soreness is proof they are getting better. Neither approach works, she says. Keep a joint still for too long and it grows weak while the tendons stiffen; push too hard and the swelling simply carries on. A colleague of hers adds that the same muddle crops up among people who have hurt a wrist. What helps, the two of them argue, is small movements done often, and stopped the moment the pain turns sharp. They end on the point their patients tend to skip: recovery is measured over whole weeks, never over a single appointment.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the healers of former times relied on an oral inheritance for want of reliable devices
this know-how was limited to a small number of practices
plant drinks were used against fever and against irritation of the throat
fragrant ointments were applied to the swollen areas
warm poultices were laid on at bedtime and taken off on rising
the drawing of blood was both dreaded and demanded
the healer's speech weighed as much as his preparations
the act of giving the illness a name already brought relief
science has kept few of these treatments but has drawn from them a lesson about waiting and trust
text: Long before healers had instruments they could trust, they leaned on what had been handed down by word of mouth alone, and that inheritance amounted to no more than a small handful of remedies. First came the brewed drinks: a bitter one to bring down a fever, a sweetened one to soothe a throat rubbed raw. Then the ointments, spread thickly over swollen skin, whose sharp smell was half the cure. Warm poultices followed, laid on at bedtime and lifted away at first light. Bleeding stood apart from the rest, dreaded and demanded by turns. And the healer's own voice counted for as much as anything he mixed: he gave the illness a name, and the naming of it already brought ease. From that tangled legacy medicine has kept very few treatments, though it did draw from it a lasting lesson about waiting and about trust.

units: the medicine in the form of a shell first goes down the passage leading to the stomach
contractions of the muscles carry out this descent
the acidity of the stomach dissolves the shell and releases its contents
the folded wall of the fine bowel takes up the active matter
the blood then carries the matter towards the organ that transforms it
this transformation lowers the strength of the remedy
the remaining part attaches to precise targets in the tissues concerned
the action rises to a peak then decreases as elimination goes on
a liquid preparation acts sooner because its active matter is already in solution
text: A swallowed capsule passes through several stages before it can do anything at all. It travels down the gullet, driven along by steady waves of muscle. In the stomach the acid juices break the shell open and release the powder held inside. From there the contents reach the small bowel, whose deeply folded lining offers an enormous surface for taking things up. The drug crosses into the blood, which carries it onwards to the liver; that organ alters part of the molecule and weakens its effect. Whatever survives travels on to the tissues it was meant for, and locks onto particular receptors there. The effect builds, peaks, then fades as the kidneys and the liver clear the substance away. A syrup takes much the same route, but starts working sooner, since the drug held in it is already dissolved.

units: a player of a stringed instrument sought advice for headaches that cut his playing sessions short
no disorder was found on the side of the eyes or the ears
the practitioner spotted a clenching of the jaws during difficult passages
this repeated clenching exhausted the muscles lying between the skull and the neck
the tension spread towards the sides of the forehead and brought on the pain
the fear of the attacks increased the contraction and kept the trouble going
the practitioner taught the musician a short release between two pieces played
she added to it an exercise of deep breathing
the headaches became rarer after one season
the musician put his trouble down to the fear of failure rather than to his instrument
text: A violinist went to see a practitioner because headaches were cutting his practice short. Nothing was wrong with his eyes, and nothing was wrong with his hearing. What she did notice was that he clenched his jaw the moment a difficult passage came up. Repeated over whole sessions at a stretch, that clenching wore out the muscles running from the skull down into the neck, and the strain then spread up to the temples, where the pain began. Because he dreaded the attacks, he tightened all the more, and so the trouble kept feeding itself. She taught him a brief release to use between one piece and the next, along with an exercise in slow and deep breathing. Within a single season the headaches had grown rare. The musician concluded that his instrument mattered less than his own fear of failing on it.

units: an unpleasant mouth smell on waking rarely comes from the stomach
it is caused above all by micro-organisms that multiply on the tongue and near the gums during sleep
the method proposed involves five actions that can be carried out without costly equipment
the teeth must be cleaned on waking and before sleeping, turning the brush towards the flesh of the gums
a thread must pass between the teeth because the brush does not reach those gaps
the tongue must be scraped gently to remove the pale film that forms on it
drinking water helps because a dry mouth sharpens the smell whereas saliva cleans
an appointment with the dental practitioner is needed if the trouble carries on
inflamed gums or a damaged tooth can keep the trouble going without being visible
text: Bad breath on waking worries a good many people, though it rarely starts in the stomach. It comes mostly from the bacteria multiplying overnight on the tongue and along the gum line. The remedy amounts to five simple habits, none of which calls for costly equipment. Brush on rising and again at bedtime, angling the bristles towards the gum rather than scrubbing away at the enamel alone. Then run floss between the teeth, since a brush can never reach those narrow gaps. Scrape the surface of the tongue gently, where a pale film gathers. Drink water steadily through the day: a dry mouth sharpens the smell, whereas saliva rinses it away. If the problem carries on despite all this, see a dentist, because inflamed gums or a damaged tooth can keep it going without ever showing themselves.

units: two opposite opinions circulate in a neighbourhood gym
one group defends sessions in a very hot cabin
these enthusiasts claim that their muscles loosen after sweating heavily
the other group prefers immersion in very cold water
the latter maintain that the pain disappears abruptly
the instructor of the place refuses to side with either of the two camps
he explains that heat softens and stirs up the circulation of the blood
he explains that cold numbs and soothes the irritation of the tissues
according to him the two methods suit different moments
he judges that sleeping enough and drinking enough counts for more than these practices
text: In a gym round the corner you can hear two camps going at each other flat out. On one side, the heat people: one session after another in a scorching cabin, and out they come dripping wet, swearing blind that every last muscle has come undone. On the other, the cold lot, who drop themselves into a tub of icy water and reckon the ache switches off all at once. The coach, for his part, just grins and sends the pair of them packing. Heat loosens you up and gets the blood moving, he points out, while cold numbs the part and settles down the swelling; both have their moment, only never the same one. What he mostly notices is that the regulars forget the plain basics: enough sleep and enough water. No cabin on earth, he laughs, makes up for short nights and meals bolted down standing.

units: the care premises are on the floor above a food shop
they comprise two rooms with little furniture
the reception room holds only seats, a plant and worn magazines
the second room is used for consultations and houses a table covered with paper, a weighing device and an instrument for measuring pressure
the boxes of medicines are stored up high and sorted by illness
