the clean equipment is kept in a drawer, each injection instrument in sealed wrapping
the tap of the basin is opened with the arm to limit the passing on of germs
the nurse receives people without an appointment on three half-days a week
she treats wounds, changes dressings and listens to the fears of those who come
the place is very quiet, only the cold storage device makes a noise
text: The surgery takes up two rooms above a grocer's shop, and nothing in it is surplus to need. The waiting area holds a row of chairs, a green plant and a pile of dog-eared magazines, and that is the whole of it. Next door is where people are examined: a narrow couch covered over in paper, an old set of scales, a blood pressure gauge fixed to the wall. Boxes of tablets sit on the topmost shelf, sorted out by complaint. A drawer holds the sterile kit, every syringe still sealed up in its sachet. By the window stands a basin whose tap is worked with the elbow, which keeps germs from travelling about. The nurse who runs the place takes people without appointments on three afternoons a week; she dresses wounds, changes bandages and listens to people's worries. The quiet in there is thick, broken only by the hum of the fridge.

units: night rest was first despised before being reconsidered
it was held at the start to be an empty gap that had to be shortened
active minds believed themselves obliged to sleep less
a later phase valued long waking hours as a mark of courage
exhaustion was then displayed as a distinction
studies carried out at night then showed intense activity in the sleeping brain
this activity includes sorting, the fixing of memories and repair
of late we count our nights and worry about a result judged poor
the writer holds that this counted watching is a mistake
he maintains that rest calls for steadiness, for darkness and for a calm mind
text: Sleep fell out of favour for a long stretch of time before it was taken seriously again, and the journey is worth pausing over for a moment. It was held at first to be an empty gap, a mere parenthesis stolen from a life, which anyone of industrious mind had a plain duty to cut short. Then came the age of the guilty sleeper: staying up late proved your mettle, and exhaustion was worn about like a badge. Later the laboratories were opened at night, and there we found a brain hard at work, sorting, fixing memories in place, mending. Lately the pendulum has swung back the other way: we count our nights, we score them, and we fret over a poor result. That strikes me as a mistake. Rest asks for no heroics and for no supervision; it asks for regular hours, for darkness and for a mind at ease.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the head of a healing plant workshop had not intended this line of work
a lasting allergic reaction, poorly soothed, pushed her to take an interest in the make-up of plant drinks
this interest led her to study plants and then to work in a place of analysis
she observed that the richness of plants changes with the nature of the ground and the moment of picking
she therefore made a check of every batch compulsory before it dries
this rule lowered her rate of production
impatient buyers left her because of these delays
the sellers of medicines trust her and take the greater part of her output
she refuses to announce cures and recalls that a plant drink soothes without treating an infection
her colleagues put the long life of the business down to this restraint
text: The woman who runs the medicinal herb workshop never set out to do this kind of work. A stubborn allergy that ordinary treatments barely touched led her to look closely at what actually went into the herbal drinks she kept being offered. That curiosity took her into the study of plants, and from there into an analysis laboratory. Since she could see that plant strength varies with the soil and with the timing of the harvest, she made a test of every single batch compulsory before drying. The rule slowed her output and drove away buyers in a hurry; in exchange it won her the trust of chemists, who now take the greater part of what she produces. She still refuses to promise cures: a herbal drink soothes, it does not clear an infection. That restraint, her staff say, is why the workshop has lasted so long.

units: a prevention scheme aimed at the staff of a company receives a mixed appraisal
the opening analysis is judged accurate
sitting still in front of a screen hardens the neck and dulls the shoulders
it also brings on pains at the joint of the hand that remedies do not wipe out for long
the solution chosen is a sound signal that cuts off the activity and suggests a short loosening exercise
the first reactions report reduced discomfort at the end of the week
the carrying out is criticised for its lack of flexibility
the signal goes off without taking account of the attention under way
many employees switch the device off after a week
the writer proposes letting each person set their own break times and adopting a discreet visual reminder
text: The prevention scheme offered to the staff at this company deserves a mixed verdict. Its opening analysis is sound enough: fixed postures in front of a screen stiffen the neck, dull the shoulders and bring on a wrist pain that no medicine clears away for long. The answer devised is an audible alert that halts the task in hand and proposes a short stretch. The idea appeals, and the early reports mention less discomfort by the end of the week. The way it has been carried out, though, is rigid: the alert goes off with no regard at all for whatever the person is concentrating on, and a good many employees switch it off altogether after a week. A remedy looks within reach, namely to let each person set their own break times, and to replace the sound with a discreet reminder on the screen.

units: the writer answers a complaint from the reader about poor sleep
the writer has spoken to a nurse at a care centre
the advice falls into three separate groups
the first group concerns what is eaten in the evening
a shortage of iron is presented as a source of lasting tiredness
the second group covers physical activity and stretching
the third group describes the conditions of the bedroom
the nurse advises seeking help if the spells come back
the writer asks for news of whatever has been tried
text: You say your evenings are restless and that sleep keeps slipping away from you. I put the question to a nurse at the centre I go to, and she sorts her advice into three groups. The first is about what goes on the plate at night: no heavy meal close to bedtime, and she reminded me that a shortage of iron keeps a stubborn tiredness going. The second is about moving: a walk each afternoon, a slow stretch of the shoulders once the light goes, nothing strenuous as night draws near. The third is the bedroom itself, which she wants cool, dark and quiet, with no screen left glowing. One remark stayed with me: if the dizziness or the shivering comes back, do not sit it out, go and be seen. Write and tell me what you have tried, and I will say whether it matches what she described.

units: a patient being interviewed describes the stages of her recovery
the first sensation mentioned is a heaviness in the limbs
a state of queasiness then arrives in waves
the first week seemed to her to have no end
the second week went by almost unnoticed
quiet and half-light helped her to improve
a nurse kneaded the back of her neck at the close of the day
a wound on her arm that was slow to heal worried her more than her diagnosis
she advises asking nothing of oneself
text: What comes first? The patient being interviewed describes a dull heaviness, as though her limbs had doubled in weight. And after that? The queasiness arrives, she says, a wave that rises and pulls back without warning. Does that stage last? She hesitates, then answers that the first week seemed to have no end, while the second slipped past almost without trace. What eased it? Quiet, half-light, and the hand of a nurse who came to knead the back of her neck as the day closed. And the nights? Sleep came back in pieces, never whole. Did she fear she would not mend? She admits that a wound on her arm was slow to close, and that this one detail troubled her more than the whole diagnosis. And her advice at the end? Ask nothing of yourself, and take slowness as an ally rather than an enemy.

units: a sports doctor explains a chain of causes to his patient
a muscle that has not been prepared stays cold and short of give
a cold fibre tears more readily under a sudden stretch
the tear brings on inflammation in that spot
the inflammation draws blood in and sets off the pain
the patient wonders about the swelling of his knee
the swelling comes from the same chain of events
cold laid on the area eases the process
using the joint too soon holds up the healing
text: The sports doctor sets out for his patient how one thing leads to the next. Skipping the warm-up, he explains, leaves the muscle fibres cold and short of give. The patient asks what difference that makes in practice. A cold fibre takes a sudden stretch badly, the doctor answers, and tears without much resistance. The tear then brings on inflammation in that spot, he adds, which draws blood towards it and sets off the pain. The patient wonders aloud about the swelling that has come up around his knee. That swelling belongs to the same chain, the doctor tells him, and a cold pack laid on the area will settle it. A muscle properly prepared, he reminds him, takes the jolts without giving way. He ends by warning that healing will drag on if the joint is used too soon, and he advises building the training back up by degrees.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: in former times slight wounds killed patients with no other illness
those who treated them saw fever and discharge without grasping where it began
infection was held at the time to be unavoidable
observers noticed a difference between the wards
the wards where hands went unwashed lost more patients
the measure adopted was the cleaning of hands and instruments
the measure was poorly received at first by those who did the caring
the mortality records ended up convincing them
the rule remains a foundation of care
text: There was a time when slight wounds carried off patients whom nothing else threatened. Those who treated them saw the fever, the shivering, the discharge, without ever tracing where the grim sequence began. The obstacle lay in a belief: infection was held to be unavoidable, almost part of the natural order. Patient observers came at last upon an unsettling regularity, for the wards where hands went unwashed lost more of their patients than the others. The remedy, austere in its plainness, was to clean the hands and the instruments before every procedure. It met sharp resistance, since the demand quietly laid blame on those who did the caring. The mortality records won the argument in the end, and the deaths fell away. That modest rule still stands as one of the pillars of care.

units: two closely related sensations are often mixed up
one gives the illusion that the room is turning
the other feels like an inward giving way with no turning
the first has its origin in the inner ear
the inner ear tells the brain how the head is tilted
the second comes from a brief drop in the blood supply to the brain
with the first it is best to sit down and fix the eyes on something still
with the second one should lie flat and raise the legs
a repeat of these episodes warrants a medical examination
text: Two sensations that lie very close together are constantly mixed up. In the first of them, the room seems to turn around you; in the second, something gives way inside, with no turning at all. The turning kind starts in the inner ear, which tells the brain how the head is tilted. The other comes from a brief drop in the blood supply reaching the brain. What helps is therefore not the same, and anyone who confuses them delays the response that would actually help. When the room turns, sit down, fix your eyes on something still and keep the neck from moving. When everything seems to drain away, lie flat and raise the legs, so that blood is brought back towards the head. A single episode of either sort means little on its own, but one that keeps returning deserves a medical examination.

units: the narrator recounts a stay at a spa centre
the treatments included bubbling baths and clay wraps
a therapist kneaded his back with some force
he describes the other guests he met there
a teenager had been sent there by his lung specialist
the food lacked flavour but was served with solemnity
he slept better than he had done in a very long while
he left lighter and convinced that rest is something you learn
text: Right, let me tell you about my week at the spa centre, because the whole thing was well worth the trip. The treatments first: bubbling baths, clay wraps, and a therapist who kneaded my back until I laughed out of sheer pain. Then the other guests: a former swimmer who talked without drawing breath, a retired woman who knew every corridor, a teenager sent along by his lung specialist and sulking about it. Then the meals: bland, honestly, but served with a gravity that made the blandness feel almost ceremonial. And the nights: I slept as I had not slept in ages, no jolting awake, no knot in the throat. The heavy hush of the corridors must have had a hand in that. I came home lighter, faintly ridiculous in a dressing gown too short for me, and sure that rest is something you learn.

units: the first check concerns the state of the shoes
a worn sole throws the stride off and wears at the knees
a warm-up of wide movements comes before the run
the calves and the thighs are loosened without forcing
the start is made at a pace that still allows talking
the speed goes up only after the first third of the route
the stop must be gradual and followed by walking
a lukewarm shower settles the muscles on returning
a sharp pain in a knee calls for skipping the next session
text: Begin by looking over your shoes: a worn sole throws the stride off balance and wears at the knees. Then give the warm-up a dozen wide movements, enough to lift the heart rate without any jolt. Loosen the calves and the thighs, never forcing a stiff joint. Set off at a steady pace, one you could hold while talking out loud. Pick the speed up only once the first third of the route is behind you. At the end, do not stop dead: keep walking, let the breath come down, drink in small spaced mouthfuls. Tell someone your route if you are heading out alone as the light fades. Once you are home again, a lukewarm shower is enough to settle the muscles. Drink again half an hour after stopping. If a sharp pain shows up in a knee, give the next session a miss and have somebody look at it.

units: there are not enough seats in the waiting room of a clinic
the closure of a nearby surgery has shifted its patients to this place
the wait before an appointment has grown longer
consultations have become shorter
questions left unanswered bring patients back once more
a care assistant says she recognises the same faces far too often
minor troubles worsen for want of steady follow-up
the management announces two more practitioners for the warm season
text: Since the autumn there have not been enough seats in the waiting room of the clinic. The surgery down the road closed, its whole list washed up here, and the effect has spread outwards ever since. Appointments drift further off, so consultations grow shorter; shorter consultations leave questions hanging, so patients come back. A mother who brought her son leaves with one question in three answered. A care assistant speaks of faces she recognises far too often. Without steady follow-up, small troubles worsen in silence: a deficiency left untreated, a wound that will not close, a blood pressure climbing with no warning. The management says two more practitioners will arrive when the warm season comes. Until then the most pressing cases are dealt with first, and everyone senses that the backlog will fall due later.

units: a first aid kit fits into a rigid case held shut by a strap
the main difficulty comes from the muddle and not from the contents
one searches through it at a moment when the hands are shaking
the answer is to split the equipment between labelled compartments
the first compartment holds what is needed to clean a wound
the second gathers dressings bandages and round-tipped scissors
the third houses gloves a survival blanket and a medical notebook
the notebook sets out current treatments and allergies
the case is kept near the front door so that a visitor can find it
text: A well-judged first aid kit fits into a rigid case that is held shut by a strap. The usual trouble is not what goes into it but the muddle inside: you rummage through it just when your hands are shaking. The answer to that is to split the contents up between clearly labelled compartments. The first takes the sterile dressings and the solution for cleaning a wound. The second holds plasters in several sizes, elastic bandages and a pair of round-tipped scissors. The third keeps disposable gloves, a folded survival blanket and a notebook setting out current treatments along with any known allergies. A recent prescription can be slipped in beside it. Kept near the front door of the home, the case stays within easy reach even for a visitor who does not know the place at all.

units: two directions of care are set against one another
the first acts once the illness has declared itself
its effect can be seen without difficulty
the second steps in before the disorder appears
its results stay out of sight since they consist of illnesses avoided
this difference in visibility explains the gap in funding
the writer holds that preventing costs less and spares suffering
the writer asks that both directions be funded equally
text: We are too quick to set the medicine that repairs against the medicine that prevents, as though one had to hand over its resources to the other. The first steps in once the illness has declared itself: it operates, prescribes, relieves, and its effect can be measured without difficulty. The second acts before any disorder appears, and its results stay out of sight, since they consist of illnesses that never happened. That imbalance of visibility explains the imbalance of the budgets. Repair can be seen; prevention cannot. Yet it ought to be granted that prevention costs less and spares whole tracts of suffering, while repair tends to arrive late. Our health institutions should fund both paths with the same steadiness, instead of treating the second as an optional extra.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the main figure first held a junior post in a care establishment
an experienced colleague urged her to train
she studied in the evenings for three years before qualifying
she won the creation of a room set aside for movement by expectant mothers
her managers resisted the request at first
she passed her experience on to carers who came from distant districts
she still runs a training session now that her working life has ended
she holds that listening works as well as a drug treatment
text: The midwife at the valley clinic started out as a care assistant. She stripped beds, wheeled trolleys about and listened to women describe pains that nobody bothered to take seriously. An older nurse kept telling her she ought to train properly. So she took evening classes, and three years later she qualified. Once she joined the ward, she pushed for a room where expectant mothers could walk, breathe and doze between contractions. Her managers dug their heels in, then gave way. Later she taught carers who came from far-off districts, showing them the small handlings that no manual has ever set down. She retired not long ago, yet she still runs a workshop where young staff learn to listen before they reach for a prescription. Patience, she says, eases as much as a well-judged medicine.

units: the most striking feature of the establishment is how quiet it is
an absorbent covering muffles the sound of movement
visitors lower their voices without being asked
the writer holds that noise breeds tiredness
tiredness spoils the mood and works against falling asleep
removing the source of sound breaks that sequence
the writer finds the communal rooms and the cooking dull
after two nights the muscular tension eases
text: What stays with you about this rest centre is not the pale brickwork but the quiet it manufactures. The corridors are wide and lined with a thick felt, and that covering swallows every footstep so thoroughly that the ear finally lets go. The effect catches you out: guests who arrive wound tight begin to speak softly, though nobody has asked them to. The reason behind it is plain, almost mechanical. Noise tires you, tiredness sours the temper, and a soured temper keeps sleep at bay. Take away the first link and the whole chain falls apart. You could fault the communal rooms for their blandness and the kitchen for its timid cooking. Set against the result, such failings weigh very little. Two nights in, the shoulders drop, the jaw unclenches, and you catch yourself dozing in a chair without a shred of guilt.

units: the writer puts the night-time cough down to the state of the bedroom
the air in the room is too dry and is never renewed
dryness irritates the lining and sets off a cough
he advises opening the window before going to bed
he explains that cold air once warmed brings moisture
he recommends turning the heating down
he suggests standing a bowl of water near the source of heat
he proposes drinking enough during the evening
he asks for a nightly note of how the symptom changes
he invites a visit to a doctor if the attempt fails
text: I am writing because that night-time cough is robbing you of sleep, and I suspect the fault lies in your bedroom rather than in your chest. The air in there never moves: the window stays shut, the radiator runs on and on, and the moisture drops below any comfortable level. A dried-out lining grows irritated and answers with a dry cough, which starts up the moment you lie flat. Here is what I would have you try for a week. Open the window a quarter of an hour before bed, even in a hard frost; cold air, once warmed indoors, holds more vapour than stale air does. Then turn the heating down a notch and stand a bowl of water on the sill. Drink enough during the evening, without overdoing it. Note each night whether the cough returns. If nothing shifts after a week, see a doctor. I will come with you.

units: the question asked compares the value of running with that of brisk walking
running places a heavier demand on the heart within a short session
walking calls for a longer session to reach an equivalent result
each running stride drives a load through the joints above the person's own weight
follow-up surveys show that the gentler habit is given up less often
walking or exercise in a pool suits an affected joint better
the writer concludes that running yields more per session and walking more across a year
text: Does the heart need running, or will brisk walking do just as well? It depends on what you are after. Running works the heart muscle harder within a short session, while brisk walking asks for a far longer outing to reach anything comparable. The pounding on the ground, though, is another matter altogether. Every running stride drives a load through the joints well above the walker's own weight, which a gentler pace spares them. A second question follows: which of the two does anyone keep up? Follow-up surveys show that the less demanding habit is given up less often. Then comes the matter of a sore knee, or a hip that sets you limping. Caution leans towards walking, or towards exercise held up by water. The verdict stays balanced: running pays more per session, walking more across a year.

units: the chemist asks the customer when the fever began
the customer reports shivering that came on the evening before
she lists a sore throat, a running nose, sneezing and aching muscles
she admits to broken sleep and night sweats
the chemist picks out three priorities in what should be done
he says an ordinary medicine is enough against a troublesome fever
he puts making up the loss of water first
he sets difficulty in breathing as the signal to see a doctor
he recommends rest for as long as the muscles stay tender
text: The chemist asked the customer how long she had been feverish. She said the shivering had come on the evening before, out of nowhere. He wanted to know what else she felt. She listed a raw throat, a streaming nose, a constant urge to sneeze and aching calves. He then asked about her nights, and she admitted that she slept badly and woke up drenched. At that point the chemist set out three priorities. First the fever itself, which an ordinary medicine settles once it becomes a nuisance. Second, making up the water she was losing, which he put above everything else, since sweating drains the body. Third, keeping watch: should her breathing turn difficult, a doctor must be seen. The customer asked whether she ought to stop moving about. He advised rest for as long as the muscles stayed tender.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: surgeons once operated without cleaning their hands
a dirty operating apron was a matter of pride at the time
one stubborn doctor compared the death rate of two delivery wards
the death rate fell where hands were disinfected
his colleagues mocked him and he lost his post
work on micro-organisms brought his idea acceptance
sterilising instruments and airing rooms then spread widely
infections following operations dropped sharply
text: Picture a hospital where surgeons went from one bed to the next without so much as rinsing their hands, proud of the filth caked on their aprons. That was simply how things were done, and nobody saw any wrong in it. Then one stubborn doctor compared two delivery wards and noticed that deaths collapsed in the one where fingers were scrubbed with a biting solution. His colleagues laughed at him, and he ended up pushed out of his post. It took the work on micro-organisms before anyone would accept what he had shown. After that everything moved fast: instruments boiled, gowns changed, wards aired between operations. You know the rest. Infections following an operation fell away, and hand-washing turned into the cheapest and most rewarding gesture medicine has. Rather a funny turnaround, is it not?

units: sitting still for a long time makes the feet swell
the calf muscles push blood upwards by squeezing the veins
staying still halts that pumping action
fluid gathers in the tissue and presses on the nerves
that pressure on the nerves explains the prickling feeling
warmth adds to the effect by widening the vessels
a shortage of water thickens the blood and hinders the flow
the trouble normally clears after a night in a healthy adult
lasting stillness raises the risk of a clot forming
doctors advise standing up, tightening the calves, drinking and avoiding tight clothing
text: After a long journey spent sitting, the feet swell and the toes feel numb. The mechanism is well known to doctors. Blood climbs from the legs back to the heart because the calf muscles squeeze the veins at every step. Sit still and that pump stops. Fluid then gathers in the tissue, the foot puffs up, and the squeezed nerves send back a prickling feeling. Warmth makes it worse, since it widens the vessels. So does going short of water, because thicker blood travels less easily. In a healthy adult none of this amounts to much, and a night is enough to put it right. The danger grows, though, when the stillness drags on and a clot forms. Practitioners therefore advise standing up regularly, tightening the calves, drinking water and keeping clear of clothing that grips the waist.

units: a bookbinder stayed bent over her bench through long sessions
a dull ache spread through her forearm and then her fingers
she dropped her tool in the middle of a session
she ignored the symptom at first, thinking it would pass
the doctor she saw measured the height of the cutting surface instead of prescribing a remedy
the bench stood two hand-widths too low
the workshop was rearranged with a raised, tilted top and an adjustable seat
short breaks were brought in every half hour
the pain went within three weeks
text: The bookbinding workshop smelled of warm glue and damp paper. The binder stayed bent over her bench from dawn to dusk, wrist folded, jaw tight with concentration. A dull ache settled in her forearm, then crept into her fingers, until one afternoon her folding tool dropped out of her hand in the middle of a session. She put it down to a passing weakness and gritted her teeth. It got worse. A sports doctor, consulted with no real hope, prescribed neither ointment nor a long rest, but measured the height of the bench. Two hand-widths too low. The top was raised, the surface tilted, an adjustable stool brought in, and a short break set for every half hour. Within three weeks the pain had gone. She tells her apprentices the story laughing: her trouble came not from her hands but from her furniture.

units: the choice between a cold and a warm application depends on the nature of the injury
cold suits a recent injury with swelling
the ice pack must be kept off the skin by a cloth
the cold application alternates spells of a quarter of an hour
heat suits a long-standing stiffness without swelling
a warm bottle is laid on for half an hour
the time must be watched by the clock and stopped if the skin reddens deeply
cold soothes and tightens whereas heat relaxes and widens
in case of doubt cold carries fewer drawbacks
text: Before you reach for a compress, decide between cold and heat, because the two do quite different jobs. For a fresh injury, a joint that is puffing up or a knock taken the day before, choose cold. Wrap the pack in a thin cloth, hold it on for a quarter of an hour, take it off for as long again, then repeat. Never lay bare ice against the skin. For an old stiffness, a knotted neck or an aching muscle with no swelling, heat is the better choice. A warm bottle, left on for half an hour, loosens the fibres and makes movement easier. In either case, time it by the clock and stop if the skin turns deeply red. Hold on to the basic difference: cold soothes and tightens, heat relaxes and opens. When you cannot make up your mind, take the cold, whose drawbacks are the smaller ones.

units: a health survey carried out in a rural area identifies three areas of weakness
the diet of the adults questioned rests on soft, sugary food
poor chewing goes with damaged teeth from middle age
nights are short and broken by waking
lack of sleep tells on alertness at the wheel and on mood
motorised trips have displaced walking even over short distances
distance from care facilities is a factor common to all three
appointments are put off until the matter becomes urgent
the report calls for travelling surgeries, dental screening among children and waymarked paths
the health authorities will study these proposals before the end of the year
text: A health survey carried out across a rural district sets out three areas of weakness. The first is diet: the adults questioned eat soft, sugary food, chew little, and show damaged teeth from middle age onwards. The second concerns sleep. Nights there are short and broken by waking, which tells on alertness at the wheel and on temper. The third bears on physical activity, since walking has given way to motorised trips, even over short distances. The authors also note one factor running through all three, the distance to care. An appointment means a long journey, and many of them put it off until the matter is urgent. The report calls for travelling surgeries, dental screening among children and waymarked paths around the villages. The health authorities will look at these recommendations before the end of the year.

units: a sports coach notices that beginners are short of breath after a single flight of stairs
a seated life weakens the breathing quietly
the heart muscle settles for reduced effort
the vessels become less elastic
night rest deteriorates in bodies that are little used
the coach advises brisk walks repeated across the week
these walks include moderate climbs
late-afternoon weariness lessens after this practice
text: At a neighbourhood training hall, the coach watches whoever comes through the door. Most of them arrive winded after one flight of stairs, and he knows exactly why. A seated life wears the breathing machinery down quietly, without ever announcing itself. Let a still spell run on and the heart muscle settles for the smallest effort it can get away with, the vessels stiffen and lose their spring, and the shortest run turns punishing. He points to a quieter consequence as well. Sleep frays, because a body asked for nothing never demands deep repair. His remedy stays modest: a brisk walk, taken again and again across the week, broken up by gentle climbs. The results show quickly. Breathing lengthens, the late-afternoon slump loosens its grip, and the mood clears. Nothing dramatic here, an ordinary cause, an ordinary correction, a chain running backwards.

units: evenings have been overrun by lit screens
falling asleep is pushed later and later
the writer refuses to blame the devices themselves
the writer blames the lack of a limit fixed in advance
he recommends choosing a stopping hour before the evening
he advises leaving the device outside the bedroom
he suggests replacing that habit with quiet reading
he holds that the mildness of a rule is what makes it last
text: Our evenings have filled up with lit screens until they overflow. Night falls, the eye fastens on a cold brightness, thought dissolves in it, and sleep slips back half an hour, then another. I distrust the easy charge. The harm does not sit inside the device, it sits in the missing boundary, the one nobody drew while tiredness had yet to take our judgement away. A blunt ban would collapse, as savage diets collapse. What I argue for is gentler, and negotiated with oneself. Settle on a stopping hour at midday, while the mind still reasons. Leave the thing outside the bedroom, so that reaching for it costs something. Put slow reading in place of the electric vigil, a low conversation, a stretch. Sleep is never rescued by heroic denial, only by a mild rule you keep without noticing that you keep it.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a rehabilitation therapist has worked with back patients since the start of his career
he contrasts two profiles among those who consult him
the first profile carries heavy loads and shows tightened muscles
the second profile stays seated and lacks muscular tone
both profiles complain of a comparable discomfort
he treats the first with stretching and heat
he treats the second with strengthening built up by degrees
he refuses to apply the same protocol to both cases
text: The therapist working out of this practice has sorted back patients into two profiles since his first year, and every examination opens with that question. One kind lifts heavy loads most of the week: the muscles sit rigid, the shoulders lock, the neck feels hard under the hand. The other kind stays parked in front of a screen: the fibres go slack, the posture caves, the abdominal girdle holds nothing up any more. Both describe the same low ache, and people conclude from that a single treatment would serve. He argues the opposite. For the first he prescribes graded stretching, heat, and a release led by the breath, so that a clenched back loosens again. For the second he insists on strengthening built up by degrees, without which no relief holds. One symptom, he says, hiding two opposite mechanics.

units: a cookery book meant for people recovering from illness is examined
the reviewer approves of the plainness of the preparations
the recipes limit fats and long cooking
the book offers pairings rich in protein
the portions are suited to a weakened appetite
the explanations about chewing are judged useful
the review faults the absence of guidance on keeping food
the conclusion nevertheless recommends the book for family kitchens
text: This collection of dishes for those recovering from illness deserves close attention, so sharply do its choices cut against the usual output. Three merits stand out. Plainness first: the author sets aside endless cooking and heavy fats in favour of plates a weakened stomach takes without protest. Balance next: every pairing brings together a source of protein and a tender vegetable, which gives a nourishing whole that never sits heavily. The portions come sized for a faltering appetite. Instruction last: the pages given over to chewing are worth more than many a longer treatise. One reservation remains. Nothing at all is said about keeping dishes cooked ahead of time, a regrettable gap for readers whose strength is low. The book stays worth recommending to any family kitchen with recovery in mind.

units: the writer of the message writes to someone close to give news
a shivering fit appeared at the end of the week
a consultation took place the following day
the carer ruled out any complication
three nights of extended rest were prescribed
a hot drink and a light soup made up the whole diet
the fever fell before the end of the treatment
the writer promises a visit as soon as he has recovered
text: I am writing from my bed, and nothing here should worry you. It began at the end of the week. A shivering fit caught me while I was tidying the kitchen, and I went to lie down feverish, unable to finish my own sentence. The following day the carer at the nearby health centre examined me thoroughly. She ruled out any complication and ordered three nights of strict rest, which I accepted without argument. The first two dragged. My whole diet was a warm infusion and a thin soup, and I dropped off as soon as the light went. Then the fever broke all at once, before the course of treatment had finished, and hunger returned like a friend who had left in a temper. I can walk the corridor now without leaning on the wall. I shall come round the moment this tiredness finally releases me.

units: the person questioned explains night-time sweating
an overheated bedroom prevents the inner temperature from dropping
that drop is what allows a proper falling asleep
the body makes up for it by producing sweat
wakings multiply because of that discomfort
the next day's tiredness follows from those interruptions
the speaker advises turning the bedroom heating down
she recommends natural fabrics rather than synthetic ones
text: You want to know why the pillow is soaked every night when you have done nothing to earn it. One sentence covers it: your bedroom is too warm. Here is the mechanism. To drop off properly your body must shed a fraction of a degree of its own heat, and if the surrounding air prevents that, it brings out the heavy weaponry and sets you sweating. So what? So you wake clammy, shove the cover off, drag it back, and the whole pantomime chops your sleep into useless pieces. Hence the heaviness of the morning, without your having stayed up late. What can you actually do about it? Turn the heating down well before bed, and let the room cool by itself. Change the bedding too: natural cloth carries the damp away, synthetics press it against the skin. Give it a week and you will notice the difference.

units: a reception nurse describes the crowding in an emergency department
most of the arrivals concern complaints of no seriousness
seriously ill patients wait longer because of that crowding
the doctor in charge points to ignorance of the other options available
a telephone line giving guidance has been set up
walk-in surgeries open in the evening
the average wait has come down since those measures
the nurse holds that informing the public must go on
text: The nurse on reception describes a waiting room already full from the moment the doors open. Most of what arrives, she says, is minor, a light sprain, a cough that will not shift, a shallow burn, and those cases push the genuinely threatened patients further down the queue. The doctor in charge of the department agrees, with a qualification. People rarely know what exists outside the hospital, he explains, so they head for the place they can name. Two measures followed. A telephone line now gives guidance before anyone sets off, and walk-in surgeries open in the evening across the area. The average wait has already come down, he notes. The nurse is cooler about it. The room will empty for good on the evening when everyone knows where to turn, she says, and not one single day before.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: carers of former times put illnesses down to corrupted air
they advised airing rooms and keeping away from unhealthy places
that explanation rested on observation without proof
the discovery of micro-organisms altered this conception
handwashing was brought into the rooms where care was given
mortality after childbirth fell afterwards
both approaches shared the same mistrust of dirt
the older approach knew nothing of the true source of contagion
text: Before anyone had learnt to look at the invisible, carers blamed the air. A thick smell rising off marshy ground, an unaired lane, a shut room: that, it was believed, was where contagion came from. So windows were opened, herbs were burnt, the low districts were avoided. The instinct was not absurd, only blind to its own reason. Then the magnifying glass showed a tiny population swarming over the fingers, and the whole picture tipped over. A dull instruction, wash your hands between one room and the next, brought the death rate among women who had just given birth down further than any fumigation ever had. Set the two doctrines side by side, honestly. Both mistrusted filth, and both prescribed much the same gestures. But the older one aimed at a shadow, while the later one could at last name what it was fighting.

units: the text describes the effects of immersion in cold water
the skin responds by tightening the vessels near the surface
blood withdraws towards the central organs
breathing quickens abruptly on contact
control of the breath limits that reaction
stimulating substances are released after coming out
heart disorders make the practice inadvisable
a short duration is advised for beginners
text: Immersion in cold water works on three separate levels, and each of them deserves its own account. Circulation comes first. On contact the vessels in the skin tighten, blood withdraws towards the central organs, and pressure rises for a short while. Breathing follows. A reflex gasp arrives the moment you go under, fast and beyond control, and taking charge of the out-breath softens that respiratory panic and makes the exercise workable. The chemical answer comes last: on getting out, the body releases stimulating messengers, which accounts for the reviving effect regular bathers describe. Two precautions frame the whole thing. Any known heart abnormality rules the practice out without medical advice, and a beginner keeps the immersion very short, never alone, never after a heavy meal.

units: a librarian suffered from pain in her wrists
she put the pain down at first to her age
a colleague pointed out the unsuitable height of her work surface
an ergonomist examined her workstation
the seat and the screen were raised
regular breaks were brought into her day
the pain went away after several weeks
she then urged the same course on her colleagues
text: The woman in charge of the town library endured a dull ache in both wrists for two seasons, and put it down at first to her age and to ordinary wear. She carried on shelving, lifting and keying in references, until a younger colleague remarked on the odd height of her sorting surface. An ergonomist was then called in. He measured the workstation, watched how her forearms sat, and gave an opinion without softening it: the seat was too low, the screen too far back, and the neck was paying for the whole imbalance. Both were raised. Short breaks were built into the day at settled intervals. Within some weeks the ache had gone, and not a single tablet had been swallowed. From then on she preached the same procedure to her team with a stubbornness nobody could talk her out of.

units: two neighbouring workshops work on opposing principles
the joiner takes material away with his cutting tool
the wood comes off as a curled ribbon
the smith reshapes hot metal without losing any of it
the bar changes shape under the blows
both craftsmen show patience of the same kind
every material warns the maker where it will resist
ignoring that warning leads to breaking the piece
text: Walk into two workshops that stand side by side and the rules seem to reverse. In the first, the joiner leans on his plane and the timber gives way under the blade; what comes off curls into a long ribbon and drops at his feet. Stroke by stroke he takes substance away, until the board runs smooth beneath the palm. In the second nothing leaves at all. The smith brings his hammer down on hot metal and the bar stretches, thickens and bends, yet not a grain of it is lost. One subtracts, the other pushes shape about. Even so, the patience is of one kind: both men listen to what they hold, sensing where it will fight and where it will yield. Timber speaks through its grain, iron through its colour. Miss that warning and the piece breaks, and the room around you goes awkwardly quiet.

units: a beginner recounts his first months in the locksmith trade
the clamping tool holds the piece without marking it
the teeth of the shaping tool clog when it is used askew
the head of the workshop makes a sheet-metal checking template
a screw tightened too far snapped off in its hole
polishing before truing means starting again
the upkeep habits include greasing the jaws
classroom theory seemed useless to him before hands-on work
text: An apprentice sets out his first half-year in the locksmith's workshop as three strings of memories. Tools to begin with: the vice that grips a piece without leaving a mark, the file whose teeth clog the moment you come at the work sideways, the sheet-metal template the foreman cuts so that every angle can be checked. Then the mistakes: a notch driven too deep, a screw forced until it snapped off in its hole, a face polished before it had been trued, which meant starting the whole thing over. Then the habits: clearing the teeth with copper wire, oiling the jaws, sorting templates by profile. Everything learnt in the classroom, he says, was worth nothing to him until he had felt the metal push back against the file. The right movement is learnt by the hand as much as by the head.

units: the workpiece must be held fast before anything begins
the marks are scored with a metal point
the cavity is roughed out first with a chisel in short cuts
the bottom of the cavity is finished with a hollow tool
a fit that is too slack weakens the joint
the male part is sawn on the outside of the line
a dry trial checks that entry takes moderate pressure
gluing happens only once that trial has gone well
text: Before a mortise and tenon joint goes together, wipe the bench clear and make sure the workpiece cannot shift a hair under the hand. Marking comes first: score both parts with a steel point, holding the gauge flat against the edge so the lines stay true. Rough out the mortise with a chisel, taking short cuts and working outwards from the middle. Finish the bottom with a gouge and leave the cheeks alone, because a slack fit will ruin the strength of the whole thing. Only then saw the tenon, keeping the blade outside the line, and bring it down to size with fine paring, a shaving at a time. Bring the two parts together dry: if they close under steady pressure from the palm, the fit is right. Glue goes on after that trial and not before, and the joint is drawn up in a press.

units: the last tannery in the valley is to stop trading
the price of power has risen steeply
the vats of the works are worn out
the expected buyer dropped the plan for want of money
the leather workshops nearby will have to buy from far off
waiting times for supplies will grow longer
the works that is closing took two trainees a year
a takeover run as a cooperative is being talked of locally
text: The last tannery in the valley is to shut its doors, and the leather workshops around it are uneasy. The chain that led here is easy enough to follow: the price of power climbed steeply, the vats were worn past repair, and the buyer everyone expected walked away for want of ready money. The consequence is already plain next door. Workshops that bought their hides a few steps from their own gate must now order them from far off, with longer waits and quality that is much harder to judge. A less obvious loss falls on training: the tannery took two trainees each year, and it was the only place nearby where vegetable tanning could be learnt. Those who run the valley speak of a takeover held as a cooperative. The makers fear the order books will empty long before anything of the sort arrives.

units: wood dust takes over the whole workshop
it works its way into the joints of the machines
it sets the man at the saw coughing
opening the windows only moves the cloud about
each machine has been joined to a flexible hose
an extraction box has been set up outdoors
a cloth filter holds back the finest particles
the waste that is collected beds a neighbour's animals
text: Push the door of that workshop open and the trouble announces itself: sawdust. It lies over the floor, clings to the beams, works into the hinges of every machine and sets the man at the saw coughing before the week is out. The windows stay open, yet the draught only walks the cloud from one end of the room to the other. What the joiner came up with is nothing clever. Each machine now feeds a flexible hose running to an extraction box that sits outdoors under a sheet of roofing. A cloth filter holds back the finest of it, and a sack catches the rest. He still sweeps, of course, but he no longer breathes his own trade. The dust, rather than going on the fire, goes to a neighbour who beds his animals on it. The air in there, he swears, smells of cut wood once more, and not of grey powder.

units: the writer weighs learning at a screen against learning at the bench
film lets a movement be stopped and taken apart
teaching in a room wastes no material
the workshop is costly and wears the machines
every attempt that fails throws timber away
only the workshop passes on the feel of the tool
a tired arm warns of pressure wrongly applied
the writer holds that the saving made in the room will be paid for later
text: Should a manual trade be learnt in front of a screen or in front of a bench? Training centres are split on it, and the comparison deserves to be made without flattery. The teaching room has a real advantage: a movement can be watched on film, stopped, taken apart, a posture corrected without spoiling a single board. The workshop, by contrast, is expensive, it wears the machines out, and every attempt that fails costs timber. Yet it gives what no screen will ever pass on: the tool trembling in the palm, the smell of a glue that is not taking, the ache in the forearm that warns of a bad line of pressure. Training that drops all of this turns out people who can explain a joint without being able to hold one. The sums are wrong, then: what the room saves, the bench pays for later.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: those in the village name her by her trade alone
her hands carry old scars
she no longer explains where those wounds came from
her tools are ranked by width on her bench
the handle of her mallet has been worn smooth by use
a grinding wheel is used to bring the edges back
she holds that a block is chosen before it is shaped
she refuses to show work that is unfinished
about ten pupils have passed through her workshop
she started as a labourer before she touched a carving tool
text: In the village she is known as the stone carver, and the title is enough for her. Her hands first: broad, dry, crossed with old cuts whose stories she no longer bothers to tell. Then the tools, laid out on the bench with something close to tenderness, the mallet with its handle worn smooth, the chisels ranked by width, the grinding wheel that brings back an edge and fills the place with a clear hiss. Then her early years: she came in as a labourer and pushed a barrow for a whole year before anyone put a chisel in her hand. Then what she holds to: a block is chosen before it is cut, a flaw is worked round rather than hidden, and unfinished work is shown to nobody at all. She has trained ten or so pupils, and three of them still carve in the valley. They will cut truly, she says, on the day they stop counting their blows.

units: a panel judges a chest by following the order of its making
the timber chosen holds an even colour
the joint marks were not taken from one single template
a gap shows at the corner set at the back
the cuts made are clean and closely fitted
the finishing stage lets the judges down
abrasive marks remain beside the metal fittings
the wax went on to a surface still carrying dust
the piece is called sound in spite of a rushed last stage
text: The chest put before the panel is best judged in the order it was built. The choice of timber comes first, and it could hardly be bettered: cut on the quarter, quiet grain, a colour that holds steady from one board to the next. The setting out already wavers, since the dovetail marks were not taken from one single template, and the difference shows at the back corner. Cutting makes up part of the ground that was lost, for the shoulders are crisp, the sockets clean, the fit close without ever being forced. Finishing is where the work falls down. Sanding was hurried, grinder marks survive beside the fittings, and wax laid over a surface still carrying dust has set fine scratches into it. What the panel will remember is a sound piece whose last stage gives away the rush of the maker.

units: the maker announces a delay of two weeks on an order
the timber set aside was soaked under a damaged sheet
its moisture is too high for the workshop to accept
using that wood would pull the panels in after assembly
the drawers would bind as soon as the heating went on
the boards have been put into the drying kiln
the work starts again on an older batch
the new colour is darker than expected
photographs will be sent at the dry assembly
text: I am writing about the chest of drawers you left with me, which will now take a fortnight longer than we agreed. The fault lies with the timber. The batch I had set aside spent weeks under a torn sheet, and it has taken up more moisture than my workshop will allow. Were I to use it as it stands, the panels would pull in once assembled and the drawers would bind as soon as the heating went on. So those boards have gone into the drying kiln and I have started cutting again from an older batch, which puts the whole job back. There is one pleasant result: the replacement timber is deeper in tone, and I shall suggest a pale wax to bring that out. I will send you photographs as soon as it stands dry, so that you can settle your choice before a drop of glue is anywhere near it.

units: a furniture restorer is blamed for the slowness of her quotes
every piece hides repairs carried out earlier
an assessment made too fast brings costs nobody planned for
she takes part of the piece apart before naming a price
this inspection is charged to the owner
half of the customers refuse to pay for it
she now offers two ways of quoting
the inspection fee is taken off if the work comes to her
disagreements with customers have almost stopped
text: What does a furniture restorer say when people complain that her quotes take too long? She lays the problem out plainly: every piece hides a history of earlier repairs, and a rushed diagnosis leads to costs nobody planned for. Asked how she works, she describes taking part of the piece apart, testing the glue lines, looking at the backs, and only then naming a price she will stand by. Asked what that care costs, she admits she charges for it and that one owner in two says no. Her answer has been to offer two quotes: a fee for the inspection, taken off the bill if the restoration comes to her, and a broad estimate for anyone who wants a figure on the spot. Since then disagreements have all but vanished. One difficulty stays: persuading an owner in a hurry that patience is cheaper than doing the work twice.

units: the metalworker describes his place of labour as a living creature
he gives the device that sends air the role of a lung
he explains that without that air the burning weakens
he likens the block he strikes on to a shoulder
he presents the gripping tools as fearless fingers
he says those tools take hold of the burning metal without faltering
he compares the hearth itself to an organ that beats
his pupil asks him which part she stands for in this anatomy
he answers that she will be the memory of the movements
text: The blacksmith spoke about his workshop as though it were some drowsing animal, and he named its limbs for her patiently, one after another. The bellows, he said, performed the office of a lung: starve the coals of that slow, deliberate breath and the burning slackens, the bar surrenders its heat. The anvil, meanwhile, served as a shoulder, absorbing the entire violence of the hammer without ever flinching. The tongs, he insisted, were fingers considerably braver than his own, since they closed upon glowing metal and never once trembled. As for the hearth, he likened it to a heart beating dully at the further end of the room. His apprentice listened without interrupting, then asked him which limb she herself stood for in this anatomy. She would be the memory, he answered, the keeper of every movement once the old man's hands had surrendered.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: weaving began as an entirely manual operation
the earliest devices held the threads upright
lumps of clay served to keep those threads taut
the worker put the crosswise thread in row by row
a device worked by foot then parted the threads to open a passage
the tool carrying the crosswise thread crossed the width in one movement
a cord and a mallet then threw that tool mechanically
the output doubled without calling for a second worker
punched cards later governed the lifting of each thread
the pattern moved from human memory to a coded support
text: Weaving lived in the fingers long before it belonged to any machinery. The earliest frames held their threads upright, weighted at the foot by lumps of baked clay, while the worker carried the crosswise thread through by hand, one patient row after another. Then arrived the frame governed by the feet: pedals lifted a whole company of threads and opened a clean passage, so the carrier crossed the entire width in a single throw. Afterwards that carrier was thrown mechanically, flung by a cord and a mallet, which doubled the output without demanding a second worker. Later still, punched cards commanded the lifting of every individual thread, and the pattern migrated out of a weaver's memory onto a coded support. Each stage removed a movement of the hand. None removed the eye that watches the tension.

units: the glassy layer is not a paint laid on the surface
the heat turns a mineral deposit into glass
the maker spreads a preparation of powders before the firing
those powders melt and then spread into one unbroken layer
the cooling sets the material without any crystal structure
that absence of crystals explains the clearness obtained
the sealing of the pores stops the liquid from seeping through
the hardness of the layer protects the wall from scratches
an uneven shrinking between the two materials brings a web of fine cracks
text: A glaze is not a coat of paint laid over the surface of a pot. It is glass, and the heat manufactures it on the clay itself. The potter coats the piece in a slurry of finely ground minerals, then surrenders it to the kiln. Under the firing those powders melt and spread into one unbroken layer; as they cool they harden without becoming crystalline again, and that is precisely where their clearness originates. Because the layer seals the pores of the wall, the vessel stops weeping and becomes fit to hold a liquid. Because the layer is hard, it equally protects the surface against every kind of scratch. An imbalance between the two materials produces a familiar defect: should the glass contract more than the clay while cooling, it splits into a web of exceedingly fine cracks.

units: a storage cupboard arrives in the workshop out of shape
its doors no longer close properly
the joiner fears that taking it apart will break the old joints
damping the panel fails because the curve returns on drying
planing the rebate makes the door gape on the opposite side
the craftsman notices that the twisting does not affect the whole height
he finds that a split rail is turning the side panel
he puts a sound rail in place of the cracked piece
he holds the joint under pressure until the glue has set
the cupboard stands true again and its doors work
text: The cupboard delivered to the workshop was standing by luck alone: one side panel had twisted and the doors no longer closed properly. The joiner hesitated to dismantle the whole thing, since the ancient joints would probably burst under the pressure. He first attempted damping the panel to persuade it straight, but the timber curled back the moment it dried. Then he planed the rebate, and discovered that the door simply gaped along the opposite edge. The answer emerged from patient observation: the side was not bowed over its whole height, it was pivoting on a single split rail. He replaced the cracked rail with a sound one, held the joint in a clamp until the glue had thoroughly set, and hung the hinges again. The panel recovered its uprightness, and both doors swung sweetly once more.

units: the text compares two ways of finishing the edge of a cloth
the hand method consists of turning the edge over twice
the iron serves to press each fold before the stitching
the hand stitches catch only one thread on the visible side
the hand finish calls for patience and moves along without haste
the stitching done by hand becomes invisible on the right side
the machine method takes up the same double fold
closely set pins hold the cloth before it goes under the needle
the machine finish stands up better to repeated washing
the machine stitching leaves a visible line on the outer face
text: Want a hem that hangs perfectly straight, with no ripples and no lumps? Weigh up the two ways of building it before you put a single stitch in. By hand, you turn the edge over, press it flat, turn it again, and work a blind stitch that catches barely a thread on the visible side. It takes an age, it demands patience and a thoroughly steady temper, but the stitching disappears completely and the cloth keeps all its softness. On the machine, you prepare exactly the same double fold, pin it closely, and run an even line along the edge of the foot. It is quick, it is strong, and it survives repeated washing far better than handwork; the trade is a line showing distinctly on the outer face. So ask yourself which matters more: that it lasts for seasons, or that nobody ever notices it.

units: a charity teaches the metal trades to adults changing career
the classes are held under the roof beams of an old market hall
the workshops are grouped by family of movement
the first workshop teaches how to lay an even bead without burning through the sheet
the second deals with assembly by pieces put in cold
the third covers the finishing treatment obtained by heating and oiling
the last workshop teaches the costing of a commission and the buying of stock
the woman in charge states that people rarely drop out over the craft
the paperwork often wears the trainees down
text: Under the roof beams of an old market hall, a charity teaches the metal trades to adults changing career, and its workshops are grouped by family of movement. The first is given over to welding, where pupils learn to lay an even bead without burning through the sheet. The second covers mechanical assembly, in which every rivet must be driven cold, into a hole bored carefully to size. The third handles finishing, and a good deal of discussion goes into the patina you draw out by heating the piece and afterwards oiling it. The final workshop is the unexpected one, and it concerns costing: pricing a commission, buying materials, promising a date you can honour. Few people withdraw over the craft itself, the woman in charge explains; the paperwork is what wears them down. A fresh group begins at the end of the season.

units: the dye workshop smells of wet ash from first light
boards cover the vats that are still cold
the water in the troughs keeps the colour of the day before
the dyer lights a fire under the widest vat
she draws a mass of undyed yarn out of a basket
steam rises and the bath takes on the shade of crushed leaves
the wool put under takes up the colour very quickly
the next stage consists of rinsing the yarn in one trough after another
the yarn hung under the lean-to drips and marks the ground
text: At first light the dye house smells of wet ash and sodden wool. The vats are still sleeping beneath their thick wooden boards, and the water inside them retains the darkened colour of the previous day. Soon the dyer kindles a fire beneath the widest of them, then lifts a skein of undyed yarn out of a basket and shakes it vigorously at arm's length to loosen the knots. Steam begins to rise, the bath turns the shade of crushed leaves, and the wool descends into it all at once, without hesitating, drinking the colour in like a sponge. The rinsing follows: the skeins travel from one trough to the next, paler each time, heavier between the fingers. By evening they hang in a close row beneath the lean-to, still streaming, each one leaving on the ground a stain of the shade it has taken.

units: the writer disputes the idea that the electronic tool makes the older method pointless
the optical device gives a vertical from its own footing
a sinking of that footing falsifies the measurement with no visible warning
the hanging weight answers to a force that never drifts
the apprentice who handles this instrument grasps in the body what he is checking
newer teams no longer question what the screen displays
they do not check a measurement by a second method
costly reworking follows from this on site
the firm puts that reworking down to a lack of attention
the writer holds that passing on the older skill is not nostalgia
text: To claim that the electronic instrument makes learning the plumb line pointless is a failure of reasoning, and the failure costs money on site. An optical device delivers a vertical immediately, but it delivers it from its own footing; let the tripod settle or the ground shudder, and the error propagates with nothing whatever to announce it. The hanging weight answers to a force that never drifts, and the apprentice who has handled it understands physically what he is checking. Lacking that understanding, newer teams no longer think to doubt the screen, nor to confirm a value by a second method. Expensive reworking follows, and the company attributes it to carelessness when it truly comes from a truncated training. Passing on the older skill is therefore no exercise in nostalgia.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the instrument maker has taken over from her old master
the custom of the workshop was thinning at the time of the handover
amateur players wanted an instrument that held its tune
those players could not afford a piece shaped entirely by hand
she refused to use a timber of poorer quality
she split the making into two separate sets
the parts with no bearing on the sound are made in batches by a workshop nearby
she shapes alone the pieces that settle the sound
the price fell by a third with no loss of tone
her old master recognised her hand on hearing the instrument
text: The instrument maker described here took over her old master's workshop at precisely the moment when its custom was thinning. She quickly identified an obstacle which no catalogue resolved: amateur players wanted an instrument that held its tune, without being able to afford a piece cut entirely by hand. Rather than descend to a timber of poorer quality, she divided her work into two separate sets. The parts with no bearing whatever on the sound, the rough neck and the ribs, now arrive in batches from a workshop nearby. The parts that settle the sound, the belly and the bass bar, she shapes alone and adjusts them by ear. The price fell by a third, the tone lost nothing at all, and her old master, who arrived to hear a finished commission, recognised his own hand in the varnish.

units: two ranges of chairs are shown in the same room
the first range comes from a workshop attached to the old joints
that range uses fitted tenons and a back bent under steam
its sturdiness commands the respect of the writer of the review
its drawing seems hesitant for want of attention paid to the outline
the second range comes from a studio using machine cutting
this second range is made in plywood
its seat meets the back with no cushion added
the object comes apart in a handful of movements
the reviewer judges that neither range clearly wins
text: Two ranges of chairs occupy the same exhibition room, and the pairing teaches you something. The first emerges from a workshop that makes a point of traditional jointing: tenons pared to fit, a back bent under steam, an oiled finish. Its sturdiness commands respect, yet the drawing hesitates, as though the maker had spent all his attention upon structure and neglected the outline. The second comes from a studio that cheerfully owns up to machine cutting and plywood. Its line is clean, the seat meets the back without any cushion added, and the whole object comes apart in a handful of movements. One regrets, however, the dryness of the edges, which no passing hand will ever soften. Neither range clearly triumphs: one will outlast its owner, the other will please the eye before tiring at the joints.

units: the narrator writes to an acquaintance who had asked for news of him
he was taken on by an elderly cabinetmaker looking for a beginner
the master handed him a tool and a piece of wood without any explanation
his first week went entirely on a single cutting movement
the sign of success was a shaving coming off unbroken
he was then allowed to smooth the surfaces the master had prepared
his first box was judged clumsy but honest
he now draws his own designs at home in the evening
he concludes that patience is learnt through practice and not through talk
he invites his correspondent to come and see the workshop
text: You asked how the workshop was treating me, and I have put off answering long enough. When the leaves turned, I walked into a narrow shop where an elderly cabinetmaker wanted a beginner. He handed me a plane and a rough board, and said nothing at all about what I should do with them. For a whole week I did one thing: push that plane, over and over, until the shaving came away in a single unbroken ribbon. Once the cold set in, he let me smooth the surfaces he had roughed out himself. By the thaw I had made my first small box, which he called clumsy but honest. Now I draw my own designs in the evening, at the kitchen table. What I have learnt here will not fit into a letter: patience comes through the hands, never through talk. Write back soon, and tell me whether you will come and see the workshop.

units: the bubbles in a casting come from filling the mould too fast
the trapped air leaves hollows that weaken the piece
pouring very slowly is not the answer
an alloy that loses its heat too early fails to fill the whole cavity
heating the mould beforehand holds off the hardening of the metal
this preheating removes the need to pour more slowly
bubbles that persist point to air escaping badly
the craftsman cuts thin channels to let the air out as the metal rises
surface flaws come back either to heat or to the path taken by the air
text: Why does a casting come out of the mould with bubbles across its face? Look first at how fast it was filled: metal poured in a rush traps air, and that trapped air leaves hollows which weaken the piece. Should the pour then be as slow as the hand can manage? No. An alloy that loses its heat on the way in stiffens before it has reached every corner of the cavity, and the shape comes out short. What does the founder rely on instead? He heats the mould before pouring, which holds off solidification without forcing him to slow the stream. And if bubbles show up all the same? Then the air is not getting out. The moulder cuts vents, thin channels that let it escape as the metal level climbs. Every blemish on the surface leads back either to heat or to the path the air had to take.

units: a visitor reports that her old book is shedding its leaves
she fears the volume will come apart completely
the specialist puts the fault down to broken sewing
the original adhesive has grown crumbly and no longer holds
he dismisses the idea of giving up on the repair
putting it right means taking the gatherings apart one by one
the old adhesive comes away with moisture
the old outside will be kept and strengthened from within
how long it takes depends on drying under a press that cannot be hurried
text: The visitor told the bookbinder that her old family volume was shedding its leaves, and that she feared the whole thing would come apart. He answered that the original sewing had snapped and that the glue, gone crumbly, no longer held anything together. She asked whether the repair was worth attempting. He assured her that it was, then set out what it involved: taking the gatherings apart one by one, lifting the old glue with moisture, and sewing afresh onto tapes. She wondered how it would look afterwards. The binder explained that the old covering would stay where it was, with a fresh lining set inside the boards, so that the work would hardly show. She asked how long it would take. He said that drying under the press kept its own pace and that nothing could hurry it. She accepted, reassured by his plainness.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: old building sites knew two ways of organising stone cutting
under the first, one worker took a block from start to finish
under the second, the stages were shared out between specialised groups
the individual arrangement gave very even pieces
it moved at a slow pace and depended on the skill available
the shared arrangement raised output
it made learning easier by isolating a single movement
it called for strict checking of the way the pieces came together
the two methods leave distinct material clues
those clues inform researchers where no written documents exist
text: Old building sites cut their stone in one of two ways. Under the first, a single mason took a block from start to finish, squaring it, dressing it and carving the detail. Under the second, each stage passed to a team that did nothing else. Work done by one pair of hands came out remarkably even, since the same judgement governed every proportion, but it moved slowly and hung on whatever skill happened to be at hand. Splitting the stages raised output, and it brought learners on faster, since each had only one movement to master. The price was strict checking as the blocks came together, or nothing would sit true. Each method left its own marks in the stone: even tool traces on the one side, scored setting-out lines on the other. Where no records survive, that is what scholars read.

units: a pottery workshop holds three families of implements
the first family serves to give the shape
flat blades bring the wall upright while it is being shaped
the second family serves to take material away
thin metal loops lighten the underside of the pot
the third family gathers the tools of the final stage
points serve to decorate or to mark the pot
beginners overrate the part played by the turning machine
a badly smoothed wall takes up the glazed coating poorly
success rests on the order of the stages more than on nimble fingers
text: Walk into a pottery workshop and you will soon find yourself sorting the tools into three families. First come the ones that give the shape: the wheel, obviously, but also ribs, those flat blades you hold against the wall of the pot to bring it upright. Then come the ones that take clay away: loop tools, thin metal loops that pare off the surplus weight under the foot. Last comes everything to do with finishing, sponges, cloths, soft brushes, and the fine points for marking or decorating a pot. Beginners tend to believe that the wheel does the work. It does not. A wall left rough will drink the glaze unevenly, and the pot suffers for it. Each family picks up what the one before it missed, and it is that order of steps, far more than clever fingers, which decides how a piece turns out.

units: the workshop in the hamlet had closed when the man running it left
a woman metalworker bought it two winters later for a small sum
she began by clearing the rubble out of the building
she found the old ventilation device in good order
a former pupil of the place came to explain how the tools were stored
the hearth was put back into service at the start of the warm season
she now makes fastenings to order
she trains two apprentices every season
she finds it harder to convince customers that handwork lasts
text: The forge in the hamlet had gone cold when its last master left. Two winters on, a welder from the next valley bought the building for almost nothing, without much faith at first in what she was taking on. She began by clearing the rubble out of the shed, and under a tarpaulin she came across the original bellows, still sound. An old apprentice of the place, told by a neighbour that someone had moved in, walked over to show her where the tongs and the swages had always been kept. The hearth was lit again as the mild weather came round. Since then she has been forging locks and hinges to order, and takes on two trainees a season. Hammering iron, she says, was never the hard part. Convincing customers that a fitting shaped by hand outlasts one stamped out by a press is another matter.

units: the leather must be softened with a greasy product before assembly
a dried-out hide splits under pressure and cannot be mended
the holes are punched in one movement with the blade held straight
a slanted hole tips the metal fastening
the head of the fastening is struck with short repeated blows
a single heavy blow deforms the seat of the fastening
the lining inside must not form any fold
a fold makes the assembly sink under use
the rim of the head is smoothed to remove the tool marks
a sharp edge ends up cutting the thread that touches it
text: Before you set a single rivet, oil the leather and let it drink right through. Dry hide splits under pressure, and a split never closes again.
