Two shops standing side by side, two opposite ways of making a living. The goods set the rhythm, and the rhythm decides what ends up in the till.

units: the argument about funding social protection overlooks three aspects
the deduction from wages is felt as a tax imposed from above
that deduction in fact pays for shared cover
the uneven earnings of the self-employed make any fixed scale unfair
the protection of the self-employed remains incomplete
some employers escape the deductions by using short contracts
farming work out to others adds to that avoidance
the writer holds that the question is one of fairness and not of bookkeeping
text: Three things go missing from the whole argument about how social protection is paid for, and they are rarely named together. The first of them is the deduction taken from wages. It feels like a tax imposed from above, when what it actually buys is cover shared among everyone. The second is the standing of the self-employed: earnings that swing from month to month make any fixed scale unfair, and their protection is still full of holes. The third, and the quietest, is the employers who slip out of paying by stacking up short contracts and farming the work out to others. Each of these turns on fairness rather than on bookkeeping. Those calling for lighter charges skirt the first; those defending the present arrangement skirt the third. Name the three pieces first, and then decide.

units: the oldest hand in the bindery joined it very young as a beginner
she was put first on cleaning and then on folding the sections
the mixing of the glues was handed to her next
she spent long seasons at the same finishing bench
she bought the customer list when the house nearly disappeared
that purchase was paid for out of her savings and two loans
she trained about a dozen young people
several of her pupils now run shops of their own
she passed the business to her last pupil, asking him not to sell cheap
text: The oldest hand in the bindery came to the place very young, as a beginner, back when leather was still sewn by hand from one end to the other. She was given the sweeping first, then the folding of the sections, and later the mixing of the glues. She stood at the same finishing bench for season after season, long enough for the top of it to hold the marks of her tools. When the house nearly went under, she bought the customer list herself, with her savings and two small loans. After that she trained a good dozen young people, several of whom now run shops of their own. Too tired at last for the press, she handed the business to her final pupil, asking one thing of him only: never sell the work cheap. She still comes in to sit by the window, and puts a word on a loose stitch.

units: the equipment recently fitted to the assembly line draws a divided opinion
tightening is driven electronically and its accuracy is not disputed
that accuracy removes the rework tied to tightening by hand
the machine now sets the pace for the operator
a badly seated part locks the station and blocks the stations before it
the shop has gained steadiness and lost flexibility
upkeep calls for electronic skills the team does not have
every breakdown means waiting for someone from outside
the share of faulty parts has dropped sharply
text: Opinion on the equipment recently fitted to the assembly line is a divided one, and reasonably so. Tightening is driven electronically now and its accuracy is beyond any argument; the rework that came with tightening by hand has simply gone away. What comes along with it is a pace set by the machine rather than by the operator. Since the cycle no longer pauses on its own, one badly seated part locks the station, and the stoppage travels back to every station before it. The shop as a whole has bought steadiness at the price of give. Upkeep has changed as well: it asks for electronic skills the team does not have, so every breakdown means waiting for someone from outside. The balance still tips the right way, because the share of faulty parts coming off the line has dropped sharply.

units: the writer ordered a kitchen and signed a detailed estimate
a deposit was paid when the order was placed
no indication of delivery has been given since
three dates in turn were announced and then missed
the writer's last message went unanswered
the writer has to rent a furnished flat, which raises his costs
he asks either for a written commitment to a firm date with compensation
or else for the deposit to be returned in full within a fortnight
he says the file will go to a consumer body if no agreement is reached
text: I am writing to you once again about the kitchen I ordered from your shop at the start of the season. I signed a detailed estimate at the time and paid the deposit you asked for, and since then not one word has reached me about delivery. Your staff have named three dates in turn, every one of which has passed, and my last message went unanswered. Because of all this I am having to rent a furnished flat, and the cost of that grows with every week that passes. Let me put a reasonable way out of this to you. Either you commit in writing to a firm fitting date, with a reduction covering what the delay has cost me, or you return the deposit in full within a fortnight. Failing an agreement between us, the file goes to the consumer body that is already handling my case. Yours faithfully.

units: the choice between an employee and a self-employed contractor comes up often in small firms
the contractor's invoice takes the place of the wage and the employer's contributions
the contractor looks cheaper in the short term
the contractor bills for each job separately
the employee takes on unplanned tasks at no extra charge
the training the employee receives then benefits the firm that paid for it
an exclusive and lasting arrangement with a contractor risks reclassification
the advice is to keep contracting for one-off and specialised needs
the advice is to hire for the core activity
text: Is it better to take someone on as staff or to bring in a self-employed contractor? Small firms keep asking the question, and the answer turns on what you set side by side. On immediate cost the contractor looks cheaper, since an invoice takes the place of a wage and of the employer's contributions. Over time the gap narrows: the contractor bills for each job, while the employee picks up whatever comes up unplanned at no extra charge. And loyalty? That leans clearly towards hiring, because the training paid for by the firm stays inside the firm. Legal risk runs the other way, though: an exclusive, long-running arrangement with a contractor can be reclassified. So which? Keep contracting for one-off, specialised needs, and hire for the work that sits at the heart of the business.

units: a shopkeeper looks back on her early days at a wholesale market
at the start she had bought too many perishable goods
unsold crates piled up behind her stall
an experienced middleman suggested that she split her orders
he advised her to watch the customers before buying anything
she wrote down in a notebook the requests she could not meet
she started up again with a narrower range
her profit doubled while her selling space stayed the same
text: The woman who ran the counter spoke about her first season at the wholesale market. She had bought far too much perishable stock at the start, she said, trusting that the buyers would follow. Unsold crates piled up behind her stall, and the smell of over-ripe fruit tightened her throat every evening as she closed up. An older middleman, who had traded in that hall for years, told her to halve her orders and to walk the aisles for a while before committing to any purchase. She kept to that advice for a whole season, jotting down in a cloth notebook what shoppers asked for and could not find, and what they left untouched however low the price. When the cold months came she opened again with a narrower range, though a chosen one. Her margin had doubled, she added with a smile, and her stall had not gained a single shelf.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: better roads transformed the economy of the countryside
poor harvests once caused local shortages that could not be made good
heavy waggons were able to travel even in the wet season
the surplus of one region made up for what another lacked
the price of grain stopped swinging sharply from place to place
growers began to raise a single crop
they kept the crop that paid them best
the hands thus freed were taken on by the workshops of the market towns
text: Better roads changed the economy of the countryside more deeply than the people who paid for them had ever expected. While the harvests travelled along muddy tracks, each farming district had to feed itself, and a failed crop left a shortage that no one could make good, since nothing could be brought in to cover it. Once heavy waggons could move even through the wet months, the surplus of one valley made up for what another lacked, and the price of grain stopped swinging sharply from one district to the next. That steadiness had an effect nobody had planned for: growers began to specialise, dropping their side crops one by one and keeping only the one that paid them best. The hands freed by that change drifted down to the market towns, where the workshops took them on without the least difficulty.

units: a workshop can hold orders and still run short of ready money
suppliers and staff are paid before the customers are
an invoice sent out is a sum owed but not yet received
payment often arrives after the outlay has been made
financial health depends on how fast money comes in
asking for a deposit brings funds in early
steady reminders sent before the due date help payment along
a body can advance the money and take on the task of collecting it
text: A small workshop can hold a full order book and still find itself short of cash the following week. The trouble lies in the timing of it: the suppliers and the staff are paid long before the customers pay anything at all. Every invoice sent out stands for money that is owed but has not yet been received, and it falls due long after the outlay has already been made. Financial health therefore rests not on profit alone, but on how quickly the money actually comes in. Three remedies are open to it. The first is to ask for a deposit when the order is placed, which brings funds in early. The second rests on steady, courteous reminders, sent out before the agreed date. The third, and the dearest, is to hand the unpaid invoices to a body that advances the money and takes on the task of collecting it.

units: two workshops in the same trade stood on the same street
the first kept about ten workers and took on every order
the second was run by a couple who turned away ordinary jobs
the larger workshop stood the slack months badly
its fixed costs ran on while its machines stayed idle
the couple came through those months without financial harm
when demand returned the large workshop raised its output quickly
the couple could then take on no further order
each of the two ways won in one season and lost in the other
text: Two binding workshops stood on the same street, only a few doors apart, and lived off the same trade. The first kept about ten workers and took on every order it was offered, the dullest ones included. The second was run by a couple who turned away any job that called for neither gilding nor chosen leather. During the slack months the larger workshop struggled: its fixed costs ran on as before while its presses stood idle. The couple, for their part, came through the same stretch unharmed, since their outgoings amounted to little more than materials and their own labour. When demand picked up, the position reversed: one of them doubled its output within a week, the other could take nothing more. Each way of working paid for its flexibility in one season and won it back in the next.

units: it is wise to read a contract of employment before signing it
the section on hours can hold an obligation to stay reachable
you should ask what pay is set for those stretches of standby
the bonus announced may be guaranteed or left to the manager's discretion
the length of the trial period and the terms of ending it are worth checking
a mobility clause binds you to move site if the employer decides
you may ask for a copy of the document and take it home
an employer who hurries the candidate into signing gives something away
text: Before you sign a contract of employment, put the pen down and read the thing through calmly. Start with the section on hours: a standby clause often slips in there, meaning stretches of time when you must stay reachable without being at work. Ask how those stretches are paid, and have the answer written into the document itself. Move on to the pay, and check whether the bonus you were promised is owed to you or left to your manager's discretion. Then look at the trial period, how long it runs and how either side may bring it to an end. Glance last at any mobility clause, which binds you to move site if your employer decides. If something escapes you, ask for a copy and take it home with you. A decent employer will not mind; one who hurries you tells you plenty about the place.

units: a stoppage began early outside a distribution depot
the night shift left their posts first
forklift drivers and lorry drivers joined them before midday
the strikers are calling for a review of a frozen bonus scale
they demand the scrapping of a computer program that tracks every movement
management refused at first to talk under pressure
a delegation was received in the evening with no result
the vehicles were sent on to two nearby platforms
deliveries to local shops fell behind
the dispute is spreading to another site of the same company
text: The walkout began at first light outside the gates of a distribution depot. The sorters on the night shift left their posts first, joined shortly before midday by the forklift drivers and by some of the lorry drivers. They are calling for a review of a bonus scale frozen for the past three seasons, and for the scrapping of a scheduling program that, as they put it, measures every movement they make. Managers said at the outset that they would not bargain under pressure, then received a delegation early in the evening. Nothing at all came of that meeting. The stranded lorries have been sent on to two nearby platforms, which in turn has held up deliveries to the local shops. A mediator is due to reopen talks tomorrow, with the stoppage now spreading to a second site of the same company.

units: a smell of grain reaches you before you enter the building
the stacked sacks give off a warmth that raises a haze
the lack of ventilation forces the doors open very early
birds come in through those openings and nobody can drive them out
constant use has worn hollows into the pans of the scales
the passing of the trolleys has cracked the brick floor
the jolting spills the contents of badly tied sacks
the staff give up sweeping because the dirt soon comes back
text: The hall smells of grain dust well before you have crossed the threshold. Under the dark roof beams the sacks rise in uneven walls, and the warmth coming off them lifts a haze that blurs the air. Because the building has never been ventilated, the handlers throw the doors wide open at dawn, which draws in a flock of grey birds that nobody manages to shift. The scales stand there in the middle, heavy, and polished by palms; used without pause from morning to night, their pans have worn into a bright hollow. The brick floor, ground down by the wheels of the trolleys, has cracked in a star under every pillar, so that the barrows jolt and the overflow from badly tied sacks spills across it in pale trails. Nobody bothers to sweep: everyone here knows the dust will be back before evening.

units: judging a help desk by the number of calls handled is a mistake of method
the measure appeals because it is easy to work out
it turns harmful as soon as it drives what the teams are paid
an employee rated on speed cuts short the awkward conversations
he passes cases on or closes requests that are badly settled
the count rises while satisfaction falls
the cost shifts on to the fresh calls of those same customers
the proposal is to weight the rate by the share of cases settled at first contact
an outside check should confirm that share
part of the work escapes measurement and rests on the judgement of supervisors
text: Judging a help desk by the number of calls it gets through is a mistake of method, and an expensive mistake at that. The measure appeals because it costs nothing to work out; it turns harmful the moment it drives what the teams are paid. An adviser rated on speed soon learns to cut short the awkward conversations, to pass the case to another department, to close a request he knows has been settled badly. The count climbs, satisfaction collapses, and the real cost shifts on to the calls those same customers make again. There is a way out of this, though it takes some nerve: weight the rate by the share of cases settled at first contact, and have that share checked by an outside audit. Accept too that part of the work resists measurement, and leave that part to the judgement of the supervisors.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman now running a yard comes from the buying side
her predecessor was trained on the workshop floor
he measured performance by the amount sent out
she measures performance by stock turnover and by deadlines met
the former manager settled tensions by talking and by his own standing
she prefers written rules posted up and binding on everyone
he allowed private arrangements while she bargains for gains shared by all
the two ways of running the place brought much the same figures
the feel of the place changed between the two managers
text: The woman now in charge of a builders' yard came to the post after a long career in buying. Her predecessor had come up from the workshop floor: he knew the tools, the machines and the tiredness of the crews, and he measured a week by the amount that went out over the loading bays. Trained in trade, she measures instead by how fast the stock turns and how reliably deadlines are met. The former manager settled disputes by talking, and by the weight of his own standing; she prefers written rules, posted up, and binding on everyone. Where he tolerated private arrangements, she bargains for something the whole yard gains. The two methods brought much the same figures, but not the same feel: under him people stayed late without counting, under her they leave on time and argue more.

units: a retraining scheme meant for workers is judged uneven
the guidance stage is valued for its searching interviews
those interviews are led by people who have worked the trade
they end in a written plan rather than a list of options
the equipment of the technical training is old and ill suited
the machines used by employers differ from those used in training
the administrative help works well because compensation claims are handled on the spot
follow-up after placement stops too soon
most people who drop out do so after the opening stage of the contract
the yearly budget rules out any lasting planning
text: The retraining scheme offered to workers in an industrial area deserves a mixed verdict, so unevenly do its parts perform. The guidance stage is sound: the interviews run long, they are led by people who have worked the trade themselves, and they end in a written plan rather than a list of possibilities. The technical training suffers from ageing equipment inherited from the closed workshops, which prepares nobody for the machines employers actually run. The administrative help convinces more: compensation claims are put together on the spot, so nobody loses income in the gap. Follow-up after placement, by contrast, stops too soon, when most people drop out once the trial period is over. Funding, finally, hangs on yearly allocations, which rules out any serious planning.

units: the writer lost his source of income after a factory shut down
he turned to restoring old furniture
he writes his letter from the place where he practises his new trade
his savings are dwindling
that fall forces him to part with his pieces sooner than planned
he is learning to haggle over prices without embarrassment
each mended object brings him new buyers
he states that dread has left him since the change
he asks the woman he writes to for a reply
text: Dear friend, I am writing from the workshop where my tools now live. When the factory shut its doors my wage went with them, and that loss opened a door I would never have pushed at unaided. I could not bear the waiting, so I retrained and turned to the restoration of old furniture. Wood asks for patience, and it has handed mine back to me. My savings are thinning, which forces me to sell each piece earlier than I intended, and so I am learning to haggle without blushing. Every item I mend brings two more buyers to the door, and that small chain keeps me upright. You will ask whether I miss the old wage. I shall tell you the dread has gone, and that this quiet outweighs the security I surrendered. Write back to me soon. I need your voice the way glue needs a steady hand to press it.

units: a firm can run short of cash even with a full order book
the gap between money coming in and payments to suppliers creates the trouble
negotiating a deposit at the time of order eases the accounts at once
short-term credit suits only a passing shortfall
borrowing applied to a lasting imbalance merely hides the harm
putting occasional tasks out to contract lightens fixed costs
the margin must be examined product by product
a range sold at a loss can swallow the profit made on the others
the gap between money in and money out must be checked every week
text: What happens when a firm settles its suppliers long before its own sales are paid for? That gap drains the cash and chokes the business, however full the order book may look. Which measure works fastest? Reworking the terms: a deposit taken when the order is placed eases the bank account at once. Should the firm borrow instead? Short-term credit suits a passing shortfall, not a settled imbalance; applied to a structural fault, it merely hides the fever. How can fixed costs be lightened? By putting occasional jobs out to contract rather than keeping a workshop half idle. And if the trouble persists? Then the margin must be examined product by product, since one range sold at a loss swallows the profit made on the rest. Which figure deserves watching? The gap between money in and money out, checked every week, long before the yearly accounts.

units: a head of human resources sets out two options to the staff representative
the first option is to take on seasonal hands
the second option is to leave the extra load with the existing teams for higher pay
the representative holds that recruitment costs more in training
he holds that the second option wears down the existing teams
the head accepts that letting people go quickly would harm the firm's name
the representative counters that exhaustion cannot be ended like a contract
both sides settle on a middle course of limited extra hands and a bonus
a further meeting is planned before the season ends
text: The head of human resources set out his thinking to the staff representative, and put two courses before him. The first was to take on seasonal hands to absorb the rise in orders. The second was to leave the extra load with the teams already in post, paid at a higher rate. The representative answered that the first course cost more in training, while the second wore down the people who were there. The head accepted that letting workers go at the first slack spell would leave the firm with an ugly name, whereas an overload can be put right within a week. The representative countered that exhaustion, unlike a contract, cannot simply be ended. Both men settled on a middle course: a limited intake of extra hands, together with a bonus for the longer hours. They will meet again before the season closes.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the porter moved bales between the harbour and the warehouse
his pay depended on the weight he carried
the broker brought sellers and buyers together without touching the goods
the sworn weigher guaranteed the accuracy of the scales
the money changer exchanged coin come from elsewhere and took a share
the crier announced fresh arrivals in public
the scribe kept the register of debts
these trades have vanished or taken another name
each of these functions answered a lasting need of trade
text: Before machines took over, trade rested on callings whose names have faded from use. The porter hauled bales between the quayside and the warehouse; paid by the weight he carried, he wore out his back before middle age. The broker never laid a hand on the goods: he brought together a seller keen to clear his stock and a wary buyer. The sworn weigher stood behind the accuracy of the scales, and without him no bargain would have held. The money changer turned coin from elsewhere into coin that would pass here, and kept a share as he did so. The crier called out fresh arrivals in the square, there being no other way to advertise. The scribe, at the end of it, wrote down what was owed, since one man's memory rarely suited another's. Such work has gone or taken other names, yet each answered a need that trade has never stopped feeling.

units: at the start the owner lives off his savings and waits for buyers
the first visitors look without buying anything
a hard stretch follows in which money goes out faster than it comes in
half of the shops close during that stretch
a core of regular buyers eventually builds up
these regulars come back every week
word passed between neighbours then brings in new buyers
the owner ends up taking on a hand
the text insists on the slowness of the process and the absence of any miracle recipe
text: Wondering what becomes of a corner shop in the weeks after it opens? At first the owner lives off his savings: he pays the rent, fills the shelves and waits. In the early weeks the custom is mostly the merely curious, who wander in, have a look round and leave without buying. Then comes a harder stretch, when money goes out faster than it comes in, and that is where half of these shops pull the shutters down for good. If the owner holds on, a core of loyal buyers gradually builds up, households that come back week after week. From then on, a word passed over the garden fence carries the business along without him. In the end, once the slope eases, he takes on an assistant and gets his breath back. Nothing miraculous about any of it: a long hill, and two good legs to climb it with.

units: a fire destroyed a textile warehouse without injuring anyone
the rolls of cloth meant for three neighbouring workshops were lost
the workshops stopped their machines for want of material
the seamstresses paid by the piece went unpaid
a distributor cancelled its seasonal order
that cancellation removed the workshops' main source of income
a manager describes a week of unbroken telephone calls
the insurer covers the goods but not the lost contracts
owners in the trade now split their stock between two distant warehouses
text: A fire in a textile warehouse brought a whole supply chain to a halt, and the shock ran further than anyone thought it could. Nobody was hurt, but the rolls of cloth held there for three neighbouring workshops were lost. With no fabric coming in, those workshops shut down their machines; with nothing made, they had no way of paying the seamstresses, who earn by the piece. Further along, a distributor cancelled its seasonal order, stripping the same workshops of their main source of income. The manager of one site says the telephone rang without a break for a week, every call bringing one more consequence. The insurer will cover the cloth, but not the contracts that melted away. Since then, owners across the trade have split their stock between two warehouses far apart, a cost they had dismissed as needless.

units: the difficulty comes from the awkwardness of naming a sum out loud
the advice is to gather one's results on a single sheet
those results must be measured in output or in customers won
the request must be made during a quiet spell
the eve of a deadline must be avoided
the request is put in one short sentence followed by a silence
the silence must be left to the other person
if the answer is no one must ask what conditions would make agreement possible
the asker comes back on the agreed day with his notes
text: Asking for a rise is like crossing a narrow footbridge: the run-up counts as much as the footing. Everyone knows the difficulty, and it lies in the awkwardness that grips the voice at the moment a sum must be named. Here is how to go about it. Gather first, on a single sheet, what you have achieved since you took the post, measured in output or in customers won. Choose next a quiet spell, never the eve of a deadline. Put your request in one clean sentence, then hold your tongue: the silence that follows belongs to the person across the desk, and you must not fill it. If the answer is no, do not argue; ask what conditions would make agreement possible, and write them down with care. Come back on the agreed day, sheet in hand. Patience is not shyness: it keeps the rope taut without snapping it.

units: two neighbouring employment areas responded differently to the same industrial decline
the first drew in vast storage and distribution sheds
that first area shows a recovered level of activity but low wages
its workforce turns over quickly
the second area funded workshops repairing machinery
recovery there was slower but median earnings are higher
both areas received equivalent public support
the length of training explains the gap between the two models
elected representatives are now studying the method they used to criticise
text: Two neighbouring employment areas have met the same industrial decline with opposite results, to the plain surprise of those who study them. The first went after vast storage and distribution sheds; its level of activity is back, but wages are flattened and the workforce turns over fast. The second chose to fund small workshops repairing machinery; its recovery came slower, and yet median earnings there now sit above those of its neighbour. Both received much the same public support, which rules out any explanation drawn from budgets. The gap rests first on the skill demanded: a sorting job is learned in a week, a repairer's craft takes two seasons. So the second area keeps its workers, while the first watches them move on. The elected representatives are now studying the method whose slowness they used to mock.

units: the hall stands on a slab worn down by passing feet
the vegetable growers occupy the north side with their stacked crates
the cheese and preserve stalls run along one of the side walls
those stalls are held by families settled there for generations
the sellers of cloth and haberdashery gather under a patched glass roof
a coffee counter takes the opposite side and serves as a place to exchange news about prices
a central aisle wide enough for two carts crosses the building
a glazed office houses the keeper who allots the pitches and collects the fee
the sloping floor carries the washing water out to a gutter outside
text: The covered market hall stands on a slab worn smooth by barrows and by boot leather. Along the north side stand the vegetable growers, their crates stacked behind them like a low wall. Down one of the side walls run the cheese and preserve stalls, held by families who have passed them on for generations. Opposite, under a patched glass roof, gather the sellers of cloth, thread and buttons. The far side holds a coffee counter, where traders settle their accounts and swap news about prices. A central aisle, wide enough for two carts, divides these quarters and carries the buyers through. At the back, a glazed office houses the keeper of the hall, who allots the pitches and collects the fee owed. The floor, gently sloped, sends the washing water out to a gutter beyond the doors.

units: at first the working week had no legal limit
employers announced the ruin of the workshops should a limit be set
after the limit came output rose
the writer explains that rise by the cost of tiredness
the weekly day of rest was fought with the same arguments
paid time off met the same opposition
none of the collapses announced at each step took place
the same arguments now serve against a shorter week
the writer accepts that an old line of reasoning may cease to hold
he demands that those who repeat a contradicted forecast explain why it failed
text: Shorter hours are forever set against the survival of firms, and the quarrel gains from being put back in order of time. At the outset the working week ran on with no legal bound, and employers swore that any limit would ruin the workshop. The limit came; output rose, because tiredness cost more than absence. Then came the weekly day of rest, condemned in the same terms, and after it paid time off, fought with equal heat. Each step carried its own forecast of widespread collapse, and each forecast was proved wrong. We now hear those very sentences again, aimed at a shorter week. A word of caution: nothing guarantees that an argument sound yesterday is sound still. But whoever repeats a prophecy already contradicted three times over owes us, at the very least, some account of why it failed.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the manager runs a food depot
winter deliveries were arriving incomplete
the shops she supplied were running short of goods
she first blamed the hauliers and the suppliers
she understood that the muddle came from her own building
heavy goods were moved closer to the doors
lanes painted on the floor now organise movement
the handlers laughed at the change at first
the walking done by the teams grew shorter
not one order was missed the following season
text: The woman who runs a food depot knows the smell of damp cardboard better than anyone alive. Winter after winter the same ordeal came round: the lorries pulled in half empty, and the shops she was meant to supply ran short faster than she could fill them. She blamed the hauliers first, then the suppliers, before admitting that the muddle began inside her own building. So she thought the whole place through again. Heavy goods went by the doors, rare items to the back, and she painted coloured lanes across the floor that nobody crossed without a reason. The handlers laughed at her to begin with, then found their gain in it: their walking grew shorter. The season that followed, not one order was missed. She talks about it without pride, as a plain thing that took her several winters to notice.

units: two assembly workshops are set against each other
the first invested in a single costly machine
that machine cuts and folds with no operator
the second workshop lines up three modest benches set by hand
the output of the integrated plant beats that of the three benches
the single machine takes many seasons to pay for itself
a breakdown of the single machine halts all production
the modest benches are mended with ordinary parts
the integrated formula turns a profit if demand is steady and heavy
the writer concludes that the choice depends on the buyers
text: Setting the two assembly workshops side by side comes down to comparing two ways of committing money. The first backed a single costly machine, able to cut and fold with nobody at the controls. The second chose three modest benches, set by hand, which one operator watches in turn. On paper the integrated plant wins: it turns out more than its rival, and the line hand merely approves the settings. Watching them work softens that verdict. The single machine takes seasons to pay for itself, and the slightest breakdown freezes everything. The three benches seldom fail together, and they are mended offhand with ordinary parts. The integrated workshop turns a profit as soon as demand holds steady and heavy; the split workshop takes fitful orders better. The choice hangs on who is buying, not on the specification sheet.

units: the writer answers a request for advice in writing
the reader is starting out in the same trade
he advises reading contracts as far as the termination clauses
a shaky engagement shows itself in its annexes
he advises checking that the employer really pays the contributions
he advises keeping your payslips
he warns against rushing the pay talk out of embarrassment
a sum badly settled at the outset weighs for a long time
he urges keeping company with people in the same trade to hear about bad employers
the writer declares himself available should trouble arise
text: Madam, you asked what I would say to a beginner entering our trade, and I answer in writing gladly, so that nothing of it should get lost. First, contracts. Read them right through, the termination clauses included, for a shaky engagement gives itself away in its annexes rather than in its title. Second, cover. Make certain your employer truly pays the contributions owed for you, ask for your payslips and put them away. Third, pay. Do not rush a talk about money out of embarrassment: a sum badly settled at the outset will follow you through whole seasons. Fourth, company. Keep close to those doing the same work, for they will point you away from the doubtful houses. Lastly, spare your strength. I wish you a calm beginning, and I remain at your disposal should any trouble arise.

units: an employment adviser answers a run of questions
she puts the starting point in taking stock of your own skills
the second stage is spotting the employers who recruit without announcing it
then comes sending applications shaped to each firm
she warns that many refusals are to be expected
discouragement often arrives before the first interview
she advises writing every step down in a notebook
keeping that notebook turns waiting into actions you can measure
she advises preparing the interview by studying what the firm does
she urges against mistaking a slow selection for an injustice
text: Where does a job search begin? The adviser we questioned pushes the expected answer aside: you do not begin by writing, you begin by taking stock of what you can really do. And next? Next comes the stage of learning to prospect, that is, to spot the employers who are recruiting without saying so yet. Then you apply, one letter after another, shaping each one to the firm it goes to. How many refusals lie ahead? More than anyone pictures, she admits, and the weariness usually turns up before the first interview. What can be done then? Keep a notebook of every step taken, so that waiting becomes a run of actions you can measure. And the interview itself? You prepare it by studying what the firm does, instead of reciting your own path. Her last word is short: a slow selection is not an unjust one.

units: a neighbour tells the narrator about his picking season
he had been taken on for the length of the harvest
his pay depended on the number of crates filled
the crop came in heavy across the whole region
the buyers imposed half the usual price
the growers sold cheap to keep the fruit from rotting
the rate per crate came down
the pickers earned less for gathering more
he means to come back next season
he will insist on a rate written down before he leaves
text: Back from his picking season, the neighbour downstairs did not mince his words about any of it. He had been taken on for the whole harvest and paid by the crate, in an orchard where you slogged from first light to last. The crop had come in heavy everywhere, he told me, so the buyers laid down the law: they offered half the usual price, and the growers had to let their fruit go cheap rather than watch it rot. Down went the rate per crate, and the pickers earned less for gathering more. He shrugged his shoulders at me. When an orchard spills over, nobody gains, not even the one selling. He means to go back all the same, because he knows the place and knows where to sleep for nothing. But he warned me he would not set off again without a rate agreed beforehand and written on a signed paper.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: before common funds an accident ruined a family of craftsmen
the workshop hung on the bodily strength of one person
records tell of widows forced to sell the tools
apprentices were sent back to the countryside they came from
the answer came from the workshops themselves with no move from those in power
every member paid in a small sum at regular intervals
the fund replaced a ruined tool and kept an injured man fed
it also paid for the burial of a master craftsman
historians stress how slowly the idea took hold
the arrangement was later taken up by the public authorities
text: Before the trades gave themselves common funds, one accident was enough to ruin a family of craftsmen. The trouble was plain to all: the workshop rested on a single pair of hands, and those hands broke. Guild records describe widows forced to sell the tools in order to eat, and apprentices sent back to the countryside they had come from. The answer grew out of the workshops themselves, with no decree behind it. Every member paid in a small sum at regular intervals; the fund replaced a ruined tool, fed an injured man, met the burial costs of a master. What strikes historians is the slowness of the invention: it took generations to accept that a risk falls lighter when several carry it. Once the principle was granted, it ran from trade to trade, and the authorities copied it far later.

units: a fixed wage is likened to a river
the earnings of a self-employed worker are likened to showers
the wage earner can plan his spending because his income is regular
the self-employed worker knows rich spells and empty ones
the difference lies in regularity and not in the amount
on identical yearly earnings the self-employed worker gets a loan with more trouble
the lender is after regularity rather than wealth
the self-employed worker has to manufacture that regularity himself
he manages it by putting aside what the plentiful seasons leave him
text: A steady wage is much like a river, while the earnings of a self-employed worker are like rain. The river holds no more water than the rain does, but it flows. Whoever draws steady pay can plan his spending, sign a lease, promise a repayment, because he knows in advance the volume that will pass beneath his feet. Whoever lives on showers crosses rich weeks and dry ones: a great deal comes in, then nothing at all. The difference lies, then, not in the amount but in the shape of it. That is what lights up an odd fact: on equal yearly earnings, the second gets a loan with far more trouble than the first. A lender is not buying wealth, he is buying regularity. And the one who lives on rain must manufacture that regularity himself, by holding back what the plentiful seasons leave him.

units: a routine inspection was aimed at a packing plant
the inspector noted faults of four different kinds
pallets of resin were stored too close to the ovens
that exposure to heat explained the warping of certain batches
the dosing unit had gone too long without calibration
the setters corrected its drift by hand without writing it down
half the night shift lacked the certificate required
the pieces thrown out appeared in no accounting record
the site manager blamed the pressure of orders
the inspector puts these faults down to checking neglected over and over
text: It was meant to be a routine check at a packing plant, and the inspector came away from it with faults of four different kinds. Materials to begin with: the pallets of resin stored by the ovens had passed the heat tolerance, which explained the warped batches. Machines next: the dosing unit was running with no recent calibration, and its drift had been made good by hand by the setters, who had written none of it down anywhere. Staffing after that: half the night shift held posts without the certificate. Paperwork last: the pieces thrown out showed up nowhere at all in the production accounts. The manager of the site pleaded the pressure of the orders coming in. The inspector replied that nothing she had just found came from haste, but from checking done badly, season after season.

units: the procedure covers the opening of a retail shop
the steps must not be swapped around
the first is to gauge what the neighbourhood wants
that gauging goes through watching the passers-by and the shopfronts nearby
declaring the activity comes before any order of stock
the lease must carry a clause allowing you to leave
the first range is deliberately narrow to spare the cash
a trial week without advertising serves to adjust the prices
a record of goods in and goods out is kept from the first sale
text: Take these steps one by one in the order given, for the opening of a retail shop allows no swapping about. Start by gauging what the neighbourhood wants: count the passers-by, note the shopfronts nearby, ask those who live round about. Declare your activity next with the register kept for it, since no stock whatever may be ordered before that formality. Negotiate the lease then, insisting on a clause that lets you leave, for a badly chosen unit is harder to quit than to take. Build your first range after that, deliberately narrow: better to run short of an item than to lock up your cash. Open the doors quietly, without any fanfare, for a trial week, so as to adjust prices and hours. Keep, lastly, from the very first sale, a record of everything coming in and everything going out.

units: the closing of a cannery has been announced
the plant bought the catch of the fleet nearby
the skippers go out less and sell direct at a loss
the boatyards have cut their staff
the shops on the main street see fewer customers
the wages that were cut are no longer spent locally
elected members are calling for an investor to take the site over
no candidate has come forward because of the cost of renewing the cold chain
an association of employees proposes buying the plant together
the outgoing management has made no answer to that proposal
text: Since the closing of the cannery was announced, the employment area around it has taken one blow after another. The plant bought the catch of the local fleet; with no outlet left, the skippers put to sea less and sell direct, at a loss. The boatyards, which lived on their repair orders, have cut their staff in turn. The shops along the main street already report fewer customers, because the wages that were cut are no longer spent locally. Elected members are calling for an investor to take the site over, yet no candidate has come forward, the cold chain needing a costly renewal. An association of employees puts up another way out: buy the plant together and turn it to goods made in small runs. The outgoing management has made no answer. What becomes of the area will hang on that reply.

units: two joinery workshops stand on the same street
the first workshop shapes wood by hand with plain tools
the second workshop uses machines and employs three workers
the workers in the second workshop mostly watch screens
the hand workshop makes little but sells at a high price
the mechanised workshop makes a great deal and sells cheaply
the hand workshop depends on its reputation to survive
the mechanised workshop depends on the flow of orders
the two owners greet each other in the evening
text: Two joinery workshops stand at either end of the same shopping street. In the first, a seasoned cabinetmaker cuts the wood by hand. His tools are plain, his movements unhurried, and every piece leaves his palms after a long run of trial and error. In the second, machines slice identical boards, and three workers spend far more time watching screens than touching timber. The hand workshop shifts few pieces, yet each one goes for a high price, since the buyer pays for patience as much as for wood. The mechanised workshop shifts a great deal, cheaply, and leans on volume to cover heavier costs. The first lives as long as the reputation of the hand lasts; the second holds while the orders keep coming. In the evening the two owners nod to each other, aware that they sell the same thing by opposite routes.

units: the writer names three weaknesses in stock management
the first weakness concerns demand forecasting
forecasts rest on old records that are never corrected
warehouses fill up with items nobody buys
the second weakness concerns the costing of stock
a surplus of goods locks up cash that is needed elsewhere
the third weakness concerns the behaviour of buyers
managers order too much for fear of running short
the writer holds that correcting the forecast alone is not enough
text: Three weaknesses eat away at stock management among mid-sized manufacturers, and they deserve to be named plainly. The first sits in forecasting. Demand is projected from old records, with no correction for past breaks in supply, so warehouses fill up with goods nobody buys. The second sits in costing. A surplus batch locks up cash that will be missed elsewhere, and a crammed storeroom soon grows expensive to keep. The third sits in behaviour. Purchasing managers would rather order generously than face an empty shelf, an understandable reflex and a ruinous one. A loss-making year seldom grows out of one isolated mistake. It grows out of three habits that feed each other. Tightening the forecast while leaving untouched whatever rewards the buyers will bring nothing better than temporary relief.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman described runs a weaving cooperative
she started as an apprentice at a hand loom
her first job was to mend broken threads
the experienced weavers were glad to hand that job over
she was later moved to the receiving of raw materials
that post taught her about prices and delivery times
she trained in accounting away from the workshop
she proposed selling without going through a middleman
takings rose and the workshop took on more staff
text: The woman who now runs a weaving cooperative began her working life behind a hand loom, as an apprentice. Her first job was to tie up broken threads, a slow and thankless chore the experienced weavers were glad to hand over. After two seasons she was moved to goods inward, where the raw materials arrived, and there she learnt about prices, delivery times and margins. She then left the workshop to train in accounting, and came back with a precise proposal: supply the retailers directly, instead of going through a middleman who took his share along the way. The cooperative hesitated, then agreed to a limited trial. Takings rose, and two more spinners were taken on. Today she runs the house she knew as a child, and hands the delicate orders to the apprentices, as was once done for her.

units: a training scheme for jobseekers is assessed
the scheme is held to be useful but badly calibrated
the modules teach skills that are too narrow
employers want candidates who can move from one post to another
trainees find work but leave it quickly
the assessor puts those departures down to the narrowness of the training
spells inside a firm produce better outcomes
the assessor recommends longer spells inside a firm
text: The training scheme under review does genuine good, though the way it has been calibrated is open to question. Its modules teach narrow skills, cut to fit a single task, while employers are asking for candidates who can move from one post to another as the order book changes. The mismatch between the two shows up in an effect that can be measured. Trainees land a job quickly enough, then leave before the probation period is out, unable to cope with the side duties handed to them. Spells spent inside a firm produce far sturdier outcomes, most likely because the trainee watches the whole chain rather than one isolated link. The assessment therefore argues for longer spells of that kind, even at the cost of trimming the theory, which looks redundant beside the manuals handed out at the start.

units: the writer tells a friend about his soap business
making the soap by hand takes up all his evenings
the profits were too thin at the outset
the cost of sending parcels swallowed the margin
the writer has cut his catalogue back to three scents
he now leaves his crates at a shared depot instead of posting each parcel
the business has paid its way since those changes
the writer asks his friend to come and see the workshop
text: I owe you news of the soap business, and this letter of mine is a good deal later than it should be. You remember what I used to moan about: making the stuff by hand swallowed every evening of mine, and the profit stayed thin. Well, I have finally put my finger on the culprit. It was the sending out. Each parcel went off on its own, with its wrapping and its docket, and the margin melted away before it ever reached the buyer. So I made up my mind. I cut the catalogue back to three scents, the ones that always sold, and stopped chasing one-off orders. My crates now go to a shared depot, and the shopkeepers come and take what they want. Since then the business pays, and I sleep. Come and see the workshop when you are passing; you will judge the difference, and you will leave loaded.

units: an economist answers questions on the funding of new businesses
she compares a bank loan with letting an investor take a stake
a loan must be repaid even when trade falls away
a loan leaves the founder in command of his own choices
an investor asks for nothing if the venture fails
an investor wants a share of the decisions and of the profits to come
she advises borrowing for a trade with steady takings
she advises taking a partner for uncertain and costly projects
text: An economist who studies how young businesses are funded has agreed to sit down and take our questions. Borrow, or bring in a shareholder? She refuses to settle the matter in a single word, and lays out the comparison. A loan, she explains, sets a repayment date that falls due even when sales sag; against that, it leaves the founder in full command of his own choices. A partner taking a stake asks for nothing if the venture fails, but he buys a share of the decisions to come and of the profits to come. So which does she recommend? A trade with steady takings carries a fixed repayment easily and does well to borrow. An uncertain project, dear to set up and slow to pay off, will seldom survive without a partner willing to wait. It comes down, she says, to how regular the money coming in is.

units: two market traders talk once the covered market has shut
the fruit seller lists her difficulties
she mentions the rent on her pitch
she mentions the crates of damaged goods
she mentions her supplier arriving late
the cheese seller answers that her own troubles are different
the cheese seller mentions the cold she has to hold steady
the cheese seller mentions her customers growing fewer
the two traders agree to share a van
text: The shutters of the covered market had only just come down when the fruit seller began the long list of her troubles. She spoke of the rent on her pitch, which climbed every season while the aisle stayed as shabby as ever. She spoke of the battered crates, of the bruised peaches no buyer would take and she herself would carry home at dusk. She spoke last of her supplier, whose van pulled up after opening, once the shoppers had already come and gone. The cheese seller listened, then said her own troubles went by other names: the cold, hard to hold steady all day long, the electricity bill that follows it, and the queue at her counter thinning week by week. For a while neither of them said anything. Then they agreed to hire a van between them and fetch their crates together before dawn.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the text traces the coming of trade associations
the early craftsmen worked scattered and without shared rules
neighbouring workshops first agreed on identical measures
the next agreement covered the length of apprenticeship
the associations then set floor prices
floor prices sheltered members from competition on rates
the associations also decided who might open a workshop
that closing of the door ended up holding back new methods
the associations lost their power as manufactories grew
text: Before any organisation existed, craftsmen in the same trade worked each on his own, with no shared measure and no common rule. The first agreement between neighbouring workshops concerned size: a plank, a pot, a length of cloth had to answer to one template, or else the buyer had no way of comparing. Next came apprenticeship, whose length and stages were laid down. Trade associations, flourishing by then, extended their grip to rates as well, imposing a floor price that sheltered their members from ruinous undercutting. Finally they kept for themselves the right to allow a workshop to open, and that closing of the door, protective at the outset, discouraged fresh methods. Once manufactories gathered hundreds of hands under one roof, the associations lost their authority.

units: the text explains why a farm product grows dearer after a poor harvest
a poor harvest cuts the quantity to be had
the buyers stay as numerous as before
scarcity pushes up the price paid to the grower
the firms that process the crop pass the rise on to their own rates
some buyers turn instead to a substitute product
the heavier demand pushes up the price of the substitute as well
prices come down again when the next harvest is plentiful
text: A poor harvest does a good deal more than empty the granaries: it sets off a chain of effects that runs all the way to the market stall. The quantity to be had falls while the buyers stay as numerous as before, so each of them agrees to pay more to secure his own share, and the price handed to the grower climbs. Firms that process the crop watch their own bills swell in the same way, and pass the weight on to the rates they charge. Part of the custom then gives up and turns to a neighbouring foodstuff. That shift has a consequence few people expect: the substitute, suddenly in heavy demand, grows dearer in its turn, even though its own harvest was an ordinary one. Balance comes back only with a generous season, when the granaries fill again and the pressure on prices slackens.

units: a bakery in a small town threw away part of its baking every evening
the baker baked the same quantity without regard to what sold
the waste threatened to unbalance the accounts of the shop
the apprentice wrote down the unsold loaves over several weeks
the record showed that the waste piled up at the end of the week
the batch at the end of the week was cut back
the loaves left on the shelves are sold cheaply before closing
the waste has fallen sharply
a neighbouring shop copied the method
text: Every evening the baker of a small valley town filled a sack with the loaves nobody had taken, and the sack went off to the farm nearby. He had baked the same quantity since the day he opened, without a glance at what actually sold, and the waste was gnawing at an already thin margin. The apprentice suggested counting. Over several weeks she wrote down in an exercise book how many loaves came back, what shape they were, which flour had gone into them. The record left no room for doubt: the waste piled up at the end of the week, when families baked for themselves. So the last batch of the week was cut by a third, and whatever still sat on the shelves half an hour before closing went at a knock-down price. The waste shrank, the till breathed, and the butcher across the road, who had watched it all, began keeping the same book.

units: a newly learnt idea leaves at first an unsteady mental trace
that trace is made firm above all during sleep
networks of neurons replay the acquired sequence during that phase
going over the material too soon after learning brings almost no gain
a slight forgetting before the review increases its effect
recalling without help fixes the material better than reading it again
specialists advise widening the gap between two reviews step by step
writing the idea down and then trying to say it back from memory produces lasting knowledge
text: Understanding an idea in class is not the end of learning it. What the brain lays down at first is a faint trace, and a faint trace rubs out easily. The work that makes it hold comes later, above all while we sleep: networks of neurons run the newly acquired sequence again and again until it settles. Go over the material straight away and you gain almost nothing, because none of it has faded yet. Wait until it has begun to slip, and the mind must rebuild what it lost, and that effort of recall fixes far more than another read-through ever will. This is why specialists on learning tell you to stretch the gap between reviews, a little wider each time. Write the idea on a card, put the card away, then try to say the whole thing back without looking: what you keep that way, you keep.

units: a bookbinding workshop came close to shutting down
its last craftsman lost the use of one of his hands
the movements of the trade had never been written down
the manager had the craftsman recorded while he described each operation
an apprentice carried out the movements while he corrected her aloud
out of it came a manual naming the commonest fault at every stage
the workshop carried on and drew applicants from far away
the injury of one man set off the writing down of a practice until then spoken
text: A bookbinding workshop came within days of shutting when its last craftsman lost the use of one hand. Nothing of the trade had ever been set down on paper; the whole of it lived in the fingers of that one man, and the manager knew it would go with him. So she had him recorded while he talked his way through every operation, from sewing the sections to gluing the spine, laying the headbands and paring the leather. An apprentice did the work with her own hands, and he watched and corrected her aloud. Out of that came a manual nobody had planned, one that named, at each stage, the mistake most people make. The workshop stayed open, and word of the manual drew applicants from far away. An injury to a single pair of hands had put a wholly spoken craft into writing for the first time.

units: the words are missing at the moment of giving back what has been noted
the method offered rests on a notebook kept for that purpose alone
every page is divided into two columns of unequal width
the wide column takes the word as it was met and a whole sentence holding it
the narrow column takes a definition worded by the learner himself
a mark is added each week the word still slips away
words gathering too many marks are copied out apart and gone over aloud
at the end of a season the notebook forms a word list belonging to its own author
text: Your notes pile up and nothing sticks to them: the moment you have to say it back, the words are not there. The remedy is a slim notebook kept for that purpose alone. Rule every page into two columns of unequal width. In the wide one, put down the word as you met it, along with a whole sentence that carries it. In the narrow one, write a definition in your own wording, never lifted from somewhere else. Each week the word still slips away from you, add a small mark beside it. Once a word has gathered too many marks, copy it out on its own sheet, then stand up and go through that sheet aloud with the definition hidden. By the end of a season the notebook has turned into a word list that belongs to nobody but you, and every entry in it carries the trace of what it cost you.

units: two local workshops announce the same aim of mending things oneself
the first workshop is run as a lecture from the front
those attending the first leave with papers they will never open again
the second workshop is built around the machines brought in by those who come
there one gets on by sitting beside someone who has already taken a similar machine apart
the organisers of the second admit that their way of doing it is muddled and noisy
those attending the second come back while those of the first grow fewer
the gap between the two workshops comes from where the question starts
text: Two neighbourhood workshops make exactly the same promise: teaching ordinary people to mend their own broken things. The first one runs like a lecture. A trainer talks from the front, holds up the tools, hands round a printed booklet, and everybody goes home with a wad of paper they will never open again. The second runs on whatever people carry through the door. You sit beside someone who has already had the back off a machine like yours, and you get on by following your own fault to the end of it. The pair who run the second are the first to call their way of doing it noisy, muddled and impossible to grade. Yet their lot turn up again the week after, while the lecture crowd thins out by the third evening. The difference is not in the kit on the table. It is in who asks the question.

units: a smell of white dust takes hold as soon as one enters the room
a worn raised platform carries a narrow table and a chair that does not match
a dark board runs the whole width of the wall and keeps strokes that will not rub out
the rows of school desks each keep a hollow groove now left unused
notches were cut into the wood by impatient hands
boxes of yellowed writings are piled along the ledge of the openings
a glazed cupboard holds rolled maps a skeleton and jars
the room now serves as a store although nothing has been taken out of it
text: Push the door and the chalk dust catches you at once, dry and faintly damp at the same time. At the far end, a low wooden platform worn hollow by boot leather carries a narrow table and a chair that never matched it. A black board runs the whole width of the wall, scored with pale strokes that no cloth will lift now. The desks stand in rows, each keeping its groove for the ink well, long dry, and its notches cut into the wood by hands with nothing better to do. Along the window ledge sit boxes of yellowed exercise papers covered in a careful hand. A glazed cupboard holds rolled maps, a wooden skeleton and dusty jars whose labels are peeling off. Nothing was thrown out and nothing replaced: the room is a store now, and you walk into it as into a memory left standing open.

units: the ease of deleting a word harms the teaching of writing
the pupil of former times left the mark of his waverings on the page
the rough draft was held to be the proof of a path of thought
the coming of electronic supports made correction invisible
a deleted mistake can no longer be read again by the one who made it
one gets better by going back over what one missed and not by handing in a clean page
the teacher deprived of the rough draft judges only an outcome
the writer argues for giving the marks of correction their standing back
text: Deleting has become too easy, and the teaching of writing loses more by it than we care to admit. A pupil once wrote in ink, and the page held on to every wavering: a crossing-out, a word called back into the margin, a sentence begun again two lines lower. The rough draft was no waste paper. It was the proof that a mind had travelled. Then came the screens, where a correction leaves no scar at all. The pupil deletes, the error evaporates, and with it goes any chance of reading that error again. Yet nobody learns by handing in a clean page. We learn by going back over what we got wrong. A teacher shown only the finished version has no sight of the thinking; a destination is marked and the journey lost. Give the crossing-out its standing back, and error becomes a tool once more.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman teaching at the workshop earlier worked as a potter
a condition of the joints forced her to give up the wheel
that injury is the reason she moved to teaching
she can no longer show a movement over a long stretch of time
she therefore cut every movement into short steps named with precision
her pupils receive words that other workshops leave unspoken
her apprentices get on faster than those trained by copying alone
being able to describe a fault before putting it right explains that lead
text: The woman who teaches at the pottery workshop spent most of her working life at the wheel herself. Inflamed joints in both wrists took that away from her, and it is the injury, not a calling, that put her in front of a class. Since she can no longer keep her hands on the clay for a whole session to show how it is done, she had to break the work into short steps and give each one an exact name: centring, opening, raising the wall, smoothing. Her pupils come away with words that most workshops never bother to say out loud, because there the thing is simply copied. That has had an effect nobody foresaw. Her apprentices move ahead faster than those taught by copying, since they can put a fault into words before they put it right. One woman's damaged wrists changed how a whole trade is taught.

units: the book of exercises is addressed to apprentice carpenters
its material making and its pictures are held to be of good quality
the rising order of the difficulties looks carefully thought out
the work shows only movements that came out right and never ones that went wrong
a learner who gets it wrong finds no page describing his fault
that absence leads the learner to lay the blame for failure on himself alone
the writer of the review suggests adding facing it the picture of the spoiled piece
he also suggests joining to that picture the question to ask oneself before it
text: The book of exercises written for apprentice carpenters has a flaw that no amount of good making can redeem. The binding is sound, the drawings are clean, and the ladder of difficulty has clearly been thought about at length. Where it fails is on one decisive point: it shows the cut that came out right, and never the cut that came out wrong. An apprentice who saws off the line finds no page telling him what a fault looks like, or what it does to the joint once assembled. He tends to conclude that the failure lies in him alone. Putting this right would cost little. Facing each plate, the makers need only set a picture of the spoiled piece, and beside that picture the question to ask when you are standing over it. That one addition would turn a handsome object into a teaching tool.

units: the reader is torn between evening lessons and going straight into apprenticeship
the writer of the letter has followed both of these paths
the evening teaching announces its programme and marks the exercises
on that path a failure costs no more than a harsh comment
the workshop announces nothing and one learns there by starting again after getting it wrong
a mistake made in the workshop is paid for in spoiled material
the writer advises beginning with the evening lessons
he recommends noting down what one fails to understand in a notebook before turning up at the workshop
craftsmen willingly take in a newcomer who brings precise questions
text: You ask me whether to take the evening lessons or go straight into the workshop as an apprentice. I have done both, and what separates them has stayed with me. The lessons come in order: you are told what will be covered, your exercises come back marked, and failing costs you nothing worse than a harsh comment on the page. The workshop tells you nothing in advance. You watch, you get it wrong, you begin again, and getting it wrong there is paid for in ruined material. What you gain is a steadiness that no lesson hands over. My advice is short. Start with the lessons, keep a small notebook of everything you fail to understand, then turn up at the workshop with those pages in your pocket. The trade takes kindly to anyone who arrives with a precise question. Write and tell me what you choose.

units: the question asked bears on what parts a trainer who marks people from one soon forgotten
the woman running a retraining centre puts the difference down to patience with being asked the same thing again
she names first the listening that lets the learner finish his mistaken sentence
she names next the cutting of the task into portions small enough to keep failure away
she names the bad example where the trainer performs the wrong movement himself before everyone
she names last the silence kept while the learner is working the answer out
the poor trainer talks too much and moves on too fast
he takes the neatness of his own account for understanding among those listening
she holds that one becomes a trainer by watching others get it wrong
text: So what makes one trainer stay with you for years while another goes clean out of your head? The woman who runs a retraining centre answers without pausing: patience with being asked the same thing again. Then she breaks it down. Listening comes first, since a good trainer lets you finish the wrong sentence instead of cutting across it. Then the slicing: the task is cut into pieces so small that failing at one is hard. Then the bad example, where she makes the wrong move herself, in front of the room, and owns it. Last of all, silence, because she keeps quiet while the learner is getting there. And the poor trainer? Talks too much, pushes on too fast, and takes the neatness of his own account for understanding in the room. Nobody, she adds, becomes a trainer by reciting. You become one by watching people get it wrong.

units: a teacher points out to her pupil that the tool warps when the force applied changes
she asks him to go through the movement again slowly
the pupil says he followed the written instructions
the pupil admits he did not grasp the wording of the final point
the teacher explains that heat swells the metal and throws off the reading
she says the source of a fault is seldom where the fault shows
the pupil notices that the cutting waste is winding badly
the pupil works out on his own that the angle of the tool must change
the teacher holds that this reasoning carries over to other machines
she reckons a trade is handed on through an understanding of cause and effect
text: The instructor warns her apprentice that the blade twists the moment his wrist pushes harder or softer. She has him set the tool down and work through the same movement again, slowly. He protests that he followed the written instructions to the letter, then owns up to never having made sense of the wording of the final point. She takes it apart for him: the hand bears down too early, the work heats, the metal swells with the heat, and the reading goes astray. Faults, she adds, seldom begin where they show themselves. The apprentice watches the swarf curling out of the cut and sees that it is winding badly. The angle of the tool has to change, he says, and gets there unaided. She agrees, and tells him that reasoning will carry him through any machine on the floor. A trade, to her mind, passes on as an understanding of what causes what, not as copied movement.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: knowledge once rested on human memory alone
the death of a teacher took part of his doctrine with him
learned circles looked for a lasting remedy
reciting together spread the effort of remembering across several people
a slip by one reciter was caught by another
setting the words down under dictation then held what speech kept badly
the method called for trained copyists and a check made term by term
mistakes of copying became the new danger
checking by two readers comparing aloud put that flaw right
the piling up of these precautions made a doctrine carry across long stretches of time
text: Before writing, all that a community knew rested on memory alone, and that left it badly exposed: when a teacher died, a portion of his doctrine went out with him. Learned circles set about finding a lasting remedy. They took up recitation in company, which spread the burden of remembering across many mouths rather than one. Where a single voice faltered, another carried the line, and the whole survived. Dictation came next, fixing on a surface what speech held badly. It called for trained copyists and a check made term by term. Slips of the pen now became the danger, and the answer to them was a second reading, two people comparing versions aloud, line against line. Piled one on another, these safeguards are why a body of teaching could cross generation after generation without buckling.

units: two ways of teaching a skilled movement exist side by side
the first has the trainer perform while the learner watches and then copies
that route suits flowing movements which words render poorly
it leaves the learner stranded once conditions shift
the second names and justifies every stage
it asks for more effort at the outset
it hands over a rule that holds in other settings
seasoned trainers run the two approaches together
they ask the learner to describe the movement he has just watched
moving between watching and speaking beds the learning down more firmly
text: Two ways of teaching a skilled movement sit side by side, and neither one works everywhere. The first is showing: the trainer performs, the learner watches, then copies. It carries flowing movements across quickly, the very ones that speech handles poorly. Its weakness appears the moment conditions shift, because the learner is left with nothing to steer by. The second is telling: every stage is given a name, an order and a reason. More effort goes in at the start, yet the learner walks away with a rule that holds elsewhere too. Trainers who have been at it a while run the two together. They demonstrate, then insist the learner recount what he has just watched, in his own words. That to and fro between the eye and the tongue beds the learning down far more firmly than either route on its own. The comparison crowns no winner, then. It points to a balance.

units: a neighbour tells of his first days in the workshop of a relative
he builds his account around three memories
he had been given the least steady bench
he grasped that the faulty piece of furniture was part of the test set for him
he laid a pattern the wrong way round and spoiled a stack of boards
the team still find that blunder funny
not one workmate explained anything of his own accord
everything opened up once he began questioning the old hands
the old hands would answer so long as they were asked
he now hands that lesson on to the beginners in his charge
text: A neighbour of mine told me about his first days in his uncle's workshop, and the whole thing came down to three memories. There was the bench: they gave him the wobbliest of them, the one that rocked as soon as any weight went on it, and he worked out soon enough that the furniture was part of the test. There was the stencil: set to mark up a run of boards, he laid the pattern the wrong way round and spoiled the lot, which the team still laugh about. And there was the silence. Nobody explained a thing. A tool went into his hand and that was that. In the end he started asking, and everything opened up. The old hands answered gladly enough.
