They simply wanted to be asked first. He passes the lesson on now to the beginners under his eye: keep quiet and you learn two years the slower.

units: the session opens with materials being handed out to those taking part
each of them is given a rough piece of wood and a template of stiff card
they check that the corner is true with a measuring tool
any warped piece is set aside at that stage
the outline of the template is carried over in one unbroken line
the trainer sends uneven markings back to be done again
after a break the measurements are carried over onto the other face
that transfer brings every discrepancy out at once
the session ends with everyone showing the mistakes they have put right
cutting is held over until the following meeting
text: In the training workshops where marking out is taught, the session opens with the handing out of materials. Each person is given a rough board and a template cut from stiff card. The square goes against the edge of the board next, so that the corner can be checked as true, and any board that has warped is set aside there and then. Then comes the marking: the outline of the template is followed with a fine point, the hand never lifting mid-line. The trainer walks the benches and sends anyone whose line wavers back to the start. A break follows. Afterwards the measurements are carried over onto the reverse face, which throws up every discrepancy at once. The session closes with everyone gathering round, each holding up the work and naming the mistake put right. No cutting happens before the following meeting.

units: adults are writing again in the room beneath a former storage building
they had left writing behind a very long time ago
a body of local residents lends the premises for nothing
with no official body over it the place spares newcomers the feeling of going back to school
the woman running the sessions says shame turns people away more than the difficulty of the subject
the shape of the room carries the voices
so those taking part hear one another read
that shared listening breeds a rivalry between them
a former factory worker has moved from copying to writing on her own
each stage of her progress leans on the one before it
text: In the low room beneath a former warehouse, a handful of adults are writing again after decades away from it. The building is lent by a cooperative of local residents, and that free loan does what no budget could have bought: since the place answers to no authority, nobody coming through the door feels they are going back to school. The woman who runs the sessions puts it plainly. Shame turns more people away than difficulty ever does. The tables are wide and the ceiling high, so voices carry, and because voices carry, everyone hears everyone else reading. Out of that listening a quiet rivalry grows. A former factory worker describes how she copied first, then dictated to the woman beside her, then wrote on her own. The chain is a patient one, yet each link holds because the one before it held.

units: this training bench can be raised and lowered
its top is pierced with holes at even spacing
beginners hold the work badly and it drifts under the tool
pegs dropped into the holes lock the work without any grip of the hand
the top is of a hard wood that still spares the cutting edges
a rail along the side holds the measuring tools
that stowing keeps the working surface clear
a container underneath gathers the waste from cutting
collecting it that way cuts down the risk of a fall
a groove at the front takes the learner's instruction sheets
text: What strikes you first about a training bench is that it rises and drops to suit whoever stands at it, and that its top is pierced with holes at even spacing. Those holes answer an old problem: a beginner grips the work badly, it creeps under the tool, and the cut wanders off the line. Drop pegs into the holes and the work sits still, with no vice and no strength of hand called for. The top is solid beech, dense enough to take a knock, soft enough to leave a cutting edge alone. A rail along the side holds the square and the rule, which stay within reach instead of cluttering the working surface. Underneath sits a tray that gathers shavings and offcuts, so that nothing ends up underfoot. At the front runs a groove where the learner tucks the instruction sheets. Every part of it answers a difficulty seen in beginners.

units: learning by heart and learning by enquiry are often held to be at odds
the writer finds that rivalry groundless
with nothing held in mind the learner merely gropes about
the learner who does no more than remember recites a contents page without knowing what lies behind it
both of them fail because they pull apart operations that belong together
memorising asks for effort at the outset and then gives effort back
it leaves the attention free for weightier work
enquiry stays costly at every stage
it teaches how to put forward a claim, test it and give it up
the writer urges that the two be combined rather than one of them chosen
text: Learning by heart and learning by enquiry are set against each other far too readily, as though one had to drive the other out. The quarrel strikes me as badly framed. A learner with nothing held in mind does not enquire at all. He gropes about, having no material to put together. A learner who has only committed things to memory recites a contents page without ever having opened the volume. Both fail, and for the same reason: they pull apart what the mind joins. Weigh the effort each of them asks for. Memorising costs at the outset and pays back later, leaving the attention free for weightier work. Enquiry costs at every stage, yet it teaches you to put forward a claim, to test it, and to let it go. One makes for speed, the other for caution. Any serious training measures out both and declines to choose.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: nobody close to her had worked at a craft before she did
her path falls into three parts
she began her apprenticeship while others of her age were still studying
she learned above all by watching an older craftswoman who said very little
she brings damaged books back and rebuilds the parts that have suffered
she turns away any commission that comes with too short a deadline
she first builds a model in plain paper to try out her choices
she keeps her teaching down to two pupils a season by choice
that limit lets her put a movement right as it happens
she will not write a book, holding that the craft passes from hand to hand
text: Nobody in her family had worked with their hands before her. The bookbinder's path falls into three parts. Training first: she took up an apprenticeship at an age when others of her years were still at their studies, and what she learned came mostly from watching the hands of an older woman who said very little. The trade next: she brings damaged volumes back, resews the sections, rebuilds the headbands, and turns away any commission that arrives with a hurried deadline. Before delicate work she builds a dummy of the book in plain paper, so her choices can be tried without the original at stake. Passing it on, last of all: two pupils a season come to her workshop, never more, since she means to catch every movement as it happens. She will not write a manual. One hand, she says, teaches another hand.

units: the writer comes away from this woodworking course in two minds
the opening sessions won him over
a booklet handed out at the start set out a clear progression
the tutor kept to a pace the newcomers could hold
the number taking part swelled because enrolments were accepted too late
those on the course had to wait because there were not enough tools
a good part of each session went by watching other people
the organiser split the group to put matters right
the writer holds that the decision came too late
he would recommend the course only if numbers are capped in advance
text: I came away from this woodworking course in two minds, and it is worth telling in order. The opening sessions really did win me over. We were handed a booklet whose contents page set out a clear progression, and the tutor kept things moving without leaving the newcomers behind. Then the group swelled, because enrolment was left open far too late. From that point on you queued for your turn at the only saw, and half a session could go by watching other people work. The organiser did respond, splitting the group in two, which I was glad enough of, though the remedy arrived very late in the day. The closing sessions clawed back a fair part of the lost ground. I would recommend the course on one condition, that numbers be capped at enrolment. The content is sound. The running of it is not.

units: the person the message is addressed to teaches a manual trade to beginners
the beginners lose control of the movement as soon as they are no longer guided
the writer blames the way the trade is taught rather than the learners
the demonstration is at present given in one stretch, with no pause
the proposed remedy is to break the run of movements into three parts
each part ends with a noticeable cue that the learner can check unaided
a short marking sheet, filled in by the learner, tells a clean result from a rough one
the writer advises keeping the breakdown in writing for the next group
text: Dear colleague, I have finally got round to your question about the learners who lose the movement the moment you let go of their hands. The fault sits in the teaching, not in them. You run through the whole sequence in one stretch, then ask them to give it back in a single go, and the memory of the movement cannot carry that much. Break the run into three parts, and end each part with a cue they can notice on their own: the tool coming to rest at a set angle, or a sound the material makes. They stop, they check, they carry on. Add a short marking sheet they fill in themselves, so that a clean result is never taken for a rough one. After a week of fumbling most of them will hold the whole run unaided. Put your breakdown on paper and keep it, because the next group will need it. Tell me how it stands up at your bench.

units: the first question sets teaching one to one against teaching a whole group
one to one bends the pace to the learner and catches a mistake as it appears
the group puts the learner in front of the reasoning of the others
the group forces everyone to say out loud what they thought they had mastered
one to one is expensive because it ties up one trainer for each learner
the group shares the effort but thins out the trainer's attention
the managers questioned advise alternating the two arrangements
one and the same marking scale applied to both arrangements distorts the comparison
text: A listener asks whether teaching one to one beats teaching a whole group. The answer turns on what you choose to measure. Working one to one bends the pace to the learner and catches a mistake as it appears, before it hardens into a habit. A group does something else. It puts each learner in front of the reasoning of the others, and it makes everyone say out loud what they had assumed they knew. A second question turns to cost. One trainer for each learner is a costly arrangement, and that is what keeps it rare, whereas a group shares the effort out but thins the trainer's attention. Must one be chosen? The managers questioned favour alternating the two. The group session lays down the common ground, the private hour clears the blockages it leaves standing. A last question concerns marking. One scale for both distorts the comparison, since they aim at different things.

units: a man working at a bookbinding workshop reports a conversation with a visitor
the visitor wanted to know what the training covered
the man sorts the learning into three groups
the first group covers knowledge of materials and of marks left by old workshops
the second group covers carrying out the movements
the third group rests on stamina, and that is the one that makes people give up
half the apprentices give up before the end of their first season
the departures come when the apprentice is asked to decide with no model to follow
the man judges success by the absence of fingermarks on the leather
text: A man who works at a bookbinding workshop described a conversation he had with a visitor. She wanted to know what the training actually covered. He told her it falls into three sorts of thing. The first is the material: telling one paper from another, picking a glue, reading the marks an old workshop left behind. The second is the hand: folding without crushing, sewing at an even tension, pressing a cover without bruising it. The third, he said, is stamina, and stamina is what sends people away. She asked how many give up. Half of them, he said, go before their first season is out, usually at the point where nobody shows them anything any more and they have to decide for themselves. She asked what best marks out a good one. He pointed at the leather. A steady hand, he said, leaves no fingermarks on it at all.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: at the outset the learner lodged with the master in order to learn a trade
the learner watched for several seasons before being allowed a tool
trade bodies then imposed set stages and a fixed length of training
the learner had to put a piece of work before the judgement of established craftsmen
a refusal obliged the learner to start the piece again
as workshops grew, the master could no longer follow each learner
the methods of the trade were then written down in books
technical schools took over, with syllabuses and examinations
the change brought steadiness and lost some of the attention given to one learner
text: To begin with, learning a trade was nothing like school. You moved in with a master, slept under his roof, and watched him work for whole seasons before anyone let you touch a tool. Then came the trade bodies, which pinned the thing down with set stages and a set length of training. You had to put a piece of work in front of established craftsmen and wait for their verdict, and if they turned it down you started it again. Workshops grew, and no master could keep an eye on every learner any more, so the tricks of the hand went into books and the learner had to puzzle them out alone. Last came the technical schools, with their syllabuses, their classes and their examinations. Every step bought steadiness and gave away a little of the care an old master could spend on one learner. Nobody has settled that argument yet.

units: reading a chapter again gives the false impression of having mastered it
the familiarity of the text is mistaken for having learnt it
rereading draws on recognition whereas the paper calls for recall
because recognition comes easily, the learner stops revising too soon
the learner then finds the gaps at the moment of sitting the paper
saying the content back with the book shut brings the gaps out
the difficulty felt during recall strengthens what is held in memory
the practical consequence is to turn every page into a question put to oneself
learners drilled that way hold more a year later without revising any more
text: Read a chapter over again and it begins to feel like yours. The words come easily, the eye slides on, and that smoothness gets mistaken for something held in memory. Researchers who study learning point to where the muddle starts. Rereading leans on recognition, while the paper calls for recall, and the two are not the same act at all. Recognition costs nothing, so revision stops early and the gaps only show up over the answer sheet. Shut the book, try to say the chapter back, and the opposite happens. It costs something, the holes appear at once, and that very struggle is what fixes the trace. A practical rule follows from it: turn every page you have read into a question you put to yourself. Learners drilled that way still hold more a year on, without having spent an hour more on revision.

units: a learner was stuck on the same line throughout the session
his voice weakened as his discomfort grew
the usual teacher took him for a slow learner
a teacher standing in for a while looked at the way he held the page
the learner tilted the sheet and followed the line with his fingernail
the teacher gave him a strip of card with an opening cut in it
the opening laid over the line stopped the words from running together
the learner first said the letters one by one, then read a whole sentence
the teacher left an account of the method on a card in a drawer
text: The boy had been stuck on the same line since the very start of the session. He ground out the syllables, went back, lost his place, and his voice thinned as the discomfort in it rose. His own teacher had simply written him off as a slow reader. A woman standing in for a week watched the way he held the page. He tilted the sheet and ran a fingernail under the line. She handed him a strip of card with a slot cut in it. He slid the slot along the line, and the words stopped running into one another. He spelled at first, then joined the syllables, then read a whole sentence without stopping for breath. She said nothing about any of it, but she wrote the method on a card and left it in the drawer of the front desk. Two seasons on, the boy was reading aloud to his class without a stumble.

units: the reader must pick one of the two methods and stay with it
the first method rests on writing the list out again and again
once the list is covered, it is written from memory and then checked
the first method suits lists that are short
the second method consists of making cards with a question and an answer
the answer is given aloud and the cards already mastered are set aside
the second method holds off forgetting better on long lists
the same mock test a week later decides between the two methods
using both together would make it impossible to tell which one worked
text: Before you set about learning a list of terms, pick one of the two methods below and stay with it to the end. The first is copying. Write the list out in full, cover it over, then put down again whatever comes back to you. Check it against the original, cross out what went wrong, and start over on a clean sheet. It puts the hand to work, and it serves well when the list is short. The second is questioning. Cut the list into cards, one idea to a card, the question on the front and the answer on the back. Shuffle them, answer aloud, and set aside the ones that give you no trouble. Over a long list this second method holds off forgetting better. Sit the same mock test a week later, and keep whichever leaves you hesitating less. Do not run both at once in that first week, or you will never know which of them did the work.

units: a training centre housed in a former market hall received reporters
its head set out three pieces of work under way
the first concerns taking in adults who are moving to another trade
half of those adults have not studied since they left school
the second rearranged the workshops so that every work station is in view
that visibility makes dangerous handling easier to watch over
the third brings forward the checking of what has been learnt, judged too late
a short check now closes each session and gives the learner a point of comparison
mentoring by former learners is meant to bring down the number who give up
text: A training centre housed in a former market hall has opened its doors to reporters. Its head set out three pieces of work under way. The first is recruitment. The centre now takes in adults moving from one trade to another, half of whom have not studied since the day they left school. The second is the building. Workshops have been rearranged so that every work station can be seen from the central aisle, which makes dangerous handling far easier to watch over. The third is the checking of what has been learnt, which trainers had complained came far too late. A short check now closes each session and gives the learner something to measure against. Asked about learners who give up, she granted that there are still many in the first season, and announced mentoring run by former learners, who know the obstacles from having cleared them.

units: a low room with whitewashed walls serves as a writing workshop for adults
each table is laid out with a sheet, a pencil and a book of models
the tutor draws a letter of unusual size on the board
the participants leaf through the book of models before writing anything
each of them then copies the letter ten times over, watching the tilt of the pencil
halfway through the session, the tutor puts the wrists back in position
the strokes become steadier as the session goes on
each of them cuts out their best line and pastes it into a shared notebook
the shared notebook hangs near the way into the room
text: A low room with whitewashed walls serves as a writing workshop for a group of adults. Before anyone arrives, each table is laid out with a blank sheet, a sharpened pencil and a book of models. The tutor opens the shutters, then draws a letter on the board at an unusual size. The others come in, settle down, and begin by leafing through the book of models without writing a thing. Each of them then copies the letter ten times over, keeping an eye on the tilt of the pencil. Halfway through, the tutor walks between the rows and puts the wrists back in position. The sheets fill with strokes that are ragged at first and steadier later. At the end, everyone cuts out their best line and pastes it into a shared notebook that hangs by the way in. The room empties, the pencils go back in their box, and the notebook keeps the record.

units: the writer disputes the idea of replacing general subjects with short courses
those short courses are cut to fit one particular job
what a job consists of changes over the course of a working life
training fitted too closely becomes useless once the equipment changes
the lasting abilities are getting through a hard manual and reasoning over a drawing
putting a precise question to a colleague is one of those lasting abilities
these abilities come by a long detour and look useless while they are being taught
that apparent uselessness makes them easy to cut from syllabuses
the writer holds that practice with no theoretical detour turns out interchangeable operatives
text: Everyone repeats that school ought to prepare people for work, and a hasty conclusion gets drawn from it. Scrap the general subjects, the argument runs, and put in short courses cut to fit one particular job. The intention is decent enough. The result is ruinous. What a job consists of will not stay the same across a working life, and training tailored that closely is worth nothing the moment the equipment changes. What lasts is the ability to get through a hard manual, to reason over a drawing, to put a clean question to the person at the next bench. Such things are picked up by a long detour, and they look useless at the very moment they are taught, which is what makes them easy to cut. So we save on what prepares people best, and pay later in retraining that fails. A workshop with no detour through theory turns out operatives that anyone could swap for anyone else.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a workshop supervisor uses two ways of teaching
the first consists in showing the movement and then having it copied
the second lets the learner work it out alone before any correction
copying gives sound results within the first week
what is learnt by copying is poorly retained
working it out alone multiplies mistakes and wastes material
the learner who has searched understands the reason for each movement
faced with a new task the copier hesitates and the searcher adjusts
the trainer blends the two approaches according to the danger of the operation
text: The man who runs the workshop teaches his apprentices in two ways, and he never tires of setting one against the other. In the first, he performs the movement himself, slows down each stage and then hands the tool over to be copied. In the second, which he trusts more, the learner is left to fumble at the material alone until he asks to be put right. Copying gives clean work inside the first week, yet it leaves a thin trace in the memory. Fumbling wastes stock and breeds mistakes, and the learner who comes through it has grasped why every movement is made. Put an unfamiliar job in front of the two and the difference shows: the copier stalls, however careful, while the one who has searched shifts his grip and carries on. So the supervisor mixes the two, keeping demonstration for the dangerous work and free exploration for the joints that can hurt nobody.

units: the reviewer notes three merits and two faults in this manual for beginners
the ideas are introduced in short linked steps
this progression keeps the reader from feeling out of their depth
difficult movements are broken down into several pictures
rival books keep to a single picture for each movement
the author avoids obscure vocabulary while staying exact
the exercises offered are judged too few
the answers placed at the end of the volume do not explain the reasoning
the book is recommended to anyone who works in an orderly way
it suits badly the reader who needs constant correction
text: Three things set this manual for beginners above comparable handbooks, and two shortcomings temper the praise. Its progression comes first: it climbs in short steps, each fresh idea resting on the one before, so that the reader never feels out of their depth. Its pictures come next, breaking every awkward movement into a run of small images where rival books make do with a single shot. Its prose comes last, refusing jargon without giving up an ounce of precision. The reservations fall on two points. The exercises closing each chapter are far too few for anyone who wants real practice, and the answers, banished to the back of the volume, say nothing about how they were reached. The book therefore suits the orderly reader, and suits far less the one who learns alone and needs a constant check on his mistakes.

units: the writer of the letter addresses his former trainer
he let a long stretch of time pass before writing
at the start he applied the instructions without grasping their sense
he went over them in the evening from memory
the workshop then handed him a complete order
he spoiled his first three pieces and thought of giving up
mending the fourth piece showed him the worth of patience
he now lays out his materials the day before and writes his mistakes down
he has been asked to train a newcomer
he finds that what he inherited above all is a way of looking at error
text: I am writing at last, after a whole season of silence, to tell you what has become of your teaching in my hands. At the start I copied out your instructions without understanding them, and went over them in my head each evening like a lesson learnt by heart. Then, in the cold months, the workshop handed me an order of my own. I ruined the first three pieces and came close to walking away. It was while mending the fourth that what you used to say about patience took on a plain meaning. Since then I lay out my tools the night before, I write my mistakes in a notebook, and I read it through before every fresh batch. Last season the woman in charge asked me to start a beginner off. I heard your own words coming out of my mouth, almost without choosing them. That was when I understood: you handed me a way of looking at error.

units: explaining an idea to somebody else improves retention
a lesson left in a notebook demands no effort of memory
putting it into words aloud forces the brain to retrieve each element
this effort of recall strengthens the memory
an unexpected question brings out a gap one knew nothing about
a gap that has been spotted can then be filled
too wide a difference in level pushes the explainer to cut his account down too far
this excessive cutting distorts what he believed he had mastered
the ideal listener is slightly less advanced but able to argue back
text: Do you hold on to an idea better once you have said it to somebody else? You do, and the reason is short. While the lesson sits in a notebook, nothing asks the memory to build it again; the moment you have to put it into words aloud, the brain goes hunting for every link, and that act of retrieval deepens the trace. And if the other person asks something you did not expect? So much the better. The question opens up a hole you would never have found on your own, and a hole once seen can be filled. Should you then explain anything to anyone at all? No. Where the difference in level is huge, the one explaining cuts his account down too far, and the trimming ends up bending what he believed he had mastered. The right partner stands a step behind you, close enough to follow, fresh enough to argue back.

units: the woman running a shared workshop describes a problem of keeping people
newcomers were dropping out after three sessions
they walked home every evening with a spoiled piece of work
a volunteer craftsman saw beginners tense up at their very first cut
the team changed the way the sessions run
a newcomer now finishes a piece begun by somebody else
he takes on the finishing only
beginners leave with a completed object and come back
the craftsman thinks this choice holds back the learning of the cut
he admits that the learners stay long enough to learn it in the end
text: The woman who runs the shared workshop made no secret of the trouble when we put the question to her. Newcomers were dropping out after three sessions, she said, because they walked home every evening holding something they had spoiled. A volunteer joiner, sitting by the bench, backed her up: he could watch hands go tight at the very first cut. So the team pulled the sessions apart and built them again. Every newcomer now ends the evening on a piece somebody else began, she explained, with nothing left but the sanding and the polishing. The beginner carries home a finished object, she added, and turns up again the week after. The joiner put a qualification on it. The scheme holds back the learning of the cut, he said, but it keeps people about long enough that they learn it in the end.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: knowledge travelled by mouth and by hand before writing
spoken narration rested on the return of the same turns of phrase
the group put right the teller's slips
handwork was learnt almost without speech
no abstract rule was taught to the beginner
the apprentice copied what he saw and was corrected physically
the true movement lodged in the muscle before it was understood
writing keeps the exact wording but loses the voice and the presence
workshop transmission dies out if the craftsman trains no successor
the two ways of passing on ended by completing each other
text: Before writing froze what people knew, everything travelled by mouth and by hand, and each road had its own laws. The spoken tale lived on repetition: the teller came back to the same turns of phrase, and the memory of the listening group pulled him up when he strayed. Handwork, by contrast, hardly used speech at all. Nobody set out an abstract rule for the beginner; the apprentice watched, copied, took a rap on the knuckles, and the true movement lodged in the muscle long before it reached the head. Once carved signs spread, the comparison turned round. The written page kept the wording untouched but lost the voice, the shading, the presence of the master. The workshop kept the movement alive and went out with the craftsman who had trained nobody to follow him. In the end the two roads answered each other.

units: the author describes four levers of lasting memorisation
going over an idea at widening intervals fixes it better
a recall that is slightly awkward strengthens the memory
putting questions to yourself works better than reading the page again
rereading creates a misleading feeling of command
shuffling exercises of different kinds slows the session down
this shuffling teaches you to name the problem before choosing a method
the brain runs the learnt sequences through again during sleep
the most useful sequences move into a steadier memory
these levers do not remove the need for repetition but make it pay better
text: Four levers hold a scrap of learning in place for good. Spacing is the first: an idea gone over at widening intervals bites deeper than the same idea gone over in one sitting, since every slightly awkward recall firms up the trace. Self-testing is the second: putting questions to yourself beats reading the page again, because rereading hands you a feeling of command that nothing has tested. Shuffling is the third: mixing exercises of different kinds drags the session out, yet it trains you to name the problem before you reach for a method. Sleep is the fourth, and while you sleep the brain runs the learnt sequences through again and moves the useful ones into steadier keeping. Not one of these levers takes the place of practice repeated; each one raises what that practice returns.

units: a beginner in bookbinding is given an order that strikes her as nonsense
her trainer forbids her to stitch before she has folded an enormous quantity of sheets
she carries out the order without believing in it
she feels she is losing a whole season
her folds come out even as the weeks pass
her fingers end by sensing the thickness of the paper without measuring
once allowed to sew she gets a straight spine and clean stitching
the trainer owns up to having been through the same ordeal and loathed it
he explains that this drudgery trains the hand and not the craft itself
a hand already schooled picks up the next movement without a struggle
text: In her first winter the young binder was given an order she took for nonsense. The master of the workshop forbade her to stitch a single section until she had folded a mountain of sheets by hand. She did as she was told and believed none of it, sure that a whole season was going to waste. Week by week her folds came out even, and then her fingers gave up measuring altogether: they felt the thickness of the paper and stopped where they should. When she was let loose on the sewing at last, the thread ran along a spine that was already straight, and not one stitch buckled. The master owned up then. He had been through the same ordeal, he said, and had loathed every hour of it. The drudgery taught nobody how to bind; it taught the hand, and a hand already schooled takes the next movement without a struggle.

units: the method starts by cutting the piece into short stretches
a memory loaded past its limit takes in nothing
a stretch of two bars lodges better than a whole page
each stretch must first be played at a slow pace
a mistake repeated beds down as firmly as a sound movement
two stretches are to be tied together once one comes out clean three times running
breakdowns happen above all at the seams between stretches
the session closes with a run of the whole thing however rough
the next day it is better to start again at the seams than at the opening
ignoring this advice leaves the opening solid and the ending shaky
text: Cut the piece into short stretches before you do anything else, because a memory loaded well past its limit takes in nothing at all: a couple of bars will lodge where a whole page simply runs away. Play each stretch slowly to begin with, since a mistake repeated beds down every bit as firmly as a sound movement, and dropping the speed keeps the fault from settling in. Once a stretch comes out clean three times running, tie it to the one beside it, for a piece gives way at the seams far more often than it does in the middle of a phrase. Close the session with a run of the whole thing, rough as it may be, so that the memory holds an outline of the shape. Next day, start again at the seams rather than at the opening, or the first bars will gleam and the ending will stay shaky right up to the concert itself.

units: a converted shed houses a neighbourhood workshop
people living nearby saw that the craftsmen who retired carried their trade off with them
the young people round about had nowhere to train
an association put together a scheme with nothing clever about it
each retired volunteer gives two half sessions a week
he takes on two beginners at most
there is neither a syllabus nor an examination
the starting point is a repair brought in by a neighbour
half of the beginners come back from one season to the next
the old hands say that explaining makes them take apart movements that had gone automatic
text: There is sanding, sawing and loud argument going on in the converted shed at the bottom of the road. Everyone living nearby knew the problem: the craftsmen who retired were carrying their trade off with them, and the young people round about had nowhere to pick anything up. An association put together a scheme with nothing clever about it. Each retired volunteer comes in two afternoons a week and takes on two beginners, no more than that. No syllabus, no examination: you start from whatever a neighbour has brought in, a wobbly chair, a shutter that sticks, and the old hand shows you as you go. The results caught the association itself off guard. Half the beginners come back from one season to the next. The old hands gain as well, since explaining makes them take apart movements that had gone automatic.

units: the training space is made up of four separate stations
the first station is for sorting and washing the raw material
marking out calls for careful checking so that faults do not appear at assembly
the assembly stage uses clamping tools worked by two people
the last station brings together sanding, finishing and the checking of dimensions
a sheet on display gives the order of operations, the tolerances allowed and the safety equipment
the instructor moves about to correct how the learners handle their tools
all the stations must have been passed through before anyone may work unsupervised
text: A training workshop for handwork is laid out as four separate stations, and each one covers its own family of movements. At the first, the raw material is sorted: the learner weighs it, grades it and washes off whatever would spoil the later steps. The second deals with marking out, where careful checking of the reference points keeps faults from turning up at assembly. Assembly follows, with vices, clamps and a screw press that two learners work between them. The last station, often thought the dullest, brings together sanding, finishing and the checking of dimensions. A sheet pinned to the wall gives the order of operations, the tolerances allowed and the protective clothing required. The instructor moves about, adjusting a grip here, straightening a posture there. Nobody is cleared to work unsupervised until all four stations have been passed through.

units: passing on a craft was at first done by watching and repeating beside an older worker
the coming of writing set the procedures down in books
moving pictures then promised a clearer explanation
the writer disputes the idea that this sequence is steady progress
each support gains in reach what it loses in human presence
a written work reaches distant readers but corrects no movement
a recording shows the movement from every angle without feeling the hesitation of the person watching
the conclusion put forward is that no support replaces the presence of an older worker
text: For a long stretch of time, a craft passed from hand to hand: the learner watched an older worker, copied, failed and began again. Writing changed that. Once the procedures were set down in books they held still, open to anyone able to read them. Moving pictures came later and promised a clearer explanation, with the diagram that unfolds and the step slowed right down. I do not accept that this sequence amounts to steady progress. Every support has gained in reach exactly what it has lost in presence. A written work finds readers no workshop would ever have taken in, yet it cannot correct a hand that shakes. A recording shows the movement from every angle and feels nothing of the hesitation in the person watching. My conclusion is short: no support replaces an older worker leaning over an unfinished piece.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: an injury to the hand marked the start of her path
she had to work out unusual grips to hold her tools
that constraint made her alert to the way each person handles an instrument
she gained a name as a very fine teacher
she breaks every movement into stages for beginners
her workshop took in learners who had been turned away elsewhere
she cut back her own output in order to teach more
that choice brought her earnings down
her former learners, now experts, still use her method
text: The bookbinder in question lost the use of two fingers when she was young, and that injury shaped the path she took. Unable to hold the folder as her fellows did, she had to work out grips nobody had shown her, which left her unusually alert to the way each person takes hold of a tool. That alertness earned her, years later, a name as a very fine teacher. Because she had broken every movement into stages to make it possible for herself, she could do the same with the movements of an awkward beginner. Her workshop began to draw learners other workshops had turned away. As demand rose she cut back her own output and gave her afternoons over to teaching. Her earnings fell because of it, though the method spread: her former learners, seasoned now, still take a movement apart the way she taught them.

units: the beginner's handbook is irritating from the opening pages
the author piles up definitions and breaks off proofs with asides
the reader finishes a chapter without knowing what has been taken from it
the material itself is judged to be good
the criticism bears on the arrangement and not on the subject matter
reading it the other way round, starting with the exercises, solved the problem
the exercises are graded and honest about how hard they are
the book then becomes a store where one looks for what is missing
the advice is to open the theory only at the point where one gets stuck
text: Honestly, this beginner's handbook irritated me from the opening pages. The writing is dense: the author piles up definitions, doubles back, drops an aside in the middle of a proof. You finish a chapter with no idea what you were meant to take from it. The maddening part is that the material is good, and only the arrangement lets it down. So I tried something odd and read the thing the other way round, starting with the exercises. That sorted it out. The exercises are graded and honest about how hard each one is. Work through them first and you learn what you are short of, then go hunting for the definition you lack. The book turns into a store you dip into rather than a corridor you are marched along. I do recommend it, then, with one instruction: begin at the end, and open the theory only where you get stuck.

units: the writer reports on two courses taken in the same term
the first brought a large group together in a tiered room
the speaker there talked without being interrupted
the second gathered a very small number round a table
the woman leading the second fell silent as soon as a question came up between the participants
the first covered a wide syllabus and left the participants passive
the second moved along more slowly and stirred up exchanges
a beginner got on faster there than a seasoned practitioner
the writer advises the second arrangement in spite of its narrower syllabus
text: Dear colleague, here is the account I promised of the two courses I sat this term, since they run against each other at almost every point. The first put a large group into a tiered room: the speaker talked, we wrote, and nobody cut in. The second gathered a mere handful of us round one table, and the woman leading it fell silent the moment a question came up between us. The first covered a wide syllabus and left us diligent but idle. The second moved along at a crawl and made us talkative, muddled at times. Where the first rewarded a good page of notes, the second rewarded a mistake said out loud. A beginner got on faster there than a seasoned practitioner, because he dared say what he had not followed. If you must choose for the team, take the second, even at the cost of covering less ground.

units: a learner asks a worker in stone what learning really is
the answer takes the shape of an ordered list
the first item is consenting to dullness
the movement repeated without end is likened to water wearing away rock
the second item is accepting what is hard
an obstacle overcome leaves a mark that ease never leaves
the third item is taking account of what the material will allow
another item is bearing the harsh correction of an older hand
the last item is forgetting what has been learnt so that the hand moves before the mind
the worker in stone refuses to put a figure on the time needed
text: What is it to learn? The apprentice puts the question to the stonecutter. The answer comes as a list, its items laid out like tools along a bench. To learn, he says, is first to consent to dullness: a movement repeated without end wears its own channel, as water wears the rock it runs over. It is next to accept what is hard, not from any love of pain, but because an obstacle beaten leaves a mark that ease never presses in. It is to listen to the material, which refuses one curve and asks for another. It is to bear the eye of an older hand who corrects and offers no comfort. And it is, at the last, to forget what has been learnt, so that the hand moves before the mind does. And how many seasons does that road take? The stonecutter smiles, wipes his chisel and says such a stretch is not counted, only crossed.

units: the instructor first asks for the power to the machine to be cut
the trainee reports that the indicator light is still flashing
the instructor explains that a residual charge remains in the capacitor
that charge has to be given time to drain away
the cover is taken off by loosening the screws crosswise
uneven tightening warps the sealing gasket
the trainee then measures a residual voltage of nothing at all
the instructor requires the operation to be entered in a register before anything is put back
the procedure only holds good if every step is dated and signed
text: The instructor started by telling the trainee to cut the power to the machine and watch the indicator light go out. She reported that the light was still flashing away. He explained that a residual charge lingers in the capacitor and that they had to wait for it to drain away in full. Then he asked her to take off the cover, loosening the screws crosswise rather than one after another round the edge. She wanted to know what lay behind that rule. Uneven tightening, he said, warps the sealing gasket. She measured the residual voltage next and gave a reading of nothing at all on the dial. The instructor accepted the measurement and had her enter the operation in the register before a single part went back on. A procedure is worth nothing, he ended, unless every step is dated and signed.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the growth in the number of town workshops changed the way trades were taught
families were no longer enough to supply the hands that were needed
masters took children from elsewhere into their own homes
living under one roof gave rise to written agreements
the agreements set out the length of service, the keep and the secrecy required
the ban on teaching outside the workshop protected what the trade was worth
that ban slowed the spread of technique
the guilds never settled the contradiction between secrecy and the renewal of the workforce
travelling workers carried the movements from one workshop to another
text: As workshops multiplied in the towns, the teaching of a trade changed in kind. Families could no longer supply the hands that were needed, so masters took children from elsewhere into their own homes. Living under one roof gave rise to written agreements: the length of service, the keep owed, the procedures that were not to be spoken of outside. Since secrecy protected what a trade was worth, teaching beyond the workshop door was forbidden, and that ban slowed the spread of technique. Out of it came a contradiction the guilds never settled: guarding the process meant starving the trade of fresh hands. When traffic between regions grew heavier, travelling workers carried the movements from one workshop to another all the same. Secrecy gave way through movement, then, and not by any decision of the masters.

units: material read over again feels familiar and that familiarity is mistaken for command of it
the student believes he is ready and then finds himself helpless later on
recognising a statement costs less effort than producing it from memory
the brain confuses these two sensations
the answer is to question oneself without looking at one's notes
the effort of recall fixes the memory even when it fails
the recalls have to be spread further and further apart
the spacing widens up to the point where forgetting becomes likely
the method gives an impression of failure although it works
text: Anyone studying alone runs into a known trap: material read over again feels familiar, and that familiarity passes for command of it. The reader shuts the notebook satisfied, then finds a week later that nothing will come. The mechanism is well established. Picking out a statement you have met before costs less effort than producing it from memory, and the brain confuses the two sensations. The answer lies in a reversal. Rather than read again, you put the question to yourself and hunt for the answer with your notes shut. The effort of recall fixes the trace far better than a comfortable second reading, even when it comes up empty. Those recalls are then spread out, close together at first and wider and wider afterwards, up to the point where forgetting grows likely. The method feels thankless: it gives an impression of failure while it works.

units: the narrator showed the same knot to two learners
the younger one managed it after one demonstration and two failed attempts
she asked no questions
the grown man listened closely and took notes
he questioned the narrator about the logic of the crossing
he did not manage the knot that evening
the man was trying to understand where the young one was content to copy
the narrator took his notebook away and covered his eyes
the man managed it quickly once he could not see
the narrator concludes that his explanations got in the way of the man's hands
text: I taught the same knot to two learners over the last season, and the pair of them still nag at me. The younger one needed a single demonstration: she took the rope, got it wrong twice running, then had it right without a word from me, and asked nothing at all. The other, a grown man, listened with faultless courtesy, took notes, and put sharp questions to me about why the crossing had to go that way. He did not get the knot right once, all evening. It was not that he learnt less well; he learnt differently, wanting to understand what the young one was content to copy. When I took his notebook off him at last and tied a cloth right over his eyes, his hands found the answer in three tries. The lesson I draw stings a little: my explanations had fed his head and tied up his fingers.

units: the steam produced while cooking drifts through the room
on contact with the cold glass this steam turns back into water
the film of water on the pane hides the view outside
the condensed water runs down and gathers at the bottom of the window
standing water swells the timber and lifts the paint
an unpleasant smell eventually spreads through the kitchen
the source of the trouble is the damp produced inside the home
letting fresh air through while cooking breaks the process
it is better to open before the film appears than afterwards
text: Steam rising from a pan does not simply vanish. It drifts across the room until it meets the cold surface of the glass, where it turns back into water and settles as a thick film that hides the street outside. Those droplets slide downwards and gather along the bottom of the frame. Left to sit, the water swells the timber, lifts the paint in blisters, and a sour smell soon spreads through the kitchen. The cause lies indoors, not in the weather: it is the damp air that cooking itself produces. Letting fresh air through while the pan is on the heat breaks the chain, since the moist air leaves, drier air takes its place, and nothing is left for the condensation to feed on. A careful occupant therefore opens the window before the panes turn white, rather than afterwards, once the damage has taken hold.

units: a sharp knock came each time the kitchen cupboard was shut
the door struck the upright instead of settling flush against it
the tenant first suspected that the timber had warped
sanding the edge down changed nothing
a lamp held close revealed play in the top hinge
the screws turned freely in holes worn too wide
splinters of wood set in glue gave the screws a firm grip again
once the glue had set the screws went back into fresh material
the door closes silently once more
the episode shows that the source of a noise rarely lies where the ear puts it
text: A sharp knock came every evening as the kitchen cupboard was shut: the left door struck the upright instead of settling flush against it. The tenant blamed the timber first, certain that damp had warped it, and sanded the edge down. Nothing changed. Then she held a lamp close and saw the trouble at once, since the top hinge had worked loose. Two screws turned freely in holes worn wide, and the panel hung slightly askew. The remedy came from an old cabinetmaker's trick: pack the tired holes with splinters of wood set in glue, leave them overnight, then drive the screws into fresh material. Since that evening the door closes without a sound. What she took from it was a small rule of thumb, namely that when a piece of furniture complains, the source rarely lies where the ear puts it.

units: the two cleaning cloths do not serve the same purpose
the kitchen cloth is thin and dries without leaving smears
the kitchen cloth suits plates and cooking surfaces
the floor cloth soaks up a large puddle
the floor cloth leaves a damp film behind it
the two must be stored apart
the floor cloth is rinsed in scalding water after use or it will smell
the kitchen cloth goes into the machine with the rest of the washing
the test for choosing is contact with food
text: Want to clean quickly and properly? Begin by distinguishing your two helpers, because they are not intended for the same job. The tea towel is thin and closely woven. It soaks up little, yet it dries without leaving smears, so keep it for plates, glasses and the hob. The floor cloth is thick and loose. It swallows a whole puddle, but it leaves a damp film behind it, hence its place on the tiles and never on the table. Store the two well apart, one folded in a drawer, the other hung over the bucket. Rinse the floor cloth in scalding water after every use, or it will begin to smell. The tea towel goes into the machine with the sheets. And if the rest escapes you, remember this: ask whether the surface touches food. If it does, reach for the towel; if not, reach for the other.

units: a voluntary group have set up a repair workshop in a disused market hall
a first bench is given over to clothing and fabric goods
trousers are taken up there and worn hems are stitched again
a second bench deals with electrical appliances
damaged power leads make up most of the electrical requests
a third bench looks after furniture
legs are glued back on there and hinges or handles are replaced
a fourth corner lends tools out for a modest membership
the queue has not shortened since the doors opened
a travelling scheme is planned for the outlying districts
text: In a disused market hall, a voluntary group have opened a workshop where things once thrown out are mended instead. The first bench takes in clothing and fabric goods: trousers are taken up, worn hems are stitched again, a torn bag strap is put right. The second deals with electrical appliances, and damaged power leads account for most of what comes through the door. The third, noticeably louder, is given over to furniture, where a chair leg is glued back on, a hinge is eased, a fresh handle is fitted. A fourth corner, quieter than the rest, lends tools out to anyone paying a modest membership. The queue, as the volunteers point out, has not shortened since the doors opened, which suggests the skill is missed more than the will. A travelling scheme is soon to serve the outlying districts.

units: at sunrise the courtyard smells of wet stone
washing done the evening before hangs on a line strung between two walls
the water dripping from the washing runs into a groove cut in the ground
by the middle of the day the air dries and the sheets fill out
a cat settles on the warm rim of the well
a wooden shutter bangs on an upper floor before falling back against the wall
late in the afternoon a neighbour comes to fetch her washing
she leaves the pegs on the line
in the evening the courtyard empties and a smell of soap lingers
the night brings the damp back to the flagstones
text: At sunrise the courtyard smells of wet stone. Washing hung out the evening before still sags on a line strung between two walls, and the drips fall one by one into a groove cut along the paving. By the middle of the day the air has dried, the sheets fill out and crack like sails. A grey cat settles on the warm rim of the well and half closes its eyes. Somewhere above, a wooden shutter bangs, holds open for a moment, then falls back against the wall. Late in the afternoon a neighbour comes down for her washing, folds each piece over her arm and leaves the pegs where they are, biting on the empty line. As evening comes the courtyard empties, and only the smell of soap hangs on between the walls. Then the night brings the damp back to the flagstones, and the round quietly begins again.

units: welding a casing shut instead of screwing it down blocks access to the parts inside
with no access the independent workshop cannot diagnose the fault
with no diagnosis no quote is offered
the owner ends up buying a replacement appliance
each step of the reasoning looks sound taken on its own
the sequence leads to scrapping an object that a minor part would have saved
as repairers grow scarce the passing on of practical skill is cut off
the knowledge is missing where the demand is rising
effective action bears on design and not on the sorting of waste
text: Refusing to repair costs more than it appears to, and the mechanism deserves a careful description. A maker who welds a casing shut instead of screwing it down removes all access to the parts inside. With no access, the independent workshop cannot diagnose the fault. With no diagnosis, it will not quote. With no quote, the owner buys a replacement. Every link looks sound on its own, and the chain as a whole ends with an object scrapped when a hinge or a seal would have kept it in service. A second effect follows, harder to see: as repairers grow scarce, the passing on of practical skill dries up, so the knowledge is missing exactly where the demand is rising. Turning this round therefore means acting at the design stage, and not at the far end, over the sorting of waste.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the alterations seamstress keeps a narrow shop in a district
she began as an apprentice in a clothing workshop
she assembled linings there one after another
the closing of that workshop left her without work
she owned only a second-hand machine and had no customers
she changed scale by mending single pieces instead of producing runs
each repair costs less than a replacement garment
her order book now runs two weeks ahead
she is handing the trade on to an apprentice
text: Behind a narrow shopfront, the alterations seamstress of the district practises a trade that many had written off. She began as an apprentice in a clothing workshop, assembling linings one after another along the production line. When that workshop shut its doors she was left without work, owning nothing but a second-hand machine and not a single customer. Her answer was to change scale. Rather than sewing runs of identical pieces, she offered to rescue garments one at a time. A hem taken up, a sandal strap stitched back, a torn pocket closed, a zip replaced: each of these jobs costs less than a replacement garment. The shop is never empty, and her order book now runs two weeks ahead. She has taken on an apprentice of her own, convinced that the trade dies unless it is handed on aloud, with the hand on the work.

units: two clothes airers are sold in the same place at very different prices
the steel model opens easily and holds a heavy load
its feet slide on a smooth floor
the aluminium model weighs half as much
the aluminium model packs away in a narrow sleeve
its drying surface is smaller
the heavy one suits large households
the light one suits cramped homes
one corrodes at the joints and the other bows under a wet load
the decision turns on the space the buyer has at home
text: Two clothes airers stand side by side on the same shelf at prices far apart, and in use the gap tells less than the packaging promises. The first, in coated steel, opens out with a single movement and holds a heavy load without sagging. Its side wings lock on a firm catch, yet its feet slide on a smooth floor. The second, in aluminium, weighs half as much and packs away in a narrow sleeve, which is what suits a cramped flat. Its drying surface is smaller, and two sheets will barely fit on it. Put to the test, the heavy one serves a large household while the light one serves a small home. Neither deserves the enthusiasm of its leaflet: one corrodes at the folding joints, while the other bows its bars under a wet towel. What decides the matter, in the end, is the space the buyer has at home.

units: the writer of the message is going away and leaves instructions for the person sharing the flat
the kitchen tap drips if it is shut too quickly
a funnel for pouring oil sits under the sink
the wardrobe door has to be lifted before it will shut
a hanger has been freed up for a coat
the hot water takes a while before it can be used
the post box fills up quickly and has to be emptied
the recycling bag goes out at the start of the week
the neighbour below knocks on his ceiling when anyone walks heavily in the evening
that neighbour sleeps while the occupants are still up
text: Hello, I am off this evening, so here are the instructions for the flat, and I hope nothing is missing. Kitchen: the tap drips if you shut it too quickly, so turn it gently; the funnel for the oil sits under the sink, alongside the floor cloth. Bedroom: the wardrobe only closes if you lift the door while pushing, and I have freed a hanger for your coat. Bathroom: the hot water takes an age to come through, so switch it on before undressing. The post box fills quickly, so empty it on your way in and leave everything on the coffee table. The recycling bag goes out at the beginning of the week, so remember to take it down. One last thing: the neighbour below knocks on his ceiling whenever anyone walks heavily after supper. Take no offence, since he sleeps while we are still up.

units: a caretaker of a block of flats describes how his week goes
he starts at first light by cleaning the shared parts
he checks the lighting on the stairs
he wheels the bins out before the collection lorry comes
he brings the bins back washed once the collection is over
the bottom hinge on the door of the bike store gives way regularly
he straightens that door every other week
he sets aside a whole stretch of time for the repairs residents report
he makes a round at the end of the day to check that everything is locked
he reckons that the steadiness of the routine protects him
text: We asked the caretaker of a block of flats to take us through his week, task by task. He starts at first light with the shared parts: sweeping the entrance hall, running a mop over the floor, checking the bulbs on the stairs. Asked what comes next, he explains that he wheels the bins out before the lorry arrives and brings them back washed once it has gone. When we ask which fault returns most often, he names the door of the bike store, whose bottom hinge gives way under the weight and which he straightens every other week. Midweek he sets aside a whole stretch of time for the repairs residents have reported. Last comes the evening round, when he checks that everything is locked. Asked whether the work tires him, he answers that the routine protects him more than it wears him down.

units: a resident from an upper floor tells the caretaker about a door that no longer locks
the catch gives way as soon as the handle is let go
water comes in through a damaged drainpipe above the door
the caretaker had already written the fault down in his logbook
he says he can do nothing without approval from the building manager
the resident points out that the delay is helping the lock to rust
the two agree to hold the door leaf with a wooden wedge
a sheet is to be used to send the water across to the street drain
the caretaker promises a written reminder before the week is out
the resident wants to gather written backing from the other occupants
text: A resident from one of the upper floors stopped the caretaker to report that the cycle store door would no longer lock. The catch, she said, slipped back the moment the handle was let go, and water was coming in through a split drainpipe above the doorway. The caretaker replied that the fault was already down in his logbook, though he could take no action until the building manager approved it. Waiting only helped the rust along, she pointed out, and the lock would seize before long. Between them they settled on a temporary measure: a wooden wedge would hold the leaf shut, and a sheet of canvas would carry the water across to the street drain. The caretaker undertook to send a written reminder before the week was out. She, for her part, offered to collect written backing from the other occupants.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: households once drew their water from a dug shaft or from a tank
you had to haul a vessel up and wait for the grit to settle at the bottom
the supply was kept in an earthenware pot standing somewhere cool
these days one movement at the household fitting brings the water
the flow no longer depends on the bodily strength of whoever draws it
the old scarcity forced people to use their washing water again
every drop that ran away was watched closely then
the plenty of today makes a leak hard to notice
progress has done away with the carrying but hidden the waste
text: Households once drew their water from a shaft sunk in the ground or from a tank that caught the rain. You hauled the vessel up hand over hand, waited for the grit to settle at the bottom, then kept the supply cool in an earthenware pot standing out of the sun. Now a single movement at the household fitting brings it, and the flow owes nothing whatever to the bodily strength of whoever happens to be drawing. The difference between the two runs deeper than comfort. Scarcity used to impose a discipline of its own: the water from washing went on to the floor afterwards, and every drop that ran away was watched closely. Where supply feels endless, that watchfulness slackens, and a leak can seep quietly for weeks on end before anyone notices. Progress has done away with the carrying, then, and hidden the waste in the doing.

units: a kitchen drawer holds tools whose purpose is often forgotten
the one with a long handle and a deep bowl lifts hot liquid out
the perforated one holds the food back while the water runs away
its holes have to be narrow so that nothing is lost
the rack lets the plates dry in the air with no help from anyone
the citrus press keeps the juice clear of the flesh and traps the pips
the bendy blade scrapes the sides of a bowl clean without marking them
each tool answers to one particular movement
text: Open a kitchen drawer and you come upon a whole set of tools whose exact purpose has quietly slipped everyone's mind. Take the one with the long handle and the deep bowl: it is there to lift hot liquid out of the pan and keep your fingers well away from it. The perforated one holds the food back while the water runs off, and its holes want to be narrow, or half of what you cooked goes down with it. The draining rack goes about its business in its own good time — you stand the rinsed plates in it, and the air does the drying with no help at all from anyone. The citrus press keeps the juice clear of the flesh and traps the pips in the bottom of its little cup. The bendy blade scrapes the sides of a bowl clean without marking them. Each of these answers to one particular movement of the hand.

units: the incident happens just before the bread shop opens its doors
the cooking appliance can no longer reach the heat it needs
the woman in charge suspects the burner first and then the ignition sensor
the first batch comes out too pale and the display stays almost empty
a young member of staff decides to look at the flue opening
burnt crumbs of bread had packed the duct and starved the flame of air
clearing the duct takes about half an hour
the next batch comes out with its usual colour and smell
the woman in charge adds that check to her weekly habits
the story then travels round the neighbourhood by word of mouth
text: It began in the hour before the bread shop opened its doors: the oven would not come up to the heat it needed. The woman in charge suspected the burner first, then the sensor that governs the ignition. The first batch came out pale, with no crust worth the name, and the display stayed all but empty while people came in, left and came back. It was a young member of staff who thought to look at the flue opening. A mass of burnt crumbs had packed the duct tight and was quietly starving the flame of air. Clearing the whole of it took the better part of half an hour, dust and all. From the very next batch onwards the bread had its usual colour again and its usual smell. The woman in charge added that check to her weekly habits, and the story went round the neighbourhood by word of mouth.

units: the shoes must be kept away from any source of heat because the material dries out
the underside is to be brushed so that the caked mud comes off
hardened dirt holds water and eats away at the stitching
a lining that feels cold and slack shows the fabric has taken in water
crumpled paper serves to draw that damp out
the wax goes on sparingly and in circles
a thick coat never sinks in and spoils the look of the surface
polishing with a woollen cloth warms the wax and closes the pores
left untended the material splits where the foot bends
text: Because leather dries out when it is left standing beside anything warm, begin by moving the pair well away from every source of heat. Brush the underside next, so that the caked mud comes away from it, for hardened dirt holds water against the material and eats slowly away at the stitching that carries it. Slide a hand into the lining: cold and slack to the touch, it has drunk yesterday's rain, and crumpled paper pressed inside will draw that damp out of it. Then work in a little wax, sparingly and in patient circles, since a thick coat never sinks in and spoils the look of the surface. Leave it to settle, then bring it up with a woollen cloth; the rubbing warms the wax, which evens out and closes the pores. Left untended, the leather will split exactly where the foot bends, and nothing will mend it.

units: the body in charge of water has published a survey of its network
a sizeable share of the water sent out never reaches the homes
the older metal pipes crack because the ground beneath them shifts
the pressure swings that come at night add to those cracks
the first measure cuts the network into stretches that valves can seal off
meters read the overnight flow so that a loss can be spotted
a flow that does not drop away at night reveals a leak
the second measure brings the pressure down because hard pressure bursts pipes
a leak in a home counts for little beside a split main under the road
text: The body in charge of the water supply has put out a survey of the network it runs. The finding is a blunt one: a sizeable share of everything that goes into the mains never reaches the homes it was sent out to. Older metal pipes crack as the ground beneath them shifts about, and the pressure swings that come with the night hours work those cracks wider still. Two measures follow from this. The first cuts the network into short stretches that valves can seal off, with meters reading the overnight flow; where that flow fails to drop away in the small hours, water is going astray somewhere. The second brings the pressure down, since driving it hard is what bursts a pipe. A tap left dripping in a flat, the engineers add, counts for very little beside a split main under the road.

units: the space in front of the building is laid with uneven paving
tubs there hold green and sweet-smelling plants
a pale wall covering throws a soft light into the lower windows
the space at the back is covered with an even concrete surface
a wall without an opening blocks the view there
wooden seats and a water point invite people to stop in the first space
the second takes the bins and the delivery vehicles
one is meant to please and the other to serve
both spaces belong to the same building
text: The yard in front of the building is laid with paving that runs uneven underfoot, and tubs stand along its edges, holding ferns and sweet-smelling herbs. Pale render on the walls around it throws a soft light back into the windows of the lower floor. Behind the very same building the ground tells another story altogether: an even concrete surface runs from one side to the other, and a wall without a single opening in it blocks the view. The front yard asks you to stop a while, with wooden seats set against the brickwork and a water point for the planting. The one at the back takes the bins and the delivery vehicles, and nobody lingers there. One space is meant to please, the other to serve. Both belong to the same building, and the contrast tells you how a place shares out its uses.

units: the writer argues for mending a damaged appliance rather than replacing it
a spare part costs far less than an unused replacement
the money saved stays in the household budget
giving up a purchase avoids the digging out of material, the journey and the packaging
taking an appliance apart teaches how it works inside
that skill then passes on to the people around
mending is said to ask for a patience few people have
shared places offer the help of a volunteer and the loan of tools
the main difficulty comes from sealed manufacture that keeps appliances shut
text: Mending a damaged appliance rather than replacing it is a choice, and the case for it stands up on several separate grounds. Money, to start with: a spare part costs a mere fraction of an unused replacement, and what is not spent stays in the household budget. Materials, next: the digging out, the journey, the packaging, all of it goes when the purchase does not go through. Skill, last of all: whoever takes a casing apart learns how the thing works inside, and that understanding passes on in turn to the people around them. Mending asks for a patience that few people have, runs the objection. It forgets the shared places where a volunteer guides your hands and lends you the tools you lack. The one real difficulty is sealed manufacture, which keeps appliances shut against anyone opening them.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman who sells fresh produce began as a child at her mother's side
she sorted the crates before trading began
she could tell how ripe a fruit was from the sound it made in her palm
her first pitch was a few boards laid across trestles
later on a wooden counter under a canvas sheet took its place
she steers undecided buyers according to what they are after
one customer wants a fruit whose stone comes away easily
another asks for grapes with no seeds in them
she is now passing her trade to her niece, who takes notes
she says she never wrote anything down and trusts what her hands remember
text: The woman who sells fresh produce in the covered market began when she was very young, at her mother's side, sorting her way through the crates before trading began for the day. She could tell how ripe a plum was, she says, from the sound it made in her palm. Her first pitch was no more than a few boards laid across trestles; a wooden counter with a canvas sheet stretched over it took their place later on. She learned to steer the buyers who cannot make up their minds: this one wants a fruit whose stone comes away on its own, that one is after grapes with no seeds in them. Lately she has been passing the trade on to her niece, who takes down every tip in a notebook. She laughs and says that she herself never wrote a thing, and that her hands remember better than her head does.

units: the shared eating place stands in an old market building
one dish only is offered at each sitting
that limit brings about a quality rarely met
buying that is not spread thin gives access to vegetables grown in the open
the work starts very early in the day
the single broth can reduce to a thickness seldom found
the bread served alongside has a crisp crust
the hard surface of the room throws the voices back and makes talking difficult
nothing is laid on for those who will not eat root vegetables
text: The shared eating place set up in an old market building is worth the walk, and that comes down to one decision taken and held to: only one dish is offered at each sitting. From that limit comes a quality rarely met. Because the buying is never spread thin, vegetables grown out in the open can be had, and the work on them starts long before the day itself does. Because there is one broth and no other to be watched, it is left to reduce to a thickness you will seldom find. The ladle goes down into a soup that is thick and almost dark, and the bread served alongside has a crust that cracks under the tooth. The room, though, works against the meal: bare tiling throws the voices back, and talking soon turns into hard labour. Nothing is laid on either for anyone who will not eat root vegetables.

units: the writer is addressing her neighbour about their two flats
the neighbour's flat sits directly beneath the roof
the neighbour closes a wooden shutter to keep the sun out
the writer's flat takes up the lowest level of the house
the writer contends with damp that lifts the wallpaper
the neighbour has to wipe away a fine grit coming through the gaps
the writer is watching a crack widen behind a radiator
the two neighbours air their flats in opposite ways
the writer suggests calling in a tradesman for both levels
text: Dear neighbour, I am writing to you about our two flats, which turn out to need rather different care.
