Yours sits directly beneath the roof, so the tiles pass their heat straight down to you, and you close the wooden shutter on the landing well before noon. Mine takes up the lowest level of the house, where a cold damp lifts the wallpaper away from the skirting board. You fight dry air; I fight wet walls. You wipe away the fine grit that drifts in through the gaps in the roof timbers, while I keep an eye on a thin crack widening behind the radiator. Even our remedies pull in opposite directions: you throw a window open for a few minutes, whereas I have to warm the room first. Might I suggest that we call in a tradesman together, so that he can look over both levels on one visit?

units: delicate laundry is best washed by hand
the water should be lukewarm and the soak short
a small amount of soap saves repeated rinsing
the fabric must not be wrung out hard
a dry towel serves to draw off the water held in the cloth
drying is done flat and away from a source of heat
stretching the damp garment does away with ironing
an old stain is soaked before any wash
boiling water would set the colour of the stain
text: Should delicate laundry be washed by hand? In most cases, yes. Lukewarm water and a short soak are kinder to the fibres than a drum spinning at full speed. How much soap? Very little. Too much lather leaves you rinsing the load twice or three times over. Should you wring it out hard? Never. Press the fabric between your palms instead, then roll it in a dry towel to draw off the water it still holds. Where should it dry? Flat, well away from any direct source of heat, on a surface that lets air move underneath. And the ironing? You can skip that altogether if you stretch the garment while it is still damp and set the crease with your fingers. What about an old stain? Soak it before any wash, and keep it clear of boiling water, which would set the colour rather than lift it.

units: the caretaker asks the narrator about noises in the night
the narrator was asleep and heard nothing
the caretaker caught sight of a figure by the letterboxes
a wooden shutter banged on the floor above
the caretaker found a key outside a door at the far end
the caretaker had no idea whose key it was
a tenant came to claim the key later on
that tenant had locked herself out while taking the bins down
the caretaker advises leaving a spare with someone you trust
text: The caretaker stopped me in the entrance hall and wanted to know whether I had heard anything at all in the night. Not a thing, I told him, for I had slept straight through until morning. He said he had first caught sight of a figure by the letterboxes, and then heard a wooden shutter bang somewhere on the floor above. So down he went with his torch, and there on the mat outside the door at the far end lay a key. Whose was it, I wanted to know. He shrugged and owned that he had no idea at all. A while later the tenant from upstairs turned up to claim it: she had let her door swing shut behind her while taking the bins down, and hadn't the nerve to wake her neighbours. He had a good laugh about that, then told me to leave a spare with somebody I trust. I rather think I shall, this very week.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: households once depended on a well or a fountain
water had to be carried bucket by bucket
washing clothes was gathered into one operation a week
the coming of indoor pipes altered domestic habits
washing broke up into more frequent operations
clothes were changed more often
the making of light fabrics grew
floors could be cleaned with plenty of water
smooth coverings pushed out the bare boards
text: Before piped water reached the home, fetching it governed the whole domestic day. A household depended on a well or a public fountain, and every drop arrived bucket by bucket, up whatever stairs there were. That is why washing was gathered into one great operation a week rather than spread about. When pipes finally ran indoors, far more changed than mere comfort. Water now came without effort, so the wash broke up into smaller and more frequent ones, garments were changed more often, and the making of light fabrics grew to keep pace. A second consequence followed close behind. Floors that had once been swept dry in a cloud of dust could be sluiced with water, and smooth coverings soon pushed out the bare boards. Plumbing, in short, reshaped both the furniture and the clothing.

units: pastry that tears puts beginners off
flour packs itself into tight lumps while it is stored
shaking the flour through a sieve lets air into it
butter straight from the cold is a solid block
pastry takes badly to a fat that is too hard
grating the butter scatters it in fragments
the fingertips can also crumble it
pastry worked too briskly shrinks back in the heat
a rest in the cold under a damp cloth slackens the mixture
text: Pastry that tears under the rolling pin has put many a beginner off for good. The fault seldom lies with the hands. It begins in the flour, which packs itself into tight little lumps as soon as it has sat a while in its bag. The cure is an old gesture: shake it through a sieve above the bowl, so that air passes through it and lightens it. Butter raises a kindred difficulty. Straight from the cold it is a solid block, and no pastry will take a fat as hard as that. Grate it, then, on the coarse side of a grater, or crumble it between your fingertips until it lies scattered in tiny flakes. Last comes the question of rest. Worked too briskly, pastry shrinks back in the heat and leaves ragged edges; left cool beneath a damp cloth, it slackens, settles, and rolls out with surprising ease.

units: the craftsman sets out two tubes of glue for the narrator
the first glue is water-based and hardens as it dries
the first glue calls for a long spell in the clamps
the second glue sets on contact with the moisture in the air
the second glue grips very quickly
the second takes to smooth surfaces such as metal
the joint made by the first glue keeps some give in it
the joint made by the second snaps under a twist
the craftsman keeps the slow glue for the load-bearing piece
a thick layer of glue holds less well than a thin film
text: The joiner who came to mend the shelf laid two tubes of glue side by side and told me they did not work alike. The first is water-based: it soaks into the grain and hardens as the water leaves it, which means a long spell in the clamps and a room that is not cold. The second sets on contact with the moisture in the air, grips within moments, and takes to smooth surfaces such as metal or ceramic. You pay for that speed elsewhere. The first leaves a joint with some give in it, one that follows the seasonal swelling of the wood, whereas the second forms a rigid edge that snaps clean under a twist. So he kept the slow one for the load-bearing rail and the quick one for the decorative beading. The commonest error, he added, is to lay it on thick: a heavy film gives way before the fibres it joins.

units: the wardrobe must be emptied altogether before starting
the shelves are wiped with a damp cloth
the surfaces are left to dry in open air
the garments are sorted into three groups
one group holds the pieces that need mending
everything kept must be washed even if it looks clean
an unseen trace of sweat draws moths during storage
it is better to fold garments flat than to hang them
a sachet of scented wood is slipped between the layers
each box is given a label stating what it holds
text: Storing clothes away from one season to the next repays a settled order. Begin by emptying the wardrobe altogether, wipe the shelves down with a damp cloth, and leave the surfaces to dry in the open air. Next, sort the garments into three groups: those you still wear, those that stand in need of mending, and those you will part with. Then wash everything you mean to keep, even what appears perfectly clean, since an unseen trace of sweat will draw moths during storage. Fold each piece flat rather than hanging it up, which spares the shoulders from stretching out of shape. Slip a sachet of scented wood in between the layers, and never anything liquid. Finally, write on a label what every box holds, and set the heaviest of them at the bottom of the stack, where they will not crush the rest.

units: a main water pipe gave way before daybreak
the break happened in a street running alongside a covered market
residents first noticed a warm puddle
the water reached the cellars of the buildings nearby
a standby crew shut off the supply to the quarter
the traders shifted their stalls to a hall close by
the technicians found that a root had worked a joint loose
the repair was finished after dark
the water stayed cloudy for a whole evening
pumps will drain the cellars the following week
text: The main gave way shortly before daybreak, in the street that runs alongside the covered market. Residents were the first to report a warm puddle spreading at the foot of a lamp post; then the paving lifted and the water reached the cellars of the buildings nearby. A standby crew arrived before the shops had opened and shut off the supply to the whole quarter. The traders shifted their stalls to the hall close by, where two taps were still running. By the middle of the afternoon the technicians had cleared the broken iron and found that a root had worked an old joint loose. The repair was finished after dark, yet the water stayed cloudy for a whole evening, and the service told residents to run it off before using it for food. Pumps will drain the flooded cellars in the course of next week.

units: the house described belongs to the narrator's uncle
the entrance passage is narrow so as to hold the heat in
the kitchen takes up the largest room
the people there eat and mend their bicycles
soaked coats are hung there to dry as well
the green paint came from the last of a tin
the upper part of the walls stayed paler for want of paint
the floor slopes towards the garden door
that slope served to let the washing water run out
a mirror throws light back onto the table
text: Walk into my uncle's house and you see at once that it was built with its back to the wind. The front door gives onto a narrow passage, because whoever put it up wanted the heat held close to the hearth. That is why the kitchen is the largest room and swallows all the traffic: people eat there, mend their bicycles there, hang up soaked coats to dry there. The walls carry a dull green that came from the last of a tin; there was not enough of it, so the upper part stayed a good deal paler. The tiled floor slopes towards the garden door, an old trick for letting the washing water run out, which is why the children's marbles all roll the same way. And since the far window looks onto a blank wall, my uncle hung a mirror opposite, to throw a little light back onto the table where the family gathers of an evening.

units: homes pile up objects that are hardly used
tidying has become an occupation in its own right
the trouble lies in the fact that objects do not circulate
a machine bought for one particular use sleeps in a cupboard
a neighbour is sometimes hunting for the very same machine
the writer rejects the moral appeal to own less
tool stores already exist in some blocks of flats
the tenants write each loan down in a notebook
these stores rest on a modest deposit and a short loan
the writer asks landlords to set aside a room for such exchanges
text: Our homes fill up with things that we use for one season only, and tidying them has become an occupation in its own right. The trouble is not that we own a great deal of it; it is that nothing circulates. A machine bought for one particular dish sleeps in a cupboard while a neighbour hunts about for the very same thing. No moral appeal to own less is going to mend that. What will mend it are quiet arrangements that make borrowing as easy as buying. Tool stores already exist in some blocks of flats, run by the tenants themselves, who write each loan down in a notebook. Where they work, they rest on three rules: a modest deposit, a short loan, and repairs shared out among the borrowers. Landlords ought to set aside a room for such exchanges, just as they set one aside for prams.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a member of staff lives on the lowest floor of the building, beside the entrance door
his duties fall into three separate groups
the first group covers the cleanliness of the shared areas
he puts a lubricant on the closing mechanisms that squeak
the second group concerns the delivery of letters
he carries the post to the door of the oldest residents
the third group consists of calming quarrels between neighbours
he hears the sides in conflict one after the other
he does not pass on what he learns about the residents' lives
he nearly always finds the owner of a lost object
text: The caretaker lives on the lowest floor of the building, in a flat wedged against the front door. Everything he does falls into three separate groups. The first is cleaning: he sweeps the stairwell, wipes down the glass panes in the entrance hall and oils the latches that have begun to squeak. The second is the post, which he sorts through at the start of each week and leaves outside the doors of the oldest tenants. The third is peacekeeping. When two neighbours fall out, he hears each of them on their own, then suggests something both can live with. What people trust most is his silence, for he knows everyone's habits and repeats none of them. They value his memory for lost property too. A key, a glove, an umbrella left behind in the lift nearly always finds its way back to its owner.

units: the piece of furniture reviewed was bought second-hand
on arrival its surface was covered with a sticky layer the seller had not mentioned
this old coating had to be stripped off entirely
the supports of the piece began to wobble the following week
simply tightening them put this fault right without taking the whole thing apart
after a season of use the overall verdict is favourable
the material stands up to very hot containers
one drawer jams when the air turns damp
no adjustment cures this jamming
the piece is judged worthwhile given its low cost
text: This coffee table came to us second-hand, and a season of steady use has settled the question. It turned up looking dull, the top hidden under a sticky varnish that the seller had said nothing about, so the whole surface had to be stripped back before anything else could be done. A week later the legs began to wobble; tightening the screws sorted that out, with no need to take the thing apart. After a season of family use, the verdict leans firmly the right way. The wood takes a scalding mug without marking, scratches rub out with a cloth, and the height suits reading as well as eating in front of a screen. One fault remains. The drawer jams whenever the air turns damp, and no amount of adjusting cures it. For what it cost, it earns its place, provided that nuisance is accepted.

units: the kitchen refurbishment has just been finished
a workman uncovered a cracked pipe behind the sink
the seeping had been going on for several weeks
the damp made the wall covering crumble at a touch
the leak had to be sealed before any finishing work
the water supply had to be cut off during the repair
the washing-up was done at a neighbour's for five evenings
costs rose and the timescale stretched out
the writer invites her correspondent to come and see the room
text: I am writing because the kitchen is finally done, and you will never guess what held the whole job up. While digging away at the wall behind the sink, the workman came upon a pipe with a crack running through it. Water had been seeping for weeks, and the plaster crumbled the moment you laid a hand on it. The split had to be sealed before anyone could think about paint. Since the repair meant shutting off the water, we spent five evenings carrying the washing-up upstairs to the neighbour. She lent us her bowl, and we came back down with the plates still warm. The upshot: the budget swelled, the dates slipped, and my temper went with them. Now that everything has dried, the room smells of fresh paint and I sit in it for no reason at all, just to look at a smooth wall. Come and see it as soon as you can.

units: workshops open to everyone take in household appliances that no longer work
a workshop coordinator answers the visitors' questions
the main obstacle is not the scarcity of parts
owners give up because they believe the inside of an appliance is out of bounds
the method chosen is to have the visitor carry out the action
the visitor lifts the lid himself and cleans the clogged part
a helper steps in when the repair goes beyond the visitor's abilities
this help takes place in full view of the appliance's owner
more objects leave in working order than are left behind
text: What is to be done with a kettle that has given up? The question comes round again and again at the repair workshops that open their doors to all comers, and the woman who runs one of them is glad to answer it. The barrier, she explains, is not a shortage of spare parts but the discouragement of the owners themselves, who are convinced that a sealed casing is none of their business. How do you shift a belief like that? By handing over the job rather than describing it: the visitor lifts the lid himself, spots the clogged filter and rinses it under the tap. And when the fault outruns what he can manage? A helper takes over, though never out of sight of whoever brought the thing in, who follows every step. The measure of it is simple. Far more objects walk out working than are left behind.

units: a resident thought the countryside better than the noise of a block of flats
her neighbour had lived in both settings
the neighbour disputed this preference
she described the sounds of wood and wind in an isolated house
she said that no voice covers those sounds in the countryside
she liked recognising the residents' steps on the stairs
the first wanted a planted plot and warm water at the outside tap
the second told apart quiet, which one chooses, from the presence of others, which one takes in
the two women reached no agreement
they greeted each other the next day nonetheless
text: The tenant downstairs held that the hush of a country house beat the bustle of a block of flats. Her neighbour answered gently that she had lived in both and believed nothing of the sort. Out there, she said, the wind worries the shutters and the floorboards creak with no human voice to cover them; you end up listening to your own solitude. Here the stairs ring with familiar steps, and every step carries a face: the nurse coming home, the student going out, the child dragging a satchel. The first woman pressed her case. She wanted a garden of her own, the smell of cut grass, warm water running from the tap outside. The second smiled and said that quiet is something you choose, whereas company is something you take in. They parted still disagreeing, and greeted one another the next day.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: before running water arrived, three techniques served to wash cloth
the first technique used water mixed with sifted ashes
this alkaline solution dissolved greasy substances
the second technique rested on blows struck with a wooden tool
the beaten cloth was then rinsed and left to drain on a hard surface
the third technique exposed the cloth spread out on damp vegetation
damp and sunlight together removed the stains
these processes damaged the fibres, whose weave turned coarse
the wear explains why cloth was counted, mended and handed down
text: Before water came into houses under pressure, the washing of linen rested on three methods that the old handbooks set out in careful detail. The first was a soak in ash water: the pieces were heaped in a tub and drenched with water thickened by sifted ashes, and the dissolved potash bit into everything greasy. The second came down to brute force. A wooden beater drove the fibres against a sloping board, after which they were rinsed and left to drain on a flat stone. The third turned on sunlight; spread over wet grass, the cloth gave up its stains to damp and daylight working together. All three of them wore the weave down, and after a dozen washes the surface felt coarse under the fingers. That wear is why household cloth was counted, mended and handed on as something of value.

units: the observation concerns a kitchen window during a cold night
preparing food releases steam into the room
this damp air meets a pane chilled from outside
the steam turns into droplets settling on the glass
the droplets merge then run down the panel
the water gathers against the horizontal piece of wood, which soaks it up
at dawn the condensation goes from the glass surface
the wood stays soaked with water despite this disappearance
the repetition of the phenomenon lifts the paint and encourages fungus
airing the room briefly after cooking stops the process at its very start
text: Watch what happens to a kitchen window over one cold night. Early in the evening, cooking sends up steam and the air of the room fills with a damp you cannot see. By the end of the meal that warm air reaches the pane, which the cold outside has chilled. The steam gives up its energy and turns back to liquid, so a fine beading settles across the glass. Later on the neighbouring beads run together, grow heavier and slide down towards the bottom of the frame. There they gather against the wooden crosspiece, which drinks in part of the water. Come dawn the mist has gone from the surface, yet the wood underneath stays soaked. Repeat that cycle through a whole season and the paint lifts and fungus takes hold. Open a window briefly after cooking and the chain breaks at its first link.

units: a bicycle was left against railings after a move
repeated rain attacked the transmission, which seized up
the workshop in the area quoted a wait of two weeks
the owner therefore took on the repair unaided
he cleaned every link with a solvent and a stiff brush
the noise of the work drew a neighbour carrying tools
the neighbour straightened the back wheel, which had play in it
this mutual help gave rise to a weekly meeting
the two men mend the objects left behind in the building
the bin store no longer holds any wrecks
text: The bicycle had been propped against the railings since the end of summer, forgotten in the rush of a move. One shower after another had eaten into the chain until the links would not turn at all. The workshop down the road quoted a wait of two weeks, so its owner set about the job on his own. He laid the frame down on a sheet, poured solvent over the metal and worked at every single link with a stiff brush. The old grease, gone tacky, came away in flakes. The scraping brought down a neighbour with an oilcan and a spanner. The back wheel had picked up some play for want of the right tool, and the man had it running true in a handful of movements. Out of that favour grew a habit: once a week the pair mend what the building gives up on, and the bin store has emptied of wrecks.

units: a door gives out a shrill noise every time it is moved
the procedure avoids calling in a tradesman
you must first find the guilty hinge by moving the door slowly
a cloth placed underneath protects the floor from drips
you use a thin oil and not a thick paste
a thick paste picks up dirt and makes matters worse
a single drop placed on the pin is enough
swinging the door several times spreads the product
you wipe off the surplus once it has run down
if the noise carries on, the upper fixing of the hinge must be tightened
text: Does your door shriek every time someone goes through, and wake you at night? Here is how to be rid of it without paying anyone. Start by tracking down the guilty hinge: ease the door open very slowly indeed and listen for where the squeal begins. Then slip a cloth underneath, because whatever runs down will mark the floor. Reach for a thin oil, never a thick grease: grease holds the dust and the trouble comes back worse than before. One drop on the pin will do. Swing the door back and forth a dozen times so the oil works its way down. Let it drain, then wipe the surplus away with the cloth. If the squeal hangs on, the top screw has probably worked loose; tighten it right home, or the door will keep leaning crookedly on its hinges. Quiet returns before the evening is out.

units: two neighbouring districts have adopted opposite strategies to revive their shops
on the high bank, a covered market was built with public money
the pitches there are offered at low rent to growers from round about
this market's attendance reaches its peak as the week ends
on the lower bank, no building received funding
local people grouped together and use an old school yard
every seller sets up a folding stand of his own there
the covered market attracts passing buyers drawn by steady opening hours
the yard keeps a nearby clientele who put up with bad weather
in both districts, the shops in the surrounding streets receive more visitors
text: Two neighbouring districts have taken opposite routes to bring their local shops back to life, and the contrast is hard to miss. On the high bank a covered market went up with public money; pitches go cheaply to growers from round about, and the crowds peak as the week ends. On the low bank not a brick was funded. The residents there banded together instead and took over the yard of an old school, where every trader brings a folding table of his own. The takings differ as much as the settings. The covered hall pulls in passing custom, won over by the shelter and by fixed opening hours, while the yard keeps a nearby following that puts up with rain and improvisation. One thing joins the two experiments. In both, the shops in the streets round about have seen more people through the door.

units: the yard gate is opened at sunrise by the caretaker
the yard floor is swept in front of the letter boxes
the plant tubs under the porch are watered after the sweeping
parcels are piled against a wall in the middle of the day
the children of the building use the yard as a play area in the afternoon
the children's racket is tolerated until dusk
a single lamp with damaged glass lights the way to the staircase
the gate is locked again and the fire exit checked before nightfall
this arrangement has never been set down in any written rules
text: The first light reaches the inner yard before anyone else does. The caretaker unlocks the gate, whose cracked latch still puts up a fight against the key, then sweeps the gritty paving stones in front of the letter boxes. The two plant tubs beneath the porch are watered once the sweeping is done. Around midday the delivery men stack their parcels against the far wall, and the passage narrows to a cluttered corridor. By afternoon the children of the building are rolling their balls across it, and the caretaker puts up with the racket until dusk. The windows light up one by one and quiet settles again. A single lamp, its glass chipped, marks the way to the staircase. Before nightfall the gate is locked once more and the fire exit checked. Nothing in this steady round has ever been set down in writing.

units: mending an appliance now costs more than buying another one
the high price of spare parts puts people off calling a repairer
appliances in working order are thrown into the recycling bins
the build-up of discards pushes up the bill for treating waste
this expense is carried by the community
the cheapest choice for one person brings the highest cost for everyone
bringing the price of parts down would be part of the remedy
making instruction manuals available is the second measure proposed
text: Mending a broken appliance now costs more than buying another one, and that reversal has quietly reshaped our everyday habits. Spare parts sell at such a price that nobody calls a repairer when a lid cracks or a handle works itself loose. The result is plain to see in the recycling bins, where machines barely used at all sit beside wobbly chairs that a screwdriver would have saved. All those discards push up the bill for treating waste, and the bill lands squarely on the community. So the loop closes: the cheapest choice for one household turns into the heaviest outlay for everybody. Breaking it would mean bringing the price of parts down and putting instruction manuals within reach of anyone who asks for them. Until that happens, the repair workshop will remain something of a curiosity.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a neighbour mends the other tenants' clothes for nothing
she has sewn since she was a teenager without any training
her sewing machine came from her mother
the table holding the machine is unsteady and propped up with cardboard
the ceiling light was too weak to tell a dark thread from dark cloth
the poor light made her seams go wrong
a tenant from downstairs found her an adjustable lamp at a second-hand market
the lamp gathers the beam where it is needed
she refuses payment and asks for a hot drink instead
text: You know the sort of neighbour I mean: the one who takes in everyone's torn clothes and hands them back mended, and never asks for anything. She has sewn since she was a teenager, without a single day of training. Her machine came down from her mother, and it stood on a wobbly table that she propped up with a folded scrap of cardboard. The trouble was the light. That dim ceiling bulb never let her pick out a dark thread against dark cloth, so her seams wandered, she lost her temper, she began again. A tenant from downstairs turned up with an adjustable lamp from a second-hand market, its shiny reflector gathering the beam exactly where she needed it. Now she takes up a frayed hem in a couple of stitches and will not hear of being paid. She asks for a hot drink, sits down, tells workshop stories, and the whole corridor gains by it.

units: two food shops face each other at the entrance to the neighbourhood
the first fills a narrow, poorly heated room
fruit in the first shop is weighed by hand
the owner of the first shop calls out his prices aloud
the second has a far wider range and clear labels
the second offers a till with no member of staff
the fruit from the narrow shop has a frank scent
the fruit from the shop opposite is even in size but tasteless
the shopper decides by mood and hardly ever by reason
text: Two food shops face each other at the entrance to the neighbourhood, and the contrast repays a moment of close attention. The first fills a cramped, poorly heated room where crates are stacked as high as the ceiling; the fruit is weighed out by hand and the owner calls out his prices aloud. The second, all gleaming windows, carries a far wider range, labels everything clearly and offers a till with nobody standing behind it. In use, the gap in quality does not follow the gap in comfort. Tomatoes from the cramped room ripen where they lie and keep a frank scent; those from the shop opposite are firm, even in size and utterly without taste. On one side you pay for discomfort and flavour, on the other for ease and blandness. In the end shoppers decide by mood, and hardly ever by reason.

units: the writer of the letter writes from the table where meals were taken together
the floor by the window is cracked and has not been replaced
the rug in the hall has lost its fringes
the teapot chipped at the spout is still used every evening
one arm of the armchair is worn through to the threads
a shawl left behind by the reader lies on that armchair
the drawer holds keys, postcards and a worn-down pencil
the plants on the ledge survive despite careless watering
the door creaks and still shuts badly
text: I am writing from the kitchen, at the table where we used to eat together. Nothing has changed, and that is what I wanted to tell you. The floor by the window is still cracked; I gave up on replacing it, it belongs to the room now. The rug in the hall has lost its fringes and I step over it without thinking. That teapot you hated, chipped at the spout, does its work every evening. One arm of the armchair has worn through to the threads, and the shawl you left behind lies folded across it. In the drawer there are your keys, a stack of postcards and a pencil worn down to nothing. Out on the ledge the plants hold on, though I water them carelessly. I tidy very little, as you know. Yet I am attached to these battered things the way one is attached to familiar handwriting. Come back whenever you like: the door creaks, and it shuts no better than before.

units: a dark ring low down on a partition wall signals damp coming through
what to do depends on how far things have gone
at the first stage the plaster darkens but stays dry to the touch
airing the room and pulling away the furniture that blocks the air is enough at this stage
a cheap measuring device confirms the trend
the covering turns spongy and gives way under pressure as the damp advances
the wall must then be sounded and a seal or a pipe checked
at the advanced stage the plaster comes away in patches
painting over it hides the sign without removing the cause
text: What should you do when a dark ring appears low down on a partition wall? The answer depends on how far the damp has got. Early on, the plaster darkens without lifting and the surface still feels dry under the fingers; airing the room and pulling away the furniture that blocks the air will usually do. A cheap meter confirms the trend in a couple of readings. Later, as the damp advances, the covering turns spongy and gives way under light pressure: now you sound the wall, trace the source, and check the seal of a joint or a pipe. At the advanced stage the plaster comes off in patches and leaves a gritty face; surface treatment is no longer enough, and the cause must go before anything is made good. And painting over it? That hides the sign, leaves the fault alone, and the stain comes back.

units: a tenant reports to the managing agent a dripping tap dating from the autumn
the agent cites the absence of a written request
the tenant states that he telephoned three times without an answer
the agent admits that the switchboard was overwhelmed and the messages went astray
with no report on record no tradesman was sent out
the leak therefore ran on and stained the ceiling of the flat below
the tiling under the sink has split
the repair will cost more than a washer changed at the start
the two agree that every call will be confirmed in writing the same evening
text: The tenant told the managing agent that the tap in the washroom had been dripping since the autumn. The agent replied that no written request had ever reached him, and that nothing could be set in motion without one. The tenant pointed out that he had telephoned three times and had never once been called back. The agent conceded that the switchboard had been overwhelmed and that those messages had gone astray. With no report on record, he added, no tradesman had been sent out, so the leak had run on. The tenant observed that the ceiling of the flat below now carried a stain, and that the tiling under the sink had split. The agent accepted that the repair would cost more than a washer changed back in the autumn. The two of them settled on a rule: every call would be confirmed in writing the same evening.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: before running water every household had to draw its water outside
this chore fell mainly to children and servants
the buckets were carried up worn and slippery steps
the water stood in badly washed vessels
disease was passed on through this stored water
local authorities first opened more places to draw from
this measure shortened the walk without making things any cleaner
piping under pressure together with treatment solved the problem
putting a tap in the kitchen did away with the household store
text: Before running water ever reached the inside of people's homes, every household sent someone out to draw it from a well or from the fountain in the street. The chore fell mainly to children and to servants, who hauled heavy buckets up worn steps that were more often than not slippery. The trouble did not lie in the tiredness alone. Water stood for days on end in badly washed vessels with a slimy bottom, and disease travelled through it. Local authorities began by opening more places to draw from, a measure which shortened the walk without making the stored water any cleaner. The lasting answer came from piping under pressure, together with a treatment of the water before it was sent out. Once a tap stood in the kitchen itself, the household store vanished, and with it the chief source of contamination.

units: bread and a biscuit left out in the air overnight change in opposite directions
the bread goes hard while the biscuit goes soft
the cause shared by both changes is water on the move
fresh bread holds a great deal of water, above all in its crumb
the water in the bread drifts off into the surrounding air and the starch rearranges itself
the biscuit leaves the oven with almost no water
the biscuit takes moisture from the air and loses its snap
a wet cloth laid over the basket keeps the crumb supple
shutting the two foods away produces two opposite effects
text: Leave a slice of bread and a dry biscuit out on the table overnight, then look at them in the morning. The bread has gone hard and the biscuit has gone soft: two opposite outcomes from one single cause, which is water on the move. Fresh bread holds a great deal of it, mostly in the crumb; that water drifts off into the air, the starch rearranges itself, and the crumb turns dry and brittle. The biscuit leaves the oven with almost none, so it takes moisture from the air, its sugars grow damp, and the snap gives way to a soft, almost spongy bite. Each of them is hunting for a balance with what surrounds it. A wet cloth laid over the bread basket keeps the crumb supple. There is the trick: shut the bread away to hold its water in, shut the biscuit away to keep water out. One tin does two opposite jobs.

units: a bunch of keys was left behind on a low wall by a bus stop
a student photographed it and then handed it in at the kiosk nearby
the kiosk keeper took stock of the items attached to the bunch
the bunch carried a letter-box key and a trolley token
a building pass with nothing written on it hung there as well
the photograph stayed taped to the kiosk window for two evenings
the neighbourhood put forward several theories about who the owner was
the porter of a block recognised the model of pass and worked out the floor
the owner had not yet noticed that her keys were gone
text: It began with a bunch of keys that someone had left behind on the low wall beside a bus stop. A student photographed them, and then handed them in at the kiosk nearby. The keeper took careful stock of what lay in front of him: a letter-box key, a dull trolley token, a worn leather fob and a building pass with nothing written on it at all. The photograph stayed taped to the kiosk window for two evenings running. Then came the theories of the neighbourhood: a nurse from the block opposite, a delivery driver hurrying to finish his round, a pensioner who walks his dog on that same corner. The pass settled the matter. The porter of that block recognised the model of pass and worked out the floor. The owner, who was told late in the afternoon, had not yet noticed that her keys were gone.

units: rainwater does not soak into tarmac surfaces
the quick runoff reaches the watercourse all at once
these sudden arrivals push the river out of its bed
the banks lose their fine sediment to the current
bare cultivated ground wears away in the same manner
perforated slabs replace the tarmac of car parks
sown cover crops open root channels that soak up the downpour
planted ditches store the runoff before handing it back to the subsoil
text: Rain that lands on tarmac has nowhere to go. It skims across the surface, fills the drains and reaches the watercourse in one sudden shove. That surge lifts the river out of its bed, and the current strips the fine silt from the banks as it goes. Bare ploughed land wears away much the same, because the downpour hits a packed crust that no root holds together. The remedies that exist all come back to a single idea: give the ground its thirst back. Planners are pulling up the tarmac in car parks and laying perforated slabs that grass can settle into. Growers sow a cover crop between harvests, and those roots bore channels that drink the downpour. Elsewhere, shallow ditches planted with reeds hold the runoff for a while, then hand it back unhurriedly to the water table underground.

units: the narrator returns to a jetty she knew as a child
she remembers damp, quiet air on her early visits
the fierce wind of her recent visit nearly tore her bag away
sheets of water were now coming over the low wall
the lighthouse keeper describes storms closer together than before
he once counted a single serious warning each season
he now counts three or four between two big tides
the narrator finds that the place of her childhood has changed character
text: I went back to the harbour jetty during the storm season, and I could barely place the spot. As a girl I used to walk out there through a soft, salty haze, with the damp settling on my cheeks and nothing much stirring. This time a gust nearly ripped the bag off my shoulder, and sheets of water were coming clean over the low wall. The lighthouse keeper told me the blows land closer together now, with far deeper troughs behind them. He used to log one bad warning a season, he said; these days he counts three or four between one big tide and the next. It is not the same coast any more, honestly. The sand has thinned by the steps, the fishermen have shifted their pots into the shelter of the pier, and the place I grew up with feels like an out-of-date map you keep out of fondness.

units: a household compost bin fits into a small space
the method falls into three parts
the bin must stand on living soil, out of full sun
wet waste and dry material have to be alternated
meat scraps are kept out of the mixture
the heap must be turned at regular intervals to air it
a dampness like that of a wrung-out sponge is what you want
the end product is a dark, crumbly material that feeds the soil
text: Composting at home takes up less room than most people expect, and the job splits neatly into three parts. The bin first: stand a slatted container straight on living soil, in the light shade of a hedge, so that worms can climb up into it. Then the material: layer wet stuff, peelings or grass clippings, with dry stuff, fallen leaves or torn brown card. Keep meat scraps out, since they draw in rodents and stall the whole process. Upkeep last: turn the heap with a fork every fortnight and check that it stays as damp as a wrung-out sponge. Too wet and it starts to stink; too dry and it goes to sleep. After two seasons you are left with a dark, crumbly material, not far off the humus of a woodland floor, which you spread around your plantings to feed the soil and hold the water in.

units: an embankment gave way before sunrise
a man on the night shift was the first to raise the alarm
the residents left with very little in their hands
the water reached the first floor of the low houses
the current fell away in the second half of the following night
a grey silt covered the streets once the water had gone
the rescue teams set pumps down on the central square
an engineer blames the failure on runoff from the hillsides
text: The embankment gave way a little before dawn, quietly, the way a seam lets go. A man on the night shift watched it open from the footbridge and set off the siren. Thick mist still lay over the village when people came out with a bag apiece, leaving their kitchen lights burning behind them. The flood climbed to the first floor of the low houses, held that level right through the night that followed, then began to slacken. What it left as it drew back was a grey silt, smooth as varnish, poured along the streets. The rescue teams set their pumps down on the central square, and the drone of the engines took the place of the water's silence. An engineer from the rivers office puts the failure down to the runoff off the stripped hillsides, which loaded the channel far beyond its designed measure.

units: the treeless plateau sheds its heat as soon as the sun goes
the heat stored in the ground leaves towards a clear sky
the air against the ground falls below its dew point
the water vapour then settles as beads on the plants
a deposit of crystals forms once the surface drops below freezing
that frozen deposit draws a white fringe along the edge of the leaves
cold air gathers in the hollows of the ground
the dips therefore freeze before the slopes that stand above them
text: On this bare, treeless plateau the surface begins shedding heat the moment the sun drops away. The ground has taken in energy through the sunlit hours, and it gives that energy up to a cloudless sky, which sends none of it back. So the layer of air lying against the ground cools faster than the air above it. Once that layer falls past its dew point, the vapour it carries can no longer stay hidden: it settles as fine beads on stems and spiders' webs, and that is dew. Should the surface drop below freezing, the deposit changes character and turns to frost, a white fringe of crystals along the edge of every leaf. Cold air, being heavier than mild air, then slides down the slopes and gathers in the hollows. The dips whiten well before the ground above them, at much the same height.

units: the author holds it unreasonable to cover fertile ground with buildings
a productive soil takes thousands of years to assemble
a mineral covering removes that resource with no way back
built surfaces make flooding worse downstream
the author would make each further development conditional on reclaiming a brownfield
he asks that the price of a plot take in its capacity to feed people
he wants the stripping of abandoned ground made compulsory
he holds these measures to be administrative rather than technological
text: It is hard to defend the habit of building over our most fertile ground without ever pricing what is lost. A productive soil takes thousands of years to assemble, one thread of humus at a time, and a concrete slab cancels it within a single building season. The loss is not merely agricultural: sealed surfaces throw the rainfall downstream, where it feeds the flooding that the towns then pay dearly to repair. Three measures would be enough to turn this around. Make each further development conditional on bringing an already built brownfield back into use. Write into the value of a plot its capacity to feed people, rather than its suitability for construction alone. Finally, require that abandoned sites be stripped back, so the subsoil is returned to the water. These are levers of public decision, not feats of engineering still waiting to be invented.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the warden looks after a waterlogged marsh
she reads the height of the water off graduated rules
she likens her work to that of a nurse
she explains that a patient and a marsh are both treated by small corrections
the man before her set out above all to drain the site
she has had the old drainage ditches blocked
the spongy growth came back after that work
the marsh now holds the water of heavy rain
text: The warden of a marsh at the bottom of a valley spends her weeks watching a soil that breathes. Graduated rules stand planted in the peat, and she reads the water off them, feels the moss between her fingers, listens for the frogs. She describes the work as a nurse's: you do not cure anyone by shaking them, you adjust, you watch, you go round again. That comparison also lights up what separates her from the man before her. He wanted the place drained, the ditches cut straight, the acreage won back for crops; she has had those channels blocked one by one. The spongy moss grew back, the brown layer thickened, and the floor of the valley began once more to drink the downpours instead of flinging them at the village below. She says the job has taught her a patience she never knew she had.

units: the visitor expected nothing of this exhibition on the climate
she came out of it thrilled
a first room throws a fine spray of water over the visitors
a great fan there works up a storm wind
a second room shows hailstones kept in the cold
a third room smells of damp woodland
the visitor finds the explanatory panels too crowded
she recommends the visit in spite of that flaw
text: Honestly, I expected nothing at all from this exhibition on the climate, and I came out of it thrilled. Three rooms, three ideas, and not a dull stretch anywhere in the place. The first one soaks you: jets throw out a salty spray while a great fan works up a gale, and you grasp at once what a battered coast puts up with. The second plays on cold. Behind a frosted pane lie hailstones collected after a thunderstorm, big as walnuts, sliced open to show the concentric rings inside them. The third goes for the nose: you step into a rebuilt patch of woodland smelling of wet moss, while a blower pushes the scent of leaf mould at you. My one complaint is with the panels, wordy and cramped, which nobody is going to read standing up. Do go anyway, and save some breath for the last room.

units: the writer sends her cousin news of a stream
the watercourse had been shut inside a concrete pipe
a group of neighbours won its return to the open air
the machines opened the pipe at the start of the cold season
willows and rushes were planted along the banks
heavy rain arrived before the young plants had rooted
the banks held despite that rise in the water
dragonflies have been seen over the reopened stream
text: Dear cousin, you asked for news of the stream, so here is how the season went. It started when the neighbours' group finally won the right to open the watercourse up again, after decades shut away inside a concrete pipe. The machines came in with the cold weather and split the slab along the whole length of the common meadow. We planted willows and rushes on the banks, mud up to our knees, and by the second week the water had found its winding line again. Then a violent downpour arrived before the roots had taken hold, and we were sure we had lost the lot; the banks held, barely nicked. Since then dragonflies patrol above the pebbles, and the children from the hamlet come hunting for larvae under the flat stones. Come and see us before the snow patches melt, you will not know the meadow.

units: the moisture laid on the leaves comes from the air itself
the night-time cooling of surfaces brings about that deposit
air loaded with vapour can no longer hold it in suspension
mist forms when the condensation happens in the air rather than on a surface
a cover of cloud stops the deposit from happening
ground rich in organic matter holds more moisture
that moisture keeps alive the organisms which break down plant debris
taking away the plant cover dries out the reserve
text: What lays that moisture on the leaves before daybreak? Nothing has fallen from the sky: the air has simply surrendered what it held. Shedding heat into the emptiness of the night, a plant's surface grows colder than the surrounding air, and the invisible vapour condenses there. That is dew. And if the chilling reaches the entire body of air, not merely a surface? Then the droplets hang where they are, and a mist spreads low across the meadow. A covered sky, by contrast, throws the heat back down and cancels the whole business. Where does the water go? The ground drinks it, all the more readily for being loaded with rotted plant matter. That store sustains the countless creatures gnawing dead leaves back into the earth. Strip off the plant cover, and you dry out the reserve first, then the quiet life depending on it.

units: two adjoining plots are set side by side by the person who manages the fruit trees
one of the plots is sheltered by a living hedge and a bank of earth
the other plot is open and exposed to the wind
the sheltered plot holds water for longer after rain
the open plot dries out quickly once the sun returns
the neighbour complains that the living hedge shades the young plants
the neighbour also complains that it harbours small mammals
the manager judges these drawbacks minor next to the water saved
helpful insects shelter in the low growth on the bank
both speakers reckon that harvests must be recorded over several cycles
text: The woman who looks after the orchard says she weighed up two neighbouring plots before deciding. A thick hedge runs along the edge of one, and a low bank of earth slows the water as it drains away. The other lies bare, with the wind sweeping across it right up to the fence. Damp lingers in the sheltered plot long after a shower, she says, while the open ground dries the moment the sun comes back. Her neighbour sees it differently. The hedge, he argues, steals light from the young shoots and gives cover to rats and mice. She has weighed that up too, and it counts for little beside the water she keeps. Helpful insects nest in the scrub along the bank, besides, and drift down to the blossom. On one thing the two of them agree: none of it proves anything unless each keeps a record of the crop, season after season.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the considered use of trees is not a recent practice
past generations picked out many uses for a single tree
the shoots springing from a stump cut to the ground served as fuel
the covering of the trunk was stripped as the sap began to rise again
this covering was used to prepare animal skins
leaves gathered at the end of the cycle fed the herds when grazing ran short
the woven living hedge served as a barrier and gave fruit
ditches at the foot of the earth banks dried the fields and held a store of water
this landscape was in truth a set of tools and not mere scenery
text: Think the careful use of trees is a recent idea? Not a bit of it. Our forebears had already sorted out what each one was good for, and their reckoning was finer than we tend to assume. Firewood came first, cut from the shoots that spring back out of a stump felled right down to the ground. Then came the bark, stripped off as the sap began to rise, and put to use for curing skins. Leaves were gathered late on and fed to the herds when the grazing ran thin. Add the living hedge, woven in place, which kept the stock in and gave berries into the bargain. And do not forget the ditches dug at the foot of the banks: they took the wet off the fields and held a store of water against a dry spell. Nothing at all was left lying about. What we take for scenery was in truth a whole set of tools.

units: the process begins on a plot left untended
in the first cycle tall grasses take charge of the ground
in the next cycle thorny plants move in
these thorny plants keep young shoots safe from animals that graze
the first trees to arrive spread by seed carried on the wind
these first trees grow fast but cope badly with a lack of light
slower species then come on beneath their cover
the edge of the wood shows the stages of the change at a glance
a fire, a violent gale or felling sends the plot back to the beginning
text: It starts with a patch of rough ground: land nobody mows any more, land that the eye reads as empty. Through the first season the tall grasses take charge and close the surface over. In the second, brambles and scrub move in, and behind the thorns the young shoots are safe from anything that grazes. Then come the pioneer trees, light things with flying seed, quick off the mark but poor at coping with shade. Underneath them slower species germinate, ready to wait many seasons before they push through the canopy. At the edge of the wood the sequence can be read in one look: low bushes in front, tall timber behind. Foresters call this a succession, and they point out that it has no fixed end. Fire, a gale or the saw sends it back to the beginning, and the whole order repeats itself.

units: the bank built to hold the water back gave way during the night
the keeper of the water works was asleep only a few paces off
he heard a dull sound followed by the bank sliding into the flow
an earlier clearing of the channel had torn out the roots that bound the edge
without those roots the silt was carried off at every rise of the water
the flood spread over the low fields and buried the crops under mud
the people living nearby blamed the rain at first
the keeper blamed the loss of the plants along the edge
shrubs with creeping roots were put back in the season that followed
the new planting now stands up to the current and holds the bank
text: On the night the embankment gave way, the man who kept the lock was asleep a few paces from the breach. He remembers a dull sound, then the slow slide of the bank into the current. What lay behind it came out later. The roots that had bound the edge together were torn out the autumn before, when the channel was dredged without much thought. With that framework gone the silt had nothing to grip, and every rise of the water took its share. The flood spread across the low meadows, drowning the fences and laying a skin of mud over the crops. The people along the water blamed the rain at first. The keeper pointed instead at the bare stumps in a row by the edge, saying the works had lost their living bones. Shrubs with creeping roots went in the season after. Now the young stems bend without breaking, and the bank holds.

units: an earth bank that crumbles in the rain ends up blocking the ditch below
the first step is to work out where the water comes in and where it sits
without that survey the planting will be washed out
the loose rubbish must be cleared and the dead stems cut off flush with the ground
the base of the trunk is left in place because its roots still bind the soil
short level shelves are cut in a staggered pattern to break the slope
shrubs with dense roots are set in and the ground is covered with shredded branches
watering is kept to the first cycle so that the roots go down for water
after two cycles scrub covers the face and the run-off no longer gathers
text: A bank that crumbles at every downpour will end up choking the ditch below it. Here is how to hold it in place for good. Work out first where the water comes in and where it sits; skip that survey and whatever you plant will be washed out. Clear the loose rubbish next, then cut the dead stems off flush with the ground, leaving the stools where they are, since their roots still bind the soil. Cut short level shelves into the face, offset from one row to the next, so that the slope is broken up. Set shrubs with dense roots along the back of each shelf, then mulch with branches shredded on the spot. Water through the first season only, or the roots will stay lazy near the surface. Check the take after heavy rain and replace anything that has dried out. Two seasons on, scrub covers the face and the run-off spreads.

units: two towns on the same watercourse settled on different answers
the floods of the previous year prompted these decisions
the first town raised its embankment and faced the foot of the bank with stone
the second bought low-lying farmland to take the overflow
pools were dug across the land that had been bought
the figures show a more evenly spread flow leaving the second town
the water held underground recovers further in the second town
leaders of the first town cite the shelter of a densely built quarter
the specialists hold that the two methods complete one another
text: Two towns on the same river settled on opposite answers after the floods of last season. The first had its embankment raised and the foot of the bank faced with stone, on the argument that protection ought to be plain to see and quick to build. The second chose instead to buy up low-lying farmland, dig pools across it and let the river spread there when it rises. Figures put before a public meeting show a clear gap. Flow leaving the second town is more evenly spread, and the water held underground there recovers further. Councillors from the first town reply that their scheme shelters a densely built quarter, which the other approach would not have covered. The engineers brought in conclude that the two answers complete one another rather than compete, and they advise using both along the valley.

units: a waterlogged patch lies below the path and is crossed on planks
the ground gives underfoot and brown water works up between the plants
three habitats follow one after another with no line drawn between them
a belt of tall hollow stems edges the entrance and shuts off the view
a thicket of low shrubs holds the middle ground
still water lingers under that thicket
a sheet of open water takes up the centre
birds, frogs and a crowd of insects use the place
the plants hold back particles and dissolved matter before they reach the ground water
text: Below the path the ground opens into a wetland, crossed on a run of planks. Underfoot it gives like a sponge, and brown water works its way up between the tussocks. Three habitats follow one after another with no line drawn between them. At the near edge a belt of tall hollow stems shuts off the view and rustles at the faintest breath of air. Beyond it lies a thicket of low shrubs, the bark smooth and supple, with dark pools of standing water held underneath. In the middle a sheet of open water takes in the sky, ringed by a soft margin that sinks under the boot. Nesting birds work the cover, frogs call from the shallows, and insects swarm over the lot. The plants act as a sieve as well, holding back particles and dissolved matter before they reach the ground water. Nothing here looks dramatic; few places nearby hold as much life.

units: the writer had no faith at first in a scrap of waste ground behind the flats
a building scheme meant to clear the growth and cover the plot
the scheme stopped when the money ran out
brambles had taken the whole plot two cycles on
the neighbours grumbled about it
a group from the street put forward cutting paths and mowing only the middle
the idea was laughed at to begin with
the birds came back and the children made the place their own
the council in the end had the plot listed as a natural space
the writer now stands up for this rough ground rather than a park laid out with a ruler
text: I had no faith in it at all, that scrap of waste ground wedged behind the flats. To begin with we were told a developer would clear the lot and cover it in concrete. Then the work stopped, the money having run out, and the plot was left exactly as it stood. Two seasons on, brambles had taken the whole thing and the neighbours were grumbling. A group from the street put forward an idea: cut a few paths through, keep the scrub along the sides and mow nothing but the middle. People laughed. Then the birds came back, the children got into the habit of tearing about in there, and the council had the plot listed at last as a natural space. My own view shifted somewhere along the way. I wanted a park laid out with a ruler; now I stand up for this useful mess. It costs next to nothing to keep and gives back more than a shaved lawn.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a long spell without rain settled the trade of this raiser of young trees
she had been growing cereals until then
her yields fell away two cycles running
she turned her driest fields over to raising trees
she had to learn to tell trees apart and judge the health of a sapling
her first orders came from her neighbours
the people who look after rivers then ordered stock from her to hold banks together
her plants take hold better elsewhere because they came up on thin soil
she now has staff on the payroll and takes in trainees
from her old trade she kept the habit of writing everything down
text: A long drought settled the trade of the woman who now raises young trees at the edge of the village. She was running a cereal farm at the time, and watched her yields fall away two seasons running. With nothing worth cutting, she turned her driest fields over to a nursery of native trees. The switch forced a second craft on her: reading bark, judging the vigour of a sapling by the colour of its sap, sowing at the right moment. Orders came from her neighbours first, then from the people who look after rivers and wanted stock that would hold a bank together. Because her plants come up on thin soil, they take hold better once they are moved elsewhere. She has three on the payroll now and trains youngsters who travel a fair way to reach her. One habit survives from the old days: she writes everything down, season by season.

units: the quiet of the machinery is the first thing this reworked valley leaves you with
the place had once been tidied to excess
the bed of the stream had been pulled straight and its banks laid in masonry
the meadows had been drained by a network of ditches
the wild things had left the place
those who carried out the repair gave the stream its bends back
whole trunks were dropped into the bed on purpose
the wood edge was allowed to creep out over the meadows
walkers struggle to find a dry way through
the tree cover keeps the air cool and the current is slowed before the town
text: What strikes you first in this valley given back to the water is that no machine is running. The place had once been tidied to excess: the stream pulled straight, the banks laid in masonry, the meadows drained down to the last ditch. The result was a corridor rather than a landscape, and the wild things had gone. Whoever carried out the repair went the other way entirely. They gave the stream its bends again, dropped whole trunks into the bed and let the wood edge creep out over the grass. You could accuse them of indulging disorder, and walkers do struggle to find a dry way through. Even so, it convinces. Under the canopy that has grown back the air stays cool, dead wood feeds the insects, and the current sheds its load before it reaches the town. A quiet success, measured less by what it built than by what it let happen.

units: the writer sends news to a close acquaintance about a plot taken back in hand
a layer of plant matter has been spread over the ground to hold the moisture
the hedge has been filled out with pieces taken from shrubs
the plants kept in place put up with a lack of water
building rubble has to be carted off because it blocks water soaking in
the writer notices that rain is held better since the work was done
roots are reaching further down than they used to
the writer asks after the food crop of the person written to
text: Dear friend, here at last is the news you asked for about the plot we took back in hand behind the house. Three jobs have kept me busy, and I will run through them in order. The first was the ground itself: I spread a thick layer of dead leaves over it, so that the damp stays put and less water lifts away. The second was the hedge, which I filled out with cuttings taken from the shrubs that stand up best to a dry spell. The third is the dreary one, carting off the heap of rubble the old shed left behind, since it stops the rain soaking in. Already the leaf layer holds a downpour better, and the roots are reaching further down than they used to. Small efforts of that sort will count for more than regret once the weather turns harsher still. Write soon, and tell me how your vegetable patch is faring.

units: a heavy fuel escaped from a store towards a watercourse
the leak went unnoticed through the first week
fishermen then saw weakened fish
a coloured film spread across the surface of the water
the technical authorities turned out only once the intake was threatened
floating devices were put in to hold back the slick
the fouled sediment was scraped away after the pumping
wildlife is coming back to the site little by little
a smell lingers on the bank in strong heat
text: So you want to know what became of the river after the trouble at the fuel store? Here it is in order. For the first week nobody noticed a thing: the heavy oil was seeping out under a cracked slab, giving off nothing you could smell from the bank. Then the fishermen started pulling up listless fish, and a coloured film crept across the still water. Was anything done quickly, you ask? Not at all, and that is the part which still rankles. Only when the slick reached the drinking water intake did the technical crew turn out. After that it moved along. Floating booms went in, the oily layer was pumped off, and the fouled silt was scraped away. And now? Now the wildlife is edging back, though the bank still gives off a tarry smell whenever the heat builds. That is roughly where matters stand today, as far as anyone can tell.

units: the spring feeding an upper district is running dry
draws made for crops have emptied the underground store
a grower fears losing his harvest without watering
a teacher asks the official about supply brought in by lorry
the official accepts that this would become necessary the following summer
the council means to cap the volumes allowed
the leaking pipes will be mended
the watering of ornamental ground will be banned
the public accepts that its own uses add to the shortage
text: The head of the water service put it bluntly to the residents gathered in the lower hall: the spring feeding the upper district is running dry. Pumping for crops, she explained, had emptied the underground store through the dry months, and one thing was now dragging another after it. A grower answered that his fields would burn without watering. A teacher asked whether the children would end up drinking water brought in by lorry. The official accepted that it would come to that by the following summer if nothing changed. The council, she added, would cap the volumes allowed, mend the leaking pipes and ban the watering of lawns. The talk ran on well into the evening, with everyone taking the point that the shortage was not the fault of the sky alone, but of what every household draws.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the channel of a harbour was silting up season after season
ships could no longer reach the quays
the merchants wrongly believed that the sea was drawing back
the river was in fact bringing down mud torn from the slopes
the felling of trees had left the hillsides bare
engineers tied the ruin of the heights to the decline of the harbour
planting was ordered on the ridges
brushwood works were set in the gullies
basins were dug to trap the mud before the shore
the depth of the navigable passage was regained
text: A thriving harbour town once watched its channel silt up, season upon season. Ships laden with salt and timber scraped the bottom, then gave up the run up to the quays altogether. The merchants feared the sea was drawing back; in truth the river was tipping into the roadstead a load of mud torn from the slopes above. Tall stands of trees had been felled for roof beams, leaving the hillsides bare, and the rain carried the soil off with nothing to check it. In time a generation of engineers grasped what tied the stripped hill to the ailing port. They had the ridges replanted, brushwood hurdles woven along the gullies and basins dug where the mud would settle before ever reaching the shore. The channel found its depth again, and the lesson outlived by many years those who had first learned it.

units: two neighbouring roofs behave differently under the sun
the first carries a dark bituminous covering
this surface takes in nearly all the radiation reaching it
the heating spoils the insulation laid beneath
the cooling plant then runs without a break
the second joins a pale render to a cover of plants
this roof throws back part of the radiation and holds rainwater
the pale version stays cooler at the same hour of reading
the planted roof weighs more and calls for steady upkeep
text: Two roofs side by side behave in opposite ways under the sun, and the covering explains it. The first carries a dark bituminous sheet, close to tar, which takes in nearly all the sunlight reaching it. Its surface grows so hot that the insulation laid beneath ages early, and the cooling plant runs without a break. The second has a pale mineral render, topped with a mat of fleshy plants. It throws back a good share of the radiation and holds rainwater in its growing layer. Read at the same hour, the pale roof stays markedly cooler than the dark one. The gap shows up on the energy bill of the building as well. Against that, the planted roof weighs more and calls for steady upkeep, which the sheet never asks for. The choice turns as much on the frame below as on the weather.

units: the keeper of a high station tells of an episode from his last season of work
the packed snow was covered with a greyish deposit
this deposit came from fires burning far away
a darkened surface takes in more heat and melts faster
the buried instruments had to be dug out twice in the same week
the slope was oddly silent at night
the usual night-time flows had gone
the observer wrote down what he saw in a notebook
readings from later seasons bore out his impression
text: The keeper of a high station tells of an episode that stayed with him through his last season of readings. He speaks first of the colour of the packed snow: instead of the expected white, the surface wore a grey veil of soot laid down by fires burning far away. He turns next to the melting, quickened because a darkened surface takes in more heat. He describes the buried instruments, which had to be dug out twice in the same week as the mantle sank. He recalls, last of all, the odd hush on the slope, stripped of the meltwater streams that usually ran through the night. Back down at the hut he entered these remarks in a bound notebook, aware that a lone story of that kind proves nothing on its own. Readings from later seasons bore him out, and the pages of that notebook seeded a much wider study.

units: the roof must be looked over and clean before any collecting
a guard is fitted at the mouth of the gutter to hold back leaves
the tank is set on firm footing and out of the sun
a collector carrying a filter joins the downpipe to the tank
the overflow must run towards planted ground and not onto the road
the water of the first week serves to rinse and is then thrown away
the tightness of the lid is tested each season
an open vessel encourages mosquitoes to breed
the store is partly drawn down before the frost to avoid a split
text: Before you start collecting rainwater at home, look the roof over carefully: a clean covering, free of moss and grime, yields clearer water. Fit a guard at the mouth of the gutter, so that the leaves are held back. Stand the tank on firm footing, out of the sun, so that warmth does not feed the algae. Join the downpipe to it with a collector carrying a filter, and check that the overflow can run into a bed of planting rather than out onto the road. Run the tap through the first week to rinse the tank, then throw that water away. Each season, test the lid for a tight seal, since an open vessel encourages mosquitoes to breed. Lastly, draw the store partly down before the frosts, or the ice will split the wall. Water gathered in this way will do for watering the garden and for cleaning tools.

units: an old coastal path has been shut off by a fence
the sea is hollowing out the foot of the rock wall
storm spells have grown more frequent
each assault carries off soft rock at the base of the slope
the upper part ends up giving way
a dwelling was pulled down over the previous cold season
its rubble still litters the beach lying below
a councillor explains that pulling back and staying both cost dear
scientists find the pace quickening with the rise of the sea
the parking areas are being shifted inland
text: Up on the cliff, the first thing you notice is the orange fencing shutting off the old coast path. The people living there will tell you straight away: the sea is hollowing out the foot of the wall, and the top follows. Since the storms started coming round more often, every swell carries off a little marl at the base of the slope, until the rock above gives way. So a house had to be pulled down over the cold season, and its rubble still litters the beach below. The councillor who handles the shoreline makes no secret of the bind: pulling back costs dear, staying put costs dearer. Scientists out measuring the retreat confirm that the pace is quickening as the sea rises. Meanwhile the parking areas are shifted inland, access is barred, warnings go up. And the fencing creeps further in each winter.

units: from a distance a wetland looks like an ordinary meadow
straight ditches were cut long ago to drain the marsh
this draining was meant to win ground for grazing
the water runs off towards a canal instead of staying in the hollows
peat left open to the air gives up its carbon
the birds that nested in the rushes have quit the site
wardens are plugging the ditches with clay
the water table is lifted and the reeds come back
boardwalks keep visitors clear of the frail ground
amphibians took to the pools from the second season
text: Seen from a distance along the towpath, the wetland looks like an ordinary meadow, grassy and cropped short. Closer to, straight ditches appear, cut long ago to drain the marsh and win grazing for stock. The water now slides off towards the canal instead of lingering in the hollows, and the bared peat gives up its carbon to the air. The birds that nested in the clumps of rush have quit the place. A team of wardens is working to turn that round: they plug the ditches with clay stoppers, lift the water table and let the reeds come back. Boardwalks steer walkers clear of the frail ground. By the second season the rewetted pools had taken in amphibians, and the sodden peat had stopped smouldering. The scene now looks a good deal less tidy, and that is exactly the sign they were waiting for.

units: the writer disputes the sporting image used to describe climate action
a contest is run alone and comes to an end at a set term
the writer offers the image of ground tended in common
each person there takes on the state of the soil left by the others
the careless gardener harms the plot next door
changing the image changes the nature of the commitments expected
a promise of figures differs from a promise of continued upkeep
the writer calls for talk of care rather than of performance
later generations will judge what has survived
text: We are fond of casting the climate effort as a race, with its winners and its stragglers. The picture is appealing, and it leads us astray. A race is run alone and comes to an end; the climate is closer to a shared garden, where each of us takes on the soil the others have left behind. In a race, whoever slows loses ground; in a garden, whoever lets a plot go lets the weeds through to the plot beside it. The switch matters: it changes what we expect of the promises made. A runner pledges a score, a gardener pledges upkeep. One of them marks a finish, the other marks a going on. We would do better, then, to speak less of records and more of care, less of standings and more of seasons. Those who come after us will not ask who ran the hardest; they will look at what is still growing.
