the second checks the display board over and over
the second gets to his feet each time a name is called out
both men say they feel the same unease
the first tells himself that he will soon know something
the second expects the worst outcome
a nurse predicts that the second will come out worn down
the nurse reckons that a word can turn a wait right around
text: In the waiting area of a hospital treatment unit, two men have sat since the same hour, called in for the same examination. The first leafs through a magazine, his shoulders low; he says his mind is on his vegetable patch. The second, taut with worry, checks the display board at regular intervals and rises whenever a name sounds down the corridor. Both of them say they feel exactly the same apprehension. The difference lies elsewhere: one tells himself he will shortly know where he stands, the other tells himself he will shortly hear the worst. A nurse who has watched such pairings for a good many years remarks that the second will come out of it worn to the bone, while the first will come out merely relieved. A word, she adds, is sometimes enough to tip a wait from one side to the other.

units: you need a thin notebook and you keep it on you for a week
each evening you write three lines and no more
the first line names the feeling that ruled, with a precise word
vague words are set aside in favour of exact ones
the second line gives the part of the body where the feeling showed
the third line names the event that came before the feeling
you forbid yourself any rereading before the week is out
reading it back too soon bends the record out of shape
at the end you spread the pages out to spot what keeps returning
the exercise is repeated in the season that follows
text: Get hold of a slim notebook, the sort that slides into a pocket, and keep it on you for a full week. When evening comes, open it on your knees and set down three lines, not one more. On the first, name the feeling that ruled the day, using the truest word you can find: not bad, but tightness, or weariness, or lift. On the second, write where it lodged itself, whether the throat, the neck or the belly. On the third, name whatever came before it, even if the link looks thin to you. Read nothing back until the week is out; reading it too soon bends the record out of shape. On the last evening, lay the pages in front of you and look for what keeps returning. You will find regular patterns that memory alone could never have held. Then shut the notebook without judging it, and begin again next season.

units: a team of researchers ran a protocol in two similar hospital units
the first stage came down to measuring without stepping in
the measurements bore on the pulse and the sweating of the nursing staff
peaks were recorded at the moment of the spoken handover between teams
the second stage imposed a short break before every handover
the instruction asked for slower breathing during that break
the third stage set the records of the two units against each other
the unit given the break showed a better variability of the pulse
the authors remain careful because the loads of each team differ
text: A team of researchers began their protocol at the start of the cold season, in two comparable hospital units. The first phase went no further than recording: heart rate and sweating were logged in the nursing staff across their shifts, with nobody stepping in at any point. When it closed, the traces showed repeated peaks at the moment of the spoken handover. The second phase brought in a short compulsory pause before every handover, with an instruction to slow the breathing. The third phase set the readings of the two units side by side. The gap widened week by week: the team given the pause showed a more favourable heart rate variability, and damp hands turned up less often. The authors draw their conclusion carefully, since the units they followed do not carry loads of the same weight.

units: the heart races and the hands go damp before speaking in front of a group
whoever feels this believes himself fragile and judges himself clumsy
the dread pushes him to avoid meetings where he will have to speak
avoidance strengthens the dread instead of easing it
breathing out more slowly than one breathes in slows the heartbeat
rehearsing the opening sentence aloud at home helps the start
it is better to tolerate the first trembling than to fight it
a relaxed friend can serve as a practice audience
the panic lessens after several repeated attempts
text: You will know the feeling. A group turns towards you, and before a single word comes out the heart is racing and the palms have gone damp. Anyone caught in that state tends to read it as proof of some private weakness, and to write himself off as clumsy. So the meetings where speaking is expected get quietly dodged, and there the trap closes, because every escape feeds the dread rather than starving it. Three plain habits open a way out. Breathe out more slowly than you breathe in, and the heartbeat follows and settles. Say your opening line aloud at home, often enough that the mouth already knows the road. Then let the first shaking happen instead of wrestling with it. A relaxed friend makes a decent practice audience. After enough attempts the panic wears thin, and the nerves become something you can carry.

units: two opposing positions circulate about the place of feelings in a team
the first demands complete restraint and allows nothing but arguments
the second prizes the open expression of anger and of grief
imposed silence sends the unease travelling underground
compulsory restraint makes colleagues quicker to take offence
expression without limit tires those who have to listen
a middle way consists in naming one's state without demanding its repair
this balance sounds obvious to state but calls for slow learning
text: Mention feelings at work and two camps form at once. The first asks for full restraint: the sound professional leaves his moods at the door and puts nothing on the table but arguments. The second prizes the opposite, anger spoken plainly, grief carried in the open in front of everybody. Each side is right about its rival and wrong about itself. Where silence is imposed, the unease does not vanish; it travels underground, and the team grow touchy over remarks that carry no weight. Where everything is poured out, the listeners tire and the meeting turns into a waiting room. What holds is the narrower path between the two: naming what you feel without asking anybody to mend it. To say you are weighed down obliges no colleague to comfort you. Ordinary to state, that distinction is slow to learn.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the listener works in the evening with a headset on a helpline
those who ring keep their anonymity
her voice stays low and never climbs
her first quality is bearing long silences
her second quality is holding on to details given early in the exchange
her third quality is a welcoming tone that promises nothing
one sparing caller took an hour before saying a whole sentence
she will never know what became of those she listened to
text: The voice comes first, low and unhurried, and it never climbs however heavy the line grows. She spends her evenings in a headset on a helpline, taking calls from shaken strangers who give no name at any point. Three skills hold the work together. Patience is the first: she lets silences run on where most of us would rush to fill them. Memory for detail is the second, so that a dog mentioned in the opening minutes comes back from her mouth much later. The third is a warm tone kept clear of familiarity, one that steadies a caller without promising a thing. She tells of a sparing man who took a full hour to produce one complete sentence. What became of him she will never learn. That is the heaviest part of the work: to walk beside people with no sequel, to shelter them for one evening, then to put the receiver down.

units: the programme under review comprises four successive stages
the opening meeting serves to list the triggers of the anxiety
the self-rating scale stays understandable without prior training
the breathing training imposes one identical pace on every participant
this single pace overlooks the differences in lung capacity
graded exposure is the best designed point of the programme
the list of feared situations is drawn up with the patient
the last meeting handles relapse prevention on a single sheet
the final verdict is mixed: rigorous middle, rigid opening, rushed ending
text: Four stages make up the programme under review, and each deserves a verdict of its own. It opens with a structured interview in which the practitioner lists what sets the anxiety off. That part holds up well, since the questions leave room and the self-rating scale stays readable for somebody with no training behind him. The breathing work that follows is harder to defend, because one pace is set for the whole room while lung capacity differs from person to person. Graded exposure, the third stage, is where the design is at its best: the ladder of feared situations is built with the patient rather than handed down. The closing session then disposes of relapse prevention on a single photocopied sheet. The overall picture is uneven, a rigorous middle weakened by a rigid entrance and a rushed way out.

units: the writer writes to explain a long absence never clearly justified
the death of his sister happened a short while ago
the grief did not lessen as he had supposed
the writer became inattentive and forgot his files
he reread the same page without holding on to its content
this scattering damaged the quality of his reports
from it he conceived a sense of being incapable
that sense led him to decline the invitations of his team
his silence was taken for contempt
he is starting therapy and wants to return by stages
text: I am writing to you about my long absence, which I have never explained to you with any clarity. My sister died a short while ago, and the effect it had on me was not the one I had supposed. I thought the grief would settle in and then thin out; it took quite another road. First it made me vague. Files slipped my mind. I would read a page and reach the bottom of it holding nothing at all, not one line of it. My reports lost their quality through that scattering, and out of the poor work grew a sense of being no longer capable. From that sense came avoidance: I stopped answering the invitations my team sent me, and my silence was read as disdain. Seen from your desk, the chain must have looked opaque. I have begun seeing a therapist, and I would like to take my duties up again by stages.

units: the question raised concerns learning to sleep when the mind stirs
insomnia feeds itself through the fear of not sleeping
the long waking then proves that fear right
the first recommendation consists in shortening the time spent in bed
that window is then widened by steps once falling asleep is quick again
it is advised to leave the bed when the night drags on
this instruction avoids tying the bed to a struggle
the effect of screens exists but it is overstated
mental stirring weighs more than screens do
text: Can sleep be learnt, when the mind refuses to switch itself off? The question comes up in consultation after consultation, and the accepted answer starts with something unwelcome. Insomnia keeps itself alive: the fear of not sleeping holds you awake, and the waking hours then prove the fear right. So what is to be done? The first piece of advice sounds wrong, because it asks for less time in bed rather than more. The window is squeezed until falling asleep goes quickly again, then widened step by step. A second question follows. Should you get up when the night drags on? Yes, say the protocols, so that the bed stops standing for a struggle. And screens? Their effect is real but blown out of proportion; a churning mind weighs far heavier. One rule survives: a restless head calms better upright than lying down.

units: the elder brother tells his sister that he does not understand their mother
their mother flares up over a tiny mishap but stays calm at bad news
the sister describes their father as working the other way round
the father falls silent during the crises and turns kind once quiet returns
the mother lets her anger out fast and forgets it fast
the father stores it up and then gives way weeks later
the brother judges the loud manner more wounding because the words land straight
the sister prefers that manner because one knows what to expect
both admit they were handed a model without choosing it
text: The elder brother was telling his sister that their mother made no sense to him. A knocked-over glass and she was shouting, while bad news arrived and she took it steadily. His sister said their father ran the other way round, mute for as long as the crisis lasted, then warm again the moment the house went quiet. One of them lets the anger out fast and forgets it just as fast, she said; the other takes everything in, keeps it, and gives way all at once some weeks on. The brother objected that the loud manner wounds more, since the words land straight in your face. His sister thought the reverse: at least you know where you stand, whereas a long silence leaves you guessing anything you like. They agreed in the end that neither way was better, and that each had been handed a model without ever choosing it.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: three readings of mental suffering came before the scientific discipline
these readings piled up rather than replaced one another
the supernatural reading put the disorder down to a force from outside
it healed through ceremonies meant to drive that force out
the reading of inner fluids explained melancholy by an imbalance of the body
it turned to bleeding, to purges and to prescribed diets
the moral reading held the sufferer answerable for his own disorder
it laid down strict hours, work with the hands and separation from others
each reading brought forth its own houses and its own vocabulary
phrases born of these readings survive in everyday speech
text: Long before the mind became a subject of study, mental suffering was read in three ways, and these piled up on one another rather than taking turns. The first was supernatural. Something from outside had entered the sufferer, and the cure lay in ceremonies meant to drive it back out. The second looked inward at the fluids of the body, blaming melancholy on an imbalance there; blood was let, purges were given, diets were laid down. The third was moral. It held the sufferer answerable for his own disorder and put its faith in discipline: fixed hours, work with the hands, separation from others. Each reading built its own houses, its own trades, its own words. Each left deposits in ordinary speech, where a black mood and a possessed mind are still spoken of. Careful clinical observation came later, and took generations to win.

units: the newborn has only three signals of feeling at his disposal
these signals are distress, settling and wide-awake curiosity
towards the end of the first year the fear of unknown faces appears
this fear shows that the child now sorts close ones from strangers
in front of a mirror the child works out at last that the smudge is on his own forehead
from that recognition are born awkwardness, pride and shame
schooling teaches that a feeling can be kept hidden
the child discovers that a soothing face can deceive
in adolescence the charge of feeling grows before the power to hold back
this gap explains how hard the outbursts of that age break
text: Watch a newborn. The whole range comes down to three signals: distress, settling and a wide-awake curiosity. Everything else is built on top of them. Near the end of the first year, unfamiliar faces begin to worry the baby, which shows that familiar people are now sorted from strangers. Then comes the discovery of the self. Put in front of a mirror, the child works out at last that the smudge belongs to his own forehead, and from that discovery come awkwardness, pride and shame. School adds a further layer: a feeling can be kept back, a soothing face may be lying, and tears come less readily with others watching. In adolescence the charge rises while the brakes are still being fitted, which is why the storms of those years break so hard. The whole structure takes decades to finish.

units: an incident on a hospital ward illustrates how a mood spreads
the ward coordinator took a painful piece of family news as her shift began
she informed no colleague of it
her speech sped up and her instructions turned clipped
the team changed its behaviour within two handovers
the exchanges grew shorter and the cross-checks fell away
the number of preparation errors doubled
the later review set aside tiredness and patient numbers as explanations
the cause held to be the silent passing on through posture, gaze and speed of voice
a short debriefing meeting put the coordination back
text: One incident on a hospital ward showed with unusual clarity how a mood spreads from person to person. The nursing coordinator, calm by habit, took a painful piece of family news just as her shift began. She said nothing about it to anybody, yet her speech sped up and her instructions came out clipped. Within two handovers the whole team had shifted: exchanges grew shorter, cross-checks fell away, and the air on the ward turned heavy. The measurable result showed in the incident book, where errors in preparation doubled. The review carried out afterwards set aside tiredness and patient numbers, both of which had held steady. What remained was the silent passing on of a mood through posture, through the eyes, through the speed of a voice. A short meeting to talk it through was enough to put the coordination back.

units: the frame that carries the roof may be of timber or of metal
this frame passes the weight of the roof into the load-bearing walls
slim pieces of wood are nailed across it to take the covering
the covering described is a dark stone split into flat sheets
this covering lets the space beneath the roof breathe
a channel set at the foot of the slope gathers rainwater
this water is then sent into a downpipe
an opening cut into the slope lights and airs the storey under the roof
this opening weakens the watertightness if it is poorly fitted
a specialist tradesman checks the whole of it before the wet months
text: Every part of a roof does a job of its own. The frame beneath, built of timber or of steel, holds the whole thing up and passes its weight down into the load-bearing walls. Across that frame run the battens, slim strips of wood nailed at intervals, and the covering hangs on them. Slate, a dark stone that splits into flat even sheets, keeps the rain out while the space underneath goes on breathing. Along the foot of each slope sits a gutter, gathering what runs off and feeding it into a downpipe, so that the walls are never left soaking. Higher up, a dormer cuts through the slope to bring light and air into the roof space; its surround asks for careful fitting, since any opening breaks the run of the covering. A roofer who knows the trade goes over every one of these before the wet months.

units: workmen were taking up a damaged floor at the top of an empty house
a workman's tool struck something hard beneath a board
an old timber covered in notches was uncovered
the person in charge of the site stopped the work

these marks showed in what order the structure was to be put together
the owner gave up the idea of replacing the structure
he chose to have it strengthened instead
the timber is left on show and protected by a pale coating
text: Work had begun with the taking up of a rotten floor, on the top storey of a village house that had stood empty through two winters. Lifting the third board, the labourer felt his bar jar against something solid. He brushed the dust aside and freed an old beam, blackened with age, its hidden face scored with a run of even notches. The foreman stopped everything. A building conservator came out the following morning, ran her palm along the grain and recognised jointing marks cut by the carpenter who first raised the roof. Each piece, she said, had been lettered before it went up, so that the frame could be assembled in its proper order, like the words of a sentence taken apart. Told of it at the weekend, the owner dropped the plan to replace the frame and asked instead that it be strengthened. The beam still shows in the ceiling, under a pale wax.

units: the moisture of the wall must be checked before a light partition goes up
a damp background stops the covering from holding
the skim comes away in flakes at the first heating if the background is wet
the setting-out line is marked with a taut string
a floor track out of level throws out every upright and ripples the finish
the bonding compound is mixed in small amounts because it sets quickly
a screw driven too deep spoils the surface and weakens the board's hold
laying jointing tape on a wet background makes it swell and then crack
a gap left at the foot of the partition protects it from rising damp
text: Before a light partition goes up, take a moisture reading of the wall behind it, for plaster will not grip a damp background and the skim comes away in flakes the moment the heating goes on. Snap the setting-out line onto the floor with a chalked string, then fix the floor track, because a track laid off the level hands its error to every upright and the finished face will ripple. Mix the bonding compound a little at a time, since it stiffens fast and a big batch ends up thrown away. Drive each screw home without breaking through the paper, or the head tears the facing and the board loses its hold. Let the work dry before skimming, as tape bedded over a wet joint swells and splits in the end. Leave a small gap along the foot of the partition too, or the least rise of damp will stain it.

units: neighbours in a low-lying area had flooded cellars after heavy rain
the trouble had lasted since the end of summer
a study was ordered by the local authority
the drainage network had been planned for ground that soaked up water
yards covered over with concrete have done away with that soaking up
the water reached the doorways of the houses and ran under the doors
the paths will be laid with a gravelly material that lets water through
channels running along the walls will take the water to a basin dug further off
the money comes from a grant and from a payment by the owners
a first stretch will be finished before the wet season
text: Since the end of summer, people living in a low-lying district have reported flooded cellars after every heavy shower. A study ordered by the local authority found that the drainage network, laid out when the ground still soaked up rain, could no longer cope once the yards had been concreted over. Nothing was taken in any more, so the water slid towards the thresholds and worked its way under the doors. The technical department have settled on an answer in two parts. The paths are to be lifted and laid again with loose gravel, which lets the rain sink away instead of throwing it back at the buildings. Shallow channels will then follow the exposed walls and carry the flow into a holding basin dug well clear of the houses. A grant to the authority covers most of the cost, the owners paying the rest. A first stretch is due before the rains.

units: two dwellings look at one another from the two sides of a narrow street
they share no feature at all
the house on the left has a pale covering on its walls
its openings are closed by painted wooden panels
above each opening on the left runs a visible oak beam
the house on the right has stone walls left bare
its openings are narrower and capped by a beam of hard stone
it is guarded by metal slats that slide instead of hinged panels
the first gives a sense of welcome, the second a sense of closing off
the entrance steps differ too, one of wood hollowed by use, the other a heavy slab
text: Two houses stand facing one another from either side of a narrow street, and they have nothing whatever in common. The one on the left shows a front rendered in pale lime wash, its tall windows shut behind wooden shutters painted grey. Over every opening a length of oak carries the wall above, barely curved, softening the flat face of the render. The one on the right answers with bare stone, the joints raked out, and its windows are narrower, each capped by a thick granite beam. No shutter swings there: metal slats instead run down in a rebate cut for them. The first looks welcoming, a little worn by the weather, while the second seems shut, heavy, cut to stand up to the wind. Even the two doorsteps part company, one of wood hollowed by feet, the other a cold slab of stone.

units: the writer holds that buildings are pulled down too easily instead of being put right
his first reproach bears on the waste of material still fit for use
careful dismantling costs more than quick destruction
his second reproach concerns the loss of the hand trades
these skills die out along with the places that taught them
his third reproach aims at the disappointing comfort of new building
new building suffers heat in the warm season and draughts in the cold one
the bill falls on whoever lives in the dwelling
his fourth reproach is that what the occupants feel for the place counts for nothing
he does not ask that everything be kept but wants proof that repair was impossible
text: Let us be blunt: we knock buildings down far too readily and mend them far too rarely. First reproach, the waste of good material. A sound roof frame, tiles fit to go back up, an oak staircase, all of it goes in the skip because careful stripping out costs more than an afternoon with a machine. Second reproach, the hollowing out of the hand trades. Who can still repoint in lime, straighten a sagging beam, split a slate without shattering it? Those skills die with the workshops that passed them on. Third reproach, the promised comfort never turns up: the freshly built one bakes in the warm months, whistles in the cold ones, and whoever lives there pays for it. Fourth reproach, what people feel for the place they have lived in weighs nothing in the decision. I do not argue for keeping everything, only for proof that no serious repair was open to us.

units: the woman spoken of grew up beside a place where stone was got out of the ground
her father worked there cutting stone out of the rock
she watched the blocks being split before doing it herself
she took up training in a workshop that put old buildings right
her first job of note was replacing a worn doorstep
she then took on harder work such as a split beam and a vault to rebuild
she set up her own workshop about ten years after she began
she employs two workers
she now teaches beginners, several of whom had never worked with their hands
she holds that this material calls for patience
text: A quarryman's daughter, the stonemason grew up beside a limestone working, watching blocks split long before she held a chisel herself. She went on to take up an apprenticeship in a yard given over to restoration work, learning to read the bed of the stone, and her first job of any weight was the worn doorstep of an old wayside inn. Heavier work followed soon enough: a cracked beam to take out and match, a vault to set back stone by stone. Ten winters or so after she began she opened a yard of her own, where two masons now work alongside her from one week to the next. Lately she gives part of each week to apprentices drawn from all sorts of backgrounds, several of whom had never handled a tool. Stone, she says, forgives impatience badly, and what she really teaches is how to slow the hand.

units: the visitor leaves this restored building with a feeling of being shut in
this feeling comes from choices of construction rather than from a quarrel over taste
an insulating skin was added in front of the old walls
this addition has sunk the windows into a deep recess
the view towards the outside is now blocked
a stretched ceiling hides the timber structure that used to be in sight
this hiding makes the place lose the size it seemed to have
the floor of gravel was replaced by a smooth surface
this surface throws the sound back and makes the noise hard to bear
the critic approves of keeping the entrance step worn by passing feet
text: You come out of this restored hall with a feeling of being shut in, and the fault lies less with taste than with the way the work was done. The designers lined the old walls with an unbroken insulating skin, so that the windows have sunk into deep throats and the eye is stopped short of the outside. The roof frame, once readable from one end of the building to the other, has gone behind a stretched ceiling, and with it goes the height that made the room feel generous. The floor of rolled gravel, replaced now by a smooth screed, throws voices back off the bare surfaces and turns a murmur into a din. One decision alone consoles: the entrance step has been kept, hollowed by generations of feet, a reminder that the place was in daily use long before anyone thought to smarten it up.

units: the writer addresses his neighbour in writing
he speaks of the channel for gathering water fixed along the shared wall
this channel has been overflowing since the recent rain
the water is spoiling the covering of the wall and laying the mortar bare
an inspection showed a blockage made of leaves and an empty nest
a fixing bracket has given way and tipped part of the channel
the writer offers to clear the channel himself shortly
he offers to change the broken brackets and put the fall right
he suggests fitting a guard so that the trouble does not come back
he asks his neighbour to agree to these proposals
text: Dear neighbour, I am writing to you about the gutter that runs along the wall our two houses share. Since last week's downpours it has spilled over halfway down its length, and the water is eating into the render, which has begun to crumble and show the mortar behind. I put a ladder up: the channel is choked with packed leaves and an abandoned nest, and one bracket has given way, so that stretch of it now tilts backwards. May I suggest three things to you. A thorough clearing out first, which I can do myself before the week is out. Then fresh brackets in place of the broken ones, which cost very little, with the fall put right towards the downpipe. Lastly a guard over the mouth of the channel, so that none of this happens again. Do let me know whether that arrangement suits you.

units: the text compares building with a timber structure and building in concrete
this comparison comes up when a client looks at two priced offers
timber allows quick putting together because the parts are made up beforehand
its lightness allows shallower foundations
timber fears water and calls for wide roof overhangs
the points where timber meets the ground need particular watching
concrete stores heat and softens swings of temperature
it also cuts down noise from outside
its making has a high cost for the environment and its drying lengthens the work
the usual answer joins a concrete base to a timber structure
text: Should one build in timber frame or in concrete? The question comes up as soon as a client sets two tenders side by side. What does timber offer? Quick erection, parts made up beforehand in the workshop, a tidy site, and a light structure that can sit on shallower foundations. What is held against it? Its dislike of water, which calls for generous roof overhangs and steady watchfulness wherever the timber comes near the ground. What does concrete offer? A mass that takes up heat, evens out swings of temperature and deadens the noise of the street. What is held against concrete? A heavy cost in the making, and a programme stretched out by the drying. So which should be chosen? In practice the two are married, a solid base carrying a light frame, and that serves the building better than a clean choice either way.

units: the visit began as an ordinary check
a poorly fixed roof element was spotted from the metal working structure
the roofing specialist reported a crack hidden under the coating
that crack was hard to see from below
the owner demanded a full survey before the work
the mason laid bare a binder crumbled by the weather
the timber frame was not damaged
the wall was strengthened with a binder made of sand and lime
the roof covering elements were put back in place
the front wall is judged stable for what follows
text: The site manager says the job began as a routine check and nothing more. Once he was up on the scaffolding, he noticed a roof tile that had worked loose near the gable end. The roofer with him saw rather more than that: a thin crack running under the render, all but invisible from the yard below. They called the owner in, she says, and the owner insisted on a full survey before anyone touched the wall. The bricklayer brought in to help reports scraping the face back with a trowel and uncovering mortar so crumbly that the rain had washed the life out of it. The timber frame underneath, by his account, had come through unharmed. The men then packed the wall out with a mix of sand and lime, and bedded the roof covering back down. The owner reckons the front will hold now without any special watching.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the exhaustion of the nearby deposits forced the builders to change material
brick took over because it weighed less and was made on the spot
the walls became thinner
the openings grew wider
curved coverings were replaced by ceilings carried on beams
the new material stood up badly to water
a lime based coating served as breathable protection
the craftsmen had to learn to judge a firing instead of a quarried block
the old buildings still keep the trace of that change
text: Once the stone beds lying near the building sites had been worked right out, the builders had no choice but to think their craft through again. Brick took over, and it did so on its own merits: lighter to lift, and burnt within reach of the wall it would become. The shape of the buildings shifted with it. Walls grew slimmer, openings spread wider, and the vault gave way to ceilings carried on beams. Since brick took damp badly, it was given a lime coat that let it breathe without holding the wet against the face. The trade moved too. A mason now had to read the burning of a batch rather than judge the grain of a quarried block. What came of that change was a way of building quicker to raise and cheaper to pay for, yet more easily hurt by water. The older buildings carry the mark of it still.

units: the breaking of a poured floor almost always has a traceable origin
an uneven settling of the support unbalances the spread of the load
water that works in makes the metal bars inside swell
that swelling widens the crack
the change is followed with a measuring device fixed on the surface
a crack that no longer moves is treated at the surface
the treatment means opening the crack on a slant then filling it with a hardening product
a crack that keeps opening reveals a problem in the ground
the ground is then stabilised by injecting a product under the footings
text: A poured concrete floor hardly ever splits without a cause you can trace. The ground beneath it shifts, settles more on one side than the other, and the load stops being shared evenly. A crack opens, hair fine at first, then wider as damp works in and swells the steel bars set inside the slab. Diagnosis starts with the width of the opening, read off a gauge glued across it and checked at set intervals. Where the reading holds steady, the repair stays on the surface: cut the crack out to a taper, blow the dust away, and fill it with a resin that sets cold. Where the reading grows, the fault lies in the ground rather than the concrete, and a binder has to be injected under the footing to even out the bearing. Skip that and you will be dressing the same wound for years, because the ground keeps giving way under the patch.

units: a craftsman took charge of putting an old farm building back in order
he found two building techniques stacked in one and the same wall
the bottom of the wall combined uneven stones and a supple binder
the top of the wall had been built later with rigid elements and a hard binder
the old part had followed the movements of the support without damage
the recent part showed breaks in various places
the cause of the trouble was not the age of the material but the pairing of two techniques
the craftsman advised taking down and rebuilding the recent part with a compatible binder
the owner ended up accepting the cost
text: The craftsman who took on the old farm building accepted the work out of curiosity as much as anything. On his first walk round he found two ways of building stacked in a single wall. The lower courses, laid by older hands, set uneven stones in a fat mortar, soft and almost alive under the thumb. The upper part, added long afterwards, held rigid blocks locked in grey cement. Where the base had taken up every movement of the ground without complaint, the later work had torn itself open in a good many places. He understood that the weakness lay not in the oldest material but in the ill judged marriage of two opposing logics. His advice was to take the newer section down and raise it again in a binder close to the old one. The owner wavered for a good while, and then agreed to the outlay.

units: you first gather the tools needed including a one wheeled carrying machine and a mason blade
the fragile areas of the wall must be taken out and the dust removed
the surface must be wetted without excess
the mix brings together sand, lime added little by little, and water
the paste obtained must stay firm enough to cling to the tool
it is laid on in three successive coats
each coat has its own job: to grip, to fill, to level
a coat must be left to dry away from a draught before the next one
the tools are cleaned straight after use
the binder is kept in a dry place
text: Before you set about rendering an old wall, put the whole of your kit together: a barrow, a bucket, a wide trowel, a float and a sieve. Then see to the background itself. Rake out the hollow patches, brush the dust off, and damp the face down without soaking it. Now mix. Tip the sand into the barrow, work the lime in a little at a time, add the water, and turn it until you have a paste soft enough to spread yet stiff enough to sit on the blade. Lay it on in three passes. The first keys into the wall, the second fills the hollows, the third brings the whole face level. Let each coat dry out of the draught before you start the next. Finish by looking after the kit. Rinse the tools straight away, empty the barrow, keep the bag of lime in a dry store, and sheet the sand heap over.

units: the week began with an incident on the site
the metal working structure had been shifted by the night wind
taking it down took up two working days
a young worker found a blocked opening under the roof
people in the area knew that story without giving it credit
the woman in charge of the project stopped the demolition
the site turned into a saving operation
onlookers come regularly to have a look at the find
the man in charge accepts the delay in handing over
text: Up on the old quarter job, the week got off to a rough start. The lads turned up to find the scaffold sitting all skew, since one windy night had been enough to shove it out of true. So it all came down again, two full days of it, and nobody grumbled. Next morning, clearing out the loft, an apprentice came across a hatch that had been sealed up under the rafters. The old hands round here had heard tell of it and never much believed it. The architect came out, stopped the demolition there and then, and the whole job swung over to saving what was left. Since then folk from the street drop by of an evening for a look at the black hole we have opened, and two neighbours even bring the men something to drink. The boss just grins. He meant to hand it over quickly, and he knows now it will be a good deal later, but it does not bother him.

units: the outside of the building gives an impression of good order
the floor set under the roof space is warping
a damaged water pipe has been throwing water against the wall for a long time
the coating on the wall is coming away in patches
a brown stain spreads with every spell of rain
the concreted surface of the passage has lost its bed of sand
the occupants tried to hide the fault under a coat of paint
that paint blistered quickly
the survey recommends dealing with the roof before anything else
text: Seen from the yard, the house looks sound enough. The pale front, the straight gable and the shutters all in line put a visitor at ease. Inside tells another tale. Under the loft the floorboards have buckled, because a split gutter has been tipping its water against the wall for seasons on end. The damp reached the timbers, lifted the render off in sheets, and left a brown ring that widens with every downpour. Lower down, the hall slab rings hollow: the sand that bedded it has been carried off by the water working through. The owners painted over the mark first, hoping to see the back of it, and the paint blistered before the next season was out, showing a background soaked right through. The survey ends plainly. Start at the roof, or everything mended below will go again before the work is done.

units: the writer finds the spread of fronts without grain worrying
a cement based coating stops the wall from shedding damp
the water held back ends up breaking the stone from within
the writer holds that we mistook keeping water out for protection
he suggests using binders that let vapour through
he advises keeping cement for the buried parts
he invites us to accept the visible ageing of a wall
he calls for craftsmen to be trained in reading old fabric
a properly coated wall lasts several generations with light upkeep
text: Our streets are being clad in smooth fronts that age badly, and that ought to worry us. A wall sealed in cement no longer breathes. It traps the wet, pins it against the stone, and in the end bursts the stone from within. We have taken keeping water out for looking after a building. The cure calls for no great feat. Go back to binders that let vapour pass, keep cement for what sits below ground, and allow a face to weather instead of demanding that it stay untouched. The trades need teaching again as well, for reading an old wall is a slow discipline that the rush of the modern site has all but rubbed out. A wall rendered as it should be lasts generations on a coat of limewash and nothing more. We would rather redo every ten years what those before us got right the first time.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman in charge of the roofing was trained by a practitioner who drew nothing
her master judged the pitch and the tightness by his senses
she works from measurements and preparatory drawings
her master repeated the trips carrying materials
she gathers her loads so as to go up only once
she grants her master one superiority: sensing the state of a frame
no set of readings takes the place of that sense
she has kept the habit of walking a roof before touching it
her jobs are shorter than at the start and just as sound
text: The roofing chargehand on this job learnt her trade from an old boy who never drew a line. She likes to set the two schools side by side. He laid a tile by eye, corrected the pitch as he walked the slope, and told whether it was tight by the sound of rain on it. She measures first, notes the falls, and sets the coursing out on paper before she goes up. He went up and down all day with a barrow, while she makes her loads up on the ground and lifts them in one. On one count, though, she grants him the better of it: he could feel the tiredness of a roof frame through his boots, and no set of readings takes the place of that. So she has kept his habit of pacing a roof over before she lays a hand on it. Calculation and touch run together in her work, and her jobs take less time than they did at the outset, losing nothing in strength.

units: the appraisal of this refurbishment falls into three aspects
the original frame was kept and quietly strengthened
that choice is welcomed because the span of the frame still reads
the finishes disappoint the writer
the coating chosen is too rigid and is already splitting near the bearing points
the unbroken concreted surface takes no account of the movements of the support
moving about inside the building is judged pleasant and clear
the sound was dealt with without any visible devices
the writer regrets that the level under the roof is closed to the public
text: The reworking of this market hall invites a measured verdict, best set out under three headings. The first is structure. The carpenters kept the original trusses and doubled them up without fuss, which deserves praise, since the span still reads from one end of the building to the other. The second heading is the finishing, and here the warmth cools. The render chosen is too hard, and has already opened at the bearings, while the slab, poured in one piece, takes no account of what the ground beneath it does. The third heading is use. The place is a pleasure to cross, the route through it stays clear, and the sound has been tamed without a single showy panel on view. One regret does remain: the loft is kept for the work teams alone, which denies the public the finest view of the vault.

units: the writer is writing from a room fitted out under the roof
the roof had been letting water in since the cold season
the water that seeped in warped the beams
the warping of the timber stopped the landing door from closing
the craftsman took the leaf off and trimmed the jamb
two lengths of the roof frame were strengthened
the writer invites the person he is writing to to sleep in this room
the room is not heated yet
text: I am writing to you from the little room under the roof, the one we called the loft when we were small. Since the cold months the covering had been letting water through, and that seeping swelled the beams until they twisted out of true. The carpenter was blunt about it. Once timber shifts, the landing door stops closing; its hinge pulled crooked and the frame went out of square. He took the leaf off, planed the jamb back, then hung the whole thing again. Two rafters were doubled up as well, since the roof load was sitting badly. The result pleases me. The pitch runs clean, resin smells right through the stairwell, and you can hear the rain without dreading it. The upstairs room is yours whenever you come. Bring thick sheets, though, because the heating does not reach it yet, and the view over the valley is worth that chill.

units: an old wall is not rendered like a recent wall
the professional compares the old wall to something that breathes
a waterproof render traps the water coming up from below ground
this trapped water brings salt deposits to the surface
the render ends up coming away in pieces
lime laid on in thin coats lets the vapour out
a surface that is too smooth must be rubbed down and wetted before rendering
this method slows the work down but keeps the wall from decaying
text: Should a wall of some age be rendered exactly the way a recent one is? The site manager we put the question to says no, and his answer turns on a single image: the old wall breathes, the young one sweats. What happens if you seal the first of them under a waterproof mortar? Damp drawn up from below stays shut in, salt blooms at the surface, the coat blisters and comes away in sheets. What does he offer instead? Lime, laid on in thin passes, so that the masonry can let its vapour out. And if the backing proves too smooth for that? Rub it down, he says, wet it thoroughly, then throw on a very loose first pass that will grip. Work goes more slowly that way, he grants, but the wall stops rotting quietly behind its skin. A front treated so will stand a whole generation before it needs doing again.

units: the foreman asks the craftsman how the floor should be fixed down
a nail goes in quickly
a nail bends without snapping under shaking
a screw holds better when something pulls on it
a screw shears if the structure moves
laying a heavy piece over joists calls for a fixing that tolerates the timber moving
a screw costs more in tools and in care
the parts meant to come apart again will be screwed down
text: The site foreman asks the joiner whether the boards of the upper floor ought to be nailed down or screwed. Nails go in fast, the joiner says, and they take knocks well, because the shank bends rather than snapping under the shaking. A screw holds far better against pull, he adds, but it shears clean off once the frame moves under load. A heavy board laid over joists needs a fixing that tolerates timber shrinking and swelling. The foreman weighs up the cost of the two methods. A screw wants a power tool and a careful hand; a nail wants a hammer and a steady rhythm. So you nail the layers that swell and shrink, the joiner concludes, and you screw down whatever you may want to lift again later. On this job, he adds, the battens go down with nails and the inspection hatches with screws.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: three great methods came before the general use of metal
the first method piles stones on one another without mortar
the steadiness of that pile comes from the weight of the blocks
the second method uses clay bricks dried without firing
the third method combines a frame and an infill covered with plaster
each way of building depended on the materials lying close by
these ways of building forced thick walls and low buildings
villages built this way are still lived in and still kept up the same way
text: Before metal came into general use, the builder's craft rested on three families of method. The first stacks chosen blocks of stone with nothing binding them, and draws its steadiness from the sheer weight of each course. The second shapes raw clay into bricks dried in the open air, bedded in a mud of the same stuff. The third raises a timber frame, packs it with a light infill, then has the whole face plastered over. Each answered to what lay close at hand: outcropping rock, river silt, the wood of a nearby forest. Each imposed its limits too, modest heights, thick walls, constant upkeep. Builders made up for that by turning the openings to the light, deepening the footings and steepening the roofs. Their legacy survives in whole hamlets, lived in still, where repairs are made with the old gestures.

units: the stages of a building job follow an order that cannot be changed
a plank fence marks the limits of the plot at the start
the footings are poured into trenches dug in the ground
the walls rise with gaps left for the doors and windows
the roof frame goes up once the masonry has dried
the covering puts the job under shelter from the rain
the pipes run through the partitions while these are still open
a render laid on a damp backing comes away
text: Nothing on a plot being made ready for a house is placed at random, since every stage sets up the one that follows. The ground is first marked out with a plank fence, which shields the disturbed soil and gives the machines their bearings. Trenches are then dug for the footings and filled with reinforced concrete. Walls rise course by course, with gaps left where doors and windows will sit. The roof frame goes up once the masonry has hardened, and the covering closes the volume, putting the work under shelter. Water and air pipes run through the partitions while these are still open. Rendering comes last, then floors, then paint. Swapping any two of these stages proves expensive: a coat laid on a damp wall lifts off, and a partition closed too early has to be opened again.

units: a lock that jammed set the whole business going
the occupants forced the door while joking about it
one push that was too rough tore the metal part out of the frame
the bottom hinge gave way under the weight of the leaf
the door dropped down and scraped along the tiles
the caretaker wanted to replace the lot
a resident who restores furniture was given time to try the repair
she took the door off and knocked the frame back true
the neighbour earned a name in the building as a woodworker
text: It all started with a sticky lock in the basement of our block. At first we shoved a bit harder, we laughed about it, we said the door had character. Then a neighbour pushed too roughly: the keep tore out of the frame and the bottom hinge ripped away. The leaf being heavy, it dropped sideways and scraped along the tiles for its whole swing. Nothing moved after that, and nobody dared force it. The caretaker wanted the lot replaced, quote in hand, but the tenant on the ground floor, who restores furniture, asked for a week. She lifted the leaf off its pins, knocked the frame back true with a mallet, fitted a fresh hinge and greased the mechanism. The lock has snapped shut ever since. That repair earned her a name across the building as a cabinetmaker, which she had never gone looking for.

units: an opening that rubs makes a room unpleasant to use
the cause is seldom in the glass
rubbing low down points to the timber having swollen
rubbing high up points to the fixings having worked loose
the shiny patch left by the contact has to be sanded
a light oil is then wiped on and left overnight
the brackets are screwed back with the holes shifted slightly
a level set on the sill lets you check that the frame stands upright
a thin packer corrects a frame that is still twisted
text: A window that sticks spoils the use of a whole room, and the fault seldom lies in the glass itself. Start by watching the gap: rubbing low down means the timber has swollen, rubbing high up means the fixing brackets have worked loose. In the first case, open the casement fully, find the shiny band left by the contact, and sand that strip down with a medium paper until it swings clear again. Dust it off, wipe on a light oil, and leave it overnight. In the second, the brackets must be screwed back, with the holes shifted a little so the screws bite sound wood. Then check that the frame stands upright, with a spirit level set on the inner sill. Should the frame still sit twisted, slip a thin packer behind the top hinge. Adjusting it patiently spares you a costly replacement.

units: two building jobs are going on facing each other
one of them is a tall block of flats
the balconies of that block arrive ready made
lifting machines set whole face panels in place
that block gains one storey a week
the other job is the putting right of an old house
the men there take the roof covering off piece by piece
they check the state of the walls and change the timber that has gone
the neighbours like the room they are promised but hold to the front being restored
text: Two building sites face each other along one street, and nothing links them but the dust. On one side a block of flats climbs, its balconies arriving from the works already moulded, with their rounded lip and all. Cranes set whole face panels down, and the front gains a storey a week. Opposite, an old house lies open like a patient on a table: the men lift the tiles off one by one, sound the masonry, replace the dead lengths of the roof frame. Where the first site glories in speed, the second keeps faith with the way joints were once made. People living nearby watch both and cannot choose. They admire the room the tall block promises, yet they cling to the scaffolding on the old front, which will give them back a street they thought lost. Neither, in their eyes, is pointless.

units: the frame carrying the building can be seen from outside
the upright posts were cut to shape with a hand tool
each post carries a horizontal piece that takes the roof frame
the walls are made of three layers one over another
a flow of air is left within the thickness of the walls
the windows have a sloping sill that throws the water off
the ground around the building is covered with draining stones
the overhang of the roof keeps the timber out of the weather
no surface has been painted
text: Seen from the yard, the shed shows its frame before anything else about it. The timber posts, squared off with an axe on all four faces, each carry a horizontal beam that takes the trusses. The walls are built up in three layers: an overlapping board skin outside, a ventilated air gap, an insulating panel fixed onto battens from within. The openings follow one pattern, a low apron below, a jutting sill cut on the slant to throw water off, a lintel in a single piece. The floor pairs a smooth slab inside with a band of draining gravel laid along the walls outside. The roof, pitched both ways, ends in a wide overhang that keeps the rain off the woodwork. Nothing has been painted: the boarding greys, the ironwork takes on a patina, and the whole thing ages without heavy upkeep.

units: building has slowly given up on lasting a long time
supple mortars were replaced by a harder binder
that binder was taken up because it sets quickly
heavy roof frames gave way to lightened structures
those lightened structures cannot be mended and have to be replaced
thick coatings were replaced by very thin layers
the guarantee on those coatings runs out before the wall wears
each of these choices was aimed at saving money in the short term
the writer calls for materials that can be mended
text: We have given up building to last, and the drift set in by stages. Masons first dropped the supple binders in favour of a stiff cement of their own, quicker to set and easier to bring to the site. Heavy roof frames then gave way to light trusses, calculated to the bone, which nobody can mend except by putting in fresh ones. Thick renders gave way at last to films so thin that their guarantee runs out long before the wall behind them tires. Every one of these stages was defended by an immediate saving; taken together they leave a stock of buildings that will have to come down before they can ever grow old with dignity. A building worth the name takes repair after repair. To ask for materials that can be mended is not a builder's nostalgia at all: it is ordinary prudence.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the site manager learned her trade through an apprenticeship
her team works on old buildings
clients mainly ask for surfaces refinished from scratch
the footings give way under the storeys that were added
the floors are held on temporary props before anything else is done
the ground is surveyed to find hidden voids
the gaps in the masonry are filled only once the building is safe
she refuses decorative finishes while the frame is still fragile
she takes the client under the floor to show the damaged timbers
text: She came into the trade as an apprentice on renovation sites, and now runs a team that puts tired old buildings back on their feet. The same argument greets her on every job: owners want their walls smooth and freshly finished, while beneath them the footings are sinking under storeys piled on over the years. Her answer is a fixed order of work. Floors go up on temporary props before anything else is touched. Only then is the ground surveyed for hidden voids. Gaps in the masonry get filled last, once the place is safe to stand in. She will not lay a decorative finish while the frame is still fragile, and that stance costs her some distinctly awkward conversations. When an owner digs his heels in, she hands him a torch and walks him under the floor, where the timbers eaten away by damp speak for themselves.

units: two neighbouring buildings stand at the end of the same street
the first is entirely glazed and reflects the sky
the second is low and built of fired brick
the old front still carries the marks of the builders' hands
the tower is judged too regular in its geometry
the house offers worn thresholds and crooked corners
the old building is criticised for being cramped and decayed
the low rooms hold the heat better
the thick walls soften the sounds
text: Two buildings stand at the far end of the same street, and the taller one overshadows its neighbour without ever winning the argument. The first is glass from top to bottom; it hands the sky straight back at you, you admire it for a minute, and then the eye slides off it altogether. The second is low, heavy, built of fired brick that the weather has smoothed, and it holds the gaze. Its front still carries the marks of the hands that laid it. Set side by side, the modest one comes off better. The tower offers a flawless geometry, the old house crooked corners and thresholds worn hollow. One is visited, the other is lived in. People often call the old place cramped and decayed, forgetting that its low rooms hold the heat and that its thick walls take the edge off noise. Beauty here comes from use rather than from line.

units: the writer sends his sister news of the building work
three jobs are running at the same time
the broken tiles have been replaced by the roofer
the joints around the flue have been filled with a flexible mortar
every window opening has been made airtight
tape has been applied along the fixed frame of the windows
the builder suggests partitioning off the back room for a study
the partition will be lightweight board with no contact with the ceiling
the walls will get a limewash coat before the cold season
text: Dear sister, here at last is the promised news from the house. Three separate jobs are running at once, so I shall take them one after another. Up on the roof, the roofer has swapped out the tiles that had broken, then gone back over the joints around the flue with a flexible mortar. At the windows, I decided to make every opening airtight: foam squeezed into the rebate, tape run along the fixed frame, and the draughts through them have gone for good. Inside, the builder suggests partitioning off the back room to make a study; the partition would be lightweight board, stopping short of the ceiling. The walls still want a coat of limewash before the cold season sets in. I shall write again as soon as the roof timbers have been checked. Give the children a kiss from me when you see them.

units: the lead designer is asked to describe how the work unfolded
a detailed inventory of the existing fabric opened the project
that survey took a whole season
the examinations brought a weakened timber frame to light
the programme had to be revised after that finding
only the frailest part was pulled down
the rebuilding relied on the foundations that were kept
the cramped site complicated the organisation between the trades
bringing the pipework back into service was the trickiest phase
text: The lead designer is invited to set out how the work unfolded, stage by stage. She replies that it opened with a full inventory of the existing fabric, taken room by room across an entire season. Asked what followed, she explains that the surveys exposed a weakened timber frame, which forced a rewrite of the programme. On the technical choices, she says the decision was taken to pull down the frailest wing alone, and to rebuild on the foundations already there. Questioned about the obstacles, she points to the trades having to work around one another on a cramped site. Asked at last what she takes from so long an undertaking, she answers that the hardest stretch was not the structural work but bringing the pipework back into service, finished a long way past the date that had been announced.

units: a carpenter explains to his apprentice that the door is catching
the fault comes from the movement of the structure and not from the door
fitting another door would bring back the same jamming
a mark on the threshold proves that the settlement is continuing
the apprentice suggests planing the bottom of the leaf
the carpenter accepts this temporary solution
the bearing of the wall will have to be taken up afterwards
the catching will return if the ground drops further
text: The carpenter told his apprentice that the door was catching because the building itself had shifted. The apprentice asked whether it ought to be replaced. No, said the carpenter: the trouble lay in the ground, so a replacement would jam exactly as this one did. He pointed to the scrape the leaf had left on the threshold, proof that the settlement had not stopped. The apprentice suggested planing the bottom of the leaf. His teacher agreed, though he warned that the trick eased the symptom without curing anything, and that the bearing of the wall would have to be taken up afterwards. With the ground still dropping, he added, the door would be catching again within a season or two. The apprentice wrote the lesson down: treat the cause, or the repair keeps coming back, and the bill with it.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: old builders wanted to roof a wide hall without a central support
a flat stone roof breaks under its own weight
the solution adopted was to lean the blocks against one another
this form sends the load out towards the side walls
timber supports held the work up while it was being built
those supports were taken away once the central block was in place
the sideways thrust pushed the walls apart
masses of masonry were added against the walls to hold them
text: Picture builders who want to roof an enormous hall without planting a single column in the middle. Their problem is plain enough: stone is heavy, and a flat roof snaps under its own weight the moment you stretch it across. So they went looking elsewhere. What they hit on was the vault. Lean the blocks against one another and the load slides out towards the walls instead of dropping straight down. The trouble was holding it all up during the build, hence the timber centring slid underneath to carry the stonework until it closed on itself. Once the keystone dropped in, the timber came away and the vault stood alone. That left the sideways push, which shoved the walls outwards; the builders answered with thick buttresses. Neat, isn't it? Every obstacle called for one more piece, and the hall stood in the end.

units: the choice between timber and masonry depends on the use of the building
a brick wall stores the heat before giving it back
a timber wall warms quickly and cools just as quickly
the heavy solution suits rooms that are occupied all the time
the light structure suits premises used irregularly
masonry calls for drying time and a large workforce
the timber parts arrive cut to size and go together without water
the prices of the two methods end up meeting
designers advise deciding by the indoor feel that is wanted
text: Timber or masonry? The question comes up on every single project, and the answer turns mostly on how the building will be used. A brick wall banks heat: it warms slowly, then hands the warmth back as the evening cools. A timber wall behaves the other way round, coming up to temperature fast and losing it just as fast. For a room that is in use without a break, the heavy option wins. For premises opened now and then, the light frame comes out ahead. The building work divides the two camps as well: masonry has to dry out and takes a large workforce, while timber panels turn up cut to size and go together without water. The final bill, though, tends to land in much the same place. Designers therefore suggest choosing by the indoor feel you are after, rather than by the fashion of the moment.

units: an elderly tenant obtains a walk through the block before its demolition
the hall floor is damaged and holds the print of the furniture taken out
the doors of the flats are shut and marked with a chalk cross
a thin partition had already been broken into by the workmen
an old wall covering appears behind the split board
the roof timbers of the top floor let a draught through
the handrail worn by use moves her more than the rest
she thanks the caretaker as she leaves
she refuses to turn her eyes towards the front of the building
text: On the eve of the demolition, the oldest tenant was granted one last walk through the condemned block. She pushed open the door of the hall first, where the cracked tiling still held the print of the furniture that had been carried out. Then she climbed towards the landings, counting the closed doors, each one marked with a cross drawn in chalk. On the third floor she stopped at a thin partition the workmen had already broken into; behind the split board lay an old wallpaper nobody had ever scraped off. She finished under the roof, where the worn timbers let a thin thread of air come through. Nothing moved her more than the stair rail, polished smooth by hands that were long gone. On her way out she thanked the caretaker, then she refused to turn her eyes towards the tall grey front.

units: the crack must be raked out down to a sound backing
the dust is removed with a brush
the edges are damped before the filler goes on
the powder must be tipped into the water and not the other way round
the paste is pressed into the hollow to drive the air out
the surface is smoothed with a wide tool running past the sides
the drying lasts a full night at least with no heating
the hardened area is then sanded and dusted down
a mineral paint is applied in two crossed coats
text: Start by raking out the crack along its whole length with the tip of a trowel, until you reach a sound backing. Brush the dust out of the groove, then damp the edges lightly: filler laid on a surface that is too dry will simply let go. Mix the paste in a clean bucket, tipping the powder into the water and never the other way round. Work it in straight away, pressing hard so that the air is driven out of the hollow. Smooth it off with a wide knife, running a little past the crack on either side. Leave it to set for a full night at least, with no heating on in the room. Sand the hardened patch with a fine abrasive, dust it down again, and run a hand over the joint to check that the repair can no longer be felt under the fingers. Finish by brushing on a mineral paint, in two coats laid crosswise.

units: entry to several buildings in a low-lying district has been barred
the families moved out have been put up in a communal hall
a body of groundwater has been swollen by repeated rain
the sand carrying the foundations has been washed away by that water
the ground has settled unevenly
stepped cracks have appeared on the fronts of the buildings
the experts judge that the old fabric could not take such movement
the stairwells have been declared unsafe
resin injections are announced to avoid demolition
text: Access to several blocks in the low-lying district was barred yesterday, and the families moved out have been put up in a communal hall. The technical services have known the cause for seasons: a body of groundwater, swollen by one downpour after another, has washed away the sand on which the foundations sit. The ground has settled unevenly, opening stepped cracks across the fronts of the buildings. The experts called in judge that the fabric, decayed already, was in no state to absorb movement of that order. As a direct result, the stairwells were ruled unsafe and the evacuation was ordered without delay. Owners are demanding a second, independent survey, since putting matters right would mean underpinning the footings. The authorities announce resin injections, failing which demolition would become unavoidable.

units: two neighbouring dwellings show opposite characters
the older one has thick mineral walls and few openings
the newer one offers wide glazed surfaces on a light frame
the old building holds its coolness better when the air is hot
the new building follows outside temperature swings quickly
the occupants of the old dwelling report a finish that soaks up water from the ground
a waterproof layer was fitted under the outer cladding of the new dwelling
the halting of air renewal worries the occupants of the new dwelling
a building trade professional holds that each construction answers a distinct aim
text: Two houses stand side by side along the same road, and you tell them apart at a glance. The older one squats low: thick stone walls, a shallow roof, hardly a window anywhere. Its neighbour rises taller, with wide panes of glass set into a slender timber frame. Through the hot months the old walls hold their coolness and warm up slowly once the air turns; the newer house tracks whatever the weather does outside and answers the slightest shift. Tenants in the old one grumble about a porous render that drinks up damp rising from the ground. Those next door praise the sealed membrane laid behind their cladding, yet they dread the stale air that gathers when the ventilation stops. A builder from round here weighs up both and refuses to pick a winner: one was raised to last without fuss, the other to burn less energy.

units: the writer holds that hasty building work spoils the look of the streets
he regrets that heavy hand-worked materials are giving way to light parts
he notes the disappearance of dwellings with irregular shapes
those irregular shapes came from awkward plots or from holdings split between heirs
current buildings repeat matching volumes stacked up without hesitation
the roominess of a home was once judged by its side spaces such as lofts and cellars
it is now judged by the number of rooms advertised
the writer refuses to call for a return to the past
he asks that a building be weighed on what it will offer the following generation
text: Building in haste has become a habit, and that habit is making our streets poorer. Look at what slips away, one item at a time. Material first: the heavy block, cut by hand with a chisel, gives way to light panels which no palm has ever smoothed. Shape next: the crooked dwelling, born of an awkward plot or of a holding split between heirs, vanishes in favour of matching volumes stacked up without a pause for thought. Use last of all: a roomy home was once judged by its lofts and its cellars, by everything tucked around the edges; now it is judged by the number of rooms printed in a listing. I plead for no return to any earlier age, and I distrust easy longing. I ask only that a building be weighed on what it will offer the generation after us, not on the speed of its site.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the craftsman began his working life sorting beams on a refurbishment site
he was learning to tell sound timber from a length spoilt by damp
he then joined a workshop that put timber together without glue or metal parts
there he took in setting out, cutting and fitting onto uneven walls
a fall from scaffolding kept him off site while he recovered
during that break he drew roof frames for other teams
on his return he set up his own workshop and took on two apprentices
he teaches that a measurement taken on the spot beats a plan received from afar
text: The carpenter started out as an apprentice on a refurbishment site, where sorting the beams fell to him. He had to tell rough but sound timber from a crumbling length eaten away by damp. After three seasons he moved to a workshop that cut its joints by hand, using neither glue nor metal fixings. There he learnt setting out, full-scale drawing, the angled cut, and then fitting onto walls that never stood quite true. A fall from scaffolding kept him off site through a long recovery; he filled those months drawing roof frames for other teams. On his return he opened up a workshop of his own and took on two apprentices. He tells them over and over again that a measurement taken on the spot beats a plan arriving by post, because an old wall shifts and no frontage is ever straight.

units: cracks ran through the building from the base to the top
a broken gutter had soaked the foundations over a long stretch of time
the water working in had dissolved the mortar and shifted the stones
the staircase had lost its steadiness
the site manager put right the origin of the trouble before its appearance
he drained the foot of the wall, made the bonding good again and changed the worn treads
that ordering explains the soundness obtained and the quietness of the result
some visitors find the result disappointing for want of any visible effect
the writer criticises the uniformity of the windows, which rubs out the trace of the older openings
the writer holds the choice defensible all the same, since ornament laid over unsteady walls would have split
text: What this refurbishment deserves credit for is chiefly what it avoided. Cracks ran through the building from the ground to the ridge, because a broken gutter had soaked the foundations over a very long stretch of time. The water working in dissolved the mortar, the stones slid out of line, and the staircase lost its footing. The site manager therefore dealt with the origin of the trouble before its appearance: he drained the foot of the wall, made the bonding good again, and replaced the worn treads. That ordering of priorities explains how solid the work now stands. It explains too how quiet the result looks, which some visitors find disappointing for want of any visible effect. The windows are too uniform, and they rub out the trace of the older openings. The choice holds up all the same: ornament laid over unsteady walls would have split apart.

units: the writer lives above a former workshop
the floor creaked under every step and disturbed the woman living underneath
packing pieces, screws and thick rugs had settled nothing
a joiner pinned down the source of the noise in a single visit
the joists were resting on a beam that had sagged
the hollow under the floor made every footfall louder
the joiner put a stout prop in the cellar and fixed the boards down again
the noise stopped that very evening
the neighbour and the writer made their peace after that repair
text: I have a spare moment, so let me tell you how the floor saga ended. Ever since I moved into this flat above an old workshop, every step set the boards creaking and woke the woman living underneath. I tried packing pieces, screws, thick rugs, and none of it made the slightest difference. Then a joiner came round to have a look and found the cause in one visit. The joists were resting on a beam that had sagged, and the hollow beneath the floor made every footfall boom. He put a stout prop in the cellar and fixed the boards down again onto fresh battens. The quiet came back that very evening. My neighbour brought me a potted plant to mark the news, and we laughed about two miserable seasons spent blaming each other. Come and see me soon, the spare room is ready and waiting for you.

units: heating costs depend on what the walls are made of and not on the age of the building
a thick wall stores heat and gives it back overnight
a lightweight partition loses its heat as soon as the heating stops
insulation works differently on an old wall and on a recent one
an old wall must let vapour through, otherwise water builds up inside its thickness
a recent wall calls for an unbroken barrier and for controlled air renewal
builders advise choosing what you can mend yourself
render is made good with a bricklayer's tool
a factory-made panel has to be replaced whole
