text: Does an old house cost more to heat than a newly built one? Well, it comes down to the walls, not to the age of the place. A thick wall soaks up heat and gives it back overnight, while a lightweight partition lets it go the moment the boiler cuts out. So what does insulation change? A great deal, though not in quite the same way on either side. On an old wall you have to let vapour pass through; otherwise water builds up inside the thickness and the wall slowly breaks down. On a recent one you want the opposite: an unbroken barrier, plus ventilation that carries the stale air away. Which should you go for, then? The one you can mend yourself, say the builders working round here. Render can be made good with a trowel; a factory-bonded panel is swapped whole or not at all.

units: the site manager laid out the refurbishment scheme for the neighbours
he built his answers around three worries
knocking out the partitions will take a fortnight and the loud machinery will stop in the late afternoon
a fine sheet will wrap the scaffolding to hold down the dust
the rubble will be damped before it is taken away
the pavement will be diverted but the shop on the ground floor will keep its own door
a woman living nearby worried about the wall she shares with her yard
the engineer promised propping and then repointing at the contractor's expense
a parent raised the question of lorries passing when the children come home
text: The site manager laid out the refurbishment scheme for the neighbours who had come along to hear him, and he grouped his answers around three worries. Noise came first: knocking out the partitions would take a fortnight, he said, and the loud machinery would stand idle from late afternoon on. Dust came next: a fine sheet will wrap the scaffolding, and a spray will damp the rubble down before it is carted out. Access came last: the pavement will be diverted, though the shop on the ground floor keeps its own door. One woman asked what would become of the wall she shares with her yard; the engineer there replied that it would be propped, then repointed, at the contractor's expense. A father raised the matter of the lorries coming through at the hour when children walk home.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: lasting homes appear once groups stop moving about
the earliest walls were branches daubed with mud and were remade after the rains
silt paste dried in the sun proved tougher than fresh daub
the moulded block could be made again exactly alike
the wall became a sum of like parts, which changed the builder's trade
firing in a kiln yielded a block that shrugged off the rains
builders then grew bold enough to pile one storey on another
the arch and then the vault freed openings from heavy timber crossbeams
every step forward rested on a repeated gesture and on a material taking over from the one before
text: Homes meant to last appear once groups stop moving about and choose to keep their stores in one place. The earliest walls are branches daubed with mud, thrown up quickly and patched after every downpour. Then comes the finding that changes everything: silt paste dried in the sun holds far better than fresh daub, and a moulded block can be made again and again, always alike. A wall turns into a sum of like parts, and that reshapes the builder's trade as much as it reshapes the house. Later, firing in a kiln yields a reddened block that shrugs off the rain, and builders grow bold enough to pile one storey on another. The arch, and after it the vault, free openings at last from heavy timber crossbeams. Every step forward rested on a repeated gesture and on a material taking over from the one before.

units: an inside wall can turn damp with no leak at all
the air of a heated home carries vapour from cooking, showering and breathing
the vapour turns into droplets when it meets a cold surface
chilled air holds less water than warm air
the cold spot often comes from a local gap in the insulation
the surface finish soaked with water ends up covered in dark patches
warming the surface by putting the fault right removes the cause
carrying the vapour away with steady ventilation also removes the cause
drying the patch alone settles nothing, since the cold surface remains
text: An inside wall can turn damp with no leak anywhere, and the physics behind it is plain enough. The air of a heated home carries vapour, given off by cooking, by showering, and by the breathing of the people who live there. That vapour drifts about freely until it meets a cold surface. There it turns into droplets, because chilled air holds less water than warm air does. The cold spot usually comes from a local gap in the insulation: a concrete lintel, a poorly protected corner, a window sill running right through the wall. Condensation settles, the surface finish grows sodden, and dark patches begin to spread. Two remedies act on the cause: warm the surface by putting the fault right, or carry the vapour away with steady ventilation. Drying the patch alone changes nothing, since the cold surface is still there.

units: a housing block of three buildings met with an incident while its roof was being redone
the firm stripped the covering off one wing before checking the frame
the inspection turned up worm-eaten timbers along the whole length
the work was halted
the temporary cover gave way under a downpour and the water spoilt the ceilings on the top floor
the residents met and refused to settle a second estimate
a mediator suggested sharing the outlay
the firm redid the ceilings at its own cost and the owners paid for replacing the timbers
the rules of the building now call for an examination of the structure before any covering is stripped
text: A housing block of three buildings ran into an instructive mishap while its roof was being redone. The firm engaged had stripped the covering off a whole wing before checking the frame beneath, and the inspection turned up worm-eaten rafters along the entire length. Work stopped, the temporary sheeting gave way under a downpour, and water ruined the ceilings on the top floor. The residents met and refused to settle a second estimate. A mediator put a way out to them: the firm would redo the ceilings at its own cost, and the owners would fund the replacement timber, which nobody could have foreseen in so old a structure. The agreement held. The lesson now sits in the rules of the building: no covering is to be stripped before the structure it shelters has been fully examined.

units: the young deer is born as the cold season ends
at birth it wears a coat covered in pale spots
through its first weeks it lies motionless among the plants
its pale fur makes it hard to tell apart from the ground
its mother moves off to feed and comes back to suckle it
that distance keeps scent away from the hiding place
once its legs grow firm it follows its mother along the tracks
the spots fade when the warmth returns
before the next cold it joins a group of its own kind
text: The cold season loosens its grip, and the fawn arrives in a clearing, too weak to follow its mother beyond a few paces. For its first weeks it lies flat among the tall grass, quite still, and the pale spots across its back blur into the dry leaves. The doe wanders off to graze, then comes back at steady intervals to suckle, so that little scent gathers about the hiding place. When the thin legs firm up at last, the youngster trails after her and learns which tracks can be trusted. Warmth returns; the spots fade and the coat darkens. There follows a season of grazing alone, of choosing tender shoots by instinct. Before the cold comes round again, it falls in with a herd and drifts with them towards the sheltered slopes. The clearing where it all began now means nothing to it at all.

units: the mare had been limping since the day before
the assistant first put the trouble down to a knock
a stone had in fact wedged itself under the animal’s foot
that stone crushed the tissue at every step
without quick action a pocket of pus would have formed
the handler cleaned out the cavity and dressed the wound
the animal was moved onto soft ground that cushions each step
the neglected state of its mane showed poor grooming
the team now checks the feet before every outing
text: The mare had been limping since the previous day, and the stable assistant put it down to a knock against a gatepost. The examination told a different story. A sharp stone had worked its way between the frog and the wall of the hoof, and it crushed the tissue at every step. Left where it lay, that pressure would have driven inflammation deep into the foot and raised an abscess awkward to drain. The handler pared out the cavity, cleaned the wound and bound it under a thick pad held by adhesive tape. Since the animal fretted at being kept still, it was led to a sandy yard whose loose footing cushioned each stride. A matted mane, the mark of neglected grooming, prompted the team to overhaul its routine. The gait ran smooth again within weeks, and the feet are now checked before every outing.

units: a claw left too long ends up wounding the underside of the paw
one should pick a moment when the animal is dozing
the base of the toe is pressed so that the claw comes out
a coloured band marks where the blood vessels run
the cut must stop short of that band
going past that limit brings on bleeding
a tool with a curved blade suits better than an ordinary clipper
it is advisable to break off the session if the animal stiffens
a treat makes the later sessions easier
text: A claw left to grow too long throws off the footing of a cat and will in time curl round and press into the soft pad beneath. The steps set out below deal with the matter without alarming the animal in any way. Choose a settled moment, some while after a meal, when the cat lies dozing across a lap. Take up one paw gently, press the base of the toe so that the claw slides clear of its sheath, and look for the pink band through which the vessels run. The cut must stop well short of that band, or a painful bleed will follow. A tool with a curved blade answers better than an ordinary clipper, whose jaws crush the horn instead of severing it. Should the animal stiffen, break off the session and take it up the next day, one paw at a time. A treat at the end makes the sessions that follow a good deal easier.

units: two neighbouring shelters take in abandoned animals
the first houses every animal in a pen of its own
the second puts compatible animals into small groups
keeping them apart cuts the spread of disease
grouping them lowers the behaviour that comes of boredom
adoptions are settled sooner in the collective setting
quarrels on the other hand break out more often there
both teams keep the same health record
they pass residents to one another as space falls free
text: Two shelters, a valley apart, take in the abandoned animals of the district, yet they work along opposite lines. The first gives every resident a pen of its own, from arrival to departure. A keeper there defends the choice on grounds of contagion: mange travels slowly when muzzles never meet. The second sorts compatible temperaments into small groups, and its director reports a sharp drop in compulsive licking and in the barking that boredom brings. The adoption books bear the difference out. Animals leave sooner from the collective site, where visitors watch them play off one another. Scuffles, though, break out more readily there, and a bitten resident has to be pulled aside at once. Both teams keep the same health record, and each passes animals to the other as soon as a space falls free.

units: the farmyard belongs to an uncle of the narrator
the cockerel has a red growth on top of its head
a hard spike stands out at the back of its legs
the hens roll about in the dry dust
the ducks have a shallow pond to themselves
the geese announce visitors with their cries
a cat sleeps on the woodpile
the uncle hands out the grain before nightfall
text: You ought to see the farmyard my uncle keeps, it is quite a show. The cockerel lords it over the lot of them: that red comb goes up the moment the gate swings, and the hard spur behind each leg makes him worth avoiding. The hens spend the whole afternoon rolling about in the dry dust with their feathers puffed out, and they get up grey from beak to claw. Down the slope a bit, the ducks have a shallow pond they empty and fill again all day long with those flat bills. As for the geese, you hear them well before you see them: let a car turn onto the track and the whole lot start shrieking together. On the woodpile a ginger cat sleeps through the racket without stirring. Then my uncle comes round with his grain bucket before dark, the same hour every evening, and it all goes quiet.

units: the earliest animal collections served to impress visitors
the beasts were shut behind narrow bars
wider cages later imitated the settings they came from
the parks began to breed threatened species
releases into the wild have been attempted
captivity weakens the habits needed for survival
the writer holds that protecting wild places must come first
he grants that some species survive only under human watch
text: The first animal collections existed to dazzle a visitor: a big cat behind narrow bars stood for power, and nobody troubled over the creature wasting away inside them. Wider cages came later, planted with trees and dug out into pools, meant to echo the settings the animals had come from. Then the parks claimed a duty of rescue: breeding scarce species, keeping books of descent, releasing stock born in confinement. That last step deserves a harder look. A predator fed at a fixed hour loses the habits that keep it alive, and its return to the wild fails more often than not. Those budgets would do more good spent on the ground itself, on wooded corridors, on rivers freed of their weirs. Let it be granted, even so, that a handful of species now hangs on under human watch alone.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the trainer grew up on an isolated farm
an accident took the sight of her father
she then trained a dog to guide her father
that success brought other requests
she turned a barn into a training space
she picks puppies for their calm in the face of noise
she refuses rewards founded on fear
her former pupils come back to consult her
text: The trainer spent her childhood on an outlying farm, among plough horses and sheepdogs. When a farm machine took the sight of her father, she set about teaching a young bitch to walk him between the house and the byre. The dog learnt to slow at every step and to lay her muzzle against his hand before any obstacle stood in the way. Word of it travelled, and families began knocking at the farm door for help of the same sort. Short of room, she cleared the barn and laid it out for training, with ramps, slippery boards and swinging doors. She picks her puppies for indifference to clatter rather than for liveliness, since a nervous animal freezes at the worst moment. Having seen what fear produces, she will have nothing to do with harsh correction. Her old pupils still come back to ask her advice.

units: the new tank of a public aquarium is assessed
the curved panes warp the shape of the fish
lighting that was too harsh brought out the glare of the scales
the fish gathered in one corner of the tank
an artificial current was added to spread the fish out
filters have softened the lighting
the visitor route stays too narrow near the entrance
the writer recommends widening that passage
the display is judged a success despite these faults
text: The tank opened in the mild season deserves a hard look before any praise. Its curved panes flatter from a distance, yet they warp the outlines as soon as one steps close: a tail fin reads far broader than it truly is. The lighting, harsh at first, set the scales glittering until the dark markings along the back were lost. The fish, put out by all that glare, packed themselves into a blind corner and went unseen. The staff have since responded on both counts. An artificial current now spreads them through the whole volume, and tinted filters have taken the edge off the beams. One serious fault remains, in the visitor route, so narrow near the entrance that groups jam there and shuffle. Widening the passage is called for. Even with these reservations, the display stands comparison with the best of its kind.

units: the writer writes to a breeder to ask for advice
he is torn between two species to keep at home
the rabbit needs a daily space to run in
the bird copes better with long absences
the rabbit gnaws any cable within reach
the bird keeps up a steady noise that is hard to bear
the writer lives in a cramped flat
he asks for a reply before his planned visit
text: Madam, I hope you will forgive my writing to you, for your years of breeding will guide me better than the leaflets I have read. I am torn between a rabbit and a bird kept for company, and each case seems to me equally sound. The first needs a space to run in every evening, without which its muscles waste away; the second takes my long absences in its stride, which weighs with me, since I am often away from home. Against that, a rabbit gnaws through any cable left within its reach, while a bird keeps up a steady whistling that my neighbours are unlikely to bear kindly for long. My own flat is cramped, and that counts heavily in the balance, with no balcony to extend it. Might I trouble you for an answer before my visit next week? I remain, with every good wish, yours faithfully.

units: the antlers of deer drop and grow again with each yearly cycle
the horns of cattle lengthen without ever falling off
antlers are made of bone
horns sit on a bony core wrapped in a hard sheath
growing antlers again calls for rich feeding
the males use these growths when they fight
the females of certain species carry horns as well
fallen antlers are gnawed by small mammals
text: One question comes up again and again on a country walk: are antlers and horns the same thing? They are not, and the clearest difference lies in what becomes of them. The rack of a stag drops away once the rutting season closes and grows back whole in the cycle that follows, while the horn of an ox lengthens without pause and never parts from the skull. What are they made of? The first is plain bone, fed while it grows by a velvety skin; the second wraps a bony core in a hard fibrous sheath. Does such regrowth cost the animal much? It does, and it calls for feed rich in minerals. What are these growths for? Males measure themselves against rivals with them. Do females go without? Not always: in certain species they carry horns too. And afterwards? Antlers shed on the ground are gnawed away by voles and squirrels.

units: a herder explains that his flock has stopped feeding
he puts the change down to the wetness of the vegetation
a neighbouring herder describes a different reaction in her own animals
the goats crowded against the fence
the herder admits he moved the drinking point
the shade of the hedge made the water too cold to drink
the young animals drank less and lost weight
the herder judges that the fault is his and not the weather's
the neighbour confesses to having made the same mistake before
text: The shepherd told it plainly: his ewes had stopped grazing the moment the wind got up. Wet grass sits heavy, he said, and an uneasy animal chews badly. His neighbour, who keeps goats on the far slope, had watched something else altogether, for her herd had crowded up against the fence and stayed there. At that the shepherd owned up. He had shifted the drinking trough closer to the hedge, and in that shade the water turned cold. Since the move the lambs had been drinking less, they were thinning, and their mothers wore themselves out calling them back. The blame, he decided, lay with a choice of his own making and not with the sky. His neighbour laughed softly at the confession, then admitted she had done exactly the same thing during the cold season before, and to the same end.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: harnessing a draught animal squeezed its throat
that pressure hampered the animal's breathing
the animal could not deliver its full power
craftsmen shifted the bearing onto the shoulders by means of a padded collar
this change raised the load the animal could pull
a head piece served to steer the animal without hurting it
a mouth device protected the drivers from bites
these inventions spread from one valley to the next by copying
text: Harnessing a draught animal once posed a blunt mechanical problem. The strap ran across the throat, and the harder the beast pulled, the tighter it squeezed the windpipe. Breathing failed before the load had properly moved, so a good share of the animal's strength went to waste. The remedy lay in shifting where the pull was borne. Craftsmen carried the bearing onto the shoulders with a padded collar, which left the throat clear under strain and raised the weight a single beast could shift. A supple headpiece was added, so that the animal could be steered without its muzzle being rubbed raw, and a light mouth guard kept the drivers safe from bites during awkward manoeuvres. The design travelled from valley to valley, copied in workshops that knew nothing of whoever had thought of it.

units: birds and mammals feed their young in different ways
chicks leave the egg almost bare
a fine insulating down protects them from the cold
bird parents bring food in from outside the nest
these journeys back and forth are very frequent
young mammals take a food made by their mother
young mammals press against one another to keep their heat
both methods answer the same nutritional need
text: Set a nestful of chicks beside a litter of young mammals and two distinct answers to one and the same requirement come into view. Chicks break out of the egg almost bare; only a thin down keeps them insulated against the cold, and their warmth depends on an adult settling over them. Every mouthful has to be fetched in from outside the nest, which binds the parents to journeys that begin at first light and end only at dusk, back and forth without pause. Among mammals the food is made by the mother herself, so that it stays within reach at all hours and no far errand is called for. The young press close against one another and hold their heat between them while the adults are away. What separates the two, then, is where the food comes from and how freely the parents may move, not the purpose being served, which stays the same in either case.

units: a naturalist made an inventory of the shelters on a wooded slope
a burrow dug under a stump housed a rodent
she never once caught sight of this occupant
a cavity under roots served as a den for a carnivore
birds had built their nests in the cracks of a fallen wall
insects lived under the loose bark of dead trunks
the shelters changed occupant over the course of the season
she handed her notes to a research team, which published them
text: A naturalist settled on a wooded slope and set about listing every shelter the ground there had to offer. She began with the burrows driven into the hillside. One of them opened out beneath a stump and belonged to a rodent she never once set eyes on, for all the hours she gave it. Next came a den wedged under a tangle of roots, lined with hair and twigs, in use by a carnivore of middling size. After that she took in the cracks of a fallen wall, where birds had jammed their nests, and then the loose bark of dead trunks, alive underneath with insects small enough to go unnoticed. What struck her hardest was the turnover: a shelter left empty had been taken over again before the season ran out. She passed her notebooks to a research team, and they published them without delay.

units: you first have to choose a spot sheltered from the wind
the feeding device is fixed high up, out of reach of predators
dry seed is poured into it
salted leftovers are to be avoided
a shallow water container is set beside it
the water must be changed as soon as it turns cloudy
the device must be washed regularly to prevent illness spreading
you have to watch the animals from a distance without going near
the food supply must not be cut off abruptly during the cold season
text: Fancy feeding the birds in the orchard without getting it wrong? Start by finding a corner out of the wind, open enough that a cat cannot climb to it. Fix the feeder well up, a good way off any low branch, then tip in dry seed, never anything salted and never sodden bread. Set a shallow dish of water beside it, a wide saucer will do, and change that water the moment it goes cloudy. Then give the whole lot a scrub in hot water every other week. Droppings build up and pass illness around, and a dirty feeder does more harm than no feeder at all. Watch your visitors from a distance and keep well back, or they will abandon the orchard altogether. One last thing, and it matters: once the cold season has begun, do not cut the food off suddenly, because they have got used to coming and they count on you.

units: the level of a body of water fell after a dry season
a strip of mud joining the shore to the islet was laid bare
land predators took this passage
the nests set on the ground were plundered
the adult birds abandoned the breeding site
part of the colony settled on a steep bank
the site managers had a channel dug to cut the islet off
pairs came back to lay the following season
the original numbers were never recovered
text: A dry season pulled the water level down, and that single drop was enough to undo the colony of birds which had long held the middle islet. As the water drew back it laid bare a tongue of mud running from the shore across to the islet, and the carnivores that prowl the bank were over it on the very first night. Nests built on open ground were ransacked, the eggs lost, and the adults deserted a site they had used year upon year. Some of the colony shifted to a steep rocky bank, harder to reach but wide open to the swell, where hardly a clutch there came to anything. Warned by volunteer watchers, the people managing the site had a narrow channel cut across the mud, so that the islet could no longer be reached on foot. The next season a share of the pairs came back to lay, though the old numbers never returned.

units: a shelter is dug into a bank between roots
brambles hide its entrance
the rains used to flood the passage
the soaked bedding turned bitterly cold for the animal
a second opening was broken through higher up the bank
a dry chamber was dug above the level the water reached
dry grasses cover the floor of this chamber
the old passage now serves to carry the rain away
text: A dark mouth sinks into the bank between the roots, screened so thoroughly by brambles that a walker would pass within a step of it and never notice. The passage runs downward, smooth, polished by fur going through it over and over. In the rains the water used to slide down along the slope and gather at the bottom of it, and the soaked bedding turned bitterly cold under the sleeping animal. So a second mouth was broken open higher up the bank, and from it a shaft climbs to a dry chamber cut above the line the water reaches. Brittle grasses, pulled from the meadow alongside, now cover its floor, and the warmth of the sleeper holds there without any effort at all. The first passage, given up as lodging, carries the rain away instead: it pours in there and comes out lower down, well clear of the bed.

units: the author compares rearing in an enclosed space and rearing on open range
the enclosed space makes every animal easy to pick out and examine
an injury is spotted early there
confinement helps parasites travel
open range builds up the animals' muscle
open range cuts down joint trouble
the scattering of the animals makes health monitoring difficult
the author recommends combining the two systems according to age and season
he asks that the decision rest on measurements and not on convictions
text: Pitting housed rearing against open range rarely settles anything, and the appetite of both camps for a single verdict does the argument more harm than good. Housing has one plain advantage over the rest: every animal can be picked out, weighed and looked over, so that a lesion shows up while it is still small. That same confinement gathers the parasites in and helps them travel through the stock from one animal to the next. Open ground works the other way about. It builds muscle and cuts joint trouble, yet it scatters the animals widely and leaves any health check to chance. A sensible holding therefore runs both systems, sorted by age group and by season, rather than raising either one of them into doctrine. What is still wanting is that the choice be settled on recorded measurements and not on conviction.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman who runs a care centre looks after injured animals
she worked as a veterinary assistant before founding her refuge
the refuge occupies an abandoned farm
she feeds the nestlings with forceps at short intervals
she straps up fractured wings and watches them heal
she teaches volunteers to take hold of a frightened animal without hurting it
she enters every arrival in a register
she releases the recovered animals well away from busy roads
she refuses to give a name to the animals taken in
text: The woman who runs the care centre gives her days to creatures that will never be hers. She trained first as a veterinary assistant, learning restraint, splinting and the reading of plates, and only later opened a refuge of her own in a farm that had long stood empty. Her work falls into fixed tasks. She feeds the nestlings with forceps at short intervals, from first light through to dusk. She straps fractured wings, watches the weight come back onto them and adjusts the dressings. She trains volunteers, showing them how to take hold of a frightened animal without hurting it or being bitten. She enters every arrival in a thick register, with the species, the injury and the outcome. And she lets the recovered go well away from busy roads, taking care never to give any of them a name.

units: a documentary book about nocturnal animals is assessed
the opening reports observations carried out in the field
this opening wins the reviewer over
the middle chapters set out measurements from experiments in captivity
this part is judged too dry to read
it nonetheless brings solid knowledge on hearing and orientation
the closing pages give protective recommendations that are too vague
the drawn plates are held to be the great success of the book
the reviewer recommends reading it all the same
text: The book opens with notebooks kept on night watches, and that opening wins you over at once: the author describes long waits, whole evenings that came to nothing, and brief meetings with animals that sensed her well before she could make them out. Then it changes character altogether. The middle chapters set out run after run of measurements taken from animals held in captivity, in prose so dry that the reading bogs down in it. Solid material on hearing and orientation is there to be had, all the same. The closing pages offer a list of protective measures, too broad, sadly, to commit anyone to anything at all. The drawn plates are another matter: they alone repay the trip, so well do they catch posture and movement. It is worth reading all the same, sagging middle and all.

units: the writer is looking after the dog of a close friend who has gone travelling
the animal whined at night behind the bedroom door
it refused to eat its ration
it damaged the floor with its claws whenever she moved away
the writer first read this behaviour as a reproach
a training specialist explained that the animal was looking for a reassuring fixed point
she was advised to keep walks at regular hours and to place the bed near the entrance
the dog now sleeps against a cloth that holds its owner's scent
text: Your dog has been with me since you set off, and I am writing to you at last as someone who has finally found the way out. For the first few nights he whimpered behind my bedroom door, turned his nose up at his bowl, and raked the floorboards with his claws the moment I stepped away from him. I took all of it as a rebuke for having let you go. A trainer put me right: the animal was hunting for a fixed point, not passing judgement on me. She told me to walk him at the same hours every day, and to shift his bed against the wall by the front door. He settles there now as soon as the light goes, curls against the cloth that still holds your scent, and waits for the latch without a murmur. He eats, he runs, and he sleeps deeply. You will come home to a calm companion, and to a rather proud friend.

units: specialists in animal behaviour refuse to treat the two kinds of group as one
in a group of grass-eaters each beast takes its cue from its nearest neighbours
no member of that group holds an overall view of the manoeuvre
among bees scouts come back and pass on directions through their movements
the colony settles on the site that gathers the most support
the first group exchanges bodily stances and changes of pace
the second group exchanges content comparable to a reasoned proposal
the first reacts almost instantly whereas the second takes several days to decide
text: Should a herd and a swarm be thought of as two settings on the same machine? Specialists in animal behaviour will not have it. Within a herd, each beast takes its cue from the animals immediately beside it, and the shape of the whole comes out of those local corrections; not one of them holds the manoeuvre in mind. A swarm works on quite another principle. Scouts return and pass on directions through the way they move, and the colony settles on whichever site gathers the most support. So what divides the two? What travels between the members. A herd passes on a stance, a quickening pace, a turn of the head. A swarm passes on something closer to a case being argued. And the pace of it? A herd answers within a fraction of a second, while a swarm weighs the matter for days before it lifts off.

units: a stock keeper set out her worries to a veterinary practitioner
she reported that the animals had been eating less grass for a week
she added that the chewing of the cud lasted a shorter time than usual
the practitioner examined the teeth of the animals
he then checked the quality of the water made available
he also judged the fodder too poor in fibre
he recommended keeping the weakened animals apart from the group
he promised to come back and check the state of the herd
text: The stock keeper set out her worries at some length to the vet who had come out to look over her animals. She told him the cattle had been cropping less grass for a week, and that they stopped chewing the cud sooner than they used to. The vet said he would work through three lines of enquiry in turn. He began with the teeth of each animal, since a single broken one is enough to put a beast off chewing. He then drew water from the trough, whose pipe struck him as clogged. Last, he judged the fodder too poor in fibre, and so ill suited to their digestion. Before leaving, he advised her to keep the weaker animals apart from the rest, to write down every refused feed, and to ring the surgery if intake did not pick up. He gave his word that he would come back before long and check on the state of the herd.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the drawing together of humans and wild animals began with a mutual acceptance
meat-eaters came to look for the waste left around the camps
the least wary individuals ended up being fed
hunting bands mixing humans and dog-like animals took shape
grass-eaters were then penned as a living store of food
these beasts were picked over for their steadiness and their fleece
the rise of sown crops created a need for animals able to pull loads
cats were suffered in order to keep gnawing creatures away from the grain stores
text: Domestication began with no decision behind it, only with a mutual putting up with. Meat-eaters prowled at the edge of hunting camps, drawn by the scraps thrown aside; the wariest slipped away, the boldest lingered and ended up being fed. Out of that closeness came the mixed band, human and dog-like animal running down game together. Grass-eaters were penned next, held at first as a larder on the hoof, then picked over for their steadiness and for the thickness of their fleece. Sown fields, once they spread, called for pulling power, and the sturdiest beasts were harnessed to the plough. Later still, cats were suffered in the grain stores, where they held the gnawing creatures away from the harvest. Every stage lengthened the roll of species bound to us, and reshaped their outline as much as their temper.

units: a thin see-through covering left by a reptile is sometimes found on the ground
the outer layer of a snake's skin does not stretch as the animal grows longer
that stiffness forces the reptile to get rid of its old covering
a fresh layer builds up beneath the old one
a fluid seeps in between the two layers and lifts them apart
the eyes of the animal turn cloudy during this phase
the snake hunts little and hides while its sight is poor
it rubs its snout against a stone to start the lifting
text: Have you ever picked up one of those see-through papery things by the side of a path and wondered what creature could have left it there? That is a snake skin, and the whole business comes down to a fault in the design. The outer layer that shields the reptile will not stretch, while the animal underneath keeps getting longer. So, sooner or later, it has to shed. A fresh layer builds up below the old one, then a fluid seeps in between the two and lifts them apart. While that goes on, the eyes cloud over to a milky blue and the poor thing can barely see. It hardly hunts at all, and tucks itself away under a stump. Once the split is complete, it rubs its snout on a rough stone, catches the rim of the old covering, and works its way out of it. What you find lying on the ground is that worn out coat.

units: a mark left in the mud near a pen set off alarm
ewes had been killed during the night
the sheep farmers put the losses down to a wild meat-eater
a naturalist judged the mark too broad for that explanation
cameras triggered by movement were set up
the pictures showed two dogs without an owner at hand
the owners of the dogs were traced and held responsible
an electrified fence and a watch kept at night put an end to the raids
text: The alarm went up over a single print in the mud, a few steps away from a pen where three ewes had been killed during the night. Sheep farmers round the valley pointed straight at a wild meat-eater and asked for leave to shoot it. A naturalist sent out to look refused to sign up to that. The pad mark seemed too broad to her, and the bites fell in the wrong places for a practised hunter. She had cameras set up along the fences, the sort that trip of their own accord when something moves. The pictures, collected the week after, showed two stray dogs with collars round their necks, no owner anywhere near. The men who kept them were traced and held to account for the losses. An electrified fence and a watch kept through the hours of darkness were put in place, and the raids ceased at once.

units: there are two methods for watching wild birds
the first consists in setting out food to draw them in
this method quickly brings in the bolder species
it alters the behaviour of the very birds one claims to study
the second consists in sitting still inside a screen of cut branches
it calls for keeping quiet through a long wait
it shows behaviour that food never brings out
it is advised to begin with the first method and then take up the second
text: Before you carry your binoculars out to the hedge, settle on one of two ways of coming near the birds, because they do not show you the same thing. The first sets out food to draw them in: a handful of seed on a board, a lump of fat hung from a branch. Bold species will turn up quickly and counting them is easy, yet what you watch are guests at a table, not free birds. The second asks you to build a screen of cut branches, to sit inside it before first light, and to keep still and quiet. The wait drags on and on, and the cold works its way into you. In return you catch the display, the squabble over a dry stalk, the heavy flight of the bird bringing home nest stuff, things a feeding board never brings out. Start with the food until the shapes grow familiar; move to the hide once the names come to you without a pause.

units: a scientific team is finishing the yearly count of a colony of sea birds
the count is made on occupied nests and not on the adults in view
breeding numbers have fallen compared with the previous season
the fish these birds depend on has moved into deeper water
the adults range further to feed
the eggs are left alone more often than before
gulls take advantage of these absences to rob the nests
the team recommends limiting the access of walkers to the foot of the cliffs
text: A team of bird specialists is coming to the end of the yearly count of a colony lodged on the coastal cliffs, and their findings fall under four separate heads. Numbers first: the count is made on occupied nests, a steadier measure than the adults in view at any moment, and the total has fallen well below the figure of the previous season. Food next: the fish the birds live on has moved away into deeper water, which stretches out every feeding trip they make. Breeding after that: the adults range further out, eggs are left alone more often than before, and gulls with an eye for a chance come in and rob the uncovered nests. Access last: the team urges that the foot of the cliffs be closed to walkers through the delicate weeks, a step it calls modest in itself but open to immediate use.

units: the mare leaves her box as the gate opens
she halts and takes in the air before going forward
she shakes her whole coat to rid it of the damp
she rolls onto her back in a sandy hollow
she eats the grass of the field for a long stretch
she makes her way to the trough set under a tree
she stays on her feet and dozes in the shade of the leaves
she waits by the gate for someone to come and bring her in
text: As the gate swings open, the mare clears the doorway of her box and halts, nostrils wide, to take in the air of the field. She goes forward a few paces, then shakes herself out at length, and the damp of the night leaves her coat in a fine spray. Then comes the roll: she folds her forelegs, tips onto her flank, rubs her back into a sandy hollow, and rises again with a thrust of the loins. She grazes after that without lifting her head, moving on in short even steps along the fence, tearing at the lush growth of the edges and leaving the coarse tufts of the middle, until the heat turns her towards the trough set under the tree. There she drinks, and stays on her feet, one hind leg resting, eyelids heavy in the shade of the leaves. Late in the afternoon she comes back to the gate and waits, quite still, to be led in.

units: wildlife parks justify their existence by the rescue of species
their opponents hold that confinement undoes the animals
the surface available is far smaller than the ground covered in freedom
this restriction brings on repeated movements in meat-eaters
the food handed out removes all active searching
animals born in captivity survive poorly once released
the writer proposes keeping these parks for species that are truly at risk
the writer suggests funding the protection of wild places with the takings at the gate
text: Wildlife parks defend themselves by pointing to the rescue of species; their critics answer that shutting an animal in undoes the very creature it claims to save. The argument is worth following to its end, because one effect draws on the next. An enclosure, however roomy, gives a surface bearing no comparison with the ground a meat-eater covers when free. Out of that shrinking come the mechanical turns along the bars that keepers know so well. Food brought at fixed hours then removes all searching, and with it any schooling in the hunt. It follows that beasts born behind wire seldom last long once returned to the wild. The conclusion seems to me to hold: keep these parks for species that are truly at risk, and turn the takings at the gate over to the defence of wild places.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the central figure looks after the animals of a shelter
she is inside the enclosure before the sky lightens
she likens her trade to that of an interpreter
a thick-coated mammal states its needs differently from a bird
she bottle-feeds the infants left without a mother
she keeps her distance when a grown animal is hurt
she compares her patience to that of someone who works a plot of ground
her colleagues credit her with sensing pain before any visible sign
she puts that reputation down to close and repeated watching
text: The keeper is inside the enclosure before the sky has begun to lighten, a bucket of seed wedged against her hip. Her trade, she says, comes closest to an interpreter's: she listens to tongues that carry no words. A shaggy mammal rubbing itself along the fence is asking for one thing; a bird beating its wings behind glass is asking for something else entirely. The newborns whose mothers have vanished she feeds from a bottle. The wounded grown ones she leaves alone, watching from the far side of the gate. Patience of this kind belongs to anyone who works a plot of ground: healing cannot be hurried, only kept company. Her colleagues swear she senses pain long before the animal starts to limp. She laughs at that, and says she only looks harder, and more often, and without any hurry at all.

units: the piece assesses a film devoted to wildlife
the assessment falls into three aspects
the steadiness of the long takes is judged excellent
one sequence follows a bird of prey settling on a branch
the added music covers the sound recorded on site
the commentary confuses two different bodily states
one passage shows young just taken off the teat
that passage is held to be the best in the film
the crew did not state how long the watching sessions lasted
text: The wildlife film shown last week is worth judging under three headings. The picture first: the long takes are held with a steadiness that never falters, and the camera follows a bird of prey right down onto its branch without a tremor in the frame. The sound is another matter. A layer of added music keeps swallowing what the recordists caught on the spot, the shifting of leaves, the settling of feathers. Then the science: the commentary runs together two distinct states, the deep torpor of a winter sleeper and the light dozing of a beast that wakes at intervals, and an argument otherwise well built is weakened by it. What redeems the whole is the passage on the young just taken off the teat, where gestures pass from one generation to the next. A pity the crew never said how long they watched.

units: the letter is addressed to a woman living in the house next door
it concerns a ginger cat that moves from one plot to the other
the writer saw it at dusk hidden under a hedge
the animal was watching birds that had come to drink
the next day it settled on a window ledge
the writer first supposed it belonged to a tenant
the worn collar and the thinness of the animal changed her mind
she gives it water but will not feed it
the animal walks badly on a hind limb
text: Dear neighbour, I am writing to you about the ginger cat that moves back and forth between our two gardens. Last week, at dusk, I caught sight of him under the hedge, flattened low, watching the birds that come to drink at the stone basin. The following morning he crossed the low wall and settled on my window ledge. My first thought was that he belonged to the tenant at the far end, until I noticed how worn his collar was and how thin he had grown. Since then I have been putting out fresh water for him, though I have stopped short of feeding him, so as not to tie him to my yard. Should you know who owns him, I should be grateful if you would pass the word on: he is walking badly on one hind leg. I am glad to discuss the matter in person. Yours sincerely, the tenant of the house alongside.

units: the wall of the egg grows thinner from the inside
the embryo draws off the calcium meant for its skeleton
a longer incubation yields a more finished young one
that young one moves about as soon as it leaves the shell
other species are born without feathers and without sight
this strategy shortens the time the female stays still over the clutch
it therefore lowers the risk of being spotted by a hunter
the adults must then feed young that cannot move
neither strategy is presented as the better one
text: What goes on inside an egg in the last hours before hatching? The shell grows thinner from within, because the embryo is drawing off the calcium its own skeleton needs. Why does one chick come out in thick down and another with bare skin? It rests on how long the incubation lasts: the longer the wait, the more finished the chick, and some are on their feet and running the moment the shell gives way. So what does a species gain by hatching its young naked and blind? It cuts short the stretch of days when the female must sit motionless over the clutch, and with that it lowers her chances of being marked by anything out hunting. The bill comes later, since the parents must then feed mouths that cannot move. Does one method win, then? Neither does. Each answers the pressures of its own surroundings.

units: someone from the neighbourhood tells of his troubles with livestock
his rabbits were digging under the fence and getting out
the runaways headed for the vegetable patch at the bottom
the man had already sunk the wire netting deeper
the animals were slipping through a gap he had not found
his daughter suggests laying a wide board flat against the fence
a digging animal starts its hole at the foot of the obstacle
it gives up when it meets a hard surface
the family nailed boards down and then tipped gravel over them
there has been no escape since
text: The chap next door stopped me at the gate to tell me about his rabbits. They had been digging under the wire, he said, and heading straight for the vegetable patch at the bottom of the plot. Had he tried sinking the netting deeper? He had, and it made no odds, because they were still slipping out through some gap he had never managed to find. His daughter, who was listening, said he should lay a wide board flat on the ground, tight against the fence. It struck me as sound: an animal that digs goes at the foot of whatever stands in its way, and once it meets something hard underneath, it gives the job up. So they nailed the boards down and tipped gravel over the wood. Not one rabbit has got out since. He still laughs about it: he was planning a wall, and his daughter settled it with offcuts.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: two ways of taming existed at the same time
the first came about without any human intention
animals drew close to the camps for the food scraps
they bred on the spot alongside people
the second way rested on a choice made by keepers
the keepers held back the quiet animals and got rid of the fierce ones
this sorting produced bloodlines that do not occur in the wild
bones found in rubbish heaps bear witness to the first process
pens and tethers bear witness to the second
the first process yielded companions and the second yielded herds
text: Two ways of taming ran side by side long before anyone wrote anything down, and researchers still tell them apart. The first owed nothing to human intention. Animals drifted in towards the camps for the scraps, put up with the people who lived there, and bred where they stood, so that the sorting happened on its own. The second was deliberate. Keepers held back the quiet beasts, got rid of the ones that turned on them, and within a handful of generations had shaped bloodlines that exist nowhere in the wild. Bones dug out of old rubbish heaps tell the first story; pens and tethers tell the second. Specialists point out that one road led to companions and the other to herds. The two overlap, of course, since a creature that came near by chance is kept on purpose one evening.

units: the piece describes what a coat reveals
a plain shade hides the animal in a stretch of sand or grass
a coat marked with spots copies foliage pierced by light
those spots wipe out the outline of the animal
ruffled hair traps air against the skin
that hair keeps a body warm without weighing it down
swimmers wear a dense pelt that holds water off the skin
every coat also gives off a scent
a dog nosing at a trunk reads there that one of its own kind went by
newborns wear a down that a breath will shift
text: A coat tells a story, and the eye needs time to read it. There is the plain shade first, which melts an animal away into a stretch of open sand or dry grass. There is the dappled coat, whose scattered shadows copy foliage pierced by light and blur the line of the back. There is the rough, wind-tousled hair that traps air against the skin and keeps a body warm without weighing it down. Then there is the close fur of the swimmers, packed so tight that water runs off it and never reaches the skin underneath. Every coat gives off a scent as well, and that scent travels: a dog nosing at a tree trunk reads there that one of its own kind went by. Last of all comes the down of the newborn, so light that a breath will move it. Colour speaks to the eye, texture to the cold, scent to memory.

units: a team strung a fine net between two poles at the edge of a copse
the birds taken were measured and weighed and then let go again
one bird ringed the season before was caught again in the same place
that recapture allowed a comparison of mass from one season to the next
the bird had lost a marked amount of weight
the loss fitted a hard winter
the technician added two measurements to the protocol
she recorded wing length and the state of the plumage
the final report calls for lasting watch over the site
the equipment was left standing for the season to come
text: The ringing season opened with a fine net strung between two slender poles at the edge of a copse. Every bird taken from it was measured, weighed on a field balance and then let go again straight away. On the third evening a bird ringed the season before turned up in the very same net, which made it possible to set the mass of one season against that of the next. The loss of weight proved marked, and it matched a winter that had been hard. The technician widened the protocol on the spot: from then on she noted wing length and the state of the feathers as well, both of them signs of wear. By the close of the season the file held dozens of usable lines. The report concluded that the site deserved watching without a break, and the equipment was left standing exactly where it was.

units: a wall sheltered from the prevailing wind should be chosen
an exposed entrance lets rain in and chills the eggs
the support must be solid because a box that sways frightens the occupants
the entrance hole must stay narrow
a wide opening makes it easy for predators to get in
the box must be set beyond the reach of cats
no branch nearby should offer a foothold
the inside must not be lined because the occupants bring their own materials
damp padding rots the brood
a clean-out at the end of the season removes parasites that would harm the next clutch
text: Before you put up a nesting box, pick a wall that is sheltered from the prevailing wind, since an entrance left exposed takes in the rain and chills the eggs beneath. Fix the back panel to something thoroughly solid: a box that sways unsettles the birds inside, and they abandon it at the first alarm. Cut the entrance hole small, because a wide one makes life far too easy for predators. Set the whole thing beyond the reach of cats, at shoulder height at the very least, with no branch nearby that might offer a foothold. Do not line the inside, since the occupants bring their own materials and damp padding holds a wetness that rots the brood. Clean the cavity out once the season is over, because the parasites that build up in the debris will spoil the clutch that comes after.

units: walkers reported that the young ducks along a canal were vanishing
an association of naturalists looked into what was happening
the concrete slope kept the young from getting out of the water
the bread thrown by passers-by drew in rodents
those rodents were wrecking the nests
the local authority sank sloping wooden ramps into the water
the young can climb these ramps unaided
signs explain that bread does the birds harm
a later count found more young alive
those in charge hold that one season is not enough to conclude
text: For weeks, walkers along the banks of a town canal had been reporting that the duck broods were vanishing. An association of naturalists looked into it and came back with two causes. The concrete slope of the bank gave the ducklings nothing to climb, so they could not get out of the water at all, and the rats drawn in by the bread that passers-by throw were working their way through the nests. The local authority first sank wooden ramps into the water, set at a steep pitch, which the young can now climb unaided. Signs went up afterwards explaining that bread does the birds harm and feeds the rodents instead. A count taken when the warm weather came round again found more young alive than the year before. Those running the scheme are careful, though: one season proves nothing, and the watch goes on.

units: groups of different animals share the same bank without falling out
the birds with webbed feet search the mud with their beaks
these birds leave star-shaped marks pressed into the mud
rodents of a stocky build live in the belt of reeds
these rodents drive tunnels and eat the young stems
their soft fur keeps the wet off them
the insects hold to the dry part of the slope
the insects feed the animals that fly above
the bank reads as three levels stacked one upon another
text: Three sets of creatures hold the edge of the pond at once, and none of them gets in the way of another. Where the mud lies softest, the web-footed birds work their beaks through the silt, and the ground behind them keeps a scatter of star-shaped prints. A little higher, in among the flattened reeds, live the short thick-bodied rodents; they drive tunnels through the bank and strip the young stems down to the pith, and their downy coats turn the wet away. The dry face of the slope belongs to the insects, hardly noticed and past counting, and everything that flies above the water lives on them. Sit still long enough and the edge sorts itself into three floors stacked one on another: open water, then mud, then cropped grass. Each floor sets its own food, its own hours, its own quiet.

units: the writer holds that public argument has not kept pace with tracking methods
counting was first done by eye and written up on paper
coloured marks then made it possible to follow one particular animal
those marks unsettled the species least willing to be approached
small transmitters now record movement without a break
these devices also measure the depth of dives and the beat of the heart
the writer holds that each advance shifts the moral problem without settling it
a light device still alters what a bird spends in energy
the writer asks that an outside body approve every fitting of a device
text: Let me put it plainly: the watching of wild populations has changed out of all recognition, and the public argument has not kept pace. At the start a person stood on a bank and counted by eye, writing the totals up on paper afterwards. Coloured rings came next, and with them the power to follow one animal rather than a blur of them, though the shyest sorts were badly unsettled by the closeness such work asks for. Now a tag records movement without a break, and reads off the depth of a dive and the beat of a heart besides. Every step forward has shifted the moral problem along instead of settling it. A tag weighs almost nothing, yet it still alters what a bird spends in the air. My own view is firm: nothing should be fitted unless an outside panel has looked at the case and agreed to it.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman who looks after the horses had not aimed at this work
an injury to the knee took her away from her first trade
this injury obliges her to move without haste
the fearful animals came close to her before the others did
she announces every movement by speaking before any touch
the unwilling animals turn biddable within a single season
neighbouring places send her the animals judged past helping
she puts her success down to a constraint of the body and not to a gift
she forbids the beginners in her charge to move at a run
text: The woman who has charge of the horses did not set out to do this work at all. An injury to the knee closed the trade she had trained for, and the stalls were what remained open to her. Because she limps, she moves without haste, and the timid animals, used to quick hands about them, were the first to come near her. Out of that enforced slowness a method grew. She learned to say aloud what she was about to do before her hand went anywhere, so that the most unwilling beasts turned biddable inside a season. Word spread, and neighbouring places began sending her the ones written off as past helping. She will not hear the word gift. The advantage, she says, was handed to her by her own body, and anyone willing to slow down would arrive at the same place. She now trains beginners, who are not allowed to run.

units: the reviewer finds the pictures of the film well made
the reviewer faults the telling for giving human motives to the animals
this lends the belief that survival follows from a considered choice
the viewer comes away moved but no better informed
the last part of the film does without any telling
these passages were shot at night with a heat camera
they follow a band of wolves crossing a wooded corridor
the want of speech makes this passage truer than the opening of the film
text: Nothing is wanting in the pictures: the framing holds, the patience shows, every surface comes through with real precision. It is the telling that lets the film down. Human motives are handed out freely, the she-wolf decides, the hawk chooses, the colony takes revenge, and the ease of it thins the whole thing, since survival begins to look like something weighed up and settled. One comes away moved and none the wiser. The cure was to hand, and the director found it in his closing part, where the night passages, taken with a heat camera, run almost without a word. A pack crosses a wooded corridor, halts, moves off again, and nothing is said over it. All at once the film is truer than anything before it. The lesson holds for the whole kind: film it and stop; explain it and betray it.

units: the writer writes to an acquaintance about two cats
the cat with striped fur was already hanging about behind the workshop
a second cat with ginger fur turned up not long ago
the striped cat hunts little and sleeps on the warmed metal sheet
the ginger cat is thin and eats greedily
the ginger cat keeps its distance from people
the writer tried feeding them in one place in two bowls
the ginger one ate what was in both bowls
the writer means to set the meals of the two animals apart
text: Do you remember that striped cat forever hanging about behind the workshop? He has a rival now, and the gap between the pair is worth a letter. The striped one hunts hardly at all, sleeps on the warm sheet of metal and waits to be waited on; a door creaks and he is already purring. The newcomer is ginger, thin, ravenous, and will not let you within three paces of him. One has worked out that people are a larder, the other that they are a threat. Where the first asks, the second helps himself. I tried feeding them at the same spot, in two bowls set well apart: a poor idea, since the ginger emptied both while the striped one stared at me as though I had sold him. So the meals will be pulled apart, one at first light and one after dark, and the pair left to it. Come and watch some evening.

units: a specialist in animal behaviour answers the questions of the reporter
the subject is the massed flights of birds above river mouths
the specialist puts forward three explanations
living in a crowd lowers the chance that any one bird is taken
the birds find food by watching those that come back well fed
the flock finds the fish in this way without a leader pointing them out
birds packed together hold their warmth better through the halts of the night
the specialist denies that any ranking exists in these flights
each bird sets its pace by the neighbours nearest to it
text: We put our questions to a specialist in animal behaviour about the massed flights of birds above the river mouths. Is there anything like an organisation behind them? Her answer comes in three parts. The first is safety: a bird that keeps company spreads the risk, and stands a smaller chance of being taken while it moves inside a shifting cloud. The second is news. Those coming home well fed are watched and followed, so the whole flock learns where the fish are lying without a leader pointing anything out. The third is warmth; pressed against one another through the halts of the night, the birds lose far less of it. Is there a ranking all the same? She will not have it. What she describes are local rules, each bird setting its pace by whoever is nearest, and a shape overhead that nobody willed.

units: the keeper of the herd comes to warn before the sun rises
he reports that one animal is missing
the neighbour holds that the mist makes the search useless
the keeper answers that the animal has been walking badly since the day before
three people set out together to look for the animal
the keeper explains that the beast follows smells instead of the herd
the neighbour catches the sound of breathing behind some scrub
the animal is found lying down and alive at the foot of the slope
the keeper carries the animal back on his shoulders
text: Before the sun was up the old keeper of the herd knocked at the shutter and said one of the beasts was missing. My neighbour, still in her shawl, told him nobody looks for a horned animal in mist and that the thing to do was wait. He answered that it had been walking badly since the day before and could not have gone far. The three of us went out. On the path he explained that the creature had a way of following smells instead of following its own kind. Then my neighbour stopped and said she could hear breathing, down below, behind the scrub. The keeper went over the edge, pushed the branches apart and called up that she was there, lying down but alive. He brought her up across his shoulders without a word of complaint. Walking home he said only that the next outing would be for her alone, and laughed quietly.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: taming reached first for the species that put up with human company
a species that lives in a crowd already knows an order of rank within it
such a species allows a stranger to take the leading place
a species that lives alone and holds ground refuses that place to a stranger
human groups kept the lines whose young would bear closeness
the animals hard to approach seldom bred within an enclosure
the sorting therefore went on without any settled plan
tamed animals show a shorter jaw and ears that hang down
these features come up together because they arise from the same cells of the embryo
text: Taming did not begin with the most useful creatures but with the most forbearing. A beast that lives in a crowd already stands somewhere in an order of rank, and will therefore let a stranger take the leading place, which one that lives alone and holds its own ground never grants. From that leaning a plain consequence follows: human groups held on only to the lines whose young could bear having people about them. The wary ones fled or struck out, and bred poorly behind a fence, so the sorting went on with almost nothing willed about it. Shape and temper then shifted together: the jaw grew shorter, the ears came down, the temper cooled, ripeness arrived later. Such features turn up as a set because they all trace back to the same cells in the embryo. Mildness was never taught. It was gathered in.

units: the frogs and their kin leave the woods for the ponds where they were born
their route crosses a road again and again
these animals with webbed feet go forward in small moves
they hold still in front of the beams of vehicles
they travel above all after the sun has gone down
a population of one place can die out within three seasons
a first measure is a low fence that leads the animals towards a tunnel
this work costs a great deal but asks for no watching over
a second measure closes the road on the nights of heaviest movement
both measures suppose that the usual routes have been found beforehand
text: When the mild season comes round, frogs and their kin leave the woods for the ponds they hatched in. The way there crosses a road more often than not, and the losses run high: these web-footed travellers advance in short hops, freeze in the beams of oncoming traffic, and set off mostly once the sun is down, at the hour when driving is still fast. A population can be wiped from a place in three seasons. Two answers have been tried. The first lays a low fence along the verge, steering the animals towards a pipe that runs beneath the surfacing; the work costs dearly but needs nobody to mind it. The second, much lighter, shuts the road on the nights of heaviest movement. Both call for the old crossing places to have been traced first, which nothing but patient watching will give you.

units: two young dogs of the same age reached the shelter on the same evening
the first dog is heavily built and carries grey patches
the first dog lets itself be touched and looks for company
the second dog takes fright at noises and comes out only once night has fallen
the staff thought the first dog would be taken very quickly
it was the second dog that left the shelter first
a household kept it precisely because it held back
this household judged its home too quiet for a restless animal
the first dog waited until the autumn
the man in charge concludes that the fondest animal is not the first to be taken
text: Nobody would have put money on the pup that kept to the back of its kennel. Two dogs of the same age had been left at the shelter on the same evening, and the staff never tired of setting one against the other. The first, heavy and flecked with grey, took handling without a murmur; she ate anything, slept anywhere, and pushed her head forward for a stroke the moment a door moved. The second flinched at the knock of a bucket and left her shelter only after dark. A week would see the first one rehomed, the keepers said. It was the second that found a household first. She was chosen for the very hiding that had counted against her, by people who said their rooms were too still to suit a restless animal. The flecked one waited until autumn. The most winning animal, says the man in charge, is never the first to go.

units: a resin put on the hair makes it grip more strongly
the hair drags the string and releases it over and over
that repetition produces a steady oscillation
the speed of the oscillation settles the note that is heard
a string on its own sets too little air moving
the vibration travels through a piece standing on the body
the body of the instrument starts moving in its turn
widening the vibrating surface makes the sound louder
text: Draw a bow across a taut string and the sound begins with a grip so small that no ear can catch it. The hair carries a dusting of resin, which leaves it faintly tacky. So the hair takes hold of the string, drags it a fraction to one side, then lets go all at once. The string springs back towards its resting place, the hair catches it again, and the cycle runs on without a break. Out of that catching and slipping comes a steady vibration, and how fast it runs decides the pitch we hear. On its own the string shifts far too little air to be heard across a room. It hands its movement instead to the bridge, a slim upright of wood standing on the belly of the instrument. The bridge sets that broad panel swinging, and the panel drives a great deal more air. The tone grows full because the vibrating surface has been made wider.

units: the head of the percussion instrument sounded dull late in the rehearsal
the conductor halts the rehearsal and sends for the repairer
dry air had shrunk the animal skin
tightening the fittings would have made matters worse
the repairer chooses to put moisture back into the room
vessels full of water are set out around the platform
the players carry on rehearsing in another room
with the give restored a slight adjustment brings the pitch back
text: The rehearsal was nearly over when the timpanist noticed that her drum had stopped answering her. Under the stick the head gave back a flat knock with no depth to it, as though every trace of tension had drained out of it. The conductor stopped the players and sent for the craftsman who looked after the instruments. He found the cause soon enough: weeks of very dry air in the hall had shrunk the natural skin stretched over the copper bowl. Turning the screws down would only have deepened the imbalance, and might well have torn the head across. He put forward something gentler, damping the air by degrees and letting the skin ease itself back. Wide basins of water were set out around the platform, and the players moved to another room to finish. By morning the head had recovered its give, and two turns of the key put the pitch right.

units: two blades must be examined before either is fitted
the soft blade bends under the pressure of a finger
the stiff blade keeps its shape when pressed
the blades have to be wetted before fitting
the fastening must not be closed too tightly
a low note is tried and then the same note high up
the soft blade speaks quickly but weakens in the top register
the stiff blade asks for more effort and stands up to loud playing
the choice rests on the tiredness felt after a long held sound
text: Lay two reeds side by side and look at both before you fit either one to the mouthpiece. The softer blade gives way under your thumb; the harder one pushes back and keeps its curve. Each suits a different job, and trying them beats trusting what you have been told. Wet both in a little warm water, then seat the first on the table of the mouthpiece and close the ligature without forcing it. Blow a long note low down, then the same note up in the top register. The soft reed speaks at once and sounds sweet, yet the high end slips away from you as soon as you press harder. The hard reed wants more support to start, gives a thicker tone and holds together when you play out. Keep whichever leaves you less tired after a long held note, not the one that charms you straight away.

units: the place where the instruments are made has lately opened to visitors
a smell of glue and cut wood meets you at the door
the space is divided into four working areas
the first area is for splitting and joining the boards
a student there shapes a part by hand without any powered tool
the finishing area is kept clear of moving air
each coat of finish dries before the next is put on
the last area allows the instrument to be tried by playing it
the person in charge says nothing leaves without being tested
one and the same wood yields instruments that sound different
text: Hot glue and freshly planed wood: that is what meets you the moment you step through the door of the workshop, which has only lately been opened to the public. Four benches share the hall. At the back sits the cutting, where boards of maple are split, turned over and glued up to form the backs. Over on the right, the fitting, where a young apprentice trims a bridge with a knife and never goes near a machine. Further along lies the varnishing room, held well clear of any draught, where a coat has to dry before the next goes on. The last bench, the busiest of the four, is for trying things out: strings go on, a bow is drawn, everyone listens. The man in charge warns visitors that nothing leaves the place unplayed. Most go away with a thought they had not expected, since two instruments cut from one board never sound alike.

units: the space is deserted late in the day before the session
the technical team lay the cables and hang two pickups
the players settle in and put their instruments in tune
the first take starts once night has come
one player fits an accessory that softens the tone
the person in charge of sound answers by moving a pickup back
stray noises can be heard during the pauses
the last take is the best one in spite of the exhaustion
the gear is packed away before the sun rises
text: Late in the afternoon the hall stands empty and the quiet inside it feels thick enough to touch. The technicians come in first, running their cables along the foot of the walls and hanging two microphones above the platform. The players drift in afterwards in twos and threes, settle without hurry and tune up in a peaceable sort of muddle. The first take begins after dark. A cellist clips a mute onto his bridge to soften the tone, and the engineer answers by drawing one microphone back. Between takes you catch the rustle of pages, a cough, a chair creaking under somebody who has shifted. Around midnight the tiredness shows in every face, and yet the take that holds together best is the last of them. The cables are coiled before the sun is up, and the hall goes back to its silence, a shade warmer than it was on arrival.

units: the absence of noise is now sold as a product
the humming of machines pushes the ear to sort very early
that protection of the hearing costs it its fineness
attention goes to masses of sound rather than to details
recorded sound is now made to survive the noise around it
such recordings in their turn deepen the listener's inattention
the writer describes a circle that feeds itself
bringing back the absence of noise is not a longing for the past
text: Quiet has turned into something we buy, and the change is worth pausing over. Machines hum on every side, so the ear learns early to sift, to push the murmur into the background and to expect nothing at all from what it takes in. That defence carries a price. Guarding itself season after season, our listening coarsens: it tells shades apart less well and settles for broad blocks of sound. What follows is music built to survive noise, squeezed and levelled, cut for the half attention of someone walking down a corridor. And since that music then fills the air everywhere, it trains the ear to attend less still, so the loop closes on itself. Giving quiet its place back has nothing to do with longing for what is gone; it is what lets sound become an event again, rather than a backdrop nobody notices.

units: the specialist opens the instrument before doing anything else
