the middle register gives out a sound that is too harsh
she checks the tuning by working on the fittings of the strings
the trouble is still there after that check
the padding of the striking parts has packed down with use
grooves have been worn into it by the contact of the strings
she refuses to change the parts and would rather restore them
she pricks the padding with points to give it back its give
she then sets the control worked by the left foot
text: Before she lays a finger on the keys, the tuner lifts off the front panel and studies the works in silence. The instrument handed to her rings hard through the middle, as though every note there were being struck too bluntly. She goes over the tuning first, string by string, with a key that turns each pin an eighth of a turn. The fault stays where it is. So she looks at the hammers and finds her answer: the felt has packed down with use, gone hard, and carries grooves worn into it by the strings. Her remedy is not to swap the parts out but to nurse them. She pricks the felt of every hammer with fine needles to give it back its spring, then smooths the surface down. Last of all she sets the left pedal, which brings the hammers nearer the strings, and plays the middle again: the roundness is back.

units: two recordings of the same work for strings are set against each other
the older recording was made in a space of great size
the resonances pile up there and soften the starts of the notes
the listener has the feeling of sitting far away
the other recording was made with the pickups very close in
every group of instruments can be told apart in it
that precision costs the sense of space
neither of the two versions is called the better one
the distant recording suits the calm passages
the close recording suits the swift passages
text: Set two recordings of one and the same score for strings against each other, and you learn more than any quarrel about taste would ever teach you. The first, taken in a wide hall, lets the resonances run into one another; the attacks come out rounded, the edges a little blurred, and you seem to be hearing the players from the far end of the building. The second, made with the microphones brought up close, lays every desk bare: you catch the scrape of the bows, the breathing, the grain of the low strings. Such sharpness costs something, for the whole loses the depth that gave the other version its breadth. Neither of them carries the day outright. The distant balance convinces in the slow movements, while the close one takes over in quick passages, where clear drawing settles everything.

units: the writer answers a request for news about his learning
the first sessions went on holding the instrument without making a sound
that early constraint spared his shoulders
the teacher asks for a breath that comes from the belly
an uneven breath makes the note waver
the fingers grow nimble on their own once the groundwork holds
hearing is the faculty that takes longest to form
the writer now catches his own faults of tuning before they are pointed out
he asks the person he writes to come and listen the following week
text: You asked me how the lessons were going, so here is what a whole season of them has left me with. Posture came first: for weeks on end I held the instrument without sounding a single note, which struck me as daft at the time and which has saved my shoulders ever since. Then the breath. My teacher insists that the air must set off from the belly and reach the mouthpiece even, or else the note wobbles and dies on you. The fingers come third, and they look after themselves well enough as soon as the other two hold up. The ear is the slowest of the lot to ripen: I am beginning to hear that I am out of tune before anyone tells me so, and that heartens me rather more than it may sound. Come round next week, bring your own instrument if you like, and judge the results for yourself.

units: she began with cleaning and tidying jobs
she was not allowed near the mixing gear during her first year
she was then given the placing of the pickups on the percussion
an accessory badly fitted on a brass instrument can spoil a take
the hardest part was keeping her remarks to herself
she ran a session on her own to cover for an absent colleague
that successful session put an end to the lowly jobs
she now teaches the trade to newcomers
her chief instruction is to trust the ear and not the eye
text: First they ask her where it all began for her. She says she swept the studio floor and coiled the cables, carried the cases of gear about, and went a whole year without once laying a hand on the desk. And after that? After that they let her place the microphones on the drums, then on the brass, where a mute sitting wrong can ruin an entire take. The hardest part of those early days? Holding her tongue when she heard a fault that everybody else was letting through. In the end she ran the desk on her own one night, standing in for a colleague who had fallen ill; the session went off well, and nobody ever handed her a broom again after that. And now? Now she trains beginners, and drills into them the one rule she trusts: you place a microphone with your ears, never with your eyes.

units: the takes recorded in the room come out muddy
the technician blames the hard surfaces of the walls
a note played takes too long to die away in the room
the player reports a hum tied to the ventilation system
the first fix is to hang absorbent material near the microphones
the second fix is to set the air duct on flexible mounts
the player fears the tone colour of her instrument will suffer
the technician promises the opposite, a gain in the high frequencies
text: The studio technician kept saying that the takes made in that room came back muddy, and he laid the blame squarely on the bare walls. A note, once played, hung on far too long; by the time it had faded, the next attack was already smeared into it. The cellist added that she could hear a low hum whenever the ventilation started up. Two fixes were put forward. The first was to hang absorbent panels close to the microphones, so that the hard surfaces stopped throwing sound back into the takes. The second was to set the air duct on flexible mounts, which would keep its shudder out of the floor. She worried about what all that might do to the colour of her instrument. The technician promised the opposite: strip out the stray echo, he said, and the top of the sound comes back, the very frequencies the room had been swallowing.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: two ways of handing music on have lived side by side over long stretches of time
the first rests on a pupil copying a master by ear
in that way nothing is set down on any material support
every performer freely alters the piece he has learnt
the second uses written signs giving the pitch and the length
writing pins the work down and lets it travel far from its maker
handing music on by ear breeds many versions
specialists find that the two routes have combined
copyists set down only an outline that performers filled out
text: Two ways of handing music on have lived side by side over long stretches of time, and the contrast between them still shapes how players work. The older one rests on the ear alone: a master plays, a pupil copies, and the piece travels through patient repetition. Nothing is set down on any material support, so every performer bends the tune a little, adds an ornament here, shortens a repeat there. The other relies on written signs that state the pitch and the length of each note. Writing pins the work down and lets it travel far from the person who made it, whereas the route through the ear breeds version upon version. Scholars are clear that the two paths never shut each other out: copyists set down no more than an outline, and it fell to the performers to fill in what the page left silent.

units: every sound comes from a quick movement that stirs the surrounding air
the first family gathers strings stretched between two fixed points
such strings are set going by plucking, bowing or striking them
a hollow box swells the movement passed on by the string
the second family gathers hollow tubes driven by the breath of the player
the pitch got from a tube depends on how much air is left free
the third family covers skins pulled tight over a frame
the fourth family covers metal bars and plates that are struck
each family is known by its colour of sound, tied to the material used
text: Every sound begins with a quick movement that stirs the air around it, and the objects able to make such a movement fall into families. The first gathers strings stretched between two fixed points: pluck them, bow them or strike them, and the shudder they give off passes into a hollow box that swells it. The second brings together hollow tubes, where the breath of the player sets a column of air going, and the pitch depends on how much of that air is left free. The third covers skins pulled tight over a frame, which answer a blow with a short, dark ring. The fourth takes in metal bars and plates that sound of their own accord once they are knocked. Each family carries a colour of its own, because the material set moving filters the overtones of the sound in its own way.

units: a neighbour takes the narrator down to the basement of their building one evening
the neighbour claims the pipes down there give out a kind of singing
the two women go down with a torch and a recorder
at first they hear only the boiler and the metal door
when the pump stops a held low note comes out
a faint high sound goes with that low note
the neighbour admits she has been hearing it for several weeks
playing the take back reveals a steady throb
a tradesman later puts it down to a valve left half shut
text: My neighbour from the flat below dragged me down to the basement one evening, swearing that the pipes down there could sing. We went with a torch and a borrowed recorder. At first, nothing: the boiler grumbling away, the metal door creaking shut behind us. Then the pump stopped, and the whole place began to ring. A low note came up out of the pipework, steady and held, with a thin whistle sitting above it. She was laughing; she said she had been hearing it for weeks and had never dared mention it to anyone. We left the machine running for half an hour. Back upstairs we played the take through, and there it was, clear, with a steady throb running under it. The plumber who came the week after sorted it out in a sentence: a valve left half shut, and a pipe whistling away like a flute.

units: capturing the sounds of a street calls for a strict method
a spot sheltered from moving air has to be chosen
air hitting the diaphragm of the microphone sets off a rumble that buries everything
the machine has to be clamped to a steady stand
a hand holding the microphone passes on audible rubbing
the phone should be switched off to keep out interference
a take should begin before the event aimed at and run on past it
the take should be listened to on headphones before leaving the place
text: Recording the sounds of a street takes far more care than people expect, and every slip shows up later at the editing stage. Pick a sheltered spot first, because moving air hits the diaphragm of the microphone and sets off a rumble that buries everything else. Clamp the machine to a stand next, since a hand holding a microphone passes on the least rub, and you end up with a rasp running the whole length of the take. Switch your phone off: held close, it can throw a short click into the recording that no amount of work will lift out afterwards. Start rolling before the event you are after and let it run on past, or the cut lands too early and the passage is no use to anyone. Listen back on headphones before you leave, because a fault caught late means going again, while one caught early takes a step sideways.

units: a railway line runs right along the playground of a school
passing trains swallow the voices of the children
teachers describe lessons broken off again and again
protective works were carried out over a season
a thick tilted wall throws the sound wave back towards the track
the windows of the building were fitted with heavier glazing
absorbent cladding was hung on the exposed frontage
the noise remains but seems clearly further off
the children can now hear the bell without straining
text: From the school playground, it is not the children you hear first but the railway running along the wall. At regular intervals a train goes by, and the squeal of wheels on the curved rail swallows the voices, the games, even the bell itself. Teachers describe lessons cut to ribbons, dictation started over and over, pupils raising their voices without noticing they are doing it. The building work lasted a season. A thick wall, tilted towards the track, now throws the wave back down onto the ballast instead of letting it clear the fence. The windows were fitted with heavier glazing, and absorbent cladding was hung across the exposed frontage. The rumble has not gone; it has moved off, as though pushed behind a curtain. Out in the yard the bell rises above the voices again, and nobody shouts to be answered.

units: two halls in the same music school sound different
the lower hall is lined with timber set on a hollow frame
its walls take the top off the sound and soften the attack
the upper hall is built of polished stone and has no hangings
its walls send the sound wave back almost untouched
quick notes there pile onto one another
a brass section gains weight in the upper hall
a string quartet loses its clarity there
teachers keep the lower hall for sessions where detail is worked out
text: The lower hall and the upper hall of the music school do not sound alike at all, and the ear picks the difference up within a bar or two. The lower one is lined with timber panels set on a hollow frame. Its walls give a little as the instrument sounds; they take the top off the note and hand back something warm and slightly veiled, in which the bite of the strings is rounded away. The upper hall is built of polished stone, with no hangings and no rugs of any kind. Its walls send the wave back almost untouched, so that quick notes pile onto one another before they have died. A brass section gains weight and body up there, while a string quartet loses its edge and its outline. Teachers therefore keep the lower hall for the sessions where detail has to be worked out, note by note and bar by bar.

units: the writer disputes the idea that music played without a break is harmless
he puts forward three objections in turn
the first objection bears on the draw made on the attention of the customer
that draw brings on a tiredness whose cause escapes the one who feels it
the second objection bears on staff exposed to the same loop of sound
those staff have no control at all over what they hear
the third objection bears on the loss of standing of music itself
the writer holds that silence is what makes a sound audible
text: It would be a mistake to treat the music that plays without a break in shops as a harmless courtesy. Three objections deserve to be set out. The first bears on attention: an unbroken stream of sound draws off part of the mental resources of whoever is buying, who listens without listening and tires without ever placing the cause of that tiredness. The second concerns the staff on the floor, for the person selling, serving or taking payment sits through the same loop from the start of a shift to the end of it, with no control whatever over what reaches their ears. The third bears on music itself, which loses its standing as an event once it becomes a hanging draped behind every activity. Silence is not a gap waiting to be filled; it is the condition that makes a sound audible at all.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the tuner of the theatre began his training very young
he sorted felts in the workshop of an instrument maker
he was first taught to hear the beats between neighbouring strings
he then spent a year replacing hammers
he also adjusted the travel of every key on the keyboard
once a tuner, he went from one concert hall to another
the heat of the lamps threatens the steadiness of the instrument
he says one false note is enough to shake the confidence of an orchestra
he now hands his trade on to two apprentices
text: The tuner at the theatre started learning the trade very young, in the workshop of an instrument maker who set him to sorting felts. He was taught to hear the beats between two neighbouring strings long before anyone put a key in his hand. A whole year then went on replacing hammers and adjusting the travel of every key across the keyboard, painstaking work that asks for a steady hand. Once he was tuning on his own, he went from one concert hall to the next, where the instrument had to hold despite the heat of the lamps and the air stirred up by a crowd. He says that one false note heard from the desk is enough to shake the confidence of a whole orchestra. He now hands the trade on to two apprentices, telling them that the ear is built by patience, and that the hand follows of itself.

units: the concert discussed took place in an old market hall
the metal roof and the concrete floor throw the sound back hard
that layout gives a metallic ring to the returning sound
the trio played more quietly to suit the place
the gaps left between the musical phrases became noticeable
the double bass suffered from too much low end in the space
the drums on the other hand gained from the acoustics
the reviewer advises standing near the stage
text: Honestly, that concert in the old market hall was worth the trip, and what struck me had as much to do with the building as with the players. The roof is sheet metal and the floor bare concrete, so the least note comes straight back at you with a metallic ring, and a loud band would turn to mush in there within a minute of starting. The trio had clearly worked that out: they played quietly, very quietly, and because of it the gaps between the phrases came to count for as much as the notes did. The double bass suffered, since low frequencies gather in a space like that one and end up as a thick paste. The drums, on the other hand, came off well, as every stroke went up into the roof beams and came back broader. One tip if you go: stand right down at the front, close to the stage.

units: the writer answers a question his correspondent had asked earlier
two stringed instruments stand in a place where such things are made
on the first, the sound starts when a finger pulls the string aside and lets it go
on the second, a bow drawn across the string brings the sound to life
the tone of the first begins fading the moment it appears
the tone of the second can be held for as long as the movement lasts
the first allows several strings to sound together
the second rarely manages more than two strings at once
the writer recommends the first for backing a singer
text: You asked me to explain how the two instruments standing in the workshop differ, so here is the answer at last. On the first, the sound comes from a finger: it pulls the string aside, then lets go, and the vibration starts with a dry snap. On the second, a bow is drawn across the string, so the tone builds gently and goes on lasting as long as the arm keeps moving. The real gap lies in the way a note begins. Pluck the first, and the note starts fading the very moment it appears. Bow the second, and you can hold the note, swell it, and cut it off exactly when you choose. There is another difference worth knowing about. The first takes several strings at once, so a whole chord sits under the hand, while the second rarely manages more than two. Backing a singer? Choose the first. Shaping one long line? Take the other.

units: the text sorts noise into three categories
the first category covers sounds that never break off
the ear stops noticing these continuous sounds
the second category gathers sounds that return at intervals
the third category concerns very short and violent impacts
an impact of that kind can damage hearing in a moment
how long the exposure lasts counts as much as how loud the sound is
three protections are named: moving away, putting up a barrier, cutting the exposure short
the hearing cells that are destroyed never grow back
text: What exactly counts as noise? The answer splits the field into three families. The first covers continuous sound, the hum of a machine among it, which the ear gradually stops registering. The second gathers intermittent sound, a chiming alarm and its like, forever announcing itself again. The third holds brief, violent impacts, able to wreck hearing in a moment. Is the racket of a building site more to be feared than the murmur of a busy road? Specialists reply that how long you are exposed weighs as much as how loud the source is. What protection is there? Three measures are advised: move away from the source, put an absorbing partition in between, cut the listening short. Can damaged hearing be repaired? The cells that die never grow back, so prevention remains the only route.

units: a learner recounts aloud a lesson he has been given
the specialist asks him to listen in silence to a key being struck
at first the learner hears only one sound
several strings in fact belong to a single key
the specialist deliberately slackens one of the strings
the learner then hears a steady pulsing
doing away with that pulsing is the aim of the operation
the specialist sounds a run of neighbouring notes
the learner tightens the moving part too far during his own attempt
by the end, two strings no longer produce any pulsing
text: The pupil talked his way through the lesson aloud, following the order in which it had happened. The tuner had begun by asking him to listen without speaking while she struck a single key. He answered that he could hear only one note. She pressed the point: three strings sit behind that key. Then she slackened one of them on purpose, and the pupil said a slow beating had come up, like a wave rising and falling back. Tuning, she explained, means getting rid of that beat. After that she played a whole run of neighbouring notes so he could hear them. At last she handed him the lever and let him turn the tuning pin. He tightened too hard, the beating quickened, and she told him to work with a lighter touch. By the end of the lesson, two strings had fallen silent for each other.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: older rooms were low and hung with cloth
sound died away quickly in them
that quick fading allowed fast successions of notes
taller stone halls were built afterwards
sound lingered there long after it had been made
fast passages turned muddy in such halls
those who wrote music then spaced their notes out and made them longer
adding padded seats and audiences cut the lingering down
musical writing grew quicker again after that
the text concludes that materials shaped music as much as taste did
text: Look at what happens to a piece of music when the room around it changes size. Rooms used to be low and hung about with cloth, and the sound in them died away almost at once. Since nothing lingered in the air, players could run through quick notes without everything turning to mush. Then taller halls went up, bare stone all round, and every sound dragged a long tail behind it. The upshot: those same quick notes came out as porridge, so the people writing music slowed down, stretched their chords, preferred held notes to ornament. Later, once such halls had been filled with padded seats and packed audiences, the ringing dropped away again. Writing picked up speed once more, and the pace tightened. Put simply, stone and cloth shaped what went on the page as much as what listeners happened to like.

units: pupils sitting at the back catch only part of the instructions
the cause lies in the surfaces of the room rather than in the speaker
bare walls throw sounds back and the returns run into one another
everybody speaks louder, which raises the noise further still
specialists call this mechanism a spiral
absorbing panels are fitted to the ceiling
pads under the chairs do away with the scraping
the layout of the tables turns voices towards the listeners
teachers strain their voices less once these changes are made
the money spent stays modest
text: In plenty of classrooms, the pupils at the back catch only half of what they are told. The fault seldom lies with the teacher's voice. It lies with the walls. A bare room throws sound back, the returns pile up, and syllables blur into one another. Everybody then speaks a good deal louder, and the level climbs further still. Acousticians call this a spiral of noise. Getting out of it takes very little indeed. Porous panels are fixed to the ceiling to soak up part of what comes back. Felt pads go under the chairs so that they no longer scrape across the floor. Tables are turned about so that every mouth faces a set of ears. Where this has been done, teachers push their voices less and pupils hold on to instructions better. The outlay stays small, and the difference is audible from the first lesson.

units: a neighbour upstairs plays an instrument with plucked strings
a neighbour on the ground floor plays a worn guitar
the narrator likens the two musics to two kinds of rain
the music from above gives separate notes parted by silences
the music from below makes a continuous fabric that cannot be counted
the power fails during a storm
the two neighbours then play at the same time without having arranged it
the narrator listens from the stairwell of the building
the mixture makes a music unlike either of the first two
the neighbours stop playing when the power returns
text: The woman who lives above me plays the harp, and the man on the ground floor scrapes away at a worn guitar. In the end I came to compare their music the way you might compare two kinds of rain. Hers falls in separate drops, each note clean, each parted from the next by a polite silence. His pours in a sheet: strings answer strings, fingers rasp, and nothing can be counted. One stormy evening the power failed across the building, and the two of them began playing at the same moment, without a word between them. From the stairwell I heard the drops land on the sheet. It was neither of the two musics: it was a third, one that neither of them could have written down. When the light came back they stopped, each door closed, and the building went back to being two flats stacked up.

units: the preparation follows three ordered stages
the room holding the most furniture is the one to choose
anything making a background noise has to be switched off
a thick cloth is hung behind whoever is speaking
the microphone goes at chin height and slightly to one side
the tilt keeps the expelled air from striking the diaphragm
the stand belongs on the floor rather than on a piece of furniture
a short stretch of silence is recorded to gauge the background noise
listening is done on headphones and not through a loudspeaker
one complete take is kept before any editing
text: Before you record a voice at home, get the room, the microphone and the session ready, in that order. The room: pick whichever one holds the most furniture, shut the windows, switch off anything that blows or hums, and hang a thick blanket behind you. The microphone: set it at chin height, a hand's width away from the mouth, tilted a little to one side so that the breath of your consonants misses the diaphragm. Stand it on a weighted floor stand, never on the table, since wood carries every knock straight up. The session: record a short stretch of silence first, which gives you a measure of the background. Then speak at a steady level, without drifting nearer or further away. Listen on headphones, never through a loudspeaker. And keep one full spare take before you cut anything at all.

units: work on a concert venue has just come to an end
complaints had been piling up over a whole season
the lower sounds became inaudible from the far rows back
an acoustic survey was commissioned and then passed to those in charge
the decision was taken to clear the vaulted ceiling
the panels that threw the sound back were removed
the armchairs were swapped for seats whose absorption never varies
the stage floor was given a rake
a musical ensemble played without an audience to test the place
those in charge will wait a full season before drawing conclusions
text: Work on the concert hall came to an end last week, closing a project the musicians had followed closely. It had been launched after a full season of complaints: once the ceiling was redone, the lower instruments vanished for anyone sitting in the back rows. An acoustic survey was commissioned and then passed to the management, which decided to open the vaulted ceiling up again. The workers went on to take down the reflecting panels, swap the armchairs for seats whose absorption never varies, and put a rake into the stage floor. A trial orchestra played behind closed doors to measure how the room answered. The readings confirmed a gain in clarity in the lower register. Performances will resume, the management announced, warning that the real verdict cannot come in before a full season of use.

units: the workshop is heard before it is seen
the craftsman strikes a heated piece of metal
each blow makes a short sound that the metal walls throw back
the pitch of the sound shifts because the metal is cooling
the sound grows higher as the material hardens
the sandy floor takes in part of what comes back
a blower keeps the fire going and makes a continuous noise
the ear grows used to that continuous noise and keeps only the blows
the quiet after the stop seems sharper than it really is
text: A forge makes itself heard well before anyone catches sight of it. The smith hammers away at a heated bar, and every blow tears out a short, almost shrill sound that bounces straight back off the metal walls. Because the bar cools as it is struck, the note keeps shifting: it climbs as the metal hardens, and it drops again once the flame has softened the bar. The sandy floor swallows part of what comes back, so the din stays bearable for anyone working in there all day. At the far end, a blower breathes over the embers, and its steady drone sits underneath everything else. Since the ear grows used to that drone, it ends up hearing nothing but the blows. When the hammer stops, the quiet seems far deeper than it truly is, for hearing keeps the trace of the sound just gone a moment longer.

units: the listener does not decide what music is played in public places
the point of playing it is to slow the customers down
the writer locates the problem in the absence of any prior agreement
no way of stopping the playback is offered
those who hear poorly are put out more than the rest
background music covers voices and makes conversation tiring
a first measure is to bring in stretches with nothing playing
these stretches would be announced at the door and would cost nothing
a second measure lowers the volume until talking becomes possible
a third measure hands the setting over to the staff of the place
text: You hardly ever choose the music you hear any more. Step into a shop, a lift, a waiting room, and a tune meets you, pitched to slow your walk along the shelves. The trouble is not taste, it is consent. Nobody ever asked whether you wanted to listen, and nobody offers you any way of stopping it. For those who hear poorly the thing is worse still: the wash of sound covers voices and makes talking exhausting. So what can be done about it? First, make silence available: a stretch with nothing playing at all, announced at the door, costs nothing and would relieve the whole trade. Second, drop the level to the point where two customers can speak without raising their voices. Third, let the staff work the controls, since they are the ones who take the loop from start to finish. None of this needs a law.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the man described builds pipe instruments
he selects seasoned wood free of flaws
he melts a metal mixture into thin sheets
these sheets are rolled to form the pipes
the pressure of the bellows must be adjusted
excessive pressure gives a harsh sound
too little pressure weakens the sound
tuning slightly alters the length of the pipes
he stops labouring when his hearing tires
text: The organ builder works slowly, and every movement he makes is a measurement. Wood comes first. He picks out seasoned boards with no knots in them and planes each one until the thickness runs even. Metal comes second. He melts tin and lead together, pours the alloy out in thin sheets, then rolls every sheet into a pipe that trembles the moment air passes through. Air comes last. He sets the pressure of the bellows, for too strong a wind turns the note shrill, while too weak a wind smothers it. Then comes the tuning, the most delicate stage of the lot. The craftsman shortens or lengthens each pipe by a hair's breadth, until the high timbre stops beating against the low one. His ear, he admits, tires long before his hands do, and that is the point at which he lays the work aside.

units: the evening opened with a short piece for the low strings
the opening sound filled the space without excess
a solo singer then performed a work with restraint
the writer stresses how young this performer is
the second half of the programme convinced less
the brass instruments covered the woodwind instruments
an untuned string instrument produced an unpleasant noise
the conductor flagged the mishap with a single glance
the closing chord hung under the ceiling of the hall
the writer judges this ensemble uneven against its ambitions
text: The evening opened with a short piece given to the low strings alone, and their thick sound filled the hall without ever swamping it. A work for solo voice came next, in which the singer shaped every phrase with a restraint one rarely meets in so young a performer. The second half disappointed. The brass, set too far forward, buried the woodwind, and the ear lost the middle line. One badly adjusted string instrument let out a brief grating noise, which the conductor put right with a glance. The closing bars drew every desk together at last, and the final chord hung under the vaulted roof for a stretch that seemed suspended. You came away with the impression of an uneven ensemble, at its finest the moment it gives up on effect, and brittle the moment it reaches for sheer force.

units: the writer is writing from a rehearsal room
the room is unheated and the air inside is damp
the damp warps the wood and slackens the strings
the instrument loses its tuning after half an hour
the retuning eats up half of the session
the person in charge found the same trouble on his bow
his request for a heater was turned down
the group falls back on a narrower room next door
the bare walls of that room amplify the low sounds
the writer asks her correspondent to bring a tuning fork
text: I am writing from the room where we rehearse, having turned up well ahead of anyone else. There is no heating in here, and the damp works straight into my instrument: the wood tightens, the strings go slack, and half an hour later the tuning has gone. Since I have to keep putting it right, I lose half the session, which wears the rest of the group down as well. The one in charge worked out the cause at last, his own bow having started to grate in just the same way. He asked for a heater and was turned down. So we fall back on the room next door, narrower than this one, where the bare walls throw the sound about and set the low notes booming. I would sooner have that fault than the cold. If you come by at the weekend, bring your tuning fork: mine has rung false since I dropped it.

units: a sound professional is asked about her hearing health
she blames the wear on quiet and lengthy mixing sessions
listening at low volume forces sustained attention
she gave up the ear protection she had bought
that protection distorted her sense of the high frequencies
she breaks off her listening at regular intervals
she holds herself to a volume ceiling she never crosses
she sometimes turns down a session when she feels worn out
the evening ringing in her ears has clearly eased
text: What wears out a sound engineer's hearing fastest? She answers without hesitating: not the concerts, but the long mixing sessions at low volume, where the ear strains after details barely there at all. And the remedy? She bought earplugs at first, she says, then let them go, since they muffle the top of the range and throw her judgement out. What works for her comes down to three settled habits. The first is to kill the sound at regular intervals and let the ear rest for a while. The second is a ceiling of loudness she never goes above, however hard the client happens to push. The third, and by far the hardest of them, is to turn a session down flat once she feels her hearing has gone. Since then, she tells us, the ringing that used to buzz around her head at night has all but stopped.

units: two professionals judge the same venue differently
the man finds the sound of the stage too dull
he blames the drapes for soaking up the high frequencies
the singer feels held up there by her voice coming back
the side walls send her own singing back to her
both note that the floor shakes with the low sounds
that shaking upsets the technician's readings
it gives the singer a rhythmic marker
she sings under her breath in the other venue to steady herself
the technician prefers a venue that adds no colour
text: The engineer and the singer do not describe the same hall. He finds the stage dull, blaming the heavy drapes, which soak up the top of the range and hand him back something soft and shapeless. She says the opposite, that the place holds her up, since her own voice comes back to her off the side walls. On one point they agree: the floor shakes as soon as the low notes rise. He treats that as a fault, the trembling muddling every reading he takes. She treats it as a prop, since she feels the beat coming up through her feet before it ever reaches her ear. Asked about the larger hall next door, she owns up to humming under her breath there to steady herself, so hollow does the silence seem. He much prefers it, saying that a space which adds nothing at last lets you hear what is played.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the writer traces early music to three movements of the hand
the first movement consists in striking
a skin stretched over a hollow shell gives a deep carrying sound
the second movement rests on breathing
a hollow pierced plant stem turns breath into a note
stopping or opening the holes varies the pitch
the third movement is that of plucking
a taut string let go gives a short-lived sound
a hollow chamber was added to lengthen the shaking
these three origins can still be read in the shape of the instruments
text: All early music comes down to three movements that the hands learned apart from one another. The first is the blow. A skin stretched over a hollow shell answers the shock and sets the air shivering around it; from there come the drums, whose rumble carries further than any voice. The second rests on breathing. A hollow stem, pierced with holes of unequal size, turns the outgoing breath into a note, and the hand that stops or frees those openings drives the pitch up or down. The third is the pluck. A string held taut between two fixed points gives a short sound when it is drawn back and released; beneath it a hollow chamber was soon added, so that the shaking might last longer and swell. The three families mingled afterwards, yet their origin is still legible in the shape of the instruments.

units: a string that is pulled swings about its resting position
that swinging squeezes then loosens the neighbouring air
the disturbance travels on from one part to the next
the air particles themselves barely move
the outer ear guides the wave towards a passage
a thin membrane begins to swing at the end of that passage
three small bones strengthen that movement
a coiled organ filled with fluid then takes in the shaking
cells fringed with hairs turn the movement into nerve signals
the rate of the swings settles the pitch that is heard
text: A plucked string swings away from where it rested, comes back, then overshoots again, and that coming and going is what we call vibration. It squeezes the air molecules alongside it, which crowd together, loosen, and pass the shove on to the next ones. The disturbance travels outwards from one part to the next, while the air itself covers almost no ground at all. Reaching the outer ear, it is funnelled into a narrow passage, at the far end of which a soft membrane begins to swing at the very same rate. Three minute bones gather that movement, strengthen it, and hand it on to a coiled organ filled with fluid. Inside, cells fringed with hairs bend over and give off an electrical signal. The nerve carries it to the brain, which reads the note as high or low from the rate of the swings.

units: a flaw in the casting had cracked a bell
the crack could not be seen without examination
it split the shaking into two parts out of tune with each other
the ringing gave a beating instead of a clean sound
those living nearby complained without grasping where the noise came from
the local assembly had the bell taken down
a specialist declared the repair impossible
she explained that welding alters the density of the metal
the bell was cast afresh from its own alloy
putting it back in service stopped passers-by where they stood
text: A flaw in the casting, which no eye could catch, had cracked the tower bell. The split ran under the lip of the bronze, and it broke the shaking into two parts that no longer agreed. Every peal therefore gave a dull beating in place of the full sound people expected, and those living nearby, with no notion of the cause, complained of a ringing that seemed to grate. The council had the thing brought down, a slow and costly job. A founder was called in. A crack, she explained, cannot be mended, for welded metal no longer holds the same density, and the timbre suffers by it. She offered instead to melt the whole down and cast it afresh from its own bronze. The recast bell went up as the cold season ended, and its first peal rang so cleanly that passers-by halted in the middle of the square.

units: the text speaks to whoever plays in an overly reverberant room
the notes pile up and blur the fast passages
the rigid walls send the sound back without soaking it up
a clap of the hands serves to gauge how long the tail runs
a rug on the floor treats the bounce between floor and ceiling
a thick fabric is hung on one wall only
covering every wall would leave the room lifeless
moving the stand round to an angle avoids building up the low sounds
a second clap allows the result to be checked
text: You rehearse in a room where every note drags on behind the next, and the quick passages turn to mush. Hard surfaces are the trouble: they send the sound back instead of soaking it up. Work through it by stages. Clap your hands once in the middle of the floor and listen to the tail; the longer it runs, the heavier the treatment will have to be. Lay a thick rug down on the floor next, since the bounce between floor and ceiling is by far the most stubborn of the lot. Hang a heavy blanket on the wall facing your instrument, never on all four, or the room goes lifeless and the top of the range is smothered. Swing the stand round to an angle last of all, because a symmetrical placing builds the low notes up and sets them droning. Clap again: if the tail has halved, leave it there.

units: a student survey compares two neighbouring urban areas
the workshop area suffers a steady mechanical noise
that constant noise ends up slipping past the attention of the neighbours
the area of the main roads shows a lower average level
sudden traffic sounds arise there without warning
it is those sudden peaks that break into rest
one resident sets the steady drone against the harsh sound
the survey also covered the night hours
night deliveries bring on ringing in the ears and tiredness
the authors conclude that the unexpected tires more than the loudness
text: Two neighbouring districts live with noise in opposite ways, and a survey run by students has just borne it out. Over on the workshop side the machines never stop, yet their drone holds steady, and the people living there say they grow so used to it that they stop hearing it. Along the main roads the average level is lower; the trouble is the horns and the squealing brakes, which come out of nowhere, and it is these brief peaks that wake you. One resident puts it plainly: a steady drone you end up forgetting, a sound that stings you never do. The students looked at the nights as well. Where the activity stops, sleep repairs itself; where the deliveries carry on, people complain of ringing in the ears and of tiredness. Their conclusion fits in a line: loudness is not what drains you, surprise is.

units: a mould is shaped in clay before the pouring
the molten metal is poured without a break
the piece cools for a whole night without being moved
the mould is broken once the metal has cooled
the surface looks reddish and unpolished when the shell comes off
a tuning specialist adjusts the pitch at the end of the process
material is taken away from the inside to change the note
the craftsman leaves a mark of his own when the result satisfies him
text: Long before any metal moves, the workshop grows hot. The founder builds up a clay mould by hand, layer on layer and without haste, then leaves it to dry beside the furnace. Once the alloy runs, he tips it in one unbroken stream and watches the bubbles rise across the surface. Cooling takes a whole night through; nobody lifts the piece or shifts it until it has gone lukewarm. Breaking out comes next. The shell splits under a mallet and uncovers a reddish flank, unpolished and still rough to the touch. The tuner has the last word. He strikes the rim, listens hard, scrapes fine shavings from the inside, then strikes again. Every pass lifts the note a shade higher. When the tone rings clean and the ringing dies away without a beat, he sets down his tool and cuts a small mark of his own into the metal.

units: shared places have grown too noisy
shops play music to hold on to their customers
machines about the house give out unpleasant beeps
each emission taken on its own seems harmless
it is the adding up of the sources that makes the din
attention comes apart and talking together costs more effort
vulnerable people now keep away from public spaces
doctors report a lasting exhaustion in those exposed to it
the writer holds that an individual answer would be useless
the writer asks those who build and those who manufacture to protect quiet
text: A quiet change deserves a moment of attention: the places we share have grown far too loud, and the fault belongs to no one in particular. Shops pipe out music chosen to hold customers on the floor a little longer. Machines about the house mark every task they finish with a shrill beep. Taken one at a time, each of these seems harmless enough; laid over one another, they build a din that nobody ever chose. Attention comes apart, talking together costs more effort, and the frailest users withdraw from public spaces. Clinicians report a lasting exhaustion among those who cannot step away from the noise. Since the cause is collective, no private remedy will serve: blocking one's ears merely shifts the burden along. It falls to those who design our buildings and those who make our machines to treat quiet as a resource.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: she began her trade in a country workshop
her first speciality was mending cracked soundboards
the mended bodies gave out a muffled sound
neither the wood nor the varnish nor the strings explained the fault
she put the blame on a layer of glue laid on too thickly
she tested hanging samples that she tapped
the least glued samples sounded better
she changed her preparation and put right the instruments already delivered
she passes the method on to pupils who come from far away
text: The woman who restores old instruments learned her trade in a country workshop, where cracked soundboards made up most of the work. One puzzle held her for whole seasons: every body she glued back together came out muffled, as though a blanket lay over it. The wood was sound, the varnish untouched, the strings at their proper tension. In the end she turned on the glue itself, laid on too thickly, holding back the movement of the board. To test the idea she made up samples, hung each one from a thread and tapped it gently. The heavily coated pieces answered with a dull thud; the lighter ones rang out. So she thinned her layer, warmed the mixture with care and went back over every instrument she had already handed on. Her customers heard the change at the first playing. She now teaches the method to apprentices who travel a long way for it.

units: the narrator compared two recorded versions of the same set of pieces
the two hearings were a week apart
the first group takes a fast and very confident pace
this first version ends up wearing the listener out
the second group slows down and blends the colours more
a passage of the fast version is out of tune between two instruments
a piece of the slow version loses its coherence
the narrator picks the second version
his reason is that it stands up to repeated hearings
text: I sat down with two recordings of the same set of string pieces, a week between them, and the gap between the two took me aback. The first group plays fast, with a dazzling confidence: the attacks snap, and you can hear the players breathe. Brilliant, yes, though wearing after a while, a brightness nobody could keep up with. The second group takes its time. Tempos stretch, colours melt together, and what sounded angular turns round and soft. The first record grabbed me; this one kept me. Neither is faultless. Among the quick players a middle passage tips into sourness, the viola and the cello never quite agreeing. Among the slow ones, a single piece sags and loses the thread. Asked which one I would keep, I do not hesitate: the second, because it survives another hearing, and another, without going stale before the end.

units: the writer is staying in a rented house beside an estuary
he chooses to relate the sounds rather than the scenery
the water strikes the supports of the building at regular intervals
the boats scrape when the level rises
a bird lets out an evening cry that he takes for a creaking door
human noises come from the quay and from a radio set
the wooden frame creaks during the night
those creaks make up a kind of tune
the writer notes down what he observes with the hour and the wind
he means to let his recordings be heard when he returns
text: I am writing from the low house we have taken by the estuary, and rather than the view I want to give you the sounds. Water comes first: a steady slap against the piles, then the scrape of hulls as the tide lifts them and sets them nudging. Birds are second. One of them lets out a thin cry at dusk that I still mistake for a door in need of oil. Third comes everything human, voices carrying up from the quay, a radio playing somewhere out of sight, a trolley rumbling over planks. The fourth caught me unawares. The timber frame itself creaks after dark, and those creaks fall into something close to a tune. All of it goes into a notebook, with the hour and the quarter the wind blows from. When I am home again I shall play you the recordings that came out well; most beat any postcard.

units: the origin of the phenomenon is older than the keeper's memory
her grandmother already knew this echo
the first returning sound she caught seemed weakened to her
she put the cause down to the wind at first
she then suspected the work of water on the rock
a rock specialist explained to her the part played by the shape of the land
she accepts that explanation without giving up her listening
the curious go away pleased once they have shouted
she waits until she is alone to say one short sentence
the voice that comes back to her sounds lower and altered
text: When did the cliff begin to answer? The keeper of the path waves the question away: it was answering long before she was born, and before her grandmother, who knew it as a girl. What did she hear on her first night up there? A call that came back to her weakened, as though the stone were reluctant to give it up. Did she look for a reason? She blamed the wind at first, then the water that eats into the face, until a passing rock specialist spoke to her of the curve of the hollow. What does she make of that answer? She keeps it, and climbs up alone at dusk all the same to hear her own voice returned to her. And the curious? They shout, they laugh, they go away pleased. She waits for them to drift off, then says one short sentence, and the wall hands it back a little lower, a little changed, and she goes down telling nobody.

units: the technical manager explained to the performer where the shrill noise came from
the microphone was picking up the sound leaving the speakers
that sound fed back into the circuit and built up on its own
the performer believed the sound level alone was to blame
the technician answered that the aim of the microphone weighed more
he advised moving the speakers behind the performer
he suggested cutting the top frequencies and the input level
he recommended never aiming the microphone at a speaker
the trial worked apart from a brief moment during a lean towards the audience
text: The stage manager took the singer aside to tell her where the whistle was coming from. Her microphone, he said, was hearing the speakers set out in front of her; that sound went back down the line into the amplifier and built on itself until it howled. She supposed the volume was to blame. Not chiefly, he told her: which way the capsule faces weighs more, since a microphone aimed at a loudspeaker listens to its own echo. She asked what could be done. Put the speakers behind you, he suggested, pull down the top frequencies, which run away first, and take a little off the input. He added a rule for the stage: never swing the microphone round towards a source, not even while taking a bow. She tried it through the sound check. The whistle stayed away, apart from one second, when she leaned out over the hall.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: spoken transmission of melodies wore down from one singer to the next
learning was done by copying a sung model
after three handings on two neighbouring groups sang differently
the first copyists set signs above the sung words
those signs showed the direction of the voice but not the gap between the notes
it was still necessary to know the tune in order to read those signs
the solution was to rule guide lines
the height of the sign on the page then showed the pitch of the note
a performer could from then on sing a piece he had never heard
that invention opened the way to writing for several voices
text: Handing a melody from one generation to the next raised a difficulty that memory alone could not settle. Singers learned by copying what they heard, and every copy drifted a little from its model; three relays on, two neighbouring communities no longer sang the same tune. Early copyists tried marks placed above the words, recalling where the voice rose and where it fell, though never how far. The help was real but partial: you had to know the melody already before the marks meant anything. What broke the deadlock was a plain graphic idea. Rule one line across the page, then a second, and set each mark at a measurable height. From that moment the page itself stood for pitch. A singer could work out a tune he had never heard, and music written for several voices at once became possible.

units: in air the widely spaced particles pass the vibration on badly
sound weakens quickly as it travels through air
in water the closely packed particles pass the vibration on without delay
the vibration travels markedly faster in water than in air
a swimmer under the surface cannot place where an engine noise comes from
that confusion comes from the signal reaching both ears too close together
metal carries the vibration better still than water
a wall of wool damps the vibration almost entirely
the same blow gives a different sound according to the material
text: Take two ways of carrying a sound over a distance. In air the wave spreads and fades: the molecules sit well apart, they hand the shake on lazily, and the message has worn thin after a short stretch. In water those same molecules all but touch. The shake passes straight from one to the next with nothing lost between, and it travels far quicker there than it ever does in air. That is why a swimmer below the surface hears a distant engine yet cannot tell where it lies: the signal reaches both ears too nearly at once for him to compare them. Solids belong in the comparison as well. A steel bar carries the tremor better still than water, while a partition of wool soaks up almost all of it. One blow, three materials, three answers: a bright clatter from the metal, a dull ring under water, a short flat thud in the wool.

units: the narrator expected a long session but not a failed one
the injured pianist had to play with one hand only
the borrowed room belonged to a dance school
its floor threw the sounds back strongly
the singer had a cold and a ragged voice
she refused to lighten her part in spite of her state
noisy building work disturbed a quiet passage
the group carried on regardless out of stubbornness
the final result turned out to be satisfying
the musicians kept those choices for the performance
text: They warned me the rehearsal would run long. Nobody warned me it would turn into a run of disasters. First blow: the pianist turns up with a bandaged finger and announces he will manage with the left hand. Second blow: the room, lent to us by a dance school, has a floor that throws everything back, so the smallest note cracks and returns doubled. Third blow: the singer has caught a cold, her voice comes out ragged, and she will not lighten her part by a single line. Fourth and finest: someone starts drilling through the party wall during the quietest passage. We kept going out of sheer stubbornness. And the thing stood up: the left hand laid down a rocking bass none of us had imagined, the ragged voice suited the words, and the ringing floor made us play softer than we ever had. On the night we asked for rugs and kept every one of those choices.

units: the clogging of the access roads comes from motorists setting off at the same moment
each driver believes that pressing on alone is in his own interest
traffic specialists see sensible choices whose sum produces the opposite effect
a first solution is to spread the start of work across the morning
staggering departures thins out the crowding at the busiest moment
a second measure gives one lane over to cars carrying several occupants
that reserved lane rewards the sharing of a vehicle
applying both measures together improves the speed and the punctuality of public transport
the main obstacle is the lack of coordination between separate decision makers
text: Why do the roads into a town centre seize up morning after morning? The cause is a dull one: nearly every driver sets off at the same moment. Each of them reckons that pressing ahead alone will save time, and the queue lengthens for everybody. Traffic engineers describe a heap of reasonable decisions adding up to an absurd result. Two remedies come round again and again. The first is to spread the leaving hour: employers stagger the start of shifts, and the busiest moment thins out across a wider stretch of the morning. The second hands one lane over to vehicles carrying more than a single occupant, which rewards those who share a journey. Where both have been tried at once, average speeds climb again and the buses keep to their timetable. So the obstacle is not a technical one. It lies in getting bodies that decide separately to decide together.

units: a delivery cyclist had ridden the same machine for seven years
his old bicycle was heavy and rattled over uneven ground
the bicycle lent by the workshop was slimmer and quicker on the flat
he expected to be won over but felt uneasy at first
the old machine forgave clumsy riding
the borrowed one reacted harshly under braking
after a week he decided that each machine had an advantage of its own
he gave the trial model back
he simply replaced his braking parts
text: Seven years on one bicycle had made the courier stubborn, and it took some persuading before he agreed to try another. His old frame was a weight, the wide bars pushed his shoulders open, and the rear mudguard rattled over every rut. The machine lent by the workshop was its opposite: slender tubing, more spokes, deep rims that carried him along the flat with no effort at all. He had expected delight. What he felt, for the first hour, was unease. The old bike forgave a clumsy line; the borrowed one punished the smallest wobble. The pads bit so hard that he nearly went over the bars. By the end of the week he had his verdict, and it was even: the light machine won on speed, the old one on trust. He gave the trial bike back and changed nothing but his brakes, which struck him as the better bargain.

units: an hour set aside for checks is advised before a long journey
the front screen has to be cleaned inside as well as outside
the mirrors are set once you are sitting where you drive
the pressure in the tyres is taken while they are not hot
the state of the brakes is seen through the opening in the wheel
the fluid levels under the bonnet have to be topped up
a level that drops quickly points to a loss from the circuit
the heaviest luggage goes at the bottom of the load space
writing the checks down makes later departures easier
text: Before a long drive, give yourself an hour and work through it in blocks. You will save yourself a sulk at the roadside. Seeing out comes first: clean the windscreen on both faces, check the wipers leave no smear, then sit where you actually drive and set each mirror from there. Wheels next: take the tyre pressures while they are cold, look along the tread for uneven wear, and peer through the spokes at the pads. Fluids after that: lift the bonnet and top up the washer bottle, the coolant and the oil, and if a level drops quickly, that is a leak and not thirst. Loading last: heavy things at the bottom of the boot, nothing loose on the back shelf, and strap down whatever sticks out. Write what you checked in a small notebook. Next time you set off you will start calm instead of guessing.

units: the first train came out of the depot before sunrise
people living nearby watched the departure from behind barriers
the freshly laid rail link serves the warehouse area and the station
the works had begun four years earlier
shifting the underground pipes was the costliest stage
laying the power cables was held up by a shortage of parts
the runs without passengers brought a track connection fault to light
the opening to the public was put off twice
traders in the area grew angry at those delays
text: The first tram rolled out of the depot before the sun was up, watched by people from the surrounding streets pressed against the barriers. The freshly laid line joins the warehouse district to the station, closing a scheme begun four years ago. The opening months went on shifting pipes and ducts beneath the ground, work nobody would ever see and by far the dearest part of the whole undertaking. Rails followed, then the overhead power cables, held up by a shortage of parts. Empty running brought to light a fault in the points at the depot mouth, put right within three weeks. The start of services to the public slipped twice, which wore down the patience of shopkeepers cut off from their custom. The engineer in charge now insists that the promised frequency will be met within weeks.

units: a narrow strip of grass runs along the roadway
the manoeuvres of passing vehicles have damaged the edge of the road
two parallel grooves have worn into that border
rain sits in those hollows instead of reaching the ditch
the trapped water softens the ground and breaks up the edge of the surface
vehicles squeezing over to the side deepen the wear
stakes driven in by those living along it are flattened by wide trailers
the low light of evening makes those deformations easier to see
this old road carries a far heavier traffic than the one first intended
text: A band of cropped grass runs beside the narrow road, and it is the grass that gives the story away. Years of awkward passing have let wheels bite into the verge, whose surface has dropped away into two long parallel grooves. Rain gathers in them instead of running off to the ditch; it soaks downwards, softens what lies beneath, and the edge of the surfacing splits away in flakes. Every vehicle that squeezes over widens the trough a little further. Those who live along the road drove in stakes to mark the limit, but the stakes lean now, torn loose by trailers built too wide. When evening comes, the low light picks out each hollow and the lane looks stitched with dark scars. From that ruined margin alone you can read the load carried by a track laid out for carts and handed over to lorries.

units: the wearing out of a road depends above all on the weight borne by each axle
the damage rises far more steeply than the mass, following a power law
one laden lorry harms the upper layer as much as a very great number of cars
engineers know this mechanism
the rules on financial contribution take no account of this mechanism
the sum asked of hauliers depends mainly on the dimensions declared
a first correction would be to charge for the load measured under each axle
sensors set into the road surface would make that measurement possible
a second correction would be to spread the goods over more axles
text: Nothing wrecks a road surface like the weight riding on a single axle. The damage does not rise in step with the load; it climbs as a steep power of it, so that one laden lorry chews through the upper layer as thoroughly as many thousands of cars. Engineers in the highways offices have known this for a long while. The rules that decide who pays take no notice of it: what a haulier is charged turns mostly on the size declared for the vehicle. Two corrections follow. Charge for the load actually pressing on each axle, read off sensors buried in the surfacing, and not for a tonnage written on a form. Then reward operators who spread the same freight across extra axles, something trailer builders have long known how to do. A network priced by the damage it takes would cost less to keep up than one priced by guesswork.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the manager of the depot first worked as a driver
she drove on services that ran at night
she holds that the two roles differ in almost everything
at the wheel the attention goes to things happening at once
in management the effects of a decision show up long afterwards
as a driver she judged her success by arriving on time
as a manager she judges it by the steadiness of every route together
she has kept the habit of listening to the sounds a vehicle makes
she values what a driver reports more than readings from instruments
text: The woman who runs the bus depot began her working life at the wheel, on the services that ran through the night. Two jobs that look neighbouring, she says, turn out to share almost nothing. Driving, your world ends at the windscreen: a signal, someone stepping off the kerb, a door that will not shut. From behind a desk the view stretches across seasons, and an order given one week shows its effect months afterwards. As a driver she measured herself by reaching the terminus on time; running the depot, she measures the steadiness of every route at once. One habit from the old job stayed with her, and she rates it highly: listening to the bodywork. A groan from an axle, reported by a driver, is worth more to her than a screen full of readings. Her former workmates grumble only that she has grown strict about deadlines.

units: the appraisal deals with a shared bicycle service opened not long ago
the mechanical design of the machines is held to be sound
the parts that wear can be changed without special tools
such ease of repair is unusual for a fleet of this sort
the docking points are too tightly gathered in the central area
spaces grow scarce in the districts that lie higher up
a user going down early finds no space on the way back
the scale of charges favours short trips and punishes long hires
the adjustment of the saddle and the height of the bars are found comfortable
text: Three things are worth weighing up in the shared bicycle service that opened not long ago. The engineering comes first, and it earns respect: a heavy frame, reinforced rims, mudguards welded rather than bolted, brake pads you can reach without a special tool. Worn parts can be swapped out, which is rare enough on a fleet of this sort. The spread of docking points is the obvious weakness. Stands cluster in the middle and thin out as soon as the ground rises, so anyone who freewheels down at dawn comes back to find every slot taken. Charges are the third matter: short hops are cheap, long hires punished hard, which suits errands but discourages anyone riding for pleasure. One kind word on comfort, though. The saddle adjusts one-handed, and the bars sit high enough for a tender back.

units: the writer puts his message together while sitting in a train
the train follows a narrow valley
he left his starting point very early with an overloaded bag
the coach at the beginning of the journey suffered a puncture
the driver mended it while grumbling about the sloping verge
the passengers had to help shift the vehicle
that incident made him miss his rail connection
someone at a ticket window sent him on to a train stopping everywhere
he finds the experience worthwhile in the end despite the delay piling up
text: I am writing this from a carriage that is following a narrow valley, and I want to give it to you in order, because the day has earned it. I left at first light with a bag far too heavy and far too much faith in my connections. An hour out, the coach picked up a puncture; the driver got the jack out, grumbled at the verge for sloping, and had us all pushing. So I missed the train I was booked on, of course. At the next halt a woman at the ticket window put me on a service that stops everywhere, and I watched hamlets go by that I would never have looked at otherwise. Around midday I shared my lunch with a couple coming back from a house move. The delay piled up and I minded none of it. I will get in late, tired, with two notebooks full. Do not pity me. I think I came out ahead.

units: the question put is whether stops with few users should be closed
the specialist in planning holds that the question is badly framed
she puts the thin custom down to the spacing of the services
a service that comes rarely drives users away
the fall in custom then serves to justify further cuts in provision
she reckons that travel booked on demand can break that circle
she insists that booking be possible by voice call as much as through the internet
she stresses that a vehicle without passengers costs almost as much as a full one
she concludes that closing a stop treats the effect and strengthens the root of the trouble
text: Should stops that almost nobody uses be closed? The engineer in charge of planning answers that the question itself is put the wrong way round. Thin custom, she explains, follows from thin service: when vehicles come rarely, people give up waiting for them, and the emptier the stop looks, the easier it becomes to cut again. We ask whether booking a ride on demand breaks that loop. She believes it can, on one condition, that a journey may be ordered by telephone as readily as through a screen, or the scheme shuts out the very people it claims to serve. On cost, she points out that a vehicle running without a soul aboard costs nearly what a full one costs, while a small bus matched to real demand trims the bill. Closing a stop, she concludes, treats the symptom and feeds the root of the trouble.

units: a depot supervisor sets out two routes for a newly hired driver
the fast road has a recently fitted safety barrier and a toll point at its entrance
the surface of the fast road is smooth and shakes the vehicle very little
the second route runs through small towns where the surface is full of holes
traffic calming humps stand before the junctions on the second route
the driver objects that the direct run is costly and dull
the supervisor states that a broken road wears the mechanical parts more than the toll costs
the driver accepts her supervisor's view and settles on the fast route
text: The depot supervisor sat the newly hired driver down and explained that the two routes available were not equivalent. One of them, he said, follows a fast road with a freshly fitted crash barrier and a toll point at the entrance; the surface stays smooth throughout, and the vehicle barely shudders. The other winds through small towns where the tarmac is pitted with holes and where a calming hump rises before every junction on the way. She pushed back at that: the direct run costs money, and the sheer monotony of it wears a person down. He answered that a broken surface eats into the suspension considerably more than the toll ever removes from the takings, and that a single swerve into an unmarked hole costs more again. She came round in the end, and settled on the fast road.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: trade called for roadways able to carry heavy waggons
the width of the ways had to let two teams pass each other
the needs of war produced straight alignments and evenly spaced staging posts
ordinary travellers were given resting places and watering points
carved markers announced the distance still to be covered
upkeep became necessary because a neglected way decays and closes over
these old concerns are found again in the networks still being built
text: The earliest organised road networks grew out of demands that had little to do with one another. Trade came first of all: a laden waggon needed a surface firm enough not to sink under the weight it carried, and the width had to let two teams pass each other without either of them drawing to a halt. Then came the needs of war, calling for straight alignments and staging posts set at even intervals, so that a column on the move could hold together without straggling. Ordinary travellers were served later, with resting houses, watering places and carved stones telling them how far they still had left to go. Upkeep settled the matter of its own accord: a way left alone sinks, fills with thorn and turns back into a track. Those same demands shape the networks still being laid today.

units: markings on the ground show where the doors will open
you have to wait for passengers to get off before boarding
two streams meeting at the doorway slow the whole exchange
once aboard it is better to move towards the middle of the carriage
the boarding step turns slippery in rain and causes falls
it is advisable to get ready to leave one stop before the intended one
forcing the door is unwise and you can come back on the opposite line
text: Arriving on the platform, your first instinct should be locating the markings painted underfoot, which show precisely where the doors will open. Then you let people off. It sounds obvious, but two streams meeting head on clog the doorway and cost the whole carriage a good minute. Once aboard, work your way along towards the middle of the carriage instead of camping beside the entrance. The step deserves attention whenever it rains: the surface turns soapy underfoot, and a fall happens more quickly than you would imagine. Getting off, be ready a stop early, bag closed, one hand free. And if you miss your moment, whatever happens, do not force the door. Leave at the following stop, cross over, and return on the opposite line. Nothing disastrous, unless you insist on rushing to mend your mistake.

units: a front tyre tore open on the lip of a hole in the road surface
the steering snatched sharply and the coach left its line
the driver gave up braking hard so as not to unbalance the lorry behind him
he let the side barrier take the rubbing of the vehicle
the passengers heard the bodywork grinding along the metal over a long stretch
the inquiry showed that the repair of the surface had been botched
the top layer had lifted away after a wet season
what the users remember is that the barrier withstood the impact
text: A burst tyre was all it took to turn an ordinary run into an emergency manoeuvre. The coach was in the nearside lane, holding a steady speed, when the front wheel tore itself open on the lip of a badly patched hole. The steering snatched, and the vehicle slewed towards the verge. Braking hard would have swung the trailer of the lorry behind into a jack knife, so the driver came off the throttle instead and let the crash barrier take the rubbing. Passengers, thrown about in their seats, heard the bodywork grinding along the metal for a long stretch before everything came to rest. The inquiry found that the surface had been patched in haste after a wet season, and that the top layer had lifted clean away from what lay beneath. What the users remember, though, is that the barrier held.

units: loading a luggage hold is a matter of method rather than strength
the bags turn up in disorder while the space available is fixed
it is advisable to sort the bags on the ground before opening the hatch
rigid containers and soft bags are put into two separate groups
the heaviest pieces go against the rear bulkhead
soft bags fill the hollows left between the cases
the luggage for the first stop is set near the opening
a well arranged load does not shift under braking
text: Loading a luggage hold asks less of your arms than of your method, and the difficulty comes down to one thing: the bags turn up in whatever order they please, while the space you have forgives nothing. So begin outside, sorting them patiently, before the hatch is even open. Rigid cases go in one heap, soft holdalls in another, and anything due to come out along the way is kept aside. Then set the heaviest pieces flat against the rear bulkhead, edge towards you; they will make a solid footing. Push the soft bags into the hollows the cases leave, much the way you would stuff a mattress with straw. Keep the space nearest the opening for whatever leaves at the first stop. A hold built like that does not shift under braking, and unloading goes off without anything tumbling out.

units: two toll collecting systems work on the same road
the barrier arrangement forces vehicles to a complete standstill
the queue stretches back at the barrier arrangement as soon as traffic thickens
the repeated pulling away raises what the lorries burn
the automatic gantry lets vehicles through without any break in speed
