the throughput measured at the gantry is markedly higher than at the barriers
the end of the braking reduces the wear of the road surface
automatic reading fails when the plates are dirty
deferred collection brings about heavier administrative handling
text: Two ways of collecting tolls now run along the same road, and the readings taken at the newly opened junction lay bare the gap between them. The barrier arrangement, with its sorting lanes, brings every vehicle to a standstill; throughput hits a ceiling, the queue stretches back as soon as traffic thickens, and the repeated pulling away drives up what the lorries burn. The overhead gantry, mounted on the slip road, lets vehicles hold their speed as they go under it; the throughput measured there runs far higher, and the surface wears more slowly once the constant braking stops. Engineers do point to a weakness: the reading fails on dirty plates, and payment falls back on billing after the event, which is a good deal heavier to handle. Smoother traffic, then, is bought with paperwork.

units: the moored vessel stretches along the whole length of the quay
a row of round openings ringed in brass runs just above the water
the level given over to vehicles looks like a vast metal hall
the boarding ramps ring out as the wheels pass over them
the cabin level is known by its narrow passageways and its numbered doors
the topmost deck takes the walkers and holds benches bolted to the floor
a lowered gangway links the stern of the vessel to the quay
two thick ropes hold the vessel against the swell
text: The moored vessel occupies the entire length of the quay, and its architecture reads upwards, level by level. Low down, the dark hull barely breaks the surface, and a line of round ports runs along it, each one ringed in brass that the salt air has dulled. Above that opens the vehicle deck, a great metal cavern where the ramps ring out beneath the crossing wheels. Next comes the cabin level, recognisable by its narrow passageways and by the numbered doors following one after another. The topmost deck is given over to walkers: benches bolted down, an unbroken rail, a signal mast, a funnel as broad as a tower. Astern, a lowered gangway reaches the concrete of the quay, and two heavy ropes, drawn taut at an angle, hold everything steady against the swell beating on the breakwater.

units: the carriageways were widened in the name of keeping cars moving
the shops were moved out to the edges where parking was plentiful
that move lengthened the distances everyone has to cover
the doubling of the lanes was followed by even thicker congestion
a recent reversal narrows the carriageways and hands space back to those on foot and on cycles
the writer refuses to see a passing fashion in this reversal
the old mistake lay in taking traffic for a fixed volume
traffic in fact depends on the lanes that are offered to it
text: Before passing judgement on the state of our streets, it is worth running back through the decisions that made them. The carriageways were widened first, in the belief that keeping cars moving would serve everybody. Shops were then pushed out to the edges, where parking was plentiful, which lengthened every journey people had to make. Congestion followed, so the lanes were doubled, and congestion came back thicker than before. Lately the order has reversed: streets are being narrowed, trees planted, room handed back to those on foot and on cycles. Call it a passing fashion if you like, but it is nothing of the sort. It corrects a mistake in reasoning several generations old, which took traffic for a fixed volume rather than a demand shaped by what is offered to it. Worth remembering before the next scheme.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the driver of the evening service had not chosen this trade at the start
she worked as a mechanic in a workshop that closed
the closing of the workshop pushed her to take her lorry licence
her mechanical experience lets her feel a worn suspension at the first speed hump
she reports faults before they cut the service short
her knowledge of the chassis makes her take obstacles gently
she had the boarding step replaced because its worn edge hindered older travellers
her route logs fewer incidents than the others
the firm has given her the training of the newly hired drivers
text: The woman who drives the evening coach never once pictured herself doing this. She started out as a mechanic in a workshop; the workshop shut, and she took her lorry licence for want of anything better. That earlier trade has come to serve her well: she can feel a tired suspension at the first speed hump, and she flags the fault up long before it strands the service. Because she knows the chassis inside out, she takes the humps gently, so her passengers no longer bump against the seat in front. She also got the boarding step changed, since a worn edge made climbing aboard risky for older travellers. The upshot is that her route logs fewer incidents than the rest, and the firm now hands her the newly hired drivers to train. She laughs about it, having only ever wanted to mend engines.

units: the coach station just opened was met with dutiful praise
the boarding bays run in one line along a single corridor
no overhead signing helps the traveller find their coach
a hurried user has to walk the whole row before spotting their departure
the hall throws back the echo and makes the spoken announcements impossible to follow
boards hung above each bay would settle the question of where to stand
absorbing materials placed under the roof would improve the hearing
the number of benches ought to be doubled
the writer judges the structure a success but its use badly thought through
text: The coach station just opened deserves better than the dutiful praise that greeted it. Its main failing is plain from the door: the boarding bays run in one long line down a single corridor, with nothing hung overhead to say which is which, so anyone in a hurry walks the whole row before spotting their coach. The hall, for its part, rings hollow and swells the announcements until nobody can make out a word. All this would amount to failure if the building offered nothing to work with; yet the remedies exist, and none of them costs much. Lit boards above each bay would settle where to stand. Absorbing panels under the roof would give the voice back its edges. As for the benches, far too few, doubling them would do. The frame is sound; it is the use of it that nobody thought through.

units: the writer has settled not far from a harbour area
he lists the vehicles he has at his disposal
the small boat belongs to his neighbour
he has learnt to cast off the rope that holds the boat
his bicycle is old and needs seeing to every week
he uses it to reach the market
an animal pulls the cart
the craftsman strengthened the pulling gear
the shared boat leaves a trail on the water
the load he has to shift decides which one he takes
text: Dear friend, now that I have established myself a short distance from the harbour, let me describe how I travel about here. There are four means, and I use each of them in turn. The first is my neighbour's rowing boat, and I have finally learnt to cast off the mooring rope without fumbling. The second is a bicycle, ancient and remarkably heavy, which I overhaul every week before riding down to the covered market. The third is a cart drawn by a donkey, with a harness that the wheelwright strengthened before the cold weather arrived. The fourth is the river ferry, which leaves a broad, unhurried trail behind it. What settles the question, I must admit, is simply whatever happens to need carrying. With every good wish, and in the sincere hope of welcoming you here before long.

units: training opens with a spell of watching at the landing stage
the novice first learns to handle the steering
he then sails as second hand on working crossings
approach drills are done in still water to begin with
the difficulty rises when a headwind is added
the test includes a crossing made in darkness
a breakdown is staged on purpose during the trial
the final berthing is carried out with no engine
the newly qualified pilot works under an old hand for a season
shipping firms are wary of pilots with little experience
text: How does the training of a river ferry pilot begin? With a spell at the landing stage, where the learner watches the manoeuvres and gets the feel of the tiller without forcing it. What follows afterwards? The candidate sails as second hand on working crossings, repeating the approaches in still water at first, then against a headwind. What closes the course? A crossing made in darkness, a breakdown staged deliberately, and a final berthing with the engine shut down. Why does that last one matter? Because it makes the crew read the current and watch the wash of passing craft. Is the certificate enough to take charge? Certainly not. The newly qualified pilot must still work under an old hand for a whole season. Shipping firms welcome such caution, and rarely hand a deck over to a beginner.

units: the courier takes off his head gear before speaking
a slippery layer covered the road surface
his two-wheeler lost its grip on a bend
the driving wheel span without biting into the ground
he insists that he did not come off
he weaved between heavy lorries to keep out of the ditch
a parcel dropped from the rack at the back
he turned back to pick the parcel up
his round ran late
he took a picture of the wheel to convince his supervisor
text: The courier set his helmet down on the table and started explaining. He said the roadway had been covered in a fine slick of mud, and that his scooter had slithered sideways on the lower bend. The back wheel, he said, span uselessly without biting the moment he opened the throttle rather too hard. I asked whether he had come off, because he was limping slightly as he came indoors. He said he had not, but that he had weaved between two heavy lorries to keep himself out of the ditch. The parcel had worked loose from the rack behind and dropped, so he doubled back to retrieve it, and his delivery round ended up running late. His supervisor, he told me, never believes stories involving mud. So he had photographed the filthy wheel before setting off again, simply to have something convincing to show.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: changing track once called for heavy work done by hand
workers had to lever the rolling stock up and shove it across
the growing number of lines made the problem sharper
a man in a repair shed thought up a device with swinging blades
one pull on a lever was enough to move those blades
from then on the train changed direction while still rolling
the system had few parts and was easy to mend
this invention helped the lines grow into a network
students of the history of engineering see a decisive step in it
text: Sending a rail waggon down another track once meant taking the whole thing apart: men levered the wheels clear with bars, then shoved the frame across by main strength. Every junction cost a morning of exhausting labour. The operators wanted a way out, for the lines were multiplying and crossings came thick and fast. A fitter in a repair shed suggested hinging two movable steel blades against the fixed rails, so that one pull on a lever would swing them aside. From then on a train changed direction while still rolling. The idea spread quickly, since it took few parts and could be mended on the spot. It also reshaped the way track was laid: builders stopped stringing out lonely lines and began weaving webs where every branch met the next. Historians of engineering call it a founding step.

units: the two ways of getting about look alike but spend energy differently
the walker has to lift his own weight at every stride
his energy drains away into a movement he repeats
the cyclist lets the saddle carry his weight
he keeps up a turning motion that the wheel holds on to
for the same effort the bicycle covers a greater distance
walking needs no machinery at all
it gets over obstacles that a wheel cannot take
the machine offers speed but stays fragile
the kind of ground should guide the traveller in choosing
text: Walking and cycling look like near neighbours, yet the way each spends energy differs sharply. The walker lifts his own weight at every stride, sets it down, then lifts it again; his effort drains away into a stubborn, repeated beat. The cyclist hands that weight over to a saddle and has only to keep a turning motion alive, which the wheel then carries on for him. Hence a striking difference: for the same effort, the bicycle takes its rider considerably further than his legs alone would manage. Walking, though, holds a quieter advantage. It asks for no chain, no inner tube, no smooth roadway, and it climbs the stair, crosses the bramble, survives the soft sand. One buys speed and pays with a fragile machine, the other buys freedom and pays in slowness. A wise traveller reads the ground before deciding.

units: the customer reports a sway that shows up at speed
the check is worked through one station at a time
the coupling part had too much play in it
that play set the load lurching on a cambered surface
the tyres showed slanting wear on the inner side
such wear gives away a fault in the tracking of the wheels
one clamp on the suspension had lost its grip
the braking system worked but was clogged up
the road test after the repair showed no sway at all
the driver had been running in that state for weeks
text: A driver left his trailer with us one wet evening, reporting a persistent sway that appeared as soon as the pace picked up. We worked through it station by station. First station: the coupling ball, where the play ran well beyond what is permitted, enough on its own to set the whole rig lurching on a cambered surface. Second station: the tyres, worn on a slant along the inner shoulder, the unmistakable sign of tracking gone out. Third station: the leaf suspension, one clamp of which had lost its grip entirely. Fourth station: the braking circuit, sound but thoroughly clogged with grime. We fitted a fresh ball, reset the axle, pulled the clamps up again and bled the lines. On the road test the sway had disappeared, and the driver owned up to having run like that for weeks on end.

units: the first check is on how hard the tyres are blown up
a soft tyre slides on wet ground
the drive is to be looked over next
the braking faces must be free of any damp
the saddle is set so that the leg is nearly straight at the bottom of the stroke
the bags are shared out on either side of the back wheel
an uneven load makes the ride unsteady on a slope
something is carried to mend a puncture
a brake test comes before joining the traffic
text: Before you set off, please work through the following operations in the order given. Begin with the tyres, squeezing each one firmly between thumb and forefinger, since soft rubber slides about on a wet roadway. Move on to the chain and its tension, then to the brake blocks, whose faces must remain perfectly clean and thoroughly dry. Adjust the saddle so that the leg comes almost straight at the bottom of the pedal stroke. Hang the panniers either side of the back wheel, matching the loads carefully on each flank; get that wrong and the machine will wander alarmingly on the very first descent. Pack a spare inner tube, a pair of tyre levers and a pump. Finish with a short run along a level path, squeezing the brakes on gradually, and only afterwards venture into the traffic.

units: a crossing structure has been shut for renovation
vehicles now take a narrow road along the heights
lorries have trouble passing one another there
the daily run to work now takes twice as long
the buses that carry people about are running late
the shops in the lower quarter are losing custom
the local authority has put link boats into service
this measure does not settle the question of goods
the metal frame had been eaten away by rust
the work should be finished before the cold season ends
text: Shutting the bridge for renovation has thrown the whole town's traffic out of shape. Vehicles now climb a narrow ridge road where lorries can barely squeeze past one another. The consequence appeared immediately: the daily run to work takes twice as long, and the works buses arrive noticeably late. Traders in the lower streets report a clear drop in custom, since shoppers give up on the detour. The council has answered by hiring two river shuttles, which link the banks at frequent intervals. The stopgap absorbs a share of those travelling on foot, yet it leaves deliveries exactly where they were. An engineer on site explains that the metal frame had been eaten away by rust, and that patching it would never have held. The work is due to finish before the cold season is out.

units: the way up is made of gravel and looks to be in poor repair
it climbs steeply and forks at the top
the hollows in the ground shake vehicles about badly
rain turns the surface slippery
the wheels lose their grip on the run into the bend
someone living nearby decided to do something about it
he brought crushed stone up to fill the holes
he cut a drain along the bank
the ground now dries out quickly
dust lifts when towed vehicles go by
text: Our gravel track has never been particularly handsome, and there is no point whatever in pretending otherwise. It climbs steeply, it turns sharply at the fork near the summit, and the ruts run so deep that a car rocks about like an old rowing boat. In rain the surface turns soapy and the wheels slither on the approach to the bend; you grip the steering wheel with both hands and hope that nothing is descending towards you. The neighbour below eventually had enough of it. He brought up a load of crushed stone, filled the hollows, then cut a channel along the embankment to carry the water away. The slope dries out quickly now and the mud no longer accumulates. Perfect it certainly is not, since dust lifts whenever a trailer passes, but one can finally drive up without apprehension.

units: the piece sets widening the roads against building up the railway
a queue of cars takes up a wide strip of ground for very few people
a train on rails carries as many people on less space
those who stand up for the car point to its being there at any hour
that advantage counts above all where few people live
towns that have widened their main roads see the jams come back
that return of saturation happens very quickly
a service running to a steady timetable takes on the growth in numbers
the writer argues for putting money first into the lasting answer
text: Should we widen the fast roads once more, or pay for extra carriages on the railway? The question deserves a cool head. A queue of private cars occupies a great width of ground to shift a mere handful of people, whereas a train on rails carries the same crowd on a far narrower strip. Those who stand up for the car object that it goes anywhere, at any hour, with no changes and no waiting; the point holds, above all away from crowded districts. Yet towns that have doubled their main roads watch the flow fill those additional lanes within a single season. A line running to a steady timetable, by contrast, absorbs the growth without choking. Our own position is perfectly plain: widening relieves briefly, timetabling relieves lastingly. Public money should go first to what does not silt up again.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the future bargewoman grew up beside a waterway
as a child she watched the boatmen make their craft fast to the quay
she began her working life as a hand on a sand barge
she learned to read the movement of the current
her training covered approach manoeuvres and slowing down
she learned to lay a heavy hull along the edge despite the wind
after long seasons she was given charge of a convoy
that convoy could tow two further craft
she now teaches her trade to beginners
she tells them to think ahead to the next manoeuvre
text: The woman who would one day steer barges spent her childhood in a cluster of houses beside a narrow waterway. From the towpath she watched the boatmen make their craft fast to the quay, then slip away at first light towards the next lock. Her working life began with a hand's job aboard a barge loaded with sand, and it was there that she learned to read what the current was doing. The training that followed was hard. She had to master the approach, to slow without grazing the bank, to lay a heavy hull along the edge while the wind pushed against her. Long seasons later she was given a convoy of her own, one that could tow two further craft behind it. She teaches beginners now, and the rule she repeats to them is plain: think of the manoeuvre after this one, because water forgives nothing done in haste.

units: a funicular now serves a very steep slope
a winding road used to provide that link
the climb now asks less effort of travellers
the shops at the top of the rise take more custom
use of the line runs past what the operators predicted
the cars are packed at busy times
the wait at the foot of the slope puts off some passengers
removing the road shuttles leaves isolated households without a service
the works are judged sound technically but wrongly sized
text: The funicular on the hillside deserves a mixed verdict. Its cars climb a slope so steep that only a winding road used to link the two levels, and the swap has cut both ways. Since the climb now costs a traveller nothing at all, the small shops at the top of the rise have won back custom they had given up on, and their takings have climbed sharply week after week. Yet use of the line has run so far past what the operators predicted that the cars leave packed all afternoon, and the queue building at the foot of the slope turns away a share of would-be passengers, who give up and walk off instead. One further effect is still argued over: the road shuttles have gone, and with them the only service reaching the most isolated households. So the works convince as a piece of engineering, and disappoint as a matter of capacity.

units: the writer of the message has moved far from where he works
his coach journey took a very long time
traffic jams made his arrival time impossible to predict
he arrived worn out before he had even begun
someone at work suggested a combined solution to him
he now reaches the station with a folding bike
he finishes the journey on a regional train
the bike lets him get past the heavy traffic
he saves half a period on his old journey
he invites the person he is writing to come and try the route
text: You asked me whether moving out had made a mess of everything. At the start, yes. The coach took forever, crawling behind a line of cars that never shifted, and I never had the faintest idea what time I would land. I turned up worn out before I had even begun. Then someone at work suggested what I ought to have thought of myself: break the trip in two. So now I set off with a folding bike, thread my way past the stalled traffic down to the lower station, and finish on a regional train, where I sit down at last with the bike tucked under the seat. It has saved me half a period on the old run, and I arrive cheerful rather than fuming. Rain is the one snag, though a cape sorts that out. Come over one quiet morning, take the spare bike, and try the route with me. You will see.

units: a specialist in urban planning answers a reporter's questions
she compares the tram with the bus on a reserved lane
the tram carries more passengers at every run
rails demand costly and lengthy works
the bus can be put into service far more quickly
the bus copes badly with heavy crowds
the tram keeps its lead on the busiest corridors
she warns against deciding without studying local demand
she judges the route to matter more than the type of vehicle
text: Lay rails, or paint a reserved lane? We put the question to a specialist in the planning of large towns. Her answer is blunt: the two options never come out equal, and the setting settles the matter. A tram, she explains, takes on far more passengers at every run and keeps moving while the general traffic stalls; against that, it demands a heavy, expensive worksite that shuts streets for whole seasons together. A bus on a protected lane starts running very quickly and can be shifted elsewhere if demand moves, yet it struggles the moment the crowds thicken, and on the busiest corridors the tram holds its lead. She refuses any clean verdict. Study what the demand actually is before you pick the hardware, she says, because a badly drawn route will ruin whatever runs along it.

units: a passenger questions a sailor on the deck of a night ferry
the sailor lists what he loves about his work
he mentions the smell of wet rope
he speaks of the noise of the chains being worked
he brings up the brightness of the beacons on dark water
he values the hush of sleeping travellers
he says he knows the regulars by their walk
he states that the crossing home never resembles the crossing out
text: On the deck of the night ferry a passenger asked the sailor what still held him to the work. He laid a hand on the rail and answered with a list, as though he had had it ready for years. He loved the smell of wet rope, he said, that thick scent which soaks into the palms and stays there. He loved the clatter of the chains being hauled before they came alongside, a din that tells you the shore is near. He loved the beacons burning on black water, counted off one by one all the way to the mouth of the channel. He loved the hush of travellers dozing against their bags under blankets rough enough to scratch. He knew the regulars by their walk alone, that careful, hesitant step on wet plating. And before he went back up to the bridge he added that the crossing home had never once resembled the crossing out.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the first heavy loads were shifted on wooden rollers
the spoked wheel took weight out of vehicles
a harness bearing on the shoulders replaced the strap that pressed on the animals' throats
that change increased the pulling power available
metalled tracks stopped the wheels sinking
wooden rails then guided the wagons in the mines
steam did away with dependence on animal strength
every advance bore on the contact between vehicle and ground
text: Before any machine existed, shifting a heavy mass meant heaving it onto wooden rollers and carrying each one round to the front again as it came free. The spoked wheel came later and took weight out of the body of the cart, so that less effort was needed to set it moving from a standstill. Then the harness changed, and that mattered more than anything else: the strap that pressed on the animals' throats gave way to a collar bearing on the shoulders, and teams could suddenly pull loads that had been out of reach. Tracks were metalled so that rims stopped sinking into the mud, and wooden rails were laid in the mine galleries to guide the wagons. Steam closed the sequence by doing away with muscle altogether. Every step attacked the same weak point, which is where the vehicle meets the ground.

units: a slowdown can appear with no obstacle and no crash
one driver brakes lightly for a trivial reason
the vehicle behind brakes harder out of caution
the amplification travels back along the queue
the queue ends up at a complete standstill
the wave of slowing moves back while the cars move forward
keeping enough space ahead softens the effect
sitting too close makes the spread worse
text: A line of cars will sometimes come to a halt although nothing blocks the road ahead and no crash has occurred anywhere on it. The mechanism behind this can be described exactly. One driver eases off for some trivial reason: a clumsy entry, a moment of inattention, a slight rise in the road. The driver behind sees the brake lights and presses a little harder, out of caution. The third driver reacts more sharply still, and the gap between them tightens. Step by step the amplification travels back up the column until vehicles a long way behind the first one must stop dead. What is odd is that this wave of slowing moves backwards while the cars themselves keep going forwards. The remedy fits into one instruction: keep a comfortable gap in front of you, and never sit on the tail of the driver ahead.

units: a coach of walkers takes a mountain track
a rockfall blocks the way above a ravine
the width of the passage rules out turning round
the driver refuses to reverse back down several bends
the passengers shift the lighter stones
a farm tractor arrives from the hamlet nearby
the tractor drags the main block aside with a chain
the journey resumes with a moderate delay
the woman driving the tractor refuses any payment
text: The coach carrying the walkers had taken a stony track that wound its way up towards the pass. Round a bend hanging over a ravine, fallen rock lay right across the way. There was no width there to turn a coach in, and the driver flatly refused to reverse down a run of bends as rough as those. The passengers climbed out and began shifting the lighter stones by hand, but the largest of them would not budge whatever they tried. A farmer from the hamlet just below turned up at last on her tractor, looped a chain round the boulder and hauled it onto the verge in three unhurried pulls. The coach set off again only moderately late, to applause from the whole group of walkers. Asked what she wanted for the job, she only shrugged, swung the tractor round and drove back down towards her cattle sheds.

units: the text explains how to choose between a night train and a long-distance coach
it advises comparing the fares of the two options first
the night train saves paying for a room
the coach calls at stops the railway ignores
the reader must check the arrival time before booking
booking a berth well away from the corridor is recommended
a soft bag is needed since there is no storage space
the coach imposes halts that break up sleep
the final choice depends on how much rest matters
text: Torn between the night train and the long-distance coach? Work through it in stages. Compare the fares of the two first, but add to the ticket price what a room would have cost you, because that is usually where the train claws back the difference. Then look at the list of stops, since the coach calls at small towns the railway passes nowhere near. Check what time you arrive before you book anything, or you will be put down before the ticket office opens. If you go by train, pick a berth well away from the corridor and bring a soft bag, or you will sleep against your luggage with your knees folded up. If you go by road, accept in advance the compulsory halts that will wake you in the small hours. Then settle it with one question: do you want to arrive rested, or to pay as little as you can?

units: a report describes the reopening of an abandoned railway line
crews have replaced the rotten sleepers
a tunnel overrun by roots has been cleared
a footbridge has been added for cyclists
people living beside the line dread the noise of night trains
local growers mean to send their goods out by rail
passengers will try the line before it opens formally
the fares have not yet been settled
text: Rusted rails that the undergrowth had been quietly swallowing for a generation are taking trains again. Several things stand out from our visit to the works now reopening the line. The track, first: the crews have pulled out the rotten sleepers and cleared a tunnel where roots had reached down as far as the ballast itself. Access, next: a steel footbridge now spans the cutting, so that cyclists need no longer scramble down the embankment to reach the far side. Worries, too: people living beside the line dread the rumble of trains at night and are already asking for acoustic screens. Hopes, last: the growers of the surrounding countryside intend to send their harvests out by rail. Passengers will ride the length of the line before it opens formally; the fare table, meanwhile, has yet to be settled.

units: a mountain road grows narrower as it gains height
the slope of the ground forces drivers to slow down
cold rain makes the surface dangerous and worsens the hold-ups
the staff in charge of the road spread sand over the carriageway
this operation is meant to stop heavy vehicles from skidding
traffic flows freely again before night falls
a hamlet high up is served by no lorry
goods are brought up there by pack animals
the people who live there approve of this limit, which spares the track
text: The road that climbs towards the pass grows narrower the higher it goes. Its harsh gradient forces drivers to ease off, and that slowing builds a solid queue from the first bend onwards. When cold rain beats down on the carriageway, the surface turns treacherous and the queue stretches further still. Maintenance crews then spread sand, since a frozen road would send the heaviest vehicles sliding. The effect is immediate: traffic finds an even rhythm again before night falls. Higher up, a steep track leaves the road and reaches a hamlet that no lorry serves. With nothing fit for wheels to run on, deliveries go up on the backs of pack animals, which keeps every parcel small. The people who live there accept the limit, because it spares the track the wear a wheel would grind into it.

units: waiting on an overcrowded platform irritates travellers a great deal
the transport network was designed for fewer users
the number of passengers has outgrown capacity while the lines stayed the same
buying extra carriages is costly and useless if the stops are saturated
the writer proposes spreading the passengers across different time slots
he cites the staggering of office hours as one possible measure
he also suggests reserved lanes and cheaper fares outside the rush
the places that tried these measures saw the peak crowding fall
most travellers would agree to leave later in return for a seat
text: Nothing wears down a passenger faster than a packed platform where the next train refuses to come. The cause is no mystery. Urban networks were laid out for a smaller population, and demand has outrun what they offer while the lines stayed exactly as wide as before. Adding carriages costs a fortune and settles nothing if the stops jam at the same hour anyway. One idea deserves a hearing: spread the demand instead of swallowing it. Stagger the opening of offices, keep lanes for shared vehicles, cut the fare on quiet journeys — none of that calls for deep pockets. Where such measures have been tried, the peak has eased with no fresh building work at all. The objection writes itself, of course: everyone guards their own timetable. Ask the passengers, though, and most would leave later for a seat.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the driver is happy to talk about the start of his working life
his old machine was in poor condition and the door shut badly
its rattling body gave away the bends in advance
the vehicle he has now is far more comfortable and much quieter
a camera has taken the place of the old mirror
passengers used to chat all the way along the route
the passengers of today stare at their screens in silence
the driver admits that the new machine is kinder to his back
he misses the smell of machinery at the moment of setting off
text: Ask the shuttle driver about his early years behind the wheel and he needs no coaxing at all. The first vehicle he had was worn out: the door never shut properly, the floor shook, and the rattling bodywork gave away a bend long before the indicator did. What he drives today has nothing in common with it. The cab is hushed, the seat adjusts at the back, and a camera has taken over from the blind old mirror. He compares his passengers too. Once, the whole village climbed aboard together and talked from one end of the aisle to the other; now each of them stares at a screen and the run goes by almost without a word. He draws no bitterness from any of it, he says, because the newer machine is kinder to his back. What he misses is the smell of a cold engine at the moment of setting off.

units: three things catch the eye at the entrance to the refurbished building
the entrance area was cramped and poorly lit before the works
glazing now brings daylight down as far as the steps
the signs pointing the way have been redrawn in large lettering
travellers in a hurry find their way without looking at a display
the old grimy seats have been taken out of the place
the new perches are few and uncomfortable
the writer judges the result favourable on the whole
the platforms are now reached without any detour
text: Three things catch the eye the moment you step into the refurbished halt. The first has to do with volume: the entrance hall, cramped and gloomy before the works, now opens under glazing that carries daylight as far as the steps. The second is the signing, redrawn in broad lettering and plain symbols, so a traveller in a hurry picks out the right platform without lifting his eyes to a display. The third is less flattering. The grubby benches have gone, and the perches that took their place are few and hard, as though the operator feared people might settle in. Even so, the verdict leans the right way. Movement through the building reads clearly, the platforms are reached without a detour, and the hush of the automatic doors comes as a pleasant surprise. One user sums it up: easier to breathe, harder to sit.

units: the person written to had warned of a soaked track after the water rose
the writer set off at first light with his luggage strapped down
the first part of the route was marked out with stakes driven into the ground
the grooves left by the wheels closed up straight away
the rain stopped halfway through the journey
the ground hardened under the wind
a steep climb forced the writer to walk and push his bicycle
he reached a shelter high up as evening fell
the warden of the shelter gave him hot soup
text: You warned me the track would be a swamp once the water had risen, and you were right. I set off at first light, panniers strapped tight, the handlebars heavy as an anchor. The opening stretch, marked out with pale stakes, dropped between hedges soaked through; my wheels cut two clean grooves that the mud sealed up behind me. Halfway along, the rain gave out and the wind dried the crust of the ground, so I rode a long hour without effort, hardly thinking about it. Then came the climb, steep and endless, and I pushed the bicycle up on foot, counting my steps. As the light went, I reached the shelter on the plateau, hands black and heart light, and the warden set a bowl of scalding soup in front of me. I am writing from the window: the valley is steaming, and I am thinking of tomorrow.

units: the energy stored by a vehicle rises with the square of its speed
doubling the speed makes the braking distance four times longer
a layer of water slides in between the rubber and the road
that layer cuts the grip and reduces the slowing obtained
the grooves in the tyre push the water out to the sides
worn tyres can no longer clear that water away
a more heavily laden vehicle needs greater force to slow as much
specialists advise widening the gap between vehicles when these conditions change
text: What is it that lengthens the stopping distance of a car already under way? The first cause is stored energy, which rises with the square of the speed: drive twice as fast and you need four times the length to pull up. And what happens once the road is wet? A film of water slides in between the rubber and the ground, the grip collapses, and the same pressure on the pedal buys less slowing than before. Do the grooves in a tyre earn their keep? They push that film out to the sides; worn away, they clear nothing and the car floats. And what about the load it is carrying? Greater mass calls for greater force to slow at the same rate, so the stop grows longer again. Engineers put their conclusion in a single line: the safety gap must widen as soon as any one of these factors changes.

units: a traveller reports that her connecting service has been cancelled
the clerk blames the disruption on a fallen branch across the track
the trouble happened near the mouth of an underground passage
a road vehicle is to run instead, leaving from the square outside
that vehicle will go round the high ground to reach the station she wants
her ticket stays valid and nothing further will be charged
the traveller fears her things are too bulky for the central aisle
a luggage hold will take her cases
a member of staff will lend a hand with stowing the bags
text: At the ticket window, a traveller reported that her connecting service had just been cancelled. The clerk answered that the whole line was affected, a fallen branch having blocked the track at the mouth of the tunnel. She asked whether anything could be arranged before dark. A coach would run instead, he explained, leaving from the square outside and reaching the junction station by going round the high ground rather than through it. Her ticket stayed valid, he added, and nothing further would be charged. The traveller then worried about her luggage, too bulky for a crowded aisle. The clerk set her mind at rest: a hold would take the cases, and a member of staff would lend a hand with loading them. She thanked him and made for the exit shown on the notice, her relief plain to see.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: carriage by water dominated before wheeled vehicles came into their own
a boat loaded with grain moved along with almost no effort
animals hauling the same cargo tired quickly on a broken surface
the gap is explained by the resistance the ground puts up
routes over land served places the current could not reach
a waterway imposes one direction and one fixed line
the two systems shared the work according to the cargo
carriage by water suited heavy loads moved without haste
the spread of paved roads tipped the balance towards the dry route
text: Long before the wheel came into its own over the longer hauls, it was water that carried the bulk of the goods. A boat loaded with grain slipped along the current at almost no cost, while a team dragging the same load over a broken surface was spent before it had covered half a stage. The difference lay in the resistance of the surface: water gives way, mud holds on. Routes over land, for their part, offered something the river never could. They went wherever people wanted them to go, the high ground included, whereas the water imposed its own line and its own direction. So the two networks divided the work between them: the barge for heavy volume that could wait, the cart for the short and supple run. Once metalled roads multiplied, that balance tipped towards the dry route.

units: the writer brings getting a bicycle ready down to three checks
he advises pumping the tyres up properly
he recommends looking over the surface of the tyre for cuts
the brake levers must be squeezed at a standstill to test the locking
friction parts worn too thin have to be replaced
bags fixed to the handlebars unsettle the steering
it is better to put the weight low down and at the back
carrying a spare inner tube and a pump saves you finishing on foot
text: Getting a bicycle ready for a long day in the saddle comes down to three checks, and not one more. Tyres first: pump them up properly, run a thumb over the whole of the tread, and hunt for the cuts where a splinter of glass may have lodged. Brakes next: squeeze the levers while the bicycle stands still, watch whether the wheel locks cleanly, and swap out any block whose grooves have worn away. Then the load: a handlebar hung with bags makes the steering twitchy, so bring the weight down low, on either side of the back wheel. One last piece of advice, plain enough — take a spare tube and a pump, because a puncture halfway round turns a fine outing into a long trudge home. A quarter of an hour of care in the shed, and you set off with an easy mind, in no fear of the first long drag.

units: the vehicle pulled out after the middle of the night with every seat taken
the engine died at the second pick-up point
it came to a halt on the verge of a fast road
the driver reported a fault in the fuel supply
a passenger trained in mechanics offered her help
they traced a clogged filter and cleared it
the journey started again after a break of roughly half an hour
the passengers applauded when the engine caught
the company handed the passenger a free travel voucher
text: It was past midnight when the coach pulled out of the terminal, every seat taken, the doors hissing, a smell of cold coffee down the aisle. At the second pick-up the engine coughed and then died outright on the verge of the fast road. The driver switched on the hazard lights and announced a fault in the fuel supply. A passenger on her way home from a course in mechanics offered to help; between them they traced a clogged filter and cleared it with a rag and a good deal of patience. The coach moved off after half an hour, to applause from the aisle. At the far end, the operator handed a free travel voucher to the woman who had rescued its driver. She replied that she had only wanted to sleep in her own bed, and that the breakdown had woken her for nothing. The others walked off retelling it down the phone.

units: one of the two cloths comes from the fleece clipped off a farmed animal
the other cloth is drawn from a plant after soaking and crushing
the crimped fibres of animal origin hold warmth by trapping air
the plant cloth yields a smooth thread that feels cool to the touch
the craftsman gives the animal fibre to cold-season clothing
the plant fibre serves for shirts because it carries damp away from the skin
the animal fibre tightens and mats together on contact with hot water
the plant fibre stands repeated washing but creases readily
text: Lay two lengths of cloth side by side on a workbench and they tell opposite stories. One begins as a fleece clipped from a grazing animal, and its crimped fibres trap pockets of air that hold warmth against the skin. The other is drawn from a plant stem, soaked until it loosens, then crushed and combed into a smooth thread, cool under the fingers. The weaver builds on that contrast. The animal fibre goes into cold-weather clothing, where a thick weave slows the escape of heat. The plant fibre goes into shirts, since it carries damp away from the body. Care pulls the two apart again. Hot water makes the animal fibre tighten and mat together, while the plant cloth survives washing after washing yet creases at the slightest fold. Choosing a cloth, then, means choosing a climate as much as a way of looking after it.

units: the narrator visits the workroom of a neighbour who sews
the visit takes place on a rainy evening
the cloths are stored by category in the workroom
close-knitted fabrics ladder the moment a pin touches them
among the tools are a battered thimble, a reserved pair of scissors and a marking chalk
the craftswoman builds a cuff and sets in a jacket lining without measuring twice
customers come back with cheap jackets that fit badly at the shoulders
the craftswoman mends these garments rather than discarding them
text: My neighbour, who sews for a living, opened up her workroom to me one wet evening, and I came away quite sure that I knew nothing at all about the clothes on my back. She started with her cloth, stacked by kind: the soft cottons, the coarse weaves that scratch the palm, the fine knits that ladder the moment a pin catches them. Then came the tools of the trade, a dented thimble, a pair of scissors nobody else may touch, a flat stick of chalk for marking lines. After that she showed me her hands at work, and there I lost the thread for good, because she builds a cuff, drops in a lining, turns a collar, and never measures twice. Last of all she talked about her customers, who bring back cheap jackets that gape at the shoulder. She laughs about them, then picks up the needle and rescues the thing.

units: the first step is to wear the trousers in front of a mirror
the wanted height is fixed with closely set pins
the original edge must be undone with an unpicking tool
a pass of the iron erases the mark of the old fold
a reserve of cloth is kept below the marked line so the work can be undone
the surplus is turned inwards then fastened
the join must not show on the visible face
the specialists advise a fitting before the pins come out
text: Taking up a pair of trousers that hang far too long is a matter of order rather than of skill, and the alteration shops all set out the very same run of steps. Put the trousers on and stand in front of a mirror, fold the cloth to the height you want, and mark that line with pins set close together. Slip them off again, undo the original hem with an unpicker, and then press the fold flat so that the old crease stops showing. Cutting comes next, and here you leave a margin of cloth below the marked line, since without it nothing can be put back. Turn the surplus inwards, pin it, and join it with a stitch that never shows on the outer face. A last pass of the iron settles and flattens the edge. Those who do this for a living advise trying the garment on before any pin comes out.

units: an idle textile mill lying in a valley has started working again
buyers have turned away from knitwear that covers itself in bobbles after few washes
these customers now ask for stronger and dearer yarn
the fleeces produced locally have regained a market value
before that the breeders destroyed these fleeces for want of a buyer
carding workshops and a dyeing place have gone back into service
the technical manager ties the state of the weaving to that of the district
the shortage of trained staff holds this revival back
text: The mill had stood idle at the foot of the valley, and now its looms are beating again. Behind the change lies a quiet shift in taste. Buyers grew tired of knitwear that bobbles after a few washes, and began asking for longer, harder-twisted yarn, whatever the extra cost. That demand gave the fleeces of the surrounding farms a market price once more, where the breeders had been burning them for want of anyone to buy. From there the effect spread outward. Carding sheds reopened, a dye house lit its vats again, and workrooms relearned how to set a neckline by hand. The technical manager puts it plainly: the weave of a jumper tells you how a whole district is faring. One shadow remains, since trained hands are scarce and the learning asks for a patience few applicants will offer.

units: the work garment described takes greater strain than an office one
the arm opening is the area that gives way first
loading the pockets pulls the front of the garment out of shape
contact with rough surfaces wears a hole through the cloth at the elbows
a triangular piece is set under the arm to follow the movement
the pocket ends are made firm by extra stitching
a removable reinforcing patch guards the elbow without taking off the sleeve
the inside of the garment can be taken out according to the season
text: A site jacket takes punishment that office clothing never meets. At the shoulder the armhole opens and shuts from first light until dusk, and the seam there gives way before anything else. At the pockets the weight of tools drags the cloth down and pulls the front out of shape. At the elbows, rubbing against rough surfaces wears the weave through to a hole. Makers answer each of these in turn. They cut the armhole wider and set a triangular gusset beneath it, so the sleeve follows the arm. They back every pocket and lock its corners with extra stitching. On the elbow they lay a patch of heavy canvas that can be swapped without taking the sleeve apart. The lining, meanwhile, unclips and comes away once the cold season ends, which stretches the life of the jacket further.

units: the text sets two wardrobes against each other
the first holds a limited number of carefully chosen garments
several of these pieces are more than ten years old and show visible mends
the second wardrobe is full of impulse buys dropped after one season
these clothes are set aside because of a slack knit or a torn buttonhole
the author rules out the explanation by financial means
the owner of the crowded wardrobe has in fact spent more
the author puts the difference down to examining how a thing is made
he suggests teaching these checks as one learns to read a label
text: Let us set two wardrobes against each other. The first holds a modest number of garments chosen slowly, several of them past their tenth year and carrying mends that anyone at all can see. The second is crammed with things bought on impulse, worn for a season, then dropped because the knit had gone slack or a buttonhole had torn at the first snag. The gap is usually blamed on money. What one actually observes says otherwise, for the owner of the crowded wardrobe has spent the larger sum. What divides the two habits is attention paid to how a thing is made. Look at a seam, tug at a loose thread, turn back a collar to judge the lining: such checks cost nothing and rule out whatever is doomed from the start. We ought to be teaching them just as we teach people to read a food label.

units: the woman described mends clothing in a cramped room of a shopping arcade
her work falls into three categories
she repairs damage such as tears and undone edges
fitting to the customer takes up the largest share of her time
factory sizes rarely suit real bodies
turning one garment into another is her favourite task
she was trained by an older professional
she refined her craft alone over twenty years
she declines to take on an apprentice in a hurry
text: The woman who alters clothes for a living works out of a narrow room at the back of a shopping arcade, and her trade falls into three parts. First come the accidents put right: a tear at the knee, a buttonhole stretched out of shape, a hem ripped away by the heel of a shoe. Then comes fitting to the body, which fills the greater part of her week, since a standard size matches almost no real figure. She takes in a back, tightens a neckline gone slack, shortens a sleeve by no more than the width of a fingernail. Last comes conversion, the part she likes best, when a dated dress becomes a skirt and a worn coat gives up its lining to another. She learned the whole craft beside an elderly tailor, then spent two decades refining it alone. An apprentice in a hurry she turns away.

units: the narrator judges his coat badly during the first cold season
at the start the collar rode up and the back went out of shape
the colour struck him as dull beside an older garment
during the second season the cloth settled to his build
the third season was very wet and the garment dried overnight
the inner part split under the arm
the repair cost a small share of the price paid at purchase
the narrator recommends this coat despite its unlovely look at the start
text: Honestly, that coat had me doubting it from the very start. Right through the first cold season the collar kept riding up, the gathers at the back puffed out oddly, and the colour looked drab beside my old jacket. By the second season the cloth had softened and had taken on the shape of my shoulders, and the lapels began to sit flat without my touching them. The third season was the best of the lot, since it rained without a break, and the surface drank the water and dried overnight, with no smell left behind. Then the lining split under the arm, and I gave the coat up for lost altogether. A repair cost a tenth of what I paid for it, and off it went for another round. My verdict: buy it, provided you accept that it looks awful to begin with. It wears better than I do myself.

units: the author writes to his sister to announce a parcel
the parcel holds a garment that belonged to their father
the damp of a space under the roof threatened the inside of the garment
the author also feared the insects that attack stored clothing
the outer cloth has stayed intact, which prompted the sending
the bottom of one sleeve is worn by the arm resting again and again on a work surface
a professional offers to take material from under the collar for a discreet mend
the author states that this kind of cloth softens when it is worn
text: Dear sister, I am writing before the crate leaves, because what is packed inside it needs a word of explanation. You will be receiving our father's blue jacket. I am not sending it out of sentiment, but because the damp up under the roof had already begun to eat at the lining, and a garment left lying in a trunk ends up as food for moths. The outer cloth has not suffered at all, and that is what decided me to save it. You will notice that the right cuff is frayed, worn thin where his arm rested on the bench and polished the weave away. A seamstress here assures me that a piece taken from under the collar would leave the mend invisible. Have the work done, and then wear it without any worry. Cloth of that kind stiffens while it sleeps and softens once it is out on a back.

units: the text deals with the insect that damages woollen knitwear
the worry arises when the cold season clothing is put away
it is the young form of the insect and not the flying adult that eats the material
traces of sweat draw this larva towards fibres of animal origin
a washed garment therefore offers little food
storing in a closed and opaque container beats an open shelf
two nights at low temperature destroy the eggs
the traditional scented sachets drive off without killing and lose their strength quickly
regular care by airing and refolding is the most reliable remedy
text: Ought we to fear the insect that riddles our woollens? The question comes round at the close of every cold season, at the moment when the knitwear is put away. It is not the winged adult that eats the mesh, but its larva, blind and tiny, drawn to animal fibre and above all to the traces of sweat soaked into it. Hence the first of the answers: a clean garment makes poor feeding. What of the storing itself? A closed, opaque cover beats an open shelf, and two nights in the cold kills any eggs laid in a seam. And the old remedies, those scented sachets tucked between the piles? They drive the creature off without killing it, and their strength fades fast. The lasting answer is a dull habit, namely taking the woollens out, shaking them, airing them, and folding them a different way.

units: the craftswoman answers her pupil's questions about the cloth kept in the workshop
she names first a light fibre used for shirts worn in the warm season
she describes a second rougher fibre meant for bags and aprons
she says that a short-pile cloth swallows the light and suits jackets made for ceremonies
she points out that a pressed material never frays and spares the trouble of finishing the edges
she buys in narrow strips an openwork cloth that she stitches onto collars
the openwork cloth costs the most because it calls for a patient hand
she holds that the choice of a material follows the purpose of the piece
she says the pupil will know the cloths by touch before knowing them by sight
text: The dressmaker answers her pupil, who wants to know what all the cloth stacked round the workshop is for. Linen comes first, cool and supple, kept back for shirts worn through the warm months. Hemp comes next, coarser under the hand, sturdy enough for bags and aprons. Velvet, she says, swallows the light, and that is why it suits jackets made for ceremonies. Felt never frays, so its edges can be left exactly as they were cut. Last of all she lifts the lace, bought in narrow strips and stitched along collars. Her pupil asks which of them costs the most. The lace, by some way, because it wants a patient hand and an eye trained on fine work. What settles the choice, she adds, is what the piece has to do, never taste on its own; and before long her pupil will know each cloth by touch before knowing it by sight.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: old cloth came from fibres drawn out of plant stems
preparing those fibres called for a soaking and then a beating
getting enough cloth to dress a single chest took several weeks
harnessing a wheel to the distaff raised what could be produced
treadle looms set the weaver's hands free
the steam engine then made the workshops larger
the price of a shirt fell so far that people of modest means could own two
fibres born of chemistry are the most recent step
these recent fibres dry quickly and hardly crease
text: Picture a workshop where thread is still drawn out by hand, wisp by wisp, and you are holding the start of this story. The oldest cloth began in plant stems. The fibres were soaked until they loosened their grip on the stalk, then beaten, then combed out straight, and whole weeks went by before there was enough to dress a single chest. Then some quick mind harnessed a wheel to the distaff, and what came off the spindle climbed sharply. Treadle looms followed, and the weaver's hands were freed for the shuttle alone. Steam took over later, the workshops swelled into something far larger, and the price of a shirt fell so far that people of modest means could keep two of them. The latest turn you are very likely wearing at this moment: threads born of chemistry, quick to dry and stubborn about creasing.

units: the wearing out of a shoe follows mechanical causes
the foot rolls its weight from the back towards the front
this way of bearing down wears the heel first and then the toe
the thinning of the outer layer takes away the cushioning
the unabsorbed shock travels up towards the knee joint
hard surfaces speed up the breaking down of the sole
a sole soaked with water loses its shape and its stiffness
makers stack layers of unequal density
the writer concludes that the stride wears the shoe out more than the material does
text: A shoe does not wear out at random, and the reason is far more mechanical than most people suppose. The foot rolls its weight from the back towards the front, so the sole meets an uneven rub: the heel goes first, the toe follows. Once the outer layer thins, the cushioning is gone and the shock travels up towards the knee joint, which is why keen walkers ache. Hard surfaces hurry the whole thing along, since nothing gives back what it takes in. Wet weather adds its share. A sole that has drunk up water loses its shape, loses its stiffness, and lets the foot slide about inside. Makers answer by stacking layers of unequal density, firm below and yielding above. The shoe holds up far better that way, yet the principle stands: it is the stride that wears a shoe out, not the material.

units: a tear spoils the front of a borrowed dress
the dress has to be given back the next day
a seam sewn edge to edge would have left a visible mark on the satin
the idea of hiding the tear under a belt is dropped
a neighbour who once kept a haberdashery looks the cloth over
the neighbour suggests adding an embroidered motif instead of mending
the embroidered motif shows a stem and three leaves
the owner of the dress notices the motif and asks where it was bought
text: A tear as wide as a fingernail ran across the front of the borrowed dress, and the woman who was due to give it back the following day felt her throat tighten. Sewn edge to edge, the split would have left a visible pucker in the pale satin. She thought of hiding it under a belt, then let the idea go, since the waist of the dress sat far too high. Her neighbour, who had kept a haberdashery years before, turned the cloth towards the window and studied it. She proposed not to mend but to add: pale thread, a stem and three leaves, worked exactly over the wound in the satin. The job filled a whole evening, the needle moving without hurry. The next morning the owner of the dress stopped short in front of the motif and asked where it had been bought. The other said it was not for sale.

units: the choice of a fastening follows the use the piece is meant for

the cord can be set finely and replaced for next to nothing
the cord asks for slow handling and works loose when the knot is badly pulled up
the metal fastener closes in one movement and holds without being watched
the metal fastener forces a fixed width that does not follow changes of measurement
lacing is advised for a work garment worn over layers of varying thickness
the metal fastener is advised for a formal jacket because it stays discreet
the edge has to be strengthened against tearing before the assembly
text: Before you settle on lacing or on a hooked fastening, think about what the garment is meant to do. A cord runs through metal rings and spreads the pull over the whole height; you can set it as finely as you like, and replacing it costs next to nothing. Against that, it wants slow hands, and it works loose the moment a knot is badly pulled up. A hook closes in one movement and holds without being watched, though it forces a fixed width on you: let the measurement shift, and the garment will not follow. For a work garment, take the lacing, because the pull has to answer the thickness of whatever is worn beneath. For a formal jacket, the hook keeps quiet and leaves the front undistorted. Either way, make sure the edge is strengthened against tearing before you put the lining in.

units: a trade gathering given over to cloth has just closed

several retailers undertake to publish the list of their subcontractors

this cut does away with the hard ridge that seamstresses had to take off
the exhibitors are waiting for these undertakings to turn into firm orders
text: A trade gathering given over to cloth closed last night, and its organisers hold on to four announcements. The first is about recycling: a group of workshops says it can pull cutting scraps back into fibre and work them into fresh yarn without weakening it. The second is about tracing, since every piece will carry a woven label giving the origin of the fibre and the place where it was dyed. The third touches how the goods are made, several retailers having undertaken to publish the list of their subcontractors. The fourth drew less notice, though the technical people seized on it: a machine now cuts the woven edge without burning it, which does away with the hard ridge that seamstresses used to take off by hand. The exhibitors are waiting to see these undertakings turn into firm orders.

units: a coat hanging near the entrance changes its look as the seasons go by
at the end of the cold season the velvet collar carries the mark of the scarf
the pile of the collar stays flattened one way
through the mild season the garment is brushed and then put away in a cotton bag
the cotton bag lets it lose its smell of smoke
during the hot spell it sleeps folded on a high shelf
it is folded with the lining outwards so as to avoid marks
a damp cloth and a warm iron take out the crease that has appeared across the back
the felt hat keeps a dent for good once the dent is pressed into it
text: The coat hangs on a hook near the entrance, and its look shifts as the seasons go by. At the close of the cold months the velvet collar still carries the mark of the scarf that pressed on it: the pile lies flattened one way and refuses to stand up again. Then the mild weather arrives, the coat is brushed and aired and then hung away in a cotton bag, where it gives up its smell of smoke. Through the hot spell it sleeps on a high shelf, folded in two, the lining turned outwards so that nothing marks the face of the cloth. When the chill comes round again it is brought out with a sharp crease right across the back, which a damp cloth and a warm iron will eventually take out. The felt hat above it goes round the same cycle, but forgives less: press a dent into it and the dent stays.

units: the writer is exasperated by how fragile mass-produced clothes are
the seams give way at the second wash and the linings split
the buyer buys again the garment he has only just worn out
the labels have worked out that quick replacement pays better than strength
makers cut the weight of the cloth and drop the reinforcements at the points of strain
an alteration workshop now turns down certain repairs for want of solid material
the writer notes that customers accept a shirt lasting a single season
the writer believes the change will come from the piled-up cost of bad buys
text: Honestly, the state of mass-produced clothing is enough to try anyone's patience. Seams give way at the second wash, linings split, and the buyer ends up buying again the jacket he has only just worn out. There is nothing mysterious behind it: the labels have worked out that quick replacement pays better than strength. So the weight of the cloth is cut, a thin fibre goes in where linen thread used to be, and the reinforcements at the points of strain quietly disappear. The alteration workshop down the road now turns certain jobs away, because there is nothing solid left for a needle to grip. And we adjust: a shirt lasting a single season strikes us as normal. My own view is that the turn will come from the purse, once the bad buys added together cost more than one garment sewn to last.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a craftsman cuts soles in a narrow room that opens onto the street
