he holds that the shape of the foot rules the model and not the other way round
text: In a narrow room that opens straight onto the street, the bootmaker has been cutting soles since the day he left school. His trade very nearly went out with him. Customers were bringing things to be mended less and less often, the leather suppliers set batches too heavy for one workshop to take, and the apprenticeship drew nobody at all. He could have closed. Instead he changed what he does: rather than wait for repairs, he now makes wooden lasts to measure for difficult feet, the ones that mass production rubs raw. His orders come from doctors and from people who work in rehabilitation. He has trained two apprentices, and one of them already puts the uppers together on her own. Asked what he is proud of, he points to a pair on the bench, its sole marked by an uneven tread, and says the foot rules, never the model.

units: two dresses are shown facing each other in a room
the first dress is cut from a dark velvet
the velvet swallows the light and hangs straight
the second dress is of unbleached lace and lets both air and eye through
the wall can be made out behind the openwork dress
the onlooker prefers the dark dress at first because of its bulk
the judgement turns round once the eye lingers
the openwork dress lays out its own drawing, in which each loop holds the next
the onlooker ends up admiring the hand that carried out the work
the heavy piece is forgotten on the way out while the light one keeps pulling the eye back
text: Two dresses face each other in the far room, and nothing about them agrees. The first, cut from a dark velvet, swallows the light; it weighs, it hangs straight, it puts a hush on everything near it. The second, in unbleached lace, lets both air and eye pass through, so that the wall shows behind it, as though the cloth were hesitating to exist at all. At first the comparison goes to the velvet, whose bulk simply commands the room. Then the eye lingers, and the balance tips the other way. Velvet offers a surface and no more, while the lace lays out its own drawing, each loop holding the next with no visible knot. In the end you admire the hand that tied it rather than the dress itself. You leave with an odd impression: the heavier piece slips your mind, the lighter one keeps pulling your eye back.

units: the writer is taking a course in making clothes
she signed up as the cold season began
the tutor handed out pieces of cloth at the first session
the first task was hemming a square of cotton without a machine
the earliest attempts were started again on two evenings running
loose stitching to hold layers is taught at the next session
that loose stitching stops the layers from shifting
a worn knee on a pair of trousers was backed with sturdy canvas
a lined skirt was finished the day before
the writer comes home with sewing kit and the intention of carrying on
text: I am writing to you from the sewing workshop I joined as the cold season set in. On the first evening the tutor handed round offcuts of cloth and set us to hemming a square of cotton by hand. My stitches wandered off the line, and I unpicked the lot on two evenings running. The week after, she showed us how to tack the layers together before any proper stitching, which stops them shifting under the needle. The step looks like wasted effort, and it saves a great deal of bother later. Mending came next: I patched a pair of trousers worn through at the knee, setting a heavier piece of canvas underneath. Yesterday I finished a lined skirt, and the tutor called the finish neat. I am coming home with a box of pins, a metal thimble and every intention of carrying on. I shall show you the whole lot when you next call round.

units: little balls forming on a knit come from the length of the fibres
fibres that are too short work their way out of the cloth
rubbing rolls those fibres together
a yarn of long, tightly twisted strands holds up better
the twist keeps the fibre ends inside the yarn
cheap articles wear out faster
how a garment is worn and looked after counts as much as its quality
a strap rubbing repeatedly on a sleeve causes the fault
a fabric shaver or a fine-toothed comb takes the balls off
that clearing leaves the colour slightly paler
text: Why does a jumper start bobbling after no more than three washes? The answer comes down to how long the fibres are. The short ones work their way up to the surface, tangle together under rubbing and roll into those little balls that leave a garment looking tired before its time. A long, tightly twisted yarn holds up far better, since the fibre ends stay locked away inside the twist. So a cheap jumper is doomed from the start? Broadly yes, though how you wear the thing and how you look after it count just as much. A sleeve rubbing all day against a bag strap will bobble in the end, even in a lovely knit. Can any of it be rescued? Certainly. A fabric shaver or a fine-toothed comb lifts the top layer away. That does leave the colour a shade paler, so go gently with the thing.

units: a customer brought in a coat whose inner cloth was coming apart
the damaged area was under the arms
the owner thought the garment was beyond saving
the inner cloth wears out before the woollen outer
that wear comes from the rubbing taken at the shoulder
putting it right takes one session at the machine
the ruined panel is replaced with fresh cloth in the same colour
the closing seam is done without a machine so as to stay discreet
the craftsman turns down repairs costing more than buying afresh
appointments are booked three weeks ahead
text: The man who runs an alterations workshop tells of a customer arriving with a coat whose lining was fraying under the arms. She had written the thing off, he says. The case is a common one: the lining, cut from a light cloth, gives way long before the woollen outer, since it takes all the rubbing at the shoulder. Putting it right takes one session at the machine. He unpicks the armhole, replaces the ruined panel with fresh satin in a matching shade, then closes the seam by hand so that no bulk shows. The coat will go on for another ten years, he adds, and he turns down any estimate that comes to more than the price of a replacement. His diary is full three weeks ahead, a sign that people are coming back to mending. Bring the coat in at the first dropped stitch, he advises.

units: colouring cloth once called for long preparation
the dyes came from crushed plants and animals
two baths one after the other did not give quite the same shade
old cloth carried the mark of whoever had worked it
a metal salt had to be added so the colour would not go at the rinse
chemical dyes overturned that practice
chemical dyes give one steady colour from batch to batch
those products stand up to washing and cost far less
old cloth told you about the harvest it came from
the text presents the steadiness gained as a loss of variety
text: Getting a clear, steady colour once called for a patience we have long since mislaid. Dye came out of pounded roots, boiled bark and crushed shells, and no two baths ever yielded quite the same shade. Cloth left the vat uneven and alive, marked by the hand that had lowered it in. The bath had to be fixed with a metal salt as well, or the colour ran away at the first rinse. Dyes born of chemistry overturned all that. They give one shade from roll to roll, they hold through washing, and they cost a fraction of what went before. The gain is real; so is the loss. Where a craftsman once read in a length of cloth the trace of a harvest and a season, we read nothing beyond a shade that can be repeated at will. Our wardrobes gained in evenness what our eyes gave up in surprise.

units: the text sets out three categories of textile material
the first category comes from animals
the fibre taken from a fleece traps air and keeps the cold out
the fibre drawn from a cocoon is smooth and glossy
the filling taken from beneath the feathers is very light and bulky
the second category comes from plants
the fibre from a stem dries quickly but creases
the third category is made industrially
those fibres come either from treated plant matter or from oil
an article combining two categories makes care trickier
text: Three families of fibre share out the contents of our wardrobes between them. The first gathers what comes from animals: wool, taken from a fleece, traps air in its crimp and keeps the cold out; silk, unwound from a cocoon, gives a smooth, glossy surface; down, gathered from beneath the feathers, weighs almost nothing and swells enormously. The second family covers what grows: cotton, drawn from a boll, soaks up moisture; linen, pulled from a stem, dries quickly but creases; hemp takes hard wear. The third is made in the works: some fibres come from treated plant matter, others from oil, and both can be spun as fine as you please. Each family sets its own care, its own wash temperature, its own way of drying. Anything mixing two families together makes that choice harder.

units: a craftsman works in a long-established quarter
a customer came in with a garment torn at the shoulder
the mishap happened the evening before an occasion
the craftsman looked at the tear through a magnifying instrument
metal fasteners were set to hold the area still
the cloth was held taut on a round support
the thread used was taken from a hidden seam of the garment
that thread was exactly the same colour as the cloth
the repair took up part of the evening
the trace showed only under a particular light
text: A tailor with premises in a long-established quarter was visited by a customer whose dress had torn at the shoulder the evening before a ceremony. He studied the tear through a magnifying glass, saw that the weave had given way across a short span, and told her the dress would be saved. He began by setting pins around the weakened area so that nothing could shift. Then he stretched the cloth over a wooden hoop, so the weave would not draw in on itself. He drew a thread out of an inner seam, one matching the colour of the dress exactly, and set about darning the tear stitch by patient stitch. The work took up a good part of the evening. By the end, the damage showed only under a lamp held at a low angle. The customer left without having to give up the outfit she had meant to wear.

units: the warmth of the water decides how washing a woollen knit turns out
water that is too hot opens the scales on the fibre
those open scales catch on one another and pack the knit tight
the garment then shrinks for good
a mild washing product is advised
rubbing and wringing by hand cause the same fault as heat
the water is to be taken out by pressing the garment in absorbent cloth
drying is done flat to avoid the garment losing its shape
this velvety material is not to be soaked but brushed dry
a light surface mark comes off with a rubber made for it
text: Before a woollen jumper goes anywhere near water, check the warmth of the bath, because that is what settles the outcome. Hot water opens the scales on the fibre; the scales then catch on one another, the knit felts, and the garment shrinks for good. Lukewarm water, by contrast, leaves the fibre as it was. A mild soap will do, since alkaline products attack those same scales. Do not rub and do not wring, because agitation felts the wool exactly as heat does. Press the garment between two towels instead, then lay it flat to dry; hung up, it would stretch under its own weight. Brushed leather follows other rules altogether. Soaking hardens its surface, so brush it dry with a soft brush, always in one direction. A light surface mark comes away with a rubber made for the purpose.

units: a sorting depot is overflowing with sacks of clothes
the place takes in ten tonnes of textile every week

the woman in charge has done this work for ten years
the main difficulty comes from materials combined in one article
an article mixing natural fibre and plastic fibre cannot be recycled
such articles end up burnt or shipped abroad
the woman in charge suggests making clothes from a single material
she calls for a label stating the make-up clearly
two towns that have opened a repair workshop destroy far less
text: In the sorting shed the sacks are stacked to the rafters and the smell of damp cloth catches in your throat. Ten tonnes come in every week, and half of it is worth nothing at all, says the woman who runs the place and has been sorting for ten years. The trouble is not the volume, she reckons, but the mixing: a tee shirt putting cotton together with plastic fibre cannot be recycled, because the two will not come apart. So it gets burnt, or shipped abroad. Her answer comes in three parts. Garments made from one material only; a label anyone can read, setting out exactly what is in the thing; and mending workshops close to the collection points. Two neighbouring towns have opened such a workshop, and the volume for destruction has dropped sharply. She hopes others will follow.

units: two outdoor garments hang next to each other
the first is made of a tightly woven woollen cloth in a dark colour
its surface feels like felt to the hand
its seams are reinforced and its collar rises very high
that garment is heavy and will last several cold seasons
the second is made of a coated fabric in a strong colour
the second squashes down enough to fit in a pocket
the second stops the wind better than the first
the second protects poorly once the air goes still
the woollen cloth covers itself in little balls while the fabric cracks at the folds
text: Two coats hanging side by side on the same rail turn out to have almost nothing in common. The first is cut from a thick woollen cloth in a deep grey, with a surface that drags at the hand like felt. Its seams are doubled, its buttons sewn through four holes, its collar rises right up to the jaw. It sits heavily on the shoulder, and it will last several winters without weakening. The second, in coated fabric of a bright blue, crumples up in a fist and folds away into a pocket. Its shiny lining slides along the sleeves and its zip runs unbroken from hem to chin. It cuts the wind better than its neighbour, yet it lets the cold through the moment the air goes still. The woollen cloth bobbles in patches, while the coated fabric cracks along the folds. One protects by its bulk, the other by its skin.

units: the shoulder of a jacket reveals how well it was made
you look at it by standing to one side
a shoulder seam falling straight means a carefully made garment
a shoulder seam that caves in signals mass production
the quality of the material is judged on the inner face of the cloth
you have to check whether the weave is tight or slack
the openings for buttons should have clean, even edges
the writer advises checking before buying whether the garment can be mended
an article with no part that can be replaced is not recommended
the writer judges that inability to mend an expensive thing
text: Nothing gives a wardrobe away like the shoulder of a jacket. Look at it from an angle: if the seam falls straight, somebody thought about the garment; if it caves in, it came off a line by the mile. The cut is judged in a second, before your hand ever reaches the cloth. The cloth itself is read on the wrong side, where you find out whether the weave is tight or slack. The finishing is read in the buttonholes, whose edges ought to be closed and even. Care, last of all, is settled at the moment of buying: a garment whose button cannot be changed and whose lining cannot be restitched deserves no attachment. A replaced lining wears as well as the first, provided a seam gives the needle something to grip. We wear things we would be helpless to mend, and that helplessness costs us more than we care to admit.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a craftswoman has taken over her family's workshop
the drying up of orders explains why she took it on
her training ran through sorting, then spinning, then the loom
she can identify a material simply by handling it
she refuses dyes that come out of industry
she draws her colours from boiled plant matter
the shades shift from one bath to the next
that variation appeals to buyers tired of standard output
rising sales have pushed her to take on a pupil
a thread held at the wrong tension spoils the whole piece
text: The weaver took over the family workshop because orders for blankets had dwindled to almost nothing. She learned the trade by stages: sorting fleeces first, then spinning, and at last weaving broad lengths of cloth. That slow apprenticeship left a mark on the way she works, for she can name a fibre by touch alone, without so much as a glance at it. Industrial dyes struck her as harsh, so she colours her skeins in baths of boiled roots and bark. No two vats give quite the same shade, and it is that very unevenness which draws customers weary of uniform cloth. Demand rose, and with it the need for help, so she took on an apprentice. The younger woman begins by learning to watch, since a thread pulled too tight will warp the whole piece. Patience, the weaver says, is no virtue here but a technical condition.

units: the speaker was disappointed by a knitted garment as soon as he put it on
the knit struck him as rough and irritating at the neck
the packaging promised a very soft material
an acquaintance who sews suggested a lukewarm wash with vinegar added
drying had to be done flat and without wringing by hand
after that treatment the knit turned supple and downy
the speaker now recommends this method to others who are unhappy
he considers the cut poor despite the improvement in feel
in his view no amount of care corrects a badly drafted pattern
he wears the garment only at home
text: That cardigan let me down the moment I tried it on. The knit felt scratchy, the collar rasped against my neck, and the wrapping had promised something soft as a cloud. I very nearly sent it back without a word. Then a friend who sews suggested a wash in lukewarm water with a splash of vinegar, followed by drying flat, never wrung out by hand. The change surprised me: the knit came out supple and almost downy, and the collar stopped prickling. Since then I pass the tip on to anyone grumbling about a rough jumper. My objection to the cut still stands, mind you. The sleeves hang too low, the shoulders gape, and no amount of washing rescues a badly drafted pattern. Put that right and the workshop would have an honest garment at a fair price. As things are, I wear it indoors and never past the front door.

units: the writer is writing from a place where clothes are repaired
the reader is hesitating between two kinds of shoe fastening
the buckled model goes on very quickly
the laced model calls for sitting down and adjusting the tension
lacing holds the joint of the foot better
the buckle often breaks at its fixing point
mending a buckle costs more than replacing laces
the writer advises lacing for uneven ground
he advises the buckle for short, repeated outings
he has set aside both pairs in the right size
text: I am writing from the alterations workshop, between fittings, because your question about shoes deserves a straight answer. You are torn between two fastenings: one shoe closes with a buckle, the other with laces. The buckle goes on in a single movement, which suits anyone heading out in a hurry. Laces make you sit down, pull them tight and check the tension across the instep, and in return they hold the ankle far better. Both kinds pass through my hands here. Buckles tend to give way at the rivet, and mending one costs a good deal more than a fresh set of laces. So if the ground underfoot is rough and broken, take the laced pair. If your day is a string of short errands, the buckle will serve. Write and tell me what you decide, for I have put aside a pair of each in your size.

units: the text asks what tells one material from another
each trade judges a cloth by its own criterion
the worker at the loom holds to weight
the woman who puts garments together holds to how a shape is kept
the one who colours holds to how much is absorbed
a plant fibre keeps creases that ironing never quite removes
the animal fibre offers a springiness that restores the shape
the most prestigious material makes those who speak of it fall silent
the most widespread fibre stirs little enthusiasm because it is ordinary
those who practise the trade know these materials with their eyes shut
text: What tells one cloth from another, if not the hand that judges it? The weaver answers by weight, the seamstress by how a piece holds its shape, the dyer by how greedily the fibre drinks. Each of them is right, and each says too little. Ask about linen and they speak of a dry coolness, of creases no iron ever quite smooths away. Ask about wool and they describe a warmth that breathes, a spring that carries the knit back to its shape. Ask about silk and their voices drop, as though the word on its own were enough. And cotton? It stirs no poetry, because it turns up everywhere and slips out of mind. There lies the riddle of these materials: they yield to description through their uses, never through their nature. Whoever handles them long enough comes to name them by touch, eyes shut.

units: a manager runs through the sequence of tasks before production starts
cutting is done on cloth laid flat and along the run of the threads
a crooked cut makes the garment twist in the wash
the person in charge of cutting says the templates were checked the day before
assembly begins with the shoulders and then the sleeves
the inner lining goes in after assembly
an employee asks whether the lining should be held with metal clips before stitching
the alignment between the clip and the stitch line is checked
the fastening is done last
the garment is done up on a dummy before dispatch to catch any misalignment
text: The workshop manager ran through the order of operations before the run began. The pieces are cut first, he said, on cloth laid perfectly flat and along the grain, or the jacket will twist the first time it is washed. The woman in charge of cutting replied that the pattern had been checked the day before and that the templates were sound. He went on: the shoulders are joined next, the sleeves are set in after that, and only then does the lining go in. One of the operators asked whether the lining should be clipped in place before stitching. The answer came back flat. Clip it, check that it hangs true, then stitch. The fastening comes last of all. Before anything leaves the workshop, the cutter added, the garment is done up on a dummy, because a misalignment shows on the stand and can still be put right.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the colour of a garment was worth more than the cloth itself
lasting dyes came from sea creatures, insects or uncommon plants
only small quantities were ever gathered
that scarcity made social standing readable on clothing
the depth of the red tones signalled the rank of a household
official rules barred certain colours to the lowest ranks
poor workshops fell back on neutral tones
the dress of ordinary people long kept a reputation for dullness
dyes drawn from an industrial residue overturned this arrangement
once bright colours became affordable, the shape of a garment replaced the dye as a mark of wealth
text: Colour once cost more than the cloth it was laid on, and that oddity weighed on the whole history of dress. Lasting pigments came from shellfish, from insects, from uncommon roots, and each of them yielded only a meagre harvest. Scarcity turned into a visible ranking, since you could read a household's standing in the depth of its reds and purples. The authorities widened the gap further by barring certain shades to the lower orders. Unable to dye within the law, humble workshops fell back on greys, browns and undyed cloth, which fixed for generations the notion that ordinary dress was drab. Then dyes drawn from a by-product of industry overturned the arrangement altogether. Once bright colour came within reach of every purse, it no longer marked out wealth, and the cut of a garment took over that office.

units: a recently made knitted garment quickly fills with small balls of fibre
this fault discourages people who have just bought one
short strands work outwards because of rubbing
these strands tangle and form visible clumps
yarns made of long, combed fibres move less against each other
it is better to choose a tight, flat knit at the time of buying
washing the garment in a protective bag reduces rubbing
a violent spin pulls out more fibres
a fabric shaver removes the clumps if the garment is stretched out flat
the operation can be repeated without damaging the knit
text: A jumper straight out of the shop soon covers itself in tiny balls of fibre, and that wear puts off whoever has only just bought it. The cause is mechanical: short fibre ends work their way to the surface under rubbing, tangle together, then build into little knots that catch the eye. Yarns spun from long, well-combed fibres slide over one another and pill far less. The first move therefore comes at the counter, where a dense, smooth knit is worth more than a fluffy one. After that, care counts as much as the material does. Washing inside a mesh bag, with no violent spin, cuts down the friction that tears fibres loose. And when knots do appear, a fabric shaver lifts them away cleanly, provided the garment is stretched flat and never pulled. The knit looks crisp again afterwards, and the treatment can be repeated without harm.

units: a woman living on the floor above owned two outdoor garments
one was made of a dense and very heavy woollen cloth
the other was cut from a waterproofed canvas and weighed little
she took the heavy garment out on evenings of strong wind
she took the light garment when it was raining
the narrator wanted to name one model as the better of the two
he borrowed the woollen garment in the rain and it soaked up water
drying it took two evenings
the light garment gave no protection from the cold
the narrator now chooses according to the state of the sky
text: The woman upstairs kept two coats in one wardrobe, and one evening she explained the difference to me. The first, thick and cut from felted woollen cloth, sat on the shoulders like a suit of armour. The second, made of oiled canvas, weighed almost nothing and folded away into a bag. She took the heavy one out when the wind bit, the light one when the rain came straight down. I wanted to settle the matter and crown one of them the better coat, and I was wrong. Caught in a downpour, I borrowed the woollen coat, and it drank the water like a sponge. Drying it out took two evenings. The other, for its part, left my back frozen the moment the cold set in. Now I stand at the wardrobe and choose by the look of the sky rather than by my own liking. Learning the hard way, my neighbour called it.

units: the text gives an ironing method that comes from professionals
a padded board, an iron with no deposit and a water spray are needed
the pockets are emptied before starting
the collar is unfastened and the cloth lightly dampened
the fabric must turn soft to the touch before the iron passes over it
the order runs from collar to cuffs, then sleeves, then back and fronts
small areas are dealt with before large ones
the heat is set for the least resistant material in the garment
a test is made on a hidden seam
the garment is left to cool on a support before being done up
text: Here is the method that professional pressers recommend for taking the creases out of a shirt without scorching it. For kit, you want a padded board, an iron with a clean plate and a spray bottle of clear water within reach. For preparation, empty the pockets, unfasten the collar and damp the cloth lightly until it turns soft under the fingers. For order of work, begin at the collar, move on to the cuffs, then the sleeves, and finish with the back and the fronts, because narrow areas come before broad ones and large panels crumple last. For heat, set the iron to suit the most delicate fibre anywhere in the garment, and test it on a hidden seam first. For putting away, let the shirt cool on a hanger before you do it up, or the damp trapped inside will press in fresh creases.

units: the smell of wet wool filled the building at opening time
the workers in charge of shearing had come the day before
the fleeces were piled against the wall
an employee pulled out the dirty locks one by one
the pressed bales were then sent to be washed
hot water rid the fibre of its grease
carding followed the drying and threw off a dust that made people cough
a worker made a trial piece with the yarn that had just been produced
the collective body wants to revive a trade killed off by buying from abroad
the order books remain far too thin
text: The shed smelled of damp wool as the doors slid open, a little before dawn. The shearers had come the evening before, and the fleeces lay heaped in downy piles along the wall. In the first hour a sorter picked out the soiled locks, one after another, without lifting her head. Around the middle of the session the pressed bales went off to be washed, where warm water carried the grease away. Later the dried fibre passed through the carding machine, and the white cloud it threw off set the visitors coughing. At the end of the line a worker knitted a sample in front of the onlookers, using the first yarn to come off the frame. The cooperative hopes to revive a trade that buying from abroad had killed off. Nothing is settled yet: orders are still thin, and the shearers are growing old.

units: a thick wool jacket soaks up water in a downpour
the wet cloth weighs on the shoulders and pulls the sleeves out of shape
the lining holds the damp for the whole evening
workshops spread a warm wax over the outer surface
the wax closes the tiny gaps without stopping the fibre from breathing
a thin membrane can be set between the wool and the lining
that film lets the vapour off the back escape and turns away the drops
the treated garment keeps its softness and its cut
brushing followed by a fresh coat of wax extends the protection
text: A heavy wool jacket drinks a downpour without a sound, and then it sits on the shoulders like a wet sponge. The cloth swells, the sleeves lose their shape, and the lining hangs on to the damp for the rest of the evening. Workshops looked for an answer that would not ruin the fibre. They spread a fine wax over the outer face, warm enough to sink in, and it closes the tiny gaps without smothering the cloth. Rain stays out, yet the jacket still breathes. Another route is to slip a thin membrane between the wool and the lining. That film lets the vapour off the back escape and turns away the drops arriving from outside. The garment keeps its soft fall, its clean cut and its comfort. Regular care stretches the effect: brush the surface, lay on fresh wax, and the protection holds for a whole season.

units: the speaker finds the choice between natural fibre and manufactured fibre a badly framed question
fine wool warms without adding weight
wool takes up sweat and releases it without smell
wool forms little balls when it rubs against a bag
manufactured fibre dries quickly and stands up to scuffing
manufactured fibre clings to the skin as soon as you exert yourself
a loose knit forgives a large meal and takes layers underneath
a tight top draws the outline of the body and demands an exact size
the speaker keeps both options and decides according to the use
text: People keep asking me whether to pick a natural knit or a manufactured fibre, and I think the question is framed wrongly from the start. The two families are not promising the same thing. Fine wool warms you without weight, it takes up the sweat off your back and gives it away again with no smell; against that, it pills the moment it rubs on a bag strap. A manufactured fibre dries fast and shrugs off scuffing, but it clings to the skin as soon as you push yourself. Look at the cut as well, because a good part of the comfort really lives there and nowhere else. A loose jumper forgives a big meal and takes layers underneath; a tight top draws the outline of the body and demands an exact size. Honestly, I keep both in the wardrobe and decide by the use I have in mind, whatever the shop assistants preach.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the dyer works in a workshop with a low ceiling
she sorts her skeins before lowering them into the bath
she identifies fibres by touch
she prepares her baths from bark and roots
her baths give a deep blue or a shifting red
she records every proportion in a notebook
without those notes a successful bath could not be repeated
her customers bring her worn woollens and speckled jackets
these customers refuse to get rid of their clothes
text: In a workshop with a low ceiling, the dyer sorts her skeins before she lowers them into the bath. Her craft comes down to three moves, and she describes them without any fuss. The first is about matter: her fingers tell a silky thread from a coarse waste, and both from a combed cotton. The second is about colour: she builds her baths out of bark and roots, then draws a deep blue or a shifting red whose strength changes under the sun. The third is about memory: she writes every proportion into a stained notebook, because a bath that works is never found again by luck. Her customers bring her tired woollens, dulled scarves, jackets of speckled cloth they refuse to throw out. She promises very little, she hands back honest, straightforward colours, and that stained notebook is worth more to her than the vat itself.

units: the narrator finds a quilted coat on a modest rail
at first he thinks it lacks elegance
the following weeks contradict that first judgement
the quilting traps a layer of warm air under the rain
the high collar keeps the wind out without gripping the throat
the cloth marked by the journeys takes on a living look
at the end of winter the garment grows lighter once the layers are removed
the narrator concludes that a garment is judged by use and not on display
text: I came across this quilted coat on a modest rail one autumn evening, and I wrote it off as graceless: too thick, too well behaved, sewn for sensible people. The weeks that followed proved me wrong. Under thin rain the quilting held a layer of warm air that nothing could scatter, and my shoulder stayed dry. When the wind began to run down the narrow streets, the high collar showed its intelligence: it closed the throat without gripping it. Then came the squalls, and the cloth, creased by all those journeys, took on a living look, almost drawn by hand, which unworn cloth never shows. At the end of winter, stripped of the layers it had sheltered, it grew light again and found a straight line. I will say it plainly: a garment is not judged on a hanger, but after a season of rain, wind and repeated journeys.

units: the reader has washed a jumper that shrank
the wool fibre is covered with microscopic scales
heat lifts those scales
the churning of the machine tangles the fibres together
tangled fibres cannot return to their original position
the shrinking is therefore beyond repair
washing must be done in cold water without a fierce spin
drying must be done flat on a towel
a rinse with vinegar added softens the knit
text: Dear neighbour, you asked what happened to your jumper, and the answer is purely mechanical. A wool fibre is not smooth: it carries tiny scales all along it, set and overlapping like roof tiles. Hot water lifts those scales away from the shaft. The drum then pushes the fibres against one another, over and over, and the raised edges catch on each other like little hooks. The knit tightens, the surface goes hard and boardy, and the garment loses a whole size. No amount of ironing will undo that tangle, since the scales stay locked into each other for good. With the next piece, wash it in cold water, spin it gently if you spin it at all, and dry it flat on a thick towel. A final rinse with a splash of vinegar softens the knit again and gives it back the easy fall it had at the start. Love from me.

units: the question is whether to give up fine knits because they pill
pilling comes from short fibres that work their way to the surface
rubbing rolls those fibres into little balls
a long twisted yarn cuts this fault down sharply
the garment must be turned inside out before washing
loads mixing in rough materials should be avoided
a fabric shaver lifts the balls without digging into the knit
the jumper must be stored folded and not hung up
a well treated garment holds up over many long seasons
text: Should fine knits be given up simply because they pill? The answer calls for a distinction. The fault begins with short fibres that work their way to the surface, and rubbing then rolls them into tight little balls. A long, well twisted yarn cuts that down sharply, and the composition label tells you more about it than the look of the garment or the price on display. What can be done with a piece already affected? Turn it inside out before washing, keep it out of loads that mix in rough materials, and run a fabric shaver over it, which lifts the balls without digging into the knit. Should storage change as well? It should: a close-fitting jumper sags at the shoulders as soon as it hangs, so it belongs folded flat. Handled that way, a fine woollen lasts many long seasons without drooping or dulling.

units: a customer hesitates between two jackets
the fitted cut flatters him but hampers the movement of his arms
the wide cut leaves freedom of movement
the customer fears the wide cut will make him look scruffy
the assistant advises taking the intended use into account
the fitted jacket suits meetings and sit-down meals
the wide jacket suits moving about and carrying bags
the assistant offers to take in the shoulders of the wide jacket
the customer leaves with the wide jacket after that offer
text: The customer stood between two jackets hanging side by side on the rail and set out his difficulty straight away. The fitted cut, he said, flattered him, and yet it locked his arm the moment he reached towards a shelf. The wide cut gave him back his freedom, at the risk of making him look scruffy. The assistant listened, then offered a useful comparison. The first jacket, she said, suits meetings and sit-down meals, where you move little and the outline counts. The second goes with moving about, with journeys spent on your feet, with bags carried on the shoulder. She added that a small alteration at the shoulders would tighten the second one without taking away its ease. The customer thought it over for a moment, then walked out with the wide jacket and the alteration agreed.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the first cloths come from stalks soaked in water
these stalks give a cool fibre that creases easily
the taming of flocks supplies a warm and springy fibre
spinning this fibre is learnt from childhood
a shining thread is obtained from unwound cocoons
this shining thread travels over long distances
a downy plant capsule gives a washable and cheap cloth
looms then produce a ribbed velvet
each new material has changed the ordinary wardrobe
text: Have you ever wondered where the cloth we wear comes from? Let us go through them family by family, without hurrying. The oldest of them come out of stalks left to soak in water, beaten and then combed: from that comes a cool fibre, pleasant in warm weather, which creases at the slightest movement. Next comes the fleece of tamed flocks, warm and springy, spun in the home by hands trained from childhood on. Later a shining thread appears, unwound from cocoons, light enough to carry along endless roads and dear enough to be kept for formal dress alone. A downy plant capsule finally gives a washable cloth, cheap to make, dressing whole populations. Improved looms add corduroy in their turn, a thick ribbed velvet. Every one of these materials has redrawn the ordinary wardrobe in its own way.

units: the fleece is taken off the animal in one piece
a wash removes the grease and the dust
carding pulls the fibres apart and lays them in one direction
twisting turns the ribbon of fibres into strong yarn
the yarn is then stretched on a loom to form a cloth
dyeing can be done on the yarn or on the finished cloth
milling in water draws the cloth together and makes it denser
cutting and stitching complete the making of the garment
text: It all starts in a sheep shed, when the shearer takes the whole fleece off in one piece. That greasy mass goes into the wash: the grease and the dust are rinsed away, the twigs are picked out, and the wool is spread to dry. Then comes carding, which pulls the tangled strands apart and lays them in a single direction. The ribbon that results goes to the wheel or the machine, where twist turns it into strong yarn. The yarn is stretched on a loom, crossed patiently with a second, and an even cloth grows steadily under the weaver's hands. Dyeing happens at this stage, or much earlier, on the bare yarn. A milling in warm water then draws the fibres closer and makes the surface denser, softer under the hand. Cutting and stitching finish the long passage from the animal to the garment worn.

units: the night watchman wears a badly worn coat
he lends this coat to an apprentice who is shivering
the apprentice discovers a lining sewn by hand
the lining holds embroidered initials and a hidden pocket
the pocket contains a piece of shining cloth
the watchman explains that this piece comes from his mother's dress
the apprentice has the coat mended by a seamstress
the watchman accepts the repair but refuses a replacement garment
text: The night watchman's coat was worn through at the elbows, and that had never troubled the man who owned it. An apprentice stood shivering outside the empty warehouse, her hands under her arms, and he held it out to her without a word of explanation. As she pulled it closed she felt a lining sewn by hand, with initials embroidered in dark thread and a pocket hidden under the seam. Inside it she found a square of silky cloth, glossy, soft as still water against her frozen fingers. The watchman said at last that the square came from a dress his mother had worn, and that he had tucked it there to keep it on him. The apprentice took the coat to a seamstress, who rebuilt the elbows and strengthened the sleeves. The watchman accepted the repair. He flatly refused the replacement coat he was offered afterwards.

units: a notebook heads the list of recommended kit
the torch in use must have a red filter to spare the dark-adapted eye
the steady mount is described as the item people neglect most
an instrument that shakes gives no usable image
the optical instrument comes only fourth on the list
a cheap model is judged good enough to start with
two eyepieces of different magnifications are recommended
a star chart is needed to find your way among the stars
going out regularly counts for more than the quality of the kit
text: Fancy a look at the night sky without spending a fortune? Start with the short list. A notebook comes first, because what you jot down beats what you half remember. Next a torch with a red filter, which spares an eye already settled into the dark. Then the mount, the bit everyone neglects and the bit that decides everything: an instrument that shakes will show you nothing. The telescope itself turns up only fourth, and a modest one is plenty for a beginner. Take two eyepieces as well, one for sweeping across a wide patch, the other for pulling in a detail. Add a star chart at the end, on paper or on a screen, or you will wander from one point of light to the next and recognise none of them. The kit counts for less than the habit. Go out often, even briefly, and your eye will learn on its own to tell what moves from what stays put.

units: the turning part of the building stayed jammed on the opening night
the guests waited outside while the trouble lasted
two technicians went up to check the mechanism
a piece of metal was caught in the rotation rail
one technician pulled the obstruction out and the other greased the gearing
the structure began to swing round again with a low rumble
the crowd first took that noise for a storm
the man in charge of the site gave an unprepared speech
the papers revealed the next day that the obstruction came from the building works themselves
text: On the opening night the dome flatly refused to turn. Guests waited on the terrace, glass in hand, while two technicians climbed the inner ladder to look at the mechanism. Wedged in the circular rail they found a strip of metal, dropped there at some forgotten moment. One of them worked it loose with a screwdriver; the other greased the gearing. Half an hour on, the whole frame began to swing round again with a low rumble that the crowd took at first for thunder. The shutter opened on a clear sky, and the man in charge of the site, plainly relieved, made a short speech he had not prepared. What he left out reached the papers the next morning: the offending strip had come from the building works themselves, a bolt left behind by the fitters, and it had very nearly wrecked an evening two years in the making.

units: hands must be dry and free of jewellery before the work begins
a greasy smear draws the particles that scratch the surface
the work is done in a closed room to keep draughts out
the disc is rinsed under lukewarm water with no cloth at all
fabric shifts the grains instead of carrying them off
every grain shifted digs a furrow that scatters the light of the stars
the water must drain off by itself before the rim is dried
repeated washing wears the reflecting film faster than the surrounding air does
text: Before you lay a hand on the mirror, dry it well and take off every ring you wear. The faintest smear of grease draws in dust, and dust will score the surface at the first rub. Set the piece down flat in a closed room, since one draught brings back onto the glass everything you have just cleared away. Rinse the disc under lukewarm water and use no cloth at all: fabric pushes the grains along instead of carrying them off, and each grain you shift leaves a small furrow that will scatter the light of the stars. Let the water drain away by itself, then blot the rim dry with a sheet of soft paper. If marks still remain, do not go at it again the following day. Wait a whole season, because washing too often wears out the thin reflecting film far quicker than a year of open air ever would.

units: the manoeuvres flown to avoid a collision are multiplying
the cause lies in the build-up of debris in low orbit
a tiny fragment can pierce a reinforced wall because of its speed
each impact breeds fresh fragments whose course becomes unpredictable
the problem therefore keeps feeding itself
the first answer is to catalogue the objects by radar
the second obliges craft to carry a fuel reserve to bring them down at the end of the mission
the third answer, still at the trial stage, plans the capture of a bulky piece of debris
text: Satellite operators report a steady rise in the number of manoeuvres flown to dodge a collision. Behind it lies a growing crowd of debris in low orbit: spent rocket parts, bolts, flakes of paint, all travelling fast enough that a chip the size of a fingernail will punch through an armoured wall. Every impact breeds fresh fragments, whose paths in turn grow hard to predict, so the risk keeps feeding itself. Agencies are testing three answers. The first is to catalogue what is up there by radar, in order to see close approaches coming. The second obliges each craft to carry a fuel reserve so that they can be pushed back towards the atmosphere once their work is done. The third, still at the trial stage, sends a chaser to seize a bulky piece of wreckage with a net or a harpoon and drag it down.

units: two neighbouring circular hollows show opposite aspects
the older one has a softened rim that has almost gone
its floor is lined with fine particles stirred by later impacts
the more recent one has a sharp wall cut into terraces
a pointed relief still stands at the centre of the recent formation
no pale streak surrounds the older formation
faint rays reach far out around the recent formation
those rays come from the material thrown clear at the impact
low light hollows out a marked shadow on the recent formation only
both formations belong to the same natural satellite
text: Two neighbouring craters offer the observer opposite kinds of relief. The older one shows a rounded rim, worn almost flat by time, and a floor lined with fine dust that later impacts have stirred over and over again. The younger raises a sharp wall cut into a run of terraces, and a pointed peak still stands on its floor. The contrast goes further than the ground itself. Around the old basin no pale streak survives; around the young one a web of faint rays stretches out a great distance, the mark of material thrown clear at the moment of the blow. Grazing light widens the gap again: the older hollow drowns in a single flat tone, while its neighbour cuts a hard, drawn-out shadow. One and the same natural satellite therefore carries, side by side, two faces of very different ages.

units: the piece raises the question of switching signs off after midnight
the writer refuses to treat the subject from the point of view of sky watchers alone
a beam aimed at the ground costs less than a beam scattered about
steady artificial brightness harms the sleep of people living nearby
it also sends migrating birds off course
a generation is reaching adulthood without having seen the milky band of our galaxy
the writer sees in that loss the end of a landmark shared by all humanity
not one of the points raised calls for complete darkness
the conclusion argues for aimed lighting, dimmed at night, and for protected areas
text: Should lit signs go off after midnight? The question deserves more than one angle, and it should not be left to those who watch the sky. Take the cost first: light aimed at the ground burns less than a beam scattered upwards. Take health next, since steady artificial brightness disturbs the sleep of people living nearby and sends migrating birds off course. Take, last, the point that looks weakest of all, the cultural one: a whole generation is reaching adulthood without ever having seen the milky band of our galaxy, and a landmark shared by all humanity is quietly lost. Not one of these points calls for complete darkness. Together they argue for lighting that is sparing, aimed downwards, dimmed after a certain hour, and for protected stretches of country where the sky stays black.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: she came into the optical workshop as a cleaner
she had no qualification at the outset
the workshop foreman gave her nothing but cleaning tasks
she took up on her own a glass disc that an apprentice had spoiled
she polished that disc through a whole night
the foreman examined the surface and put her on the bench
she could feel under her thumb flaws that no instrument of the day could measure
the delicate orders were kept for her
she passed on to two apprentices the rule never to force the glass
her last mirror is still in use and the team using it does not know who she was
text: She came into the optical workshop as a cleaner, very young, with no qualification behind her and nobody to speak for her. The foreman handed her buckets and sawdust, and nothing more. One evening she took up on her own a glass disc that an apprentice had spoiled, and she polished it until daybreak. The next morning the foreman held the surface up to a lamp, studied it, then put her on the bench. She never left it again. She learned to feel under her thumb a dip that no instrument of the day could measure, and the most delicate orders ended up at her place. Towards the end she trained two apprentices, repeating a single rule to them: never force the glass. The last mirror she polished still serves under a dome in the hills, and the team using it has no idea who she was.

units: the show traces the birth of a star and then its end
the images are judged unusually sharp
that quality comes from the scanning of genuine archive plates
the pace never slackens at any point
the lack of pauses ends up blunting the wonder of the audience
the unbroken music adds a needless weight of emphasis
the commentary explains too much and leaves nothing to imagine
the reviewer holds that a shorter show would have stayed with people longer
text: The show impresses, and that in the end is what undoes it. The seats tilt back, the vault lights up above you, and in one sitting you watch a star take shape, swell, and then collapse. The images have a sharpness you rarely meet, because the team scanned genuine archive plates one by one before setting them in motion. But the pace never slackens for a moment, and that want of breath produces the opposite of what was wanted: after a run of cosmic disasters, the viewer in the seat simply stops being amazed. The music, unbroken as well, adds a weight of emphasis the subject never needed. The commentary, for its part, explains far too much and leaves nothing to be guessed at. A shorter sitting, broken by silences and by a sky held still, would surely have stayed with people far longer.

units: the letter arrived the day before the sun was covered over
the person written to says he is giving up on watching
he pleads the want of an instrument and the want of nerve
the writer suggests pricking a sheet of card with a needle
the card held above a page throws an image shaped like a crescent
that method rules out any risk to the sight
a pale ring may close around the disc if cloud comes over
having no instrument invites you to watch the ground, the birds and the temperature
the writer asks for an account of what was felt
text: Your letter reached me the day before the eclipse, and I read it standing in the cold. You tell me you are giving up on watching, having neither an instrument nor the nerve for it. Let me put something else to you. Take a sheet of card, prick it with a needle, hold it at arm's length above a white page: the sun will draw a crescent there of its own accord, thinning as you watch, and your sight will be in no danger. If cloud comes over, do not go indoors. A pale ring may then close around the disc, and that circle alone is worth the walk out. As for having no instrument, it obliges you to look about you rather than up: the colour of the ground shifts, the birds go quiet, the air turns cold in a moment. None of that calls for equipment, or for any outlay. Write and tell me afterwards what you felt, and not what you thought you ought to feel.

units: the question concerns the difference between two rings seen around a heavenly body
the distinction lies in the matter crossed and in the optics at work
the first ring forms in high cloud made of ice crystals
those crystals bend the light through a fixed angle
the ring obtained is wide, whitish and steady in size
the second ring forms in low cloud full of droplets or in a veil of particles
it comes from diffraction and not from bending
that ring is narrow, coloured and pressed against the disc
its width varies with the size of the particles
a wide pale ring points to ice, a tight iridescent ring points to droplets or grains
text: A reader asks us how a halo differs from a corona, given that both of them wrap the body in a ring. The answer lies in the matter the light crosses and in the optics at work. A halo forms in very high cloud made of ice crystals with six faces, which bend the rays through a fixed angle; the circle you end up with is wide, whitish, and much the same size from one occasion to the next. A corona forms instead in low cloud loaded with droplets, or in a thin veil of fine dust, and it comes of diffraction rather than bending: that ring is narrow, coloured, pressed close against the disc, and its width follows the size of the particles. So keep one simple practical test in mind. A broad pale ring points to ice; a tight ring shot through with colour points to droplets or to small grains.

units: a neighbour recounts a night of observing
the instrument was set up on a balcony late in the evening
she first took a blurred streak for a plane
the sky then cleared
she recognised the comet that had been announced
she woke her brother, who grumbled before joining her
she noticed the object shifting between two glances
she plans to go again the next night, better equipped
text: My neighbour was still laughing about her night at the eyepiece when she told me the whole of it. She had set the instrument up on her balcony late in the evening, once the light had drained out of the sky. At first, she said, she could make out nothing but a smear of brightness, which she put down to a passing plane. Then the cloud broke up, and she saw where she had gone wrong: the pale streak she had been squinting at for half an hour was the comet everyone had been talking about. She woke her brother, who grumbled at being hauled out of bed and came out in his slippers all the same. Between one look and the next, she noticed, the thing had shifted along. She means to go up again the following night, with a flask and a blanket, having shivered for hours without once noticing.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: glassmakers learned to polish even surfaces
the first instruments stopped distorting the images
stars until then invisible became observable
observers moved from description to measurement
star catalogues grew richer and more reliable
blurred patches turned out to be groups of stars
steadier mounts had to be built
a craft of precision mechanics was born of that need
text: Better lenses reshaped the study of the sky far beyond anything their makers had in mind. Once glassmakers worked out how to polish a surface evenly, the earliest instruments stopped bending what they showed, and stars nobody had ever seen came within reach. That sharpness had a further effect: observers gave up describing what they remembered and began measuring what lay in front of them. Catalogues grew thicker and steadier, and faint patches long taken for smears turned out to be crowds of separate stars. Mounts had to be rebuilt as well, since a trembling tube threw away everything the glass had gained. Out of that need came a whole craft of precision mechanics, with its worm screws, its gearing and its counterweights. Step by step, the glassmaker's bench changed the way the night sky was questioned.

units: a diffuse brightness hides the stars above built-up areas
the cause is the beam of lamps aimed upward
particles held in the air scatter that beam
faint stars become impossible to pick out
observers have to travel away from towns
tilting the lamps towards the ground and hooding them solves the problem
places that have applied this measure see their galaxy again
the measure also helps sleep, birds and spending
text: A milky glow now sits over every built-up area, and the stars behind it go out one by one. The trouble starts with lamps that throw part of their beam upward, where dust and damp air scatter it in every direction. A dome of brightness gathers above the rooftops, and the weaker stars simply drown in it. Anyone after a dark sky has to drive further and further out to find one. The cure costs next to nothing: tilt the fittings towards the ground and hood them so that no light escapes above the horizontal. Towns that have done so watch the pale band of our own galaxy come back over their squares. Residents sleep less fitfully, migrating birds find their bearings again, and the lighting bill drops. A dark sky has not been lost for good; it is waiting for someone to reach for the switch.

units: a stock farmer brings in a dark stone found on his land
a specialist compares it with an already authenticated sample
the two blocks look alike from the outside
cutting them open reveals differences inside
the authenticated sample holds frozen droplets and metal
the farmer's stone holds only stretched cavities
it comes in fact from foundry waste
magnetic pull explains the usual confusion
analysis of the metal content settled the question
text: A stock farmer carried a black stone into the laboratory, picked up in one of his fields and, he was certain, fallen out of the sky. The technician set it beside a reference sample, a meteorite recovered from a desert and catalogued long before. The two might have been twins: dark crust, surprising heft for their size, edges worn smooth. Cutting them open pulled their histories apart. The reference piece showed tiny frozen droplets, the beads found throughout the oldest rock, along with a bright metallic web that came up under polishing. The stone from the field held nothing but stretched bubbles, the mark of foundry slag cooled far too quickly. A magnet clung to both, which is why finders are so regularly misled. Only the ratio between two neighbouring metals settled it, and the farmer went home with an old lump of industrial waste.

units: preparing a session follows a settled order
power and backup lighting come first
a red torch keeps night vision from being spoiled
the optics must be aligned and cleaned before dark
the finder is set on a distant target while it is still light
the mount must stand on firm ground
the axis of the mount must point at the pole star
the observer should plan for clothing and a hot drink
the charts are gathered last of all
text: Getting ready for a night at the eyepiece works best in a settled order. Power comes first: a charged battery, cables coiled, a red torch so that notes can be read without wrecking your night vision. Optics next: the mirror aligned, the eyepieces wiped with a proper cloth, the finder trained on some distant landmark while there is still daylight to do it by. Then the mount, legs spread wide on firm ground, its axis swung round until it points at the pole star, so that tracking stays smooth for hours. Comfort deserves the same care: layers of clothing, a hot drink, a seat you can adjust, because sitting still chills you faster than you would think. Last of all, gather the paperwork, sky chart, target list, notebook and pencil. A wasted night rarely comes down to the kit; it comes down to something forgotten in the rush out of the door.

units: the craft left its parking orbit on instruction from the ground
short burns corrected a sideways drift
the pictures sent back showed at first a grey cratered plain
the ground proved rougher than expected
the original landing site was given up during the descent
sharp-edged boulders lay across the planned zone
a faint signal confirmed contact with the ground
dust thrown up by the thrusters settled without a cloud
drilling is announced after a recharging phase
text: The probe left its parking orbit shortly before dawn, on instructions sent up from the control room. All the way down its thrusters fired in short bursts, trimming out a sideways drift that had been spotted the day before. The pictures relayed home showed a grey plain pitted with shallow craters, and then ground a good deal rougher than anyone had allowed for. Halfway through the descent the team gave up on the site they had chosen, since sharp-edged boulders were sitting right across it. Contact was confirmed by a faint signal, arriving with the usual travel delay, to applause in the room. A side camera then caught the dust thrown up by the nozzle, which settled straight back without hanging in the air. Drilling, the mission leads said, would begin after a rest period, the lander having to charge its batteries in the sunlight first.

units: the crew spend their breaks at the observation window
the planet looks blue and streaked with white
the speed of the craft brings sunset round again and again
the lack of gravity sets loose objects floating
every piece of kit has to be fixed down or strapped
water pulling back leaves sandbanks in view
the glazing is thick and built up in several layers
a speck of grit at that speed would pierce an ordinary wall
passing into shadow brings condensation
text: Put your face to the window and you see at once why the crew spend every break here. Below, a blue marble streaked with white slides past, near enough that you can pick out the bends of the rivers. The craft moves so fast that dusk keeps coming round again: the sky catches fire, goes out, and catches fire once more. Inside, nothing ever drops. Weightlessness sends pens drifting up to the ceiling, so every tool has to be strapped down or held by a magnet. Along one coast a paler fringe shows through, because the water has pulled back off the sandbanks there. The glazing is thick, built up in layers, since a speck of grit travelling at that speed would go clean through an ordinary wall. When the station swings into shadow the pane mists over, and you wait for the warmth to come round again.

units: low orbit is filling with dead craft and fragments
each fragment travels fast enough to pierce a hull
each collision breeds fresh fragments
some altitudes risk becoming unusable
the lack of a binding rule keeps everyone idle
every craft ought to carry the means to leave its orbit at the end of its life
a passive tracking device would make avoidance more reliable
recovery vehicles ought to capture the heaviest wrecks
the cost of these measures is small against the loss of access
text: Must we wait for a serious collision before anything is done? Low orbit is filling up with wreckage: spent rocket stages, dead satellites, splinters left behind by destructive tests. Every one of those shards moves fast enough to punch through a hull, and every impact breeds fresh shards, which puts whole bands of altitude at risk of becoming unusable. Operators pass the blame round between them, no binding rule obliging any of them to act. Three steps would turn this round. Require, first, that every craft carry enough propellant to drop itself out of orbit once its work is over. Impose, second, a passive tracking device, so that avoidance manoeuvres stop resting on guesswork. Fund, third, tugs able to grapple the heaviest hulks. The bill looks steep until you set it against the loss of an access our networks take for granted.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a cataloguer of nebulae worked from a desk
her colleagues observed directly under the dome
cloud often cut their sessions short
she examined photographic plates through a magnifier
she measured the spread and the shade of pale patches
her colleagues offered impressions, she offered measurements
a single plate took up a whole session
one scratch was enough to spoil the examination
she told two kinds of diffuse object apart
those who came after inherited her classification
text: The woman who kept the register of nebulae hardly ever left her desk, and it was from there that she saw further than the colleagues posted under the dome. They watched on perhaps one night in two, and cloud shut them down more often than not. She sat over photographic plates instead, holding pale smudges side by side, measuring how far they spread, noting their shade through a magnifier. Where the others wrote down an impression, she wrote down a figure. Her patience was that of a needleworker: one plate swallowed a whole session, and a single scratch across the glass could ruin the lot. In the end she sorted the fuzzy objects into two families, the one woven out of gas, the other made of stars beyond counting. Those who came after inherited a classification that no run of nights under the dome would have produced.

units: the instrument tested belongs to the cheapest range
the mirror gives sharp stars right to the edge of the field
the mount lacks weight and shakes at the slightest touch
every focusing move sets off a wobble to be waited out
the eyepiece supplied gives a narrow field and a soft image
the diagonal throws unwanted reflections
the finder adjusts without tools and holds its alignment
the manual says nothing about adjusting the mirrors
the verdict advises replacing the mount first
text: The budget instrument we put through its paces deserves judging part by part, with no allowances made. The optics first: the main mirror has an honest figure to it, and stars stay as points right out to the edge of the field, which is more than the price would lead you to expect. The mount next, far too light, shuddering at a touch, so that every twist of the focuser sets off a wobble you must simply wait out. The accessories disappoint. The eyepiece in the box gives a cramped field and a soft image, while the diagonal throws stray reflections across bright stars. The finder, to be fair, adjusts by hand and holds its alignment from one night to the next. Then the manual, hurried in the writing and silent on adjusting the mirrors, which the buyer will be facing inside a week. Verdict: a decent tube on a mount not up to carrying it.

units: the writer explains what got her out of bed so early
an observing club had flagged the passing of a celestial body
the clear sky decided her to take her telescope along
she drove for a good while before reaching the spot
the planet passed very close to the lunar disc and was then hidden
the steady air made the image very sharp
she made out detail she cannot reach from home
the cold delayed the settling of the instrument to the outside temperature
she invites the person she writes to to come with her the following night
text: You wanted to know what dragged me out of bed before dawn, so here is the whole story. The observing club had flagged a very close passing, and since the sky looked like staying clear, I loaded the telescope into the back of the car. Three quarters of an hour of driving, frozen fingers, and what a sight it was. The planet skimmed the edge of the lunar disc, then went behind it all at once, with no fading. The air was so steady that the image barely shivered, and I picked out detail that I never manage to get from my own balcony. The night being bitter, the tube took an age to settle to the outside air, so I spent a long stretch stamping about and breathing into my gloves. Now I understand what the old observers meant. Come out with me tomorrow night, and you will see the difference straight away.

units: the interview deals with the crowding of the near orbits
craft that have stopped working keep circling the globe after their mission ends
a collision throws off a swarm of fragments
a tiny strike can pierce a tank
a tiny strike can tear off a receiving element
the specialist recommends a planned descent designed in from the outset
she also proposes catching the debris already up there with a net or a harpoon
the debris caught would be steered towards a controlled fall into the sea
she judges the solution workable only if the operators take up one common rule
text: Should we be alarmed at how crowded the low orbits have become? The engineer we spoke to answers without hedging: craft that have stopped working carry on circling above our heads long after their working life has ended, and every knock throws off a swarm of fragments. What does a working satellite risk? A tiny strike is enough to pierce a tank or tear an aerial away. Her remedy? First a planned descent, paid for and designed in while the craft is still being drawn up. Then a clear out of what is already up there, debris caught in a net or on a harpoon and steered down to a safe fall into the sea. Is that workable? She believes so, provided that the operators take up one common rule and hold to it. With no shared constraint, she says, each operator pushes the cost onto the next one.

units: the keeper of the dome asks the narrator which he prefers, watching directly or recording
the narrator admits he cannot choose
she describes the human gaze as a brief act that leaves no trace
she describes the recording device as a tool that piles up moments
this piling up brings out what is too faint for the eye
the narrator objects that a drawing keeps something of the feeling
she grants that a sketch holds the memory of an evening
she states that a bare image tells nothing on its own
she concludes that photographing means handing your memory over
text: The woman who looks after the dome asked me which of the two I preferred, the eye or the sensor. I told her that I had never managed to choose between them. So she set the pair of them side by side for me. The eye, she said, takes hold of a moment the way a hand takes hold of a pebble, fast and leaving nothing behind; the sensor waits, gathers, piles moment upon moment until whatever is very faint rises slowly into view. I objected that an observer's drawing holds a warmth no machine can give. She smiled and granted me that much: a sketch carries a whole evening in it, while a bare image carries nothing at all. Then came the line I have kept. Looking is remembering with your eyes; photographing is handing your memory to a device. We stayed under the open slit until the cold drove us out.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the history of sky watching falls into families of instruments
the earliest tools rested on measuring angles by naked sight
those tools leaned on tables copied out by hand
the lens telescope came next
the lens telescope suffers from a fault of colour
the mirror removed that fault but makes the instrument heavier
the mirror made very wide apertures possible
the sensitive plate gave access to bodies invisible to the eye
electronic sensors and aerials carried observation beyond the visible
each family of instruments inherited the methods of the one before
text: The story of sky watching falls neatly enough into families of instruments. The earliest of them measured angles by naked sight alone and leaned on tables copied out by hand, generation after generation. Then came the telescope built round lenses, which shut the gaze inside a closed tube but never shook off a stubborn fringe of colour. Then the mirror, heavier to carry, free of that fringe, and open to apertures that ground glass could never reach. Then the sensitive plate, able to probe bodies far too faint for the retina. Then, last of all, electronic sensors and linked arrays of aerials, which carried observation clean out of the visible range. None of these families drove out the one before it. Each inherited its ways of measuring, its catalogues and, more often than not, its mistakes.

units: a star forms from a cloud of cold gas that gives way
the drawing in heats the centre until fusion starts
fusion halts the collapse of the cloud
there follows a long settled period of steady burning of the fuel
the fuel running out swells the envelope and cools the surface
the outer layers drift apart and seed the medium with heavy elements
a dense core is left at the centre and cools without end
the heaviest bodies close with an explosion
the blast of that explosion squeezes the clouds nearby and sets off new births there
text: A star begins its life in a cloud of cold gas that gives way under its own weight. As the cloud draws in, its heart grows hotter and hotter, until fusion takes hold and the collapse is halted. There follows a long and settled stretch of life, during which the star burns through its fuel at a steady rate. Once that store starts to run low, the envelope swells out of all proportion and the surface cools; the star turns into a reddish giant. Its outer layers drift away in the end, seeding the medium around them with heavy elements. At the centre nothing is left but a dense, scorching core, which cools from then on without ever having done. The heaviest stars take a far more violent road and close with an explosion whose blast squeezes the clouds nearby, where fresh stars will be born.

units: an amateur left his listening station recording while he was away
a power cut threw the clock of the station out
the files stacked up with no date to go by
the amateur nearly deleted the lot
he opened the last file and heard a short signal that kept returning
he passed the trace on to a university observatory
a researcher there picked out an onboard transmitter that had been taken for dead
that craft spoke only when its panels caught the sunlight at one precise angle
the faulty clock had shifted the listening into the one favourable window
text: An amateur radio listener had got into the way of leaving his station to record on its own while he was away. A power cut threw the clock out, so the files stacked up with no date to go by, and he came close to erasing them all. Out of plain curiosity he opened the last one of them anyway, and found a short signal returning at even intervals. Since that beat meant nothing to him, he passed the trace on to a university observatory. There a researcher recognised the signature of an onboard transmitter that everyone had taken for dead an age ago. Starved of power, the craft spoke only when its panels caught the sunlight at one precise angle. The faulty clock, by shifting every listening session, had dropped the recording into the single window in which the object had anything to say.

units: soft images come most often from the setting of the mirrors and not from the sky
the instrument must go outside half an hour before observing
the heat held inside the tube spoils the image
the eyepiece is swapped for a pierced cap to check the centring
through that cap you should see circles nested one inside another
an off centre is put right with the screws of the bottom mirror
the screws must never be tightened right down
you then aim at a bright star and throw it out of focus to get a ring
an uneven ring is corrected by an eighth of a turn of the screw concerned
text: The instrument you have just bought is giving you soft, mushy images and you are beginning to lose patience? Nine times out of ten the mirrors are out of line, not the sky. Here is the drill to follow. Carry the thing outside a good half hour before you aim at anything, or the heat shut inside the tube will smear the lot. Take the eyepiece out, drop a pierced cap in its place and look through: you should see a set of neatly nested circles. If the centre sits off to one side, work on the bottom mirror with the screws behind it, a shade at a time, and never tighten one right down. Put the eyepiece back, aim at a bright star and throw it slightly out of focus, and you get a ring. That ring should look even all the way round. If it bulges on one side, turn the matching screw an eighth of a turn, no more.

units: a new receiving array is going up on a dry plateau
the engineers set this site against an observatory placed outside the atmosphere
the two installations look at the same bodies
the one on the ground can be lengthened and mended part by part
the craft in orbit has to work with nobody to touch it
the one on the ground is hampered by air that muddles the signals
the craft in orbit has vacuum in front of its shell
the one on the ground has power in plenty
the craft in orbit has to save every scrap of energy
those in charge hold that the two approaches complete each other
text: On the dry plateau where the latest receiving array is going up, the engineers like to set their site against an observatory lofted clear of the atmosphere. Both of them look at the same bodies, and there the likeness comes to an end.
